  All five operators follow yq over every pair of kinds (captured against v4.53.3: 180 error rows, the key of a container aside): `-` over two scalars says `cannot be added to` as yq does, `*` names both operands (`cannot multiply !!float with !!str`, which was reversed for a float on the left), `/` and `%` say `cannot be divided by` and `cannot modulo by`, and a container operand is named with its key.
  The key is `()` here, since a value carries none; the exit status is 1 in both.
  `succinctly jq` keeps jq's wording.
- **yq: `/=`, `%=` and `//=` are refused unless `--jq-extensions` is passed** (#6981). yq v4.53.3 has no such operators: it reads `/`, `%` or `//` with a missing operand and stops (`'/' expects 2 args but there is 1`), where `succinctly yq` took them for jq's compound assignments and wrote `{"a":2.0}`, `{"a":0}` or `{"a":4}` for `.a /= 2`, `.a %= 2` and `.a //= 3` on `a: 4`. They now fail with a parse error naming the flag, as a jq-only builtin does (#1512); with the flag, and in `succinctly jq`, they behave as before (the text `eval(...)` runs does not see the flag, as for every gated name: #7012). `+=`, `-=`, `*=` and `|=` are yq's own and are unchanged. Found by a grammar differential fuzz of yq-mode programs against yq.
- **`SUCCINCTLY_SIMD=sse2` also clamps the x86_64 JSON index builders** (#7318). The variable used to lower only the YAML parser's dispatch; `succinctly jq` and the other JSON routes always built their index with the AVX2 kernel on an AVX2 CPU, so the SSE2 kernel ran through the CLI only on a CPU without AVX2. It now selects the SSE2 kernel there too (it still only lowers the level, never raises it), and the `sse2-dispatch` x86_64 CI leg re-runs the JSON-reading CLI suites with it set. No change when the variable is unset.
- **macOS release binaries no longer run on macOS 11** (#7321). The `succinctly-macos-arm64` archive is now built for
  macOS 12.0 (`MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET` in `.cargo/config.toml`), not rustc's default of 11.0 on arm64. `cargo install
  succinctly --features cli` builds for the default target and still runs on macOS 11. `succinctly dev compare jq` now
  times a copy of the binary stripped as the release archive's is, not the unstripped `target/release/succinctly`.
- **`succinctly jq` negates a number literal as jq 1.8 does: the result is still a literal** (#7453). jq 1.7.1 turned `-1.500` into the double `-1.5`; jq 1.8 keeps the decimal (jqlang/jq#3242, fixing the bug jqlang/jq#2704), and `succinctly jq` now follows it. `-1.500` prints `-1.500`, `-1e1000` `-1E+1000`, `-9007199254740993` keeps every digit, and `-1` compares with an input `-1.00000000000000000001` exactly (unequal). The same holds for `-(1.500)`, `-$x` and `-.` on an input or `--argjson` literal. As in jq 1.8, a zero negates to positive zero (`-0` is `0`, `-0.0` is `0.0`), and a negated literal is a fresh value for `path()` (`[-1] | path(.[0] | -1)` is refused). A computed number is negated as before. `succinctly yq` is unchanged.
- **`succinctly jq --run-tests` says the option is not supported** (#7715). jq 1.7.1's manual documents `--run-tests [file]`, jq's runner for its own test files, which `succinctly jq` does not implement; it refused it as `Unknown option --run-tests`, and now prints `jq: --run-tests is not supported: succinctly jq does not run jq's test files` (exit 2), recorded in `docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`. As in jq, the words after it are not read as options.
- **`succinctly dev compare jq` sizes each binary stripped** (#7383). Section H compared files as built: an unstripped `succinctly` (cargo keeps the symbol table) against pinned jq builds that keep their debug info, two thirds of jq's file on Linux, so the ratio read 11x on a Ryzen 9 7950X where the stripped binaries are 27x (24.8 MB against 0.91 MB for the shipped `cli` build at 73f049b2c; 19.9 MB against 0.85 MB, 23.5x, on an Apple M4 Pro). Each tool is now also sized as a copy stripped with plain `strip`, as `release.yml` strips the archive (`stripped_bytes` in `results.json`), shown as the size to compare beside the as-built size; the table notes that the `succinctly jq` row is by default the harness's own build, which adds `bench-runner` to the shipped feature set.
- **The published crate ships the library and the CLI only, and CI holds it under 8 MiB** (no issue). `tests/` and `benches/` left `include` in `Cargo.toml`, which took the `.crate` `cargo package` writes from 10,434,790 bytes, 51 KB under crates.io's 10 MiB upload limit, to 6,504,486 bytes (6.2 MiB); the `[[bench]]` targets are dropped from the packaged manifest, as the examples already were, and the tests run from a checkout. The `include` patterns are anchored at the root, so the `README.md` of every `docs/` directory no longer ships either. `scripts/crate_size.py check --verify` packages the crate, builds it from its own files with `--features cli` and fails over 8 MiB; it runs in a new `Crate package` CI job, in `release.yml` before the GitHub release is created (`cargo publish` runs last, so an over-limit crate used to leave a release half done), and in the pre-push `crate-size` gate.
- **`succinctly dev compare jq --render-docs` and `--write-docs` regenerate the by-category geomean table of `docs/guides/choosing-jq.md`** (#6916). The table (pass-through, navigation, early exit, transforms, streams, startup-bound; one column per committed platform run) was copied from the reports by hand; it is a `compare:jq-categories` block now, built from `docs/compare/jq-<platform>.json` by the same code as the other blocks, and held by a test that fails when the committed guide does not quote the committed runs. The grouping by query name is `QUERY_GROUPS` in `src/bin/succinctly/compare/docs.rs`, and a test checks that no query is in two groups.
- **`rust-version` is now 1.89.0, the oldest toolchain that builds the crate, and CI checks it**. It said 1.73.0, which nothing built with: the committed `Cargo.lock` needs 1.85 (edition-2024 dependencies such as `indexmap`, `hashbrown` and `clap`, which cargo 1.84 cannot parse), and the `simd` feature's AVX-512 VPOPCNTDQ popcount kernel needs 1.89 on x86_64, where its intrinsics stabilized. Without `simd`, or on aarch64, 1.85 builds the library and the CLI. A new `MSRV` job reads `rust-version` from `Cargo.toml` and runs `cargo check --locked` with that toolchain on x86_64 Linux, for the library with default features and for `--features cli,simd,regex,serde`; the floors are in `docs/guides/release.md` (MSRV Policy).

### Removed

- **The `unshared-containers` cargo feature** (#5841). It was the measurement-only A/B holdout for #2999's shared (`Rc`) containers: it rebuilt the pre-#2999 layout (object map behind a `Box`, array `Vec` inline, every clone a deep copy) and was never meant to ship. ADR-0024 recorded that experiment's numbers in 2026-09, and nothing has measured with it since. Removing it also deletes 1,240 `ignore = "holdout ..."` test attributes, about 270 `cfg` sites in `src/jq` and the x86_64 `holdout` CI leg. A build that names the feature now fails to resolve it, and `--all-features` builds the shipped container layout.
- **`YamlError` loses `MultiDocumentNotSupported` and `FlowStyleNotSupported`, and becomes `#[non_exhaustive]`** (#5954).
  Both variants have been `#[deprecated]` and never constructed since 0.3.0 (multi-document streams and flow style are parsed),
  so no release has returned them. A downstream `match` that names either must drop the arm, and one without a wildcard arm
  needs one, since the enum is now `#[non_exhaustive]`: a later removal is then not a break. `TagNotSupported` was returned by
  0.7.0 and earlier, so it stays for one more release: it now says `since = "0.8.0"` and that it is removed in 0.9.0.
- **`jq::document::collapsed_fields_checked` is removed** (#7311).
  Its two callers, the JSON writer's object arm and `map(f)` over an object, now take a plan of the fields a
  repeated key changes instead of the materialized field list it returned. A downstream caller can take
  `effective_fields_checked(fields, true)`, which returns the same collapsed list for an object that repeats a
  key and every field otherwise.

### Performance

- **yq: `-C`/`--colors` streams its output instead of buffering all of it first** (#808).
  The colorizers now run over the cursor streamers' output as it is written, so colored output keeps the
  M2 fast path's memory and early output: `-C '.'` on a 100 MB document peaks at 278 MB instead of
  523 MB on an Apple M4 Pro and 259 MB instead of 414 MB on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (`-C -o=json '.'`:
  278 MB instead of 774 MB, and 259 MB instead of 665 MB), the same as uncolored output, and
  `-C '.' | head` sees its first output after 0.34 s instead of 1.43 s (M4 Pro; 0.49 s instead of 1.71 s
  on the 7950X). With `-0`, colored output is checked for NUL one result at a time, as uncolored output
  already was. The colors are unchanged except where a list item's "does it start with a key" lookahead
  used to read past its own line or result: with `.[]` over records that end in a list, the last item of
  each record (`- category_0` before the next record's `id: 1`) is no longer colored as a key, and
  neither is an item whose apostrophe (`- don't`) is closed by a quote on a later line.
- **yq: a compound or alternative assignment builds the document once, not twice** (#1414, landed in #4591).
  `.users[0].age += 1`, `.users[].age += 1` and `.users[0].age //= 0` reuse the document and resolved paths
  the no-op check already built instead of building them again for the write: -6.3% to -9.1% wall-clock at
  1, 10 and 50 MB on both an Apple M4 Pro and an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (10 MB `+=`: 795.9 ms -> 731.4 ms and
  1421.5 ms -> 1317.3 ms), output identical; plain `|=` is unchanged.
- **yq: `--ascii-output` no longer instantiates every JSON streamer a second time** (#1993).
  #1983's fix for `--ascii-output` dropping duplicate keys wrapped each sink in a concrete escaper, which
  monomorphized the streamers twice and cost the default `-o json` path +0.49% on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (all 8
  rows slower). The escaping arm now streams through one shared `dyn` sink: the release binary is 62 KB
  (Apple M4 Pro) and 74 KB (7950X) smaller and the 7950X's default path reads -1.12% median with 2 of 8 rows
  slower; the `--ascii-output` path itself pays about +1% for the virtual calls. Output identical.
- **yq: JSON input on the `--slurp` / `--inplace` DOM fallback is indexed once, not twice** (#2296). The
  nesting-depth pre-check built a `JsonIndex` and the materialization step then built a second one over the same
  bytes. The built cursor is now handed on, with the check still ahead of any materialization (same
  `nesting depth exceeds limit of 128` message and exit code). `-i -p json '.metadata.version = "2"'`,
  interleaved A/B on an Apple M5 Max (min / median of 21 runs, output byte-identical): 50 MB −2.8% / −3.7%;
  within noise at 1 MB (+3.8% / −0.2%) and 10 MB (−0.6% / +0.7%), where startup and the write dominate.
- **yq: `key`, `path` and `parent` read once per member of a wide YAML mapping or sequence are linear, not quadratic** (#2784). `[.[] | key | path] | length` over a flat `kN: N` mapping took 2.84 s at 5k keys and 200 s at 40k (4x per doubling); it takes 0.02 s and 0.16 s (2x per doubling). The scan that finds a member in its parent resumes from the member the last scan found, as JSON's has since #3702/#3839; YAML opted out because block-sequence items are unwrapped from their `-` nodes, which `YamlCursor::next_element` now steps over the way `uncons_cursor` does. Interleaved A/B on an M4 Pro and a Ryzen 9 7950X, output identical on every row: mapping and sequence (items on the `-` line, on the next line, and mixed) of 2,000/4,000/8,000 members, `-96.0%` to `-99.8%`; the walk-route holdouts (`key | line`, `.`, `[.[]] | length` at 100,000 members) read -0.33% and +0.73%, with retired instructions unchanged to 0.02-0.11%. `parent | length` stays quadratic, which is #2574.
- **yq: `key | tostring` and `key | @format` no longer re-materialize the key node** (#2789).
  `key` emits the key node since #2763, so a one-stage `tostring` or `@format` after it missed the owned
  shortcut and went through the cursor (+49% / +58% on `[.[] | key | tostring]`). A string-decoding value
  now takes the shortcut: `[.[] | key | tostring] | length` over 1.6M keys, 763.9 ms -> 483.7 ms on an
  Apple M4 Pro and 1137.4 ms -> 798.8 ms on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X; `@json` -22% to -26%, output identical,
  bare `key`, `key | line`, `path` and `.` unchanged. `.[] | key` then no longer finds each key node again
  from its value (a sibling hop and a second decode, +23-30% on `[.[] | key]`): the iteration already holds
  the node, and hands it over. 1.6M keys, interleaved min of 11: `[.[] | key]` -14.2% on an M4 Pro and -7.4% on
  a 7950X, `key | line` -14.5% / -10.9%, `key | tostring` -14.4% / -6.5%; `[.. | path]`, `keys_unsorted`, `.`
  and a `select` between the two within noise, peak memory unchanged.
- **jq: the compact-echo gate checks a wide object's keys with one exactly sized table** (#3333). Past 16 keys `scan_canonical_object` grew a `KeyHashes` table from empty, so on a wide object every key was probed once and rehashed about once more (83 instructions per key, 6.9% of `wide` 2 MB `-c .`). It now collects the key hashes and settles them at the closing `}` in a table sized for exactly that many keys. Interleaved wall-clock, `-c .`: `wide` 2 MB (136k keys) −25% on a 7950X and −22% on an M4 Pro, 560k and 700k keys −25% to −31%, arrays of 1,000-key objects −17% and of 100-key objects −9% to −10% on both, 17-24-key objects −5% to +1%; 7950X instructions −6.7% on `wide`. Objects of 16 keys or fewer are unchanged in instructions (`users` and `data` read within the layout band against a holdout). Output is identical on every row and the same objects are declined (the 786,432-key ceiling is unchanged); a repeated key inside a wide object is now found at the end of the object rather than at the key, so a repeat near the front of a 136k- or 700k-key object (which still ends in the full re-render) costs 2% to 4% more wall-clock and 5% more instructions. A sort of the collected hashes was measured and rejected: a further −7% to −10% on the 7950X at 136k keys and above, but +5% to +10% worse on the M4 Pro at every width above 17 keys and +5% to +7% worse on the 7950X at 100 and 1,000 keys.
- **jq: `length`, `keys | length` and the identity print of a wide object no longer scan each key twice or sort every key hash** (#3343). `census`, the key-only walk behind those queries, found each key's closing quote once to hash it and again to check the `:` after it; one scan now answers both (`keys_unsorted` shares it). It also sorted all `n` key hashes to learn that none repeats; from 128 to 2^21 keys a bitset prefilter now sorts only the few hashes that land on a bit another hash had set, with the sort as the fallback, so the answer is the same. On perf-guard's 2 MB `wide` fixture (159 K keys) `length` falls 12.2% in instructions on a 7950X (245.6 M to 215.7 M) and 9.3% in wall-clock (median, interleaved), the identity print 6.5% and 6.3%, `keys_unsorted` 2.5% and 2.9%; on an M4 Pro `length` -9.0%, `.` -6.8% (10 MB: -12.3% and -8.3%). `map(length) | add` over equal objects of 32,768 keys: -10.6% (7950X), -11.8% (M4 Pro); 8 keys per object is unchanged (the prefilter starts at 128). Output is identical, error text and exit status included, across 1,098 comparisons on 122 documents. Peak RSS rises by up to 0.6 MB at 159 K keys and 3.1 MB (5%) at 1.9 M. An exactly sized hash table (4% to 12% slower on the 7950X), an in-place radix partition (slower on both) and a gap-scan fast path (3% slower on the identity print) were measured and not kept; see `docs/parsing/json.md`.
- **yq: an array of the document's own nodes streams instead of copying the document first** (#3475).
  `[.users[] | select(.age > 30)]`, `[.[]]`, `[.users]` and `.users | [.[]]` print from the nodes' cursors, as
  `map(select(...))` already did, where the DOM route copied the whole sequence into an owned value and a comment
  tree before printing a byte. Over comment-free records on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (interleaved A/B, same output):
  at 100 MB, `[.users[] | select(.age > 30)]` peaks at 262 MB instead of 2,350 MB and takes 2.7 s instead of
  7.2 s (-62%), and `[.users]` peaks at 261 MB instead of 4,813 MB and takes 2.3 s instead of 12.6 s (-81%);
  at 1 MB and 10 MB they take 56% and 61% (`select`) and 79% and 82% (`[.users]`) less, and `map(select(...))`
  is unchanged. With `-o json` the same shapes peak at 262 MB instead of 1,055 MB and 1,182 MB and take 19-33%
  less time. On an Apple M4 Pro the same two shapes take 48% and 68% less at 100 MB (46-47% and 66-68% at 1 and
  10 MB) and peak at 442 MB instead of 2,347 MB and 274 MB instead of 4,857 MB. Only a body that is navigation to one node, or navigation that fans out with `.[]` and goes on
  through `.`, `.[]` and `select(...)`, streams; a stage that computes, a `.a` after a fan-out, a slice or a `,`
  keeps the old route. A YAML document with an alias keeps it, because the streamers would write an `*alias` whose anchor the array does not
  hold; a comment does not (#6736, and the document's own foot comment for `[.]`): over a 10 MB file with a comment
  before every tenth record, `[.users[] | select(.age > 30)]` takes 331 ms instead of 818 ms (-60%) and `[.users]`
  285 ms instead of 1,545 ms (-82%) on the 7950X, with the comments kept. The default `yaml generate` file, which
  starts with a comment and is the one this issue names: `[.]` peaks at 35 MB instead of 401 MB at 10 MB, and at 100 MB
  at 242 MB instead of 3,667 MB (the same as `.`) and takes 2.1 s instead of 10.7 s (-81%). An element that fails to decode, or a complex key that collides with another, is
  still found before the first byte is written.
- **jq: `path(f)`, `paths(f)` and the other path consumers no longer build what a swallowed `.[]` and a `catch empty` handler throw away** (#3728). #3722 stopped `path(f)`'s two cursor walkers formatting `Cannot iterate over ...` for a `.[]?` over a scalar; the path resolver (`//`, `first`, `try`) and the owned evaluator `paths(f)`, `any`, `all` and `IN` run their filters through still did, and `try .. catch empty` ran its empty handler over a re-indexed copy of the caught error. Allocation-site sampling attributed the cost to three places: the handler (42% of `path(try .[] catch empty)`), the message the resolver's `try`/`?` arms formatted, and `eval_each_owned` re-indexing a scalar before it answered `.[]?` (twice per node for `paths(f)`). A bare `catch empty` now returns before seeding or running its handler, a `.[]?`/`try .[]` over a trackable scalar answers nothing without stepping `.[]`, and `eval_each_owned` answers it before the re-index bridge. jq mode only; a handler that is not `empty`, an untracked value (`1 | .[]?` still raises jq's path error), a container and every yq-mode query evaluate as before, and output (stdout, stderr and exit status) is identical to the parent binary on 1,558 query/document pairs, including documents jq cannot read. Allocator calls over 2,000 integer members: `[.[] | path(try .[] catch empty)] | length` 66,004 -> 10,014, `path(first(.[]?))` 22,014 -> 10,014, `path(.[]? // .)` 38,024 -> 26,024, `paths(.[]?)` 56,014 -> 32,014 (what `paths(.)` costs). Interleaved A/B, min of 9, 0 output differences, 300,000 and 1,200,000 integer members: Ryzen 9 7950X `path(try .[] catch empty)` -75.8%/-76.1%, `path(try .[])` -41%, `path(first(.[]?))` -36%/-38%, `paths(.[]?)` -33%, `path(.[]? // .)` -27%, `path(try error("x") catch empty)` -39%; Apple M4 Pro -74.7%/-75.4%, -43%/-45%, -40%/-41%, -34%/-33%, -31%/-29%, -43%; `.. | path(try .[] catch empty)` over a 4 MB array of arrays -50% on both. Rows the change does not reach (`path(.)`, `paths(.)`, `path(. // .)`, `try error("x") catch .`, `.name? // .` over records) read -1.8%..+1.6% against a control noise floor of -0.8%..+2.4%. Not changed: `del(.[]?)` (its cost is `del`'s owned bridge, 32,024 calls for `del(.)` alone) and `path(.[])?` (the `?` is outside `path`, so no bare-`.[]` boundary exists to shortcut); both read -1.6%..+1.6% on both boxes. `perf-guard` (cachegrind, 7950X) against the parent binary: every row within 0.2%.
- **jq: a slice right after `[.. | parent?]` no longer re-indexes the whole array** (#3824). `[.. | parent?] | .[0:2] | length` is an array holding `n` shared copies of the document, and the slice stage was not one the owned navigation peel (`projection_peel`) took, so the reindex bridge wrote the array out in full (quadratic in its size) to read two elements: 3,611 M, 13,953 M and 54,518 M instructions and 121 MB, 594 MB and 1,620 MB peak over 1,200, 2,400 and 4,800 inner arrays on an Apple M5 Max. A leading slice is now taken natively, with the same `slice_owned_value_read` every other owned slice uses (arrays, strings, `null`, and yq's object rule; a target it cannot slice still goes to the bridge for its error): 242 M, 453 M and 871 M instructions and 21 MB, 32 MB and 55 MB, the cost of `[.. | parent?] | length` itself. On a 7950X (wall-clock, min of 5, interleaved) 210 ms, 763 ms and 3,004 ms become 18 ms, 35 ms and 68 ms. Output is identical to the previous build across 38,896 slice/tail/value/wrapper combinations in both modes. `first` and `last` after the same array stay quadratic (#4068).
- **yq: a fan-out that skips elements of a wide YAML sequence or mapping reads `key`/`path` in linear time** (#3846). `[.[] | select(.a > 3) | key]` over a mapping was quadratic because the slot scan rebuilt the parent's field list (which walks every member for `<<` merge keys) at each position that was not the previous one's neighbour, and `[.[] | select(.a.b % 3 == 0) | .a | tostring | [key]]` over a block sequence climbed with `enclose` because an item sits under its `-` node and failed the remembered-parent depth test. The scan now resumes from the member it remembers before building the parent's value, and `DocumentCursor::element_depth` lets a block-sequence item count as a direct child. Interleaved A/B, output identical on every row, `-47%` to `-99.1%` on an M4 Pro and a Ryzen 9 7950X: mapping skip 8,000/16,000/32,000 members 402/1572/6347 ms -> 16.5/29.6/56.5 ms (M4 Pro); block sequence skip 32,000/64,000/128,000 items 165/523/1815 ms -> 68/133/262 ms (M4 Pro), 244/792/2807 ms -> 90/179/359 ms (7950X). Neighbour fan-out, non-fan-out and JSON rows read within -1.7% to +1.2% on both boxes. Out-of-order reads still restart the scan, as before.

A bind used to decode its whole source whether or not `$x` was read, so `. as $root | .users[] | .name` decoded the entire document for a variable it never named (6.5x the memory and 4-5x the time of the same filter without the bind). The node is now held as a name (`Expr::DeferredVar`) that each read re-resolves to a cursor, when the body never names `$x` (a subtree; a scalar is decoded as before and kept only if that decode failed) or when `$x` is only read where the ambient input is provably a node of the same document (`deferred_bind_is_sound`: at the bind's input, or a member read under `.[]`; not after a stage that may leave no cursor such as `.missing`, `1`, `length`, nor inside `map`, `reduce`, `path(...)`, a `def` or string interpolation, which keep the eager decode). Apple M5 Max, release build, instructions retired (min of 3-5, interleaved against the commit before) and peak RSS, `users` documents of 0.7 / 7 / 26 MB: `. as $x | 1` -72% / -86% / -87% instructions and 17 MB -> 10 MB / 81 MB -> 18 MB / 262 MB -> 42 MB; `. as $r | .users[] | .name` -57% / -66% / -66%; `.users[] | . as $u | .name` -56% / -64% / -65%; `. as $x | .users[] | select(.age > 20) | .name` -45% / -50% / -51%; `. as $r | .users | map(.age + 1) | length` -51% / -58% / -59%; `.users[] | . as $u | {id: $u.id, a: ($u.age + 1)}` -30% / -32% / -33%. Scalar binds (`.users[] | .name as $u | $u`), `reduce`, dollar-parameter `def` calls, `path(.a as $y | ...)`, a recursive `fib($n)` and `succinctly yq` over YAML (including an alias/merge-key document) are within +-0.5%, which is the harness's noise on a loaded laptop (one binary read +0.9% and +0.3% across two runs). Output identical on every row. A whole-node read decodes the node at most once per bind, as the eager bind did (#4036). On a document with a member the index cannot read, `. as $x | 1` and `. as $x | $x.a` now answer and `. as $x | $x` echoes the node as `.` does, where they raised at the bind; anything that decodes the node still raises where it does (`docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`). Pinned by a differential sweep of deferred against decoding binds over generated bodies and documents through both the collecting and the streaming entry (`deferred_bind_agrees_with_the_decoding_bind_3856`, mutation-checked), the predicate's table (`src/jq/deferred_bind.rs`), and `test_deferred_bind_matches_jq_3856` against `/usr/bin/jq` 1.7.1.

  walk's order and error rules, and jq's), where it first built the whole document as an owned tree. `first(recurse(.[]?; true))`
  over a 7 MB `users` document, Apple M4 Pro, release: 0.09 s and 81 MB peak RSS -> 0.01 s and 18 MB (what `first(..)` costs);
  collecting every node is unchanged (0.11 s, 117 MB). `succinctly yq` takes it too since #4095.

Each binary operator asked `settles_before_consumer` of its left operand first, and refusing an operand that calls no `def` means walking all of it, so in `1 + 1 + ... + 1` every one of N operators re-walked everything below it (N² node visits) to refuse a right operand that is one literal. The operator now probes the right operand with an 8-node budget first and the left only if that cannot decide (`settles_both`); an operand the probe refuses ends the question on either side, and which operands settle is unchanged. `map(<N terms>)` over 20,000 numbers on an Apple M-series, `succinctly jq` user time against the commit before, interleaved: 50 terms 0.30 s → 0.15 s, 100 terms 1.01 s → 0.29 s, 200 terms 3.95 s → 0.60 s (about 2x per doubling, was 4x); `succinctly yq` 100 terms 1.11 s → 0.33 s. A right-nested chain (`(.*1) + ((.*1) + ...)`), a chain of `def` calls, `sum_to(800)` and `fib(18)` are within ±2%. Output identical. Pinned by `settles_both_refuses_on_a_small_operand_without_the_big_walk_3885` (mutation-checked). A chain whose operands all call a `def` still re-walks its left side per operator, bounded by the 1024-node analysis budget.

  every field into a per-record buffer where the M2 path echoes the span after one scan. A cursor whose text is already the compact record is now written straight from the document (`print_json` for a `LazySeq` element, `write_output_jq_value` with no record buffer for a top-level one), and the `LazySeq` arm takes that scan as its validation. On `users` (36.6 MB, 349,525 records), interleaved A/B: `[.users] | .[0]` -69%/-67% wall (M4 Pro/7950X), peak RSS 99 -> 54 MB; `[.users]` -76%/-74%; `[.users, .users]` -81%/-80%; `.users` unchanged (-2%). A document the scan refuses falls back to the unchanged path: pretty-printed input is neutral (-2%..+0.4%), and one non-canonical token at the very end of a 36 MB element costs +5-8% on the `[.users]` shapes (the refused scan runs twice). Output is byte-identical and a malformed element still prints nothing. Pinned by `canonical_span_implies_validate_cursor_ok_3909` (the scan never accepts what the walk refuses, across the depth ceiling) and `test_cursor_printed_inside_a_lazy_array_echoes_or_rerenders_3909`.
- **jq: a keyed lookup into a wide document object is a hash probe, not a walk of its members** (#3913). `.big[$k]`, `$b[.]` for a `$b` bound to a node of the document being read, `getpath(["big", $k])` and a literal `.big.k` each walked every member of `big` on every lookup, so 10,000 lookups into a 10,000-key object took 3.5 s (350x the same read once `tostring` made the key an owned value and `$b` the decoded map). An object the walk would raise on (a non-string key, an unpaired tail, a stray trailing comma) is never indexed, nor is one whose repeated keys would make the build quadratic, so the same lookup raises the same error it always did, a repeated key still resolves to its last occurrence, and only the winning member's own `,`/`:` delimiters are checked, as before. Measured on an Apple M4 Pro, release build, 10,000 lookups, min of 3: `$b[.]` 0.61 s -> 0.11 s at 1,000 keys and 3.46 s -> 0.09 s at 10,000; `.big[$k]` 0.62 s -> 0.10 s and 3.60 s -> 0.09 s, within noise of the `tostring` row at both sizes; the index costs about 32 bytes per key (3 MB at 100,000 keys). At most four indexes and two million members are kept per evaluation, and an object whose index was dropped goes back to the walk rather than being rebuilt; a wider object keeps the walk. Single-lookup shapes are unchanged to within the ±1% layout band (`.big.k5000.v` -0.1% instructions, `.users[0].name` 0.0%, `keys_unsorted` -0.1%, `to_entries` 0.0%; `.users[].name` and a `select` over every record read +0.3% to +1.3% instructions with wall-clock inside noise). JSON documents only: YAML mappings keep the walk, and `has($k)`/`path(.big[$k])` have their own walks.

A `,` stage that does not head its pipe (`[.users[] | ., .]`) ran the owned route, and a `?`/`try` around an array forced it to learn whether it fails; both decoded every node the array holds, and answered a decode failure for a value nothing read. On a 14 MB `users` document, release, Apple M4 Pro, interleaved A/B with identical output: `[.users[] | ., .] | length` 286.7 ms and 290 MB -> 33.9 ms and 42 MB (`-88%`), `[.users, 1]? | length` 150.0 ms and 144 MB -> 25.2 ms and 26 MB (`-83%`); the comma-array holdouts (`[.users, .users]`, `[(.users, .users) | .[0]]`, `[.users[0] | .name, .age]`) read within the control's range. Over an unreadable value `[.[] | ., .] | length` and `[.a, .b]? | length` now answer (`4`, `2`) like `[.a, .b] | length`; printing the array still raises. jq mode only.
- **jq: a `,` array no longer reallocs its node list per record** (#3923). #3919's route ended every array with an unconditional `shrink_to_fit`, so the per-record `[., empty]` and `[.name, .age]` shapes paid a
  realloc each: `.users[] | [., empty]` was +4.0% instructions (+3.6%/+2.7% wall) on a 7950X against the commit before #3919. The list is now shrunk only from 64 nodes, which is what the 300k-element case it
  exists for needs; output is identical, and against the commit before #3919 the row reads -2.2%/-3.0% wall and `[.name, .age] | @csv` -5.4%/-5.2%. Pinned by
  `test_comma_array_shrinks_only_a_long_node_list_3923` (both sides, each mutation-checked).

Measured on an Apple M5 Max (release, interleaved A/B, min of 3, 5,000 / 15,000 records): `+= ($r.score | floor)` 1.27 s / 11.15 s → 0.03 s / 0.08 s, `= ($r.score // 0)` 1.76 s / 16.04 s → 0.04 s / 0.10 s, `= $r.score + 1` 3.40 s / 31.87 s → 0.04 s / 0.10 s, `(… = $r.score) // 0` 1.72 s / 13.31 s → 0.03 s / 0.07 s, with the control `= $r.score` unchanged at 0.03 s / 0.08 s. Output is identical to jq 1.7.1 on every row; an operand that raises still goes to the evaluator's route and text. An explicit `==`/`!=` on a container loop variable keeps its identity marker (#3896) and is unchanged.
- **jq: a `reduce` assignment under an `as` bind no longer copies its accumulator every step** (#3978). `$r.name as $n | .[$n] = $r.score` and `$r as $s | .[$s.name] = $s.score` were quadratic because `Expr::As` was not an assignment, so `owned_assign_step` declined and the whole object was re-copied per record. A closed bind source (one value, no read of `.`) is now substituted into the body and the write happens in place; nested binds, a shadowing rebind and an outer `//` recurse. Measured on an Apple M5 Max (release, interleaved A/B, min of 3, 5,000 / 15,000 records): `$r.name as $n | .[$n] = $r.score` 0.89 s / 7.91 s → 0.03 s / 0.07 s, `$r as $s | .[$s.name] = $s.score` 1.35 s / 11.92 s → 0.03 s / 0.08 s, the control `.[$r.name] = $r.score` unchanged at 0.02 s / 0.06 s. Output is identical to jq 1.7.1 on every row. Pinned by `fold_assign_step_copies_nothing_3138` (zero forced copies for both shapes; 1,000 `make_mut` without the change).
- **jq: a chain whose operands all call a `def` no longer re-walks itself once per operator** (#3997). `def f: .+1; map(f + f + ... + f)` re-asked `settles_before_consumer` of its whole left operand at every operator, up to the 1024-node analysis budget each time, so N terms cost N walks and doubled the time about 3-4x. The walk's answer is a function of the subtree alone, so each `Expr::Arithmetic` now remembers it with the nodes the walk cost (`ArithSettleMemo`), and a walk that reaches a remembered node charges the same cost and skips the descent. The result and the budget left are exactly what walking gives, so which operands settle (#3296, ADR-0025's `fib`/`sum_to` depth behaviour) is unchanged; only the settle analysis outside a `def` body remembers, a clone starts empty, and the memo is outside `PartialEq`/`Debug`. `map(<N terms>)` over 20,000 numbers, `succinctly jq` user time against the commit before, interleaved, min of 7-9: 25 / 50 / 100 / 200 terms 175 / 521 / 2,199 / 7,402 ms → 128 / 259 / 645 / 1,288 ms on an Apple M5 Max (-27% / -50% / -71% / -83%, about 2x per doubling) and 219 / 594 / 1,909 / 6,859 ms → 147 / 286 / 570 / 1,184 ms on a Ryzen 9 7950X (-33% / -52% / -70% / -83%); `succinctly yq` 100 terms -67% / -63%; a right-nested chain -71% / -69%; `sum_to(800)` and `fib(18)` within ±1.4% on both. Output identical to the commit before in jq and yq mode, and to `jq` 1.7.1. Pinned by `remembered_settle_walk_equals_the_cold_walk_3997` and `a_def_call_chain_is_walked_once_not_per_operator_3997` (both mutation-checked).

  so a single call holds nothing past itself. The kept copy lives to the end of the evaluation, not of the call, so a query
  that allocates heavily after a looped `path(f)` holds one document copy on top of it (peak RSS on a 10,000-key

- **jq: `has($k)` on a wide document object is a hash probe after the second lookup** (#4002). `has` walked the object's members on

  registers the object and the second lookup builds, then every lookup probes, the per-object key index #3913 added for
  `.big[$k]`. An object whose walk could raise depending on the name (a key that will not decode, a missing or doubled
  `,`/`:`) keeps the walk and gets no speedup, so output and errors are unchanged. `[.ks[] as $k | .big | has($k)] | length` over 3,000 keys, interleaved A/B (Apple M4 Pro, release):
  1,000-key object 62.8 -> 5.6 ms (11x), 10,000 keys 596 -> 7.1 ms (84x), 100,000 keys 5.85 s -> 17 ms (338x); objects of
  8-100 members are unchanged.
- **yq: a keyed lookup into a wide YAML mapping is one hash probe, not a walk of every key** (#4003). JSON documents got a per-object key index in #3913 (350x at 10,000 keys); a YAML mapping kept the walk, so `[keys[] as $k | .[$k] | .a]` over a 32,000-member mapping took 36 s and over 128,000 members more than 100 s. The same index now serves a YAML mapping once it has been read by key twice and walked at least 64 members, when every key is a plain string: an alias key (yq never matches one by name), a collection key (matched to `""` alone) and a mapping with a `<<` merge key (whose entries no member spells) keep the walk, and the index answers as the walk does, the last duplicate winning. Measured (M4 Pro, release, output identical): that query is 0.75 s at 32,000 members, 0.17 s at 64,000 and 0.21 s at 128,000; `. as $l | [keys[] | $l[.].b]` 0.11 / 0.17 / 0.27 s against 38 s / >100 s. A lookup read once, or a mapping under 64 members, costs what it did. `has("k")` of such a mapping is answered from the same index (`. as $d | [keys[] | . as $k | $d | has($k)]` over 16,000 / 64,000 / 128,000 members: 0.05 / 0.12 / 0.22 s, from over 30 s).
- **jq: a `reduce`/`foreach` assignment whose right side compares a container loop variable with `==`/`!=` no longer copies its accumulator on every step** (#4005, a #3944 follow-up). `reduce .[] as $r ({}; .[$r.name] = ($r.a == $r.b))` was quadratic: an explicit equality on `$r` marks it as a storage-sharing marker so jq's `jv_equal` identity short-circuit holds (#3896), and a marker made the in-place assignment step decline. The step now reads a marker by value, declining only when its answer is a container that carries a marker's node, so none of the binding's identity reaches the accumulator (a container built from scalar reads is fresh and is written in place; `.[$r.name] = {a: ($r == $r), t: $r.tags}` still copies, because `$r.tags` is a node of the marker). Apple M5 Max, release build, interleaved A/B (box under load, three reps, minimum): 2,500 / 5,000 / 10,000 / 15,000 records `($r == $r)` 308 / 1,255 / 4,849 / 8,693 ms to 12 / 20 / 31 / 33 ms, `($r.a == $r.b)` 337 / 1,435 / 4,598 / 9,754 ms to 13 / 21 / 25 / 30 ms; the unmarked control `($r.score > 50)` is unchanged (17 / 30 / 40 / 49 ms against 17 / 30 / 41 / 51 ms). Output identical to `jq` 1.7.1 on every row, NaN-bearing containers included (`reduce ([nan]) as $a ({}; .x = ($a == $a))` stays `{"x":true}`).

A wide array (64+ elements) that has been walked twice is now indexed on its third length lookup (the node id of every element, built by the same checked walk, so a malformed array still raises exactly what it raised), and later reads are O(1). 0.7 MB / 2.8 MB: 1,114 ms / 17.7 s -> 22 ms / 84 ms on a 7950X and 848 ms / 13.4 s -> 17 ms / 56 ms on an M4 Pro; the 300-read array row 4.31 s -> 70 ms and 3.21 s -> 52 ms. Read once or twice, an array costs what it did (instructions -0.03% to +0.28% for a single read, +1.1% / +1.6% for an array read exactly twice). Numbers and the 7950X placement caveat in `docs/parsing/json.md`.
- **jq: a deferred `as` bind decodes a node it reads whole at most once** (#4036). #3856's lazy bind (`. as $x | body` leaves the node undecoded until `$x` is read) kept the eager decode for a body that read the whole node under an iteration (`. as $x | .users[] | {r: $x}`, `select($x == .)`, `$x | tojson`), because the eager bind's embed-table entry shared one decoded copy across every read and a deferred read had no entry to hit, so it decoded the node per element (0.18 s against 6.7 s on a 1.4 MB document); a body naming the node bare `k` times decoded it up to `k` times (`. as $x | $x == .` +78%, `. as $x | {r: $x}` +17%). A deferred bind now registers a *lazily filled* entry for its node: the first materialization builds the value as before and fills the entry, and every later one is handed the same `Rc`. Those bodies defer, the one decode moves to the first read (and is not paid when no element reaches it), and the entry is invisible to the resolver that certifies identity for `path()`, so what `path()` accepts is unchanged. A member chain something consumes under an iteration (`$x.users | length`, `$x.users[0]`), and a bare `$x` that a navigating stage follows (`$x | .users[$i]`), keep the eager bind (#4035). Without `std` there is no table to hold the entry, so a repeated whole-node read stays eager there. Apple M5 Max, release build, instructions retired and peak RSS against the commit before (`users` documents of 0.06 / 0.7 / 4.9 MB; baseline noise +-1%, measured with an unchanged second copy of the baseline): `. as $x | $x == .` -20% / -44% / -48% (101 -> 58 MB RSS at 4.9 MB); `. as $x | .users[] | select(.id < 0) | {r: $x} | .r.users[0].id` (no element reaches the read) -24% / -53% / -59% (59 -> 16 MB); `. as $x | .users[] | $x | length` -25% / -52% / -59%. Rows that still read the node once or on every element decode it once either way and are within the noise: `. as $x | {r: $x} | .r.users | length` +0.2%, `. as $x | .users[] | select(.id < 300) | {r: $x} | .r.users[0].id` +0.5%. Scalar binds, `. as $x | 1`, `. as $r | .users[] | .name`, `. as $r | .users[] | select(.id == $r.meta.n) | .name` (a member read registers no entry) and `reduce` are within +-1%. Output identical on every row. Not measured on x86_64. Pinned by the lazy entry's own tests (`lazy_entry_fills_once_and_shares_the_copy_4036`, mutation-checked by disabling the fill and the pop), the differential sweeps against the decoding bind, and `test_deferred_bind_whole_node_reads_match_jq_4036` against `/usr/bin/jq` 1.7.1.
- **jq: an object holding document nodes no longer decodes them** (#4044, #3856 Phase 2). `{a: .users}` decoded every member at construction, so a program that only moved or counted a subtree paid for a full decode. Apple M5 Max, release build, instructions retired / peak RSS (min of 3), `users` documents of 0.2 / 7 / 22 MB: `{a: .users}` 121 M / 2,460 M / 7,430 M -> 54 M / 493 M / 1,425 M and 11 / 81 / 219 MB -> 0 / 25 / 58 MB (the cost of `[.users]`); on the 7 MB document `{a: .users} | .a | length` 1,701 M -> 277 M, `{a: .users} | .a[0]` 1,700 M -> 277 M, `{meta: .users[0], data: .users}` 2,479 M -> 522 M, `.users[] | {u: .}` 2,881 M -> 947 M, `.users[] | {u: .} | .u.name` 2,636 M -> 938 M, `.users[] | {u: ., n: .name}` 3,608 M -> 1,724 M. Per-record small objects and the stages after one are unchanged or cheaper (`.users[] | {name, age}` -12%, `.users | map({id}) | length` -11%, `.users[] | {u: .} | .u.age > 30` -1%, `[.users[] | {u: .}]` -3%, `.users[] | {n: 1}` +0.9%). On a 7950X (wall-clock, min of 5, interleaved): `{a: .users}` 166 -> 30 ms, `{a: .users} | .a | length` 140 -> 21 ms, `.users[] | {u: .}` 134 -> 45 ms, per-record rows within -6% / +2%. Output is identical to the previous build across 1,008 filter/tail/flag combinations, and 130 filters against `/usr/bin/jq` 1.7.1 are pinned. Visible consequences (`docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`): an object holding a node that fails to decode answers `length`, `keys` and a well-formed member and raises when printed or read (`{x: .b} | length` over `tru` is `1`, where it raised); `--preserve-input` keeps a repeated key inside a node the object holds (`{a: .dup}` prints `{"a":{"k":1,"k":2}}`, as `[.dup]` does); `{a: .} | .a | first(map(f) | .[])` (and `limit(1; ...)`, `| map(f) | .[0]`, `| map(f) | first`, `| nth(0; ...)`) yields the first element like the document's own spelling instead of raising on a later element, because `.a` is now a node, not an owned copy (an object with a literal member keeps the owned route and the old answer); and the library entries `eval_with_cursor*`/`eval_each_with_cursor*` return `GenericResult::LazyObject` where they returned `Owned(Object)` (`into_owned`/`collect_owned` report a node's decode failure as `Err`). yq mode, a repeated or computed key, a fan-out member and a construction held inside another are unchanged.
- **jq: navigating into a large owned value no longer re-indexes all of it** (#4052). `(.|tojson|fromjson) as $x | .users[] | {r: $x} | .r.users[0].id` serialized and indexed the whole 63 KB `{r: $x}` at every element to read one field, so it was quadratic in the document: 66 M, 2,448 M and 21,595 M instructions over 6 KB, 64 KB and 196 KB `users` documents on an Apple M5 Max. The owned navigation peel (`projection_peel`) checked that a pipe had a stage behind its first before it looked inside that stage, and `.r.users[0].id` reaches it as the one stage of a pipe, with nothing behind it; the peel declined and the bridge took the whole object. A lone nested pipe is now flattened first: 43 M, 110 M and 259 M instructions on the same three documents, and 3.5 ms -> 2.4 ms, 113 ms -> 6.4 ms and 993 ms -> 14.8 ms wall-clock on a 7950X (min of 5, interleaved), with identical output in both modes (630 stage/wrapper pairs against the previous build). The cost no longer depends on whether an `as` binding happens to be in scope.
- **jq: a stage that never reads `.` no longer re-indexes the value it is handed** (#4053). `. as $x | .users[] | [$x] | 1` serialized and indexed the whole array `[$x]` at every element only to evaluate the literal `1` (the `{r: $x}` twin never did), so it was quadratic in the document: 58 M, 2,173 M and 19,434 M instructions over 6 KB, 64 KB and 196 KB `users` documents on an Apple M5 Max. A stage built from literals, arrays and objects of them, and the operators over them (`1`, `"s"`, `{a: 1}`, `[1, 2]`, `1 + 2`) is now answered from the expression alone, as an owned-assign right side already was (#3138): 37 M, 55 M and 96 M instructions on the same three documents, and 3 ms -> 2 ms, 100 ms -> 3 ms and 919 ms -> 7 ms wall-clock on a 7950X (min of 5, interleaved), with identical output in both modes (880 stage/wrapper pairs against the previous build). A stage that reads `.` (`type`, `keys`, `not`) still takes the bridge.
- **jq: `first`/`last` right after `[.. | parent?]` no longer re-index the whole array** (#4068). The owned navigation peel took `.[0]`/`.[-1]` but not the builtins, so `[.. | parent?] | first | length` (an array of `n` shared copies of the document) wrote the array out in full and indexed it to read one element: 2,579 M, 9,787 M and 38,184 M instructions and 62 MB, 192 MB and 693 MB peak over 1,200, 2,400 and 4,800 inner arrays on an Apple M5 Max. In jq mode a leading `first`/`last` over an array or `null` is now taken natively (jq defines them as `.[0]`/`.[-1]`): 242 M, 453 M and 870 M instructions and 21 MB, 32 MB and 55 MB, the cost of the array itself. yq (its own `first`) and any other target (an object or scalar raises in the bridge's words) still take the bridge. On a 7950X (wall-clock, min of 5, interleaved) 136 ms, 498 ms and 1,960 ms become 19 ms, 35 ms and 69 ms. Output is identical to the previous build across 13,520 first/last/tail/value/wrapper combinations in both modes.
- **yq: `recurse(.[]?; cond)` walks cursors instead of materializing the document** (#4095). Under `--jq-extensions`, for a `cond` that yields at most one value, `succinctly yq` now takes the cursor walk jq mode took since #3867, where it built the whole alias-expanded document as an owned tree first. Over a 100 MB `users` document, `first(recurse(.[]?; true))` is 75.5% faster on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X and 73.6% on an Apple M4 Pro, collecting every node 58.0% and 50.2%, and `length > 0`, `type` tests and `. != null` conditions are 35.5% and 28.0%, 33.0% and 13.3%, and 21.1% and 5.6% faster. Every one of the 21 rows measured is faster on the 7950X; on the M4 Pro the only slower ones are a pair of comparisons joined by `and` (`. != null and . != false`, 3.9% to 4.7% slower). Over a 26-level alias ladder (2^26 leaves once expanded), `.root | first(recurse(.[]?; true))` takes 4.3 ms on the M4 Pro and 1.8 ms on the 7950X where it took 16.9 s and 37.8 s (and over 8 GB). In jq mode a bare `recurse(.[]?; . != null)` over a 10 MB JSON document is 62.9% and 54.9% faster, its collecting form unchanged. A comparison of `.` or `type` with a literal is decided without the general evaluator, which also stops a container being copied whole to be compared. Interleaved A/B against `c31f900b8` on both machines, output identical on every row.
- **jq: a position read before the element the slot scan last found steps back to it instead of rescanning from the first element** (#4101). `[range(length-1;-1;-1) as $i | getpath([$i]) | tostring | key | 0] | length` visited n(n+1)/2 elements in the scan that finds an element in its parent (8,002,528 at n = 4,000, against 1,089 for the same reads in ascending order). The scan now walks back from the remembered element (`DocumentCursor::prev_element`, `prev_sibling` for JSON) when the node ids put the read within 256 elements behind it, and takes the parent of such a position from the remembered extent rather than `enclose`; a read further back (near the start, or a stride past 256) is not attempted and costs what it cost before. Interleaved A/B, output identical on every row: descending reads of 16,000/32,000/64,000 elements read -50.7%/-50.8%/-51.4% on an M4 Pro (1.82 s to 0.90 s, 7.18 s to 3.53 s, 28.8 s to 14.0 s) and -51.2%/-51.9%/-51.8% on a Ryzen 9 7950X, which is the same query read in ascending order (13.92 s against 13.97 s at 64,000 on the M4 Pro). The first-and-last zig-zag and two interleaved distant fan-outs read -2.2% to -3.9% and -0.1% to -3.0% on both chips, and ascending reads -0.8% to +0.2%. The in-order and non-fan-out rows (`.`, an in-order and a skipping fan-out over 100,000 elements, a 300 x 300 matrix, `paths` over 20,000 records) are inside the A/A control's range on both chips, with retired instructions -0.16% to +0.14% (M4 Pro) and -0.02% to +0.11% (7950X, cachegrind). These queries stay quadratic: each `.[$i]` read in a path context is itself an O(i) sibling walk, which this does not touch. YAML and a mapping's members keep the scan from the first element.
- **yq: a wide mapping's members no longer cost a scan of the mapping each** (#4102). Two per-position costs scaled with the number of siblings. `BalancedParens::enclose` (a node's `parent`) walked backward one word at a time to the parent's open, so on the k-th member of a mapping it cost k siblings' worth of words; it now skips whole L0/L1/L2 blocks with the min-excess index `find_close` already uses. And every `value()` of a mapping read all its keys to look for a `<<` merge key; a document with no `<<` (or escape that can spell one) in its text now answers that once, from one byte search. Measured on a 128,000-member mapping, `[.[] | document_index]` and `[.[] | head_comment]` go from 3.4 s to 0.18 s and `[.[] | parent | tag]` over 16,000 members from 14.3 s to 0.05 s; `.` on a 10 MB document retires 15-25% fewer instructions (M4 Pro, `users`, `nested`, `comprehensive` and the wide mapping, output identical), and `[.[] | select(.a > 3) | key]` on the wide mapping 55% fewer. `[.[] | keys | length]` on `users` retires 2% more: the one-off byte search. `length`, `keys` and `has` of a mapping still count its members each time, so a fan-out calling them on the parent stays quadratic, as does a computed-key lookup (#4003).
- **jq: a scalar crossing the owned-evaluator bridge no longer builds a full JSON index** (#4154).
  `OwnedValue::reindexed` serialized a one-token document and ran the general index build
  over it, whose balanced-parentheses directories alone are eight `Vec`s, so `del(.)`,
  `paths(.)` and `del(.[]?)` over a scalar paid 16-18 allocator calls per member. A scalar
  root's index follows from its length, so it is now written directly: 8-10 per member
  (`[.[] | del(.)]` over 2,000 integers: 32,024 -> 16,024 calls). Interleaved A/B, min of 15,
  output identical: `[.[] | del(.)]` over 100k-1M integers -24% to -26% on a Ryzen 9 7950X and
  an M4 Pro (flat across sizes), 300k strings -25% / -21%; a container-rooted control
  (`[.[] | del(.a)]` over 100k objects) -1.3% / +1.1%, within noise.
  `succinctly yq -R` takes the same index (#4220): interleaved A/B, 11 repetitions, output
  identical on all 12 configurations per machine, over line-per-record files of 13,329,
  131,638 and 1,300,229 lines (1, 10 and 100 MB), base the commit before #4173. `.[0:3]`
  -23% to -25% on the 7950X and -8% to -14% on the M4 Pro, `test("age")` -5% to -6% / -4% to
  -6%, `. + "x"` -1% to -3% / -3% to -4% (inside the 7950X control's range), and `.`, which
  does not cross the bridge, -2% to 0% on both. Controls (the base against a copy of itself):
  median -0.05% / -0.79%, per-row range -1.7%..+5.3% / -2.1%..+1.3%, the 7950X's
  `test("age")` rows alone reading +3.6% to +5.3%.
- **jq: `path(f)` for a lone `//`, `first` or `try` leaf allocates 2-4.5x less per scalar member** (#4155). A path expression the cursor walkers decline runs through the path resolver in `eval.rs`, which cloned the whole expression to flatten it (only to ask whether it ends in a bare iterate), evaluated a `.` over a scalar to clone the value back out, cloned a field's name before knowing the lookup found anything, and walked the empty path a `.` resolution names. Each is now skipped (a lone leaf is not flattened, a scalar `.` is borrowed, the clone waits for the one arm that reads it, an empty path is emitted directly). Allocator calls over 2,000 integer members (`examples/alloc_probe_3022`): `[.[] | path(. // .)]` 24,024 to 10,024, `path(.a? // .)` 34,024 to 12,024, `path(first(.a?))` and `path(try .a catch empty)` 18,014 to 4,014, `path(.[]? // .)` 26,024 to 10,024; `path(.)` is unchanged at 6,024. Interleaved A/B over a 250,000-integer array and a 150,000-member array of integers and `{"a":n}` objects, output identical on every row: -20% to -39% on an M4 Pro (medians) and -11% to -25% on a Ryzen 9 7950X, with the unchanged `path(.)` rows inside the noise (M4 Pro -0.9%/+0.7%, 7950X +0.4%/+0.7%; a same-binary control on the M4 Pro read +0.2%). The `Cannot index number with "a"` message a `?` drops over a scalar is still built per member.
- **jq: `path(.[])?` and `try path(.[])` no longer format the `Cannot iterate over ...` message the `?` drops** (#4157). #3689/#3722/#3728 settled a bare `.[]?` over a scalar without stepping it, but `path(.[])?` has `path(...)` as the boundary's body, so `path_iterate_step_generic` still formatted the message (a preview string and an owned copy of the scalar, 7 allocator calls per member) for the `?` to discard. The value boundaries (the four `?`/`try` arms and the owned evaluator `paths(f)`, `any` and `IN` run their filter through) now recognise a `path(.[])` body, with no handler or `catch empty`, through a predicate of its own; the one `.[]?` uses also serves the path walkers, where `path(...)` is not a path expression and `path(path(.[])?)` must still raise jq's path error, so it is not widened. jq mode only; a container, a handler that is not `empty`, an undecodable string or unreadable number (still raised, as `?` never swallows it) and every yq-mode query evaluate as before, and stdout, stderr and exit status are identical to the parent binary on 5,510 query/document pairs and to `/usr/bin/jq` 1.7.1 on 4,060 of them. Allocator calls over 2,000 integer members: `[.[] | path(.[])?] | length` 14,013 -> 13, `[.[] | paths(path(.[])?)] | length` 50,013 -> 18,013. Interleaved A/B, min of 11, 0 output differences, 300,000 and 1,200,000 members: Apple M4 Pro `[.[] | path(.[])?]` over integers -75.8%/-78.1%, over strings -78.4%/-80.0%, `try path(.[]) catch empty` -86.8%/-88.5% and -87.4%/-89.0%, `[paths(path(.[])?)]` -65.8%/-65.3% and -70.3%/-70.9%; Ryzen 9 7950X -62.4%/-62.4% and -66.3%/-65.5%, `try ... catch empty` -81.6%/-81.2% and -81.2%/-80.5%, `[paths(path(.[])?)]` -59.8%/-60.4% and -59.6%/-59.5%. Rows the change cannot reach (`[.[] | path(.)]`, `[.[] | path(.[]?)]`) read -2.1%..+3.2% on the M4 Pro and -2.3%..+2.7% on the 7950X, and `path(.[])?` over 100,000 and 400,000 three-element arrays (the gate declines them) reads +0.6%..+1.8% and +0.5%..+1.4%, inside that band. A container-member `[paths(path(.[])?)]` also reads -45%..-51%, since `paths(f)` visits the scalars below each member.
- **jq: a run over a large document no longer counts newlines for a location nothing reads** (#4160). The default document loop resolved every value's `(at <file>:<line>)` line before evaluating, a scalar pass over the whole input, though only a diagnostic reads it and the M2 fast path never does; on the M2 fast path it is now resolved only if an error is reported, and every path counts in 64-byte chunks that vectorize. Two effects are in the numbers, so each row says which it exercised (interleaved A/B, output identical on every row). The chunked count alone, on **general-path** rows (`length` is not an M2 builtin per `can_use_m2_streaming`, and `[.[]?] | length` costs the same instructions with `--arg`, which disables M2, as without): `length` and `[.[]?] | length` -1.6% on a Ryzen 9 7950X and -1.9% on an M4 Pro (21 reps, every row faster; controls +0.03% / -0.61%). The lazy resolution on rows that really take M2, 21 reps: `.users[0]`, `.users[-1]` and `.users[]` on a 1.35 to 6.9 MB `users` document -2.5% / -3.2%, NDJSON `.name` -4.6% / -4.5% and NDJSON `-c .` -5.1% / -5.2% (7950X / M4 Pro; controls within +-1.4%). The identity fast path `-c .` on a single 2-10 MB document is -3.1% / -2.6% (15 reps; control +0.2% / -1.2%). For `.users[0]` the lazy route is under 1% of the instructions saved (0.7%) and the chunked count is the rest; on per-value NDJSON the lazy route is the larger share (about 6.1 M against 3.9 M instructions on a 2 MB file). Wall-clock did not separate the two effects. `find_matching_close`, the other term the issue names, is unchanged.
- **jq: a computed-index loop over a wide array in a path context is linear, not quadratic** (#4162). A non-negative index read in a path context (`[range(0;length) as $i | getpath([$i]) | tostring | key | 0]`, `[range(length-1;-1;-1) as $i | .[$i] | key | 0]`) makes no length lookup, so #4035's element index never served it and each read walked to its index: 14 s at 64,000 elements, 4x per doubling, ascending and descending alike. An array read that way is now answered from a prefix of element ids that the reads extend: a read inside it is O(1), a read beyond it resumes the walk where the last one stopped, so no element is walked twice. It starts on an array's third wide read, as #4035's index is built on the third length lookup, and the value route (which reads the length first) stays on #4035's rule. 16k / 32k / 64k elements: 936 ms / 3.65 s / 14.4 s -> 31 / 61 / 121 ms ascending and 909 ms / 3.60 s / 14.3 s -> 11 / 22 / 43 ms descending on a 7950X, 908 ms / 3.56 s / 14.1 s -> 31 / 56 / 106 ms and 887 ms / 3.51 s / 14.1 s -> 11 / 19 / 32 ms on an M4 Pro. An array read once or twice costs what it did, bar registering it (+1.2% / +1.4% instructions over 20,000 hundred-integer arrays, wall-clock -3.9% to +1.3%); one read exactly three times pays for recording and gains nothing from it (+4.7% / +6.1% instructions, +0.1% / +3.8% wall-clock on hundred-integer arrays, the worst case). Numbers and the 7950X placement caveat in `docs/parsing/json.md`.
- **jq: `nth($i)` before `key`/`path` no longer materializes the array on every read** (#4163). `nth(n)` is jq's `.[n]`, but the generic evaluator did not know that: a plain read went through the whole-input bridge, and a position read (`nth($i) | tostring | key`) left the cursor walk for the owned identity route, so 16,000 reads of a 16,000-element array took 113 s where `.[$i]` takes 0.83 s (Apple M5 Max laptop, release; 3,000 elements: `nth($i) | tostring | key` 4.5 s to 0.03 s, a plain `nth($i)` 8.7 s to under 0.01 s). `nth` now takes the computed-index arm of the evaluator and of the path-context walk. The slice shape `.[$i:][0]` is separate (a slice builds its tail, see #4195).
- **jq/yq: two fan-outs that alternate between distant offsets of one wide array no longer rescan it from the first element on every read** (#4164). The scan that finds an element in its parent remembered one element per parent, so `[(length/2|floor) as $h | range(0;$h) as $i | (getpath([$i]), getpath([$i+$h])) | tostring | key | 0] | length` evicted its own cursor on every read: 5,939,529 elements visited at n = 4,000 (`.[$i]` form), 2,562 now (3,090 for `getpath`/`nth`). A parent now keeps two remembered scans (the table is still four); a read that resumed from one replaces it, a read that started from the first element is added beside the parent's other one, and a read steps back from a later scan when that one is nearer than the earlier. Interleaved A/B, output identical on every row, min of 5: the interleaved shape at 16,000/32,000/64,000 elements reads -42.1%/-42.7%/-43.0% on an M4 Pro (1.57 s to 0.91 s, 6.23 s to 3.57 s, 24.8 s to 14.1 s) and -41.8%/-42.2%/-42.4% on a Ryzen 9 7950X, and the first-and-last zig-zag -95.2%/-97.7%/-98.9% (M4 Pro: 689 ms to 33 ms, 2.70 s to 63 ms, 10.7 s to 119 ms) and -94.9%/-97.5%/-98.7%. The ascending and descending controls move -0.6% to +0.6% on both chips. On a YAML sequence, where `.[$i]` is not itself linear in `$i`, the interleaved shape is 1.18 s, 4.61 s, 18.2 s at 10,000/20,000/40,000 items before (4x per doubling) and 34 ms, 68 ms, 154 ms after (2x) on the M4 Pro (1.98 s, 7.80 s, 31.2 s to 41 ms, 97 ms, 263 ms on the 7950X). The JSON interleaved shape stays quadratic in wall-clock (14.1 s at 64,000 on the M4 Pro) because each `.[$i]` in a path context is itself an O(i) sibling walk (#4162), which this does not touch. Non-fan-out rows (`.`, an in-order and a skipping fan-out over 100,000 elements, `paths` over 20,000 records, YAML `key`/`path` over 40,000 items) read -2.3% to +0.9% on the M4 Pro and -2.0% to +0.4% on the 7950X, inside the A/A control (-2.1% to +1.0% and -1.3% to -0.8%); the one exception is a 300 x 300 matrix read in order, +2.2% on the M4 Pro (-1.7% on the 7950X) at -0.14% to +0.42% retired instructions, so the delta is not extra work (consistent with code layout; no padding holdout was run). Three or more interleaved fan-outs still replace one another.
- **jq: `[.[] | ., 1]`, `[.[] | ., . | length]` and `[.[] | (., .)?]` keep the nodes they hold instead of decoding them** (#4166). #3922's `,`-stage array route took only a pipe of pure navigation, so a computed branch beside a navigation one, a computed stage after navigation branches, and a `?` around a group of navigation branches ran the owned route and decoded every node the array holds. The route now takes each shape whose order it keeps: computed branches with nothing after them, navigation branches with any tail, and `(a, b)?` over navigation, where a catchable raise ends that output's group as in jq. On a 14 MB `users` document, release, Apple M4 Pro mini, interleaved A/B with identical output (min wall): `[.users[] | ., 1] | length` 173.5 ms -> 37.6 ms (`-78%`) and 182 MB -> 46 MB, `[.users[] | ., length] | length` 211.4 ms -> 70.5 ms (`-67%`), `[.users[] | ., . | length] | length` 285.1 ms -> 109.4 ms (`-62%`), `[.users[] | (., .)?] | length` 306.8 ms -> 36.9 ms (`-88%`) and 290 MB -> 42 MB; the holdouts (`[.users[] | ., .]`, `[.users[], 1]`, `[.users[] | .id, .name]`, an owned prefix that declines) read within `+-1.4%` (median, idle re-run, 21 reps). Over an unreadable value `[.[] | ., 1] | length` and `[.[] | (., .)?] | length` now answer like `[.[] | ., .] | length`; printing the array still raises. jq mode only.
- **jq: `to_entries`, `.[]`, `map_values`, `paths` and the printer's `[.]` / `{a: .}` over a wide object no longer sort every key hash to look for a repeated key** (#4169). They now use the bitset prefilter #3343 gave `length` (`any_hash_repeats`, 128 to 2^21 keys), which sorts only the few hashes that land on a bit another hash had set, so the answer is the same. Because both paths build the full field list first, the sort was a small share of their cost: on a 2 MB `wide` object (159 K keys) `to_entries | length` runs 1.7% fewer instructions and `[.]` 2.7% fewer on a 7950X (1.6% and 2.0% on an M4 Pro), and median wall-clock falls 0.3% to 3.1% from 159 K to 1.9 M keys on both, except `[.]` on the M4 Pro at 1.55 M to 1.77 M keys, which is flat. Arrays of 32- to 512-key objects stay within the measurement band (instructions -0.3% or less), and peak RSS is unchanged. `keys_unsorted` past 786 K keys keeps its sort: the prefilter was up to 4.1% slower there on the M4 Pro (1.55 M to 1.77 M keys) for at most about 2% elsewhere; see `docs/parsing/json.md`. Output is identical, error text and exit status included, across 742 comparisons.
- **jq: the top-level document splitter finds a container's end over a 64-byte mask, not byte by byte** (#4177). After #4172 removed the line counter, `find_matching_close` plus its string scan was the second-largest term of `jq -c .` over a large document: 15-19% of instructions on `wide` and `users` (about 12.7 Ir per input byte on `wide`), 5% on `comprehensive`. `json::light::container_end` now classifies `"`, `\`, control bytes and the container's own brackets once per 64-byte block and answers each hit with a `trailing_zeros`, so the bytes between hits and the per-string scan entry are gone: 3.7 Ir/byte on `wide` 2 MB, 119.0 M total instructions against 137.8 M (-13.7%), `users` -11.6%, `comprehensive` -4.4%, 6.9 MB of 85-byte NDJSON records -6.0%, 2 MB of 8-byte NDJSON records -1.3%. A bracket inside a string is a hit the mask cannot tell from one outside, so the first one in a string swaps the block's mask for one without the brackets until the string ends (a string made only of the container's own brackets was +24% on a 7950X and +60% on an M4 Pro before that). Interleaved A/B wall-clock against `main`, output identical on every row, 21 reps, medians: Ryzen 9 7950X `wide`/`users` -8.9% to -13.6%, `comprehensive` -5.2% to -6.1%, pretty-printed -13.4%, a 5 MB array of 0-256-byte strings -5.3% to -22.6% and of escape-bearing strings -26.5% to -27.9%, arrays of tiny objects/arrays -16.0% and -18.4%, bracket-only strings -2.2% to -11.4%, tiny NDJSON records -2.6% and -2.8%; Apple M4 Pro `wide` -5.2% to -6.1%, `users` -5.1% to -10.1%, `comprehensive` -2.5% to -2.7%, pretty-printed -3.6%, plain strings -4.8% to +0.7%, escape-bearing strings -18.0% to -19.5%, tiny objects/arrays -7.3% and -5.0%, bracket-only strings -5.9% to +1.0%. 20 MB of 8-byte NDJSON records, the shape a per-call block classification cannot help, reads +1.4% and +3.5% on the M4 Pro (same-binary control: -3.3% to -0.6%) and -2.6% and -2.8% on the 7950X.
- **jq: `.[$i:][0]` and `.[$i:] | length` no longer build the whole slice to read one element or a count** (#4195). A computed slice converted every element in its range into an owned array, so reading one element (or the length) through it cost O(tail) and a loop over it was quadratic. `E[a:b][k]` (an integer-literal `k`, negative counting from the slice's end) and `E[a:b] | length` now resolve the slice's range and read it directly, converting only the element named. Reading each of 3,000 elements from the back (`[range(length-1;-1;-1) as $i | .[$i:][0]]`): `| length` 3.10 s to 3 ms and `[0]` 2.39 s to 5 ms on a Ryzen 9 7950X, 1.70 s to 4 ms and 1.71 s to 6 ms on an Apple M4 Pro; at 16,000 elements 97.7 s to 9 ms and 76.2 s to 20 ms (7950X), 48.5 s to 9 ms and 49.0 s to 19 ms (M4 Pro). Output is unchanged in `jq` and `yq` mode; the one observable difference is that the other elements of the range are no longer converted, so a malformed element the read does not name no longer raises, as with `.[k]` and `length` (jq rejects such a document at parse). A slice with no such read (`.[$i:$i+8] | 0`, still O(n) per slice) and the position form (`.[$i:][0] | key`) are unchanged.
- **jq: a scalar crossing the owned-evaluator bridge reuses its index buffers** (#4217).
  After #4154 a scalar `ReindexedDoc` still allocated its text and three index buffers (the
  interest bits, their rank and the leaf's parentheses word) and freed them a moment later,
  once per scalar a query bridges. A dropped scalar document now hands those buffers to the
  next one on the thread, so a crossing in steady state allocates only its text: 3 fewer
  allocator calls per member on every row (`[.[] | del(.)]` over 2,000 integers: 16,022 ->
  10,022; strings 20,022 -> 14,022; booleans and nulls 12,022 -> 6,022). Each live document
  keeps its own index, so `document_token` still tells two of them apart.
  Interleaved A/B, min of 15, output identical: `[.[] | del(.)]`, `paths(.)` and
  `del(.[]?)` over 300k-1M integers -6.0% to -9.1% on a Ryzen 9 7950X and -5.0% to -6.8% on
  an M4 Pro, 300k strings -7.6% to -8.4% / -4.4% to -7.5%; a container-rooted control
  (`[.[] | del(.a)]` over 100k objects) -0.2% / -0.2%, within noise.
- **jq: `del(.[]?)` and `del(.)` over scalars copy no expression tree per member** (#4218).
  A scalar crossing the owned-evaluator bridge paid ten allocator calls for `del(.[]?)` and
  eight for `del(.)`, four of them `Expr` boxes cloned only to be read: `eval_builtin`
  rebuilt the `Expr::Builtin` node its dispatcher already held, and `builtin_del` copied
  its path into a one-element `Vec`. Both now borrow (the path is copied only while a yq
  alias table is installed): `[.[] | del(.[]?)]` over 2,000 integers 20,024 -> 12,022
  allocator calls, `[.[] | del(.)]` 16,024 -> 12,022; output unchanged. Interleaved A/B on an
  M4 Pro (min of 15, output identical): `[.[] | del(.[]?)]` over 300k integers -19.1%, over
  300k strings -13.9%; `[.[] | del(.)]` -11.3% / -7.0%; container members
  (`[.[] | del(.a)]` over 100k objects) -6.4%. The remaining six calls per member are the
  scalar reindex bridge (#4154) and the scalar's two decodes.
- **jq: `path(f)` for a lone `.` leaf over a scalar member (`. // .`, `first(.)`, `.a? // .`) allocates what `path(.)` does** (#4226). #4155 left these at 5 allocator calls per member against `path(.)`'s 3: the resolver built a one-element `Vec` of branches that it emptied into its sink on the next line, and allocated a fresh root path-prefix node on every call. The branch now goes straight to the sink, and under `std` the root is a handle on one per-thread node (`no_std` still allocates). The third term, the member's own copy (a boxed number literal), stays: a bare `Int` is not interchangeable with a number literal under jq's `jv_identical`, so skipping it needs a cursor route, not a cheaper copy. Allocator calls over 2,000 integer members (`examples/alloc_probe_3022`): `[.[] | path(. // .)]` and `path(first(.))` 10,024 to 6,024, `path(.a? // .)` 12,024 to 8,024; `path(.)` is unchanged at 6,024. Interleaved A/B over 250,000- and 1,000,000-integer arrays and a 150,000-member array of integers and `{"a":n}` objects, output identical on all 15 configurations: -10% to -14% on the integer rows and -5% to -7% on the mixed rows on an M4 Pro (medians), -6% to -12% and -1% to -5% on a Ryzen 9 7950X, with the unchanged `path(.)` rows inside the noise (same-binary control: M4 Pro +0.1% median, 7950X +0.5%). Split by term, the `Vec`-free emit alone reads -5.1% (M4 Pro) and -1.2% (7950X) across the `//` rows, and the shared root a further -4.4% and -3.5%. The time gap to `path(.)` does not close with the allocation gap (`. // .` over the integer array is still 1.5x `path(.)` on the 7950X and 1.6x on the M4 Pro), so what remains is the resolver's per-call machinery, not allocation.
- **jq: `.a?` / `.[N]?` over a scalar inside `path(f)` no longer builds the `Cannot index` message it drops** (#4227).
  A `?`/`try` around a bare field or index lookup (no handler or `catch empty`) now settles a non-null scalar
  without stepping it, as #3728 did for `.[]?`: `[.[] | path(.a? // .)]` over 2,000 integers goes from 8,022 to
  6,022 allocator calls (the settled `path(.[]? // .)` twin) and `path(.a?)` from 4,013 to 2,013, one call per
  member. Interleaved A/B on a 1M-integer array (Apple M5 Max, not idle): `path(.a? // .)` 290.8 -> 218.4 ms,
  `path(.a?)` 149.9 -> 102.6 ms. `null` (which indexes to `null`), containers, slices, a malformed value and yq
  mode still take the step; output is unchanged.
- **yq: a `{...}` with a `select` or a `.[]` in a pair no longer pays for the fold on every record** (#4240). #4193 sent every construction with an operand that might be empty through yq's fold up front, +9% (two entries) to +16% (five) on a 7 MB document. An empty operand always empties the cross product, so the cross product is now built first and the fold runs only for a record whose construction came out empty: -5% to -8% against #4193's route on a 7-14 MB `users` document (M4 Pro, interleaved, control range -2% to +2%), and within noise of the fan-out it replaced. The trade-off: a construction that is empty for every record is built twice, which reads +54% on a document where `select` drops every record (`.users[] | {"n": .name, "s": (.score | select(. > 1e8))}`) -- slower than #4193's route there, though no slower in output. Side effects in such an operand are not run twice.
- **jq: `try path(.[]) catch LITERAL` over a scalar no longer builds the `Cannot iterate over ...` error its handler ignores** (#4280). #4157 settled `path(.[])?` and `try path(.[]) catch empty` this way, and #3704 `try .[] catch LITERAL`; a literal handler around `path(.[])` still built the payload (a preview string and an owned copy of the scalar) and ran the handler over a re-indexed scalar document. `[.[] | try path(.[]) catch "c"] | length` over 2,000 integers makes 2,022 allocator calls, down from 18,022, the same as `try .[] catch "c"`. Output is unchanged: the literal for a scalar, the paths for a container, and an undecodable string still escapes.
- **jq: `del(.)`, and `del(.[]?)` over a scalar or empty container, no longer cross the
  reindex bridge** (#4283). Both targets have the same paths whatever `.` is, so the owned
  evaluators (both of them: `eval_generic`'s and `eval.rs`'s eager and streaming routes) now
  answer them directly: `del(.)` is `null`, and `del(.[]?)` over a scalar, `[]` or `{}` is the
  input itself, not written out, indexed and decoded back (its number-literal spelling kept). The
  only allocation left per member is the member's own decode (`[.[] | del(.[]?)]` over 2,000
  integers: 6,022 -> 2,022 allocator calls; strings 10,022 -> 2,022; booleans and nulls
  2,022 -> 22). jq mode only: yq answers both differently and keeps its route.
  Interleaved A/B on an M4 Pro (first revision), min of 15, output identical: `[.[] | del(.)]`
  and `[.[] | del(.[]?)]` over 1M integers -47%, 300k strings -57% to -58%, 1M mixed scalars
  -46% to -48% wall-clock. Final code, instructions retired (min of 3, M4 Pro): those rows
  -52% / -64% / -53% to -54%, `map(del(.[]?))` -46% / -58% / -46%; a container control
  (`[.[] | del(.a)]` over 200k objects) +0.2%, and `succinctly yq -R` `del(.)`/`del(.[]?)`
  over 300k lines -0.2% / -0.1%.
  Ryzen 9 7950X, final code, interleaved A/B pinned to one core, min of 15, output identical:
  the same rows -45% / -51% / -46% to -47%, `map(del(.[]?))` -52% / -58% / -54%; container
  control -1.2%, `yq -R` -0.2% / -0.6%, against a base-vs-base control of -1.0% to +0.3%.
- **jq: a computed-slice read no longer converts the array per read for `| key`, `| tostring | key`, a document-bound `$a[$i:][0]` or an owned-array `$a | .[$i:][0]`** (#4286). #4251, #4315 and #4321 fused `E[a:b]` followed by `[k]`, `length`, `first` and `last`, but four reads still converted the whole array per read, so a loop over them was quadratic: `.[$i:][0] | key` and `.[$i:][0] | tostring | key` went through the path-context walk, which converted the target array and then the slice; `.xs as $a | $a[$i:][0]` was refused by the fusion's gate (a bound value is a `TrackedVar`, not a plain `Var`); and `$a | .[$i:][0]` over an owned array (a constructed or `map(...)` result) wrote the whole array out and indexed it again. `key` is now answered from the slice's range, the bound variable is accepted by the gate, and the owned array is read in place. Over 4,000 elements, `[range(length-1;-1;-1) as $i | .[$i:][0] | key] | length` takes 6.3 ms (was 8,034 ms) on an Apple M4 Pro and 3.5 ms (was 9,991 ms) on a Ryzen 9 7950X; `| tostring | key` 5.9 ms (was 12,916 ms) and 3.6 ms (was 17,466 ms); `$a[$i:][0]` over a document-bound `$a` 10.3 ms (was 2,504 ms) and 10.6 ms (was 3,682 ms); `$a | .[$i:][0]` over an owned `$a` 10.2 ms (was 1,482 ms) and 10.0 ms (was 2,086 ms). The old times quadrupled per doubling of the array; the new ones grow 1.3x to 1.7x, as the `.[$i]` floor does (1.2x to 1.7x on the same two machines), and the already-fused control row and the floor row are unchanged (release builds, interleaved min of 3). Like the other fused reads, they convert only the element they name (`key` converts none), recorded in `limitations.md`. `key` is fused for jq mode, a non-negative index inside the slice and a read that is the whole pipe; everything else keeps the walk. `path(.[$i:][0])` is #4356.
- **jq: a slice reads only its range, so a narrow window of a wide array is no longer O(length)** (#4287). `.[$i:$j]` collected every element of the array before taking its range, so a loop slicing a small window out of a large array was quadratic. A slice now reads only the elements in its range: by index once the array has been read three times (#4035's element index), and otherwise in one walk that counts the array and keeps only the elements a slice with non-negative bounds can hold. Slicing every 8-element window from the back of an array (`[range(length-1;-1;-1) as $i | .[$i:$i+8] | 0] | add`) on a Ryzen 9 7950X: 192 ms to 6 ms at 3,000 elements, 758 ms to 10 ms at 6,000, and 5.35 s to 25 ms at 16,000; on an Apple M4 Pro, 131 ms to 7 ms, 500 ms to 10 ms and 3.5 s to 22 ms. One slice of a million-element array is 10-24% faster on the 7950X and 6-11% on the M4 Pro (`.[$i:$i+2]`, `.[-2:]`), and a slice of almost all of it (`.[:-1]`) is within 2% of before on both. Output is unchanged in `jq` and `yq` mode, including errors: a malformed element inside the range still raises, one outside it still does not, and an array with a malformed delimiter is read as before.
- **jq: `E[a:b] | first`, `| last` and a `?` on the slice or the read no longer build the slice** (#4288). #4251 fused `E[a:b][k]` and `E[a:b] | length` so a loop over them stopped being quadratic; `first`, `last`, `E[a:b][0]?` and `E[a:b]?[0]` still built the whole tail per read. `[range(length-1;-1;-1) as $i | .[$i:] | first | .a.b] | length` over 3,000 elements takes 7.4 ms (was 1,470 ms) and over 6,000 elements 10.6 ms (was 5,804 ms): the old time quadrupled per doubling, the new one is linear. `last` and the two `?` forms match (`[0]?` 6,762 ms before at 6,000), and the already-fused `.[$i:][0]` control row is unchanged (10.4 vs 10.5 ms). Release builds, Apple M5 Max, interleaved min of 3; x86_64 not measured. `first` and `last` are jq's `.[0]` and `.[-1]`, so the fused read applies in jq mode only; yq keeps today's route. A computed index (`.[$i:][$k]`), a literal-bound slice and the `| key`/`| path` reads are unchanged. Like #4251's reads, the fused ones convert only the element they name, recorded in `limitations.md`.
- **jq: `[(.users, [1]) | .[0]]`, `[(.users, length) | .]`, `[(.users, .users)?]` and `[.users[] | (., 1) | .]` keep the nodes they hold instead of decoding them** (#4294). The `,`-head route took only a pipe of pure navigation, only the `,`-stage route recognised a `?` group, and neither ran a tail after a computed branch, so these shapes ran the owned route and decoded every node the array holds. A `?` around navigation branches is now a guarded group as the whole body or at the head too. A computed branch may be followed by further stages when no stage before the pipe's last has an effect or reads the input state (#4293's predicate) and none reads path context. On a 14 MB `users` document, release, Apple M4 Pro mini, interleaved A/B, 15 reps, identical output (min wall): `[(.users, [1]) | .[0]] | length` 176.6 ms -> 25.0 ms (`-86%`) and 158 MB -> 26 MB, `[(.users, length) | .] | length` 175.7 ms -> 22.5 ms (`-87%`), `[(.users, .users)?] | length` 270.0 ms -> 22.7 ms (`-92%`) and 258 MB -> 26 MB, `[.users[] | (., 1) | .] | length` 255.1 ms -> 51.4 ms (`-80%`) and 182 MB -> 46 MB. The #4166/#3922 holdouts read within `-1.9%..+0.2%` (median). jq mode only.
