- **jq: `E[a:b][$k]` with a computed index no longer builds the slice** (#4317). #4251 and #4315 fused `E[a:b]` followed by a literal `[k]`, `length`, `first` and `last`; a computed index (`.[$i:][$k]`) parses as an index expression over the slice, not a pipe, so it still built the whole tail per read. `0 as $k | [range(length-1;-1;-1) as $i | .[$i:][$k] | .a.b] | length` over 3,000 elements takes 8.6 ms (was 1,667 ms) and over 6,000 elements 11.3 ms (was 6,376 ms): the old time quadrupled per doubling, the new one is linear, and the `[0]` control row is unchanged (10.3 vs 10.4 ms). The `?` form matches (13.8 ms against 5,777 ms). Release builds, Apple M5 Max, interleaved min of 3; x86_64 not measured. Fused only for a key that is one integer-valued number; a fractional, string, `null` or fanning-out key keeps the ordinary route, which answers or raises it as before. Like the other fused reads, it converts only the element it names, recorded in `limitations.md`.
- **jq: a literal-bound slice read, `.[2:][0]`, no longer builds the slice** (#4323). #4195, #4288, #4315 and #4317 fused `E[a:b]` with a computed bound followed by a read; a literal bound (`.[2:]`) has no native arm in the generic evaluator, so it fell to the full evaluator, which converted every element of the array on each read. `[range(length) as $i | .[2:][0] | .a.b] | length` over 4,000 `{"a":{"b":i}}` elements took 10.8 s on a Ryzen 9 7950X and now takes 5.9 ms; 2,000 elements 2,686 ms to 4.4 ms, 1,000 elements 641 ms to 3.4 ms. The old time quadrupled per doubling; the new one grows 1.3x per doubling, where the `.[$i]` floor grows 1.3x. `[-1]`, `length`, `first`, `last`, a negative end (`.[:-2][0]`), a `?` on either stage and a computed index (`.[2:][$i]`) are covered, 4,000 elements run in 2.8-6.6 ms against 10.1-11.2 s. A bracket read behind navigation (`.a[2:][0]`) is covered; a navigated slice followed by a separate `| length`/`first`/`last` stage (`.a[2:] | length`) is covered by #4406. Release builds, 7950X pinned to one core, interleaved min of 3, output identical to the old binary on every row; the unfused spelling `(.[2:])[0]` is unchanged (the control). Like the computed form, the fused read converts only the element it names, so a malformed value elsewhere in the array no longer raises (`.[0:3][0]` on `[1,1.2.3,3]` is `1`; jq rejects the document at parse), recorded in `limitations.md`. Library `succinctly::jq::eval` over a materialized value is a separate route and unchanged.
- **jq: `path(.[$i:][0])` no longer builds the slice per read** (#4356). A computed slice of the pipe's own input followed by an integer-literal index (`path(E[a:b][k])`, and through it `=`, `|=` and `del`) built the slice in the resolver and then wrote it out and re-indexed it through the bridge to step into it, so a loop over reads at a moving bound was quadratic. It is now answered from the slice's resolved range at both places, naming the slice's component as the bounds were spelled and then the index as written (`path(.[1:][-1])` ends in `-1`; an index past either end of the slice is `null`). Over 4,000 elements, `[range(length-1;-1;-1) as $i | path(.[$i:][0])] | length` takes 9.7 ms (was 1,995 ms) on an Apple M4 Pro and 12.3 ms (was 2,237 ms) on a Ryzen 9 7950X; over 2,000 elements 6.5 ms (was 503 ms) and 6.8 ms (was 538 ms). The old times quadrupled per doubling; the new ones grow 1.5x and 1.8x, as the `path(.[$i])` floor does (1.5x and 1.8x on the same two machines), and the floor and the already-fused value-read control are unchanged (release builds, interleaved min of 5, one core on the 7950X). jq mode, a trackable array and bounds that never read `.`; a float-spelled index, a generator bound and yq keep the general route, recorded in `limitations.md`.
- **jq: `--stream` walks each document's events one at a time** (#4397). The first cut kept every event of every document before the program ran; a program that reads `.` now takes the next event out of its document as it asks for it (memory proportional to the depth on top of the document), and one that uses `-s` or `input`/`inputs` still keeps them. On a 10.8 MB array of 120,000 records `jq --stream -c .` peaked at 622 MB with the events kept and 310 MB walked one at a time (jq 1.7.1: 2.4 MB, which streams the parse as well); the output is byte-identical to jq's (md5).
- **jq: a navigated literal slice read by a separate stage, `.a[2:] | length`, no longer builds the slice** (#4406). #4323 fused `.a[2:][0]` and `.a | .[2:] | length`, but `.a[2:]` followed by `| length`, `| first`, `| last` or `| .[k]` parses to a pipe whose first stage is the nested chain `.a[2:]`, which the fusion did not see, so every read converted the whole tail of the array. The fusion now looks through that one nested pipe when every stage before the slice is a pure path (`.a`, `.a.b`, `.a[0].b`), under a postfix `?` on the slice too, and the computed index `.a[2:][$k]` is covered with it. `[range(1000) as $i | .a[2:] | length] | length` over `{"a":[{"a":{"b":i}}, ...]}` took 936 ms for 2,000 elements and 1,871 ms for 4,000 on an Apple M4 Pro, now 3.9 ms and 4.4 ms; on a Ryzen 9 7950X (pinned to one core) 1,329 ms and 2,570 ms, now 2.5 ms and 2.7 ms. `first`, `last`, `.[k]` and `.a[2:][$k]` move the same way: 971-2,179 ms before, 4.3-4.9 ms after (M4 Pro, 2,000 and 4,000 elements). The old time doubled per doubling; the new one grows 1.1x. Release builds, interleaved min of 7, output identical to the old binary on every row, and the fused controls (`.a | .[2:] | length`, `.a[$i:] | length`, `.a[2:][0]`) unchanged; instruction counts on the perf-guard matrix move +0.0% (7950X). Like the head form, the fused read converts only the element it names (`limitations.md`, "A fused slice read does not validate the rest of the range"); a parenthesised `(.a[2:]) | length` and a path that can fan out or fail quietly (`.a[]?[2:]`) keep the ordinary route.
- **jq: `.[$i:][-1] | key` and `.[$i:][0] | .a | key` no longer walk the whole array per read** (#4408). #4286 answered `E[a:b][k] | key` from the slice's range, but only for a non-negative `k` inside the slice and a `key` straight after the read; a negative index, an index outside the slice and a field step before the `key` went through the path-context walk, which converts the target array and then the slice per read, so a loop over them was quadratic. The fusion now takes an index of either sign as written (jq keeps it in the path as written, so the key is `k` itself, in or out of the slice) and field steps before the `key` (the key is the last field's name; the one element the steps read is converted, `null` outside the slice, and a step over a scalar still raises through the walk). Over 4,000 elements, `[range(length-1;-1;-1) as $i | .[$i:][-1] | key] | length` takes 22 ms (was 9,085 ms) and `.[$i:][0] | .a | key` 23 ms (was 7,374 ms) on an Apple M4 Pro (release build, one run each, box not idle); the old times quadrupled per doubling of the array and the new ones are flat. Output is identical to the previous build on 7,776 filter/document combinations and to `/usr/bin/jq` 1.7.1's `path(...) | last` on the 2,592 of them jq answers.
- **jq: `path(try .a)` and `path(try .a catch empty)` take the same cursor walk as `path(.a?)`** (#4412). `try E` and `try E catch empty` are `E?`, but the walk only recognised the `?` spelling, so a `try` fell to the route that copies the input and wraps the copy in an `Rc` on every `path(f)` call: two allocator calls per scalar member against one for `path(.[]?)`. The walk now takes both spellings in jq mode (a handler that runs, `catch .`, or a body that is not navigation keeps its route; yq mode keeps the materializing route, because the walk counts a repeated mapping key once more). `[.[] | path(try .a)] | length` over 1,000,000 integers took 140.2 ms on an Apple M4 Pro and now takes 95.7 ms (`path(.a?)`: 96.3 ms); on a Ryzen 9 7950X (one core) 192.6 ms to 130.1 ms (`path(.a?)`: 129.7 ms). `try .[0]` and `try .a catch empty` move the same -31% to -34%, `try .[]` -19% to -20% (it reaches `path(.[]?)`'s floor, 112.9 ms and 152.9 ms). Allocator calls for 2,000 members: `.[] | path(try .a)` 4,000 to 2,000. Release builds, interleaved min of 9, output identical on every row; `path(.a?)`, `path(.[]?)` and `path(first(.a?))` unchanged. `path(first(f))` keeps the materializing route: the walk collects every path before delivering one, which would make `path(first(.[]))` O(n) in memory.
- **yq: numbering the documents of a stream, and streaming a document whose aliases follow their anchors, no longer cost the square of the document** (#4871). `document_index` found a document's place by counting the documents before it, so `select(document_index == 5)` over a stream of 64,000 two-key documents took 12.4 s; it now binary-searches a list of document positions built once on first use (0.05 s). And a far hop forward in the YAML position cursors (`EndPositions`/`AdvancePositions::get_sequential`: an alias read after its anchor, then the next alias) scanned the interval bitmap word by word across the whole gap; past four select samples' worth of ones it now uses the sampled select the backward jumps already used. `yq -o=json .` over 256,000 anchors followed by 256,000 aliases takes 0.31 s, from 8.9 s. Output is byte-identical (M4 Pro, release). Ordinary documents keep the short scan: `users`, `nested`, `comprehensive`, `sequences` and a 128,000-member mapping retire within about 1% of the previous instruction count on `.`, `.[]`, a tag walk, `keys` and `to_entries` (the +0.4% on `.` is the same on every corpus with no query-specific cause: layout).
- **jq: `paths(f)` over a wide object is linear, not quadratic** (#4875). `paths(f)` read each path's node back by scanning the object's members for the key, at every path, so `[paths(type == "number")]` over a 32,000 / 64,000 / 128,000-member object took 2.3 / 10.6 / 35 s; it now looks the key up in the map (0.66 / 0.12 / 0.21 s on an M4 Pro, output identical). A survey of 25 per-position steps over wide JSON objects and 23 over wide arrays found no other shape that grew faster than its input.
- **yq: a float read from JSON prints without a per-number allocation, and the tie-break correction skips its exact check unless a tie is possible** (#4915).
  #4897 made a JSON-sourced float print through yq's float formatter, which cost +28% instructions on a 17 MB array
  of ordinary floats (`yq -p json -o json .`, 9.12 G against 7.11 G). The streaming printer now formats an
  ordinary-magnitude float into a stack buffer and only takes the allocating path for a scientific magnitude or a last digit of
  `3`, and `correct_shortest_decimal_tiebreak` rejects a non-tie with one `u64` remainder (`5^k | 2n - 1`) before its exact
  arithmetic. Same bytes out; 7.55 G instructions on that file (+6% over the plain write, -17% against main) and 6.95 G
  against 8.11 G on a mix with 20% exponent forms. Measured on an Apple M-series with `/usr/bin/time -l`.
- **yq: a float in scientific notation, and an ordinary one ending in 3, print without allocating** (#4923). `format_float_yq`'s scientific branch built `{f:e}`, a mantissa `String` for the tie-break correction and the final `mantissa e sign exp` `String`: three to four allocations per number, which #4917 had removed only for ordinary magnitudes. The streaming printer now formats the digits into a stack buffer, asks the tie-break question about them (`shortest_decimal_is_wrong_tie`, the decision `correct_shortest_decimal_tiebreak` already made, split out so it needs no `String`) and writes the `e+NN` spelling piece by piece; an ordinary float whose last digit is `3`, which still built two `String`s for the same question, uses it too. Output is byte-identical (JSON and YAML, 8 MB of mixed numbers) and `format_float_yq` stays the definition the tests compare against, including the exact decimal ties past the threshold. Interleaved A/B, release builds, 15 runs, `yq -p json -o json .` on an Apple M5 Max (instructions retired, median): 2 MB with 20% scientific numbers 0.950 G to 0.886 G (-6.7%), 8 MB 3.699 G to 3.440 G (-7.0%), 8.8 MB all scientific 5.169 G to 3.994 G (-22.7%; wall -17%), and 7.9 MB with none 3.330 G to 3.301 G (-0.8%, the ordinary floats ending in 3). Not measured on x86_64.
- **yq: printing a YAML document of many block records is linear, not quadratic** (#4939). The U+2028/U+2029 prefilter #4865 added to the streaming writer (`YamlString::may_hold_unicode_line_separator`) searched for its lead byte from each plain or single-quoted scalar to the end of the *document buffer*, so every such scalar printed cost O(document). It now scans only the scalar's own bytes. `sort_by(.id)` over a root array of two-field block records, interleaved A/B against the previous `main` binary on an Apple M5 Max (min of 3-5 runs, output byte-identical): 8,000 records 114.9 ms → 14.2 ms (−87.6%), 16,000 427.7 → 23.8 ms (−94.4%), 32,000 1,665 → 43.9 ms (−97.4%), 64,000 6,557 → 83.8 ms (−98.7%); the identity filter `.` over the same 64,000 records 6,419 → 35.5 ms (−99.4%). Time per doubling went from 4x to 2x. `.[0]` (no scalar is printed past the first) is unchanged (−4.3%, within noise).
- **jq: `reduce .[] as $r ({}; .[$r.name] = $r.score)` is linear again** (#5243). Since #5223 a path target whose index key was anything but a bare variable (`.[$r.name]`, `.[.k]`, `.[$i + 1]`) counted as dynamic and ran on the path-mode interpreter, which copied the accumulator on every step. Such a key only computes a value (jq runs it as a subexpression), so the target is static and runs on the streaming walkers again, as before #5223. Measured on a Ryzen 9 7950X (release builds, interleaved, output identical to jq 1.7.1): 0.357 s → 0.009 s at 5,000 records, 1.417 s → 0.016 s at 10,000, 5.665 s → 0.031 s at 20,000 (jq: 0.03 s). A key that can retry a `?//`, calls a function, uses a label or an input builtin, or holds a dynamic path target of its own still runs on the interpreter; one that reads a succinctly extension (`.a[line | tostring]`) is still refused. Like every other `reduce` on the shipped evaluator, the idiom is bounded again by the documented 100,000-step `reduce`/`foreach` budget (#2079), which the interpreter does not have.
- **jq: a `reduce` whose assignment target needs the path-mode interpreter no longer copies its accumulator on every step** (#5256). `reduce .[] as $r ({}; getpath([$r.name]) = $r.score)` (and `|=`, `+=`, a conditional target `(if c then .[$r.name] else empty end) = ...`) went through `assign_native`/`modify_native`, which wrote each path while the path evaluator still held the document, so every step copied the whole container (quadratic in the number of steps; jq writes in place). The writes now wait for the paths to finish (at most 4,096 paths are held back; a longer run writes as it goes, as before), after which the accumulator is held alone and is written in place. An error the paths raise after an earlier path is raised after that path's write, so a write's own error still comes first, as in jq 1.7.1; a target whose paths have an effect of their own (`input`, `debug`, a `label`) is written as it goes, as before. Measured on an Apple M5 Max (release builds, 3 runs each, ~80 ms process-spawn floor included, output identical to jq 1.7.1): `getpath([$r.name]) =` 0.270 s → 0.087 s at 5,000 records, 0.925 s → 0.084 s at 10,000, 3.61 s → 0.080 s at 20,000 (jq: 0.08 s); `|=` 0.251 s → 0.080 s, 0.895 s → 0.088 s, 3.45 s → 0.088 s; `+=` 0.257 s → 0.079 s, 0.941 s → 0.083 s, 3.59 s → 0.086 s. A `label` in the target, or a variable that binds the accumulator (`. as $acc | ...`), still copies it on every step, as jq's own do; a `def` in the program is a different route (#5263).
- **jq: `reduce .[] as $r ({}; .[$r.name] |= (. // 0) + 1)` and `reduce .[] as $r ([]; .[length] = $r.score)` are linear again** (#5263). A `reduce`/`foreach` assignment whose key, right side or update filter reads the accumulator (`(. // 0) + 1`, `if . == null then 1 else . + 1 end`, `length`, `.n`) declined the in-place write and copied the accumulator on every step, quadratic in the number of steps (jq writes in place). Such an operand, when it is a single-output expression with no effect, is now evaluated on the state before the write, so the fold hands the state to the write unshared. An operand that raises or yields nothing still takes the evaluator's route and text. Measured on an Apple M5 Max (release builds, interleaved, min of 3, ~80 ms process-spawn floor included, output identical to jq 1.7.1): the counting idiom `|= (. // 0) + 1` 0.88 s → 0.09 s at 5,000 records, 3.12 s → 0.08 s at 10,000, 12.75 s → 0.08 s at 20,000 (jq: 0.09 s); `.[length] = $r.score` 0.38 s → 0.08 s, 1.42 s → 0.09 s, 5.55 s → 0.08 s; `.[$r.name] = length` 1.25 s → 0.09 s, 4.87 s → 0.09 s, 19.9 s → 0.09 s (jq: 0.37 s at 20,000). The same holds when the key or filter calls a parameterless function of the program's own (`def f: ascii_downcase; reduce .[] as $r ({}; .[$r.name | f] = $r.score)`, `def inc: (. // 0) + 1; ... |= inc`) whose body is such an expression: 3.72 s → 0.14 s and 4.72 s → 0.08 s at 20,000 records (jq: 0.08 s). On the path-mode interpreter, which runs a program whose assignment target needs it, `length` and `type` of a string, array, object or `null` are now answered in place instead of re-serializing the whole state for the shipped evaluator, so a key such as `.[length]` no longer costs the size of the accumulator on every step. A recursive `def`, or one with parameters, still copies the accumulator on every step.
- **jq: `reduce .[] as $x ({}; .[$x.name] |= (. // []) + [$x.id])`, `reduce .[] as $x ({}; setpath([$x.id | tostring]; 1))` and `reduce .[] as $x ([]; . += [$x])` are linear** (#5271), when the accumulator is large and the array each step extends is small (many groups; a single group that itself grows to thousands of elements still copies that one array on every step, as it did). Each declined the in-place write of a fold step and copied the accumulator on every step, quadratic in the number of steps (jq: linear, or quadratic only for `. += [$x]`). An array literal in a state-reading operand (`[]`, `[$x.id, $x]`) is now one value like the rest, `setpath(P; V)` takes the in-place step with `P` and `V` evaluated before the write, and `. += X` (and `. |= . + X`) combines the moved state when both sides are arrays, objects or strings; any other pairing, and a `setpath` or operand that raises, still takes the evaluator's route and text. Measured on an Apple M5 Max (release builds, interleaved, min of 3, ~80 ms process-spawn floor included, output identical to jq 1.7.1): the grouping idiom 0.96 s → 0.08 s at 5,000 records, 3.69 s → 0.08 s at 10,000, 15.2 s → 0.08 s at 20,000 (jq: 0.09 s); `setpath([$r.name]; $r.score)` 0.73 s → 0.09 s, 2.73 s → 0.09 s, 10.9 s → 0.08 s (jq: 0.09 s); `. += [$r.score]` 0.42 s → 0.08 s, 1.43 s → 0.09 s, 5.56 s → 0.08 s (jq: 0.48 s at 20,000); `. += {($r.name): $r.score}` 0.76 s → 0.09 s, 2.75 s → 0.08 s, 11.0 s → 0.09 s (jq: 1.46 s).
- **jq: `reduce range(N) as $x ({}; .a |= (. // []) + [$x])`, `.a = .a + [$x]`, `.a = (.a // []) + [$x]` and `.a += {($x|tostring): 1}` extend the one growing value where it is** (#5273). Growing a single array or object in one field was quadratic in jq too, but ours had a 12x larger constant on the `|=`/`=` spellings: they evaluated the old value or the whole accumulator through the evaluator, then summed a clone of the old value, so nothing could extend in place. The step now answers those shapes itself and, for two arrays, objects or strings, takes the old value out of its slot for the `+` (`.a += R` and `.a |= . + R` too), at a path of any length (`.a.b += [$x]`), which makes the loop linear. Any other pairing, a right side that reads `.`, and a step that raises still take the evaluator's route and text. Measured on an Apple M5 Max (release builds, interleaved, min of 3, ~80 ms process-spawn floor included, output identical): `.a |= (. // []) + [$x]` 0.26 s → 0.09 s at 5,000 steps, 0.94 s → 0.09 s at 10,000, 3.75 s → 0.08 s at 20,000 (jq 1.7.1: 0.31 s at 20,000); `.a = .a + [$x]` 3.91 s → 0.08 s at 20,000; `.a = (.a // []) + [$x]` 3.81 s → 0.08 s; `.a += {($x|tostring): 1}` 0.42 s → 0.08 s, 1.58 s → 0.09 s, 5.96 s → 0.09 s (jq: 1.32 s at 20,000); `.g.l |= (. // []) + [$x]` 3.83 s → 0.09 s and `.g.l = .g.l + [$x]` 3.80 s → 0.08 s at 20,000; `.a += [$x]` 0.54 s → 0.08 s. The unrelated counting folds are unchanged (`.i += 1` over 1,000,000 steps 0.08 s → 0.08 s).
- **jq: a `reduce`/`foreach`/`until`/`while` that slices its state (`.[1:]`, `.[:-1]`) no longer writes the whole state out as JSON on every step** (#5274). A fold whose UPDATE is a slice with literal bounds took the evaluator's bridge each step, so peeling a 16,000-element array 3,000 times cost 2.4 s. The slice is now a cut of the owned value: an array the step owns outright is cut in place (a `memmove`), a shared one is cut into a new array, and a string is cut by codepoints; `null`, a number or an error stays the evaluator's, in jq mode only. Measured on an Apple M5 Max (release builds, min of 3, ~80 ms process-spawn floor included, output identical to jq 1.7.1): `reduce range(0; 3000) as $i (.nums; .[1:])` 0.41 s → 0.01 s on 4,000 elements and 2.36 s → 0.03 s on 16,000 (jq: 0.005 s); `.[:-1]` 2.40 s → 0.005 s; `until(length < 5000; .[1:])` over 16,000 elements 6.31 s → 0.06 s (jq: 0.008 s). The cut is still O(elements kept) where jq's slice is a view of the same buffer.
- **jq: a fold whose UPDATE is an `if`, a chain of `+`, or an append to a field no longer copies its state on every step** (#5279, #5273). Three fold shapes took the evaluator's bridge, or copied the array they extend, on every step: `reduce .[] as $x ([]; if $x.id % 3 == 0 then .[:-1] else . + [$x.id] end)` (an `if` whose condition is one value the step can settle, closed or reading the state, is a branch choice, and the chosen branch is a step of its own); `reduce .[] as $x (""; . + $x.name + ",")` (a left-associated chain `(. + a) + b` is applied link by link to the moved state); and `.l += [$x.id]`, `.l |= . + [$x.id]`, `.o += {k: v}` (the field is taken out of its slot, extended where it lies and put back, where it was copied because the state still held it). Any other pairing, a condition that raises, and a step that fails keep the evaluator's route and text. Measured on an Apple M5 Max (release builds, interleaved, min of 3, ~80 ms process-spawn floor included, output identical to jq 1.7.1): the `if` fold 0.24 s → 0.09 s at 5,000 records, 0.67 s → 0.08 s at 10,000, 2.57 s → 0.08 s at 20,000 (jq: 0.08 s); the string chain 0.20 s → 0.11 s, 0.52 s → 0.09 s, 1.98 s → 0.08 s (jq: 0.08 s); `.l += [$x.id]` 0.08 s → 0.08 s, 0.19 s → 0.08 s, 0.51 s → 0.08 s (jq: 0.40 s); `.o += {k: v}` 0.25 s → 0.09 s, 0.88 s → 0.09 s, 3.44 s → 0.09 s (jq: 1.48 s). A pipe of two assignments (`.l += [$x] | .n += 1`) still copies the field on every step.
- **jq: a fold whose UPDATE is a pipe of assignments no longer copies the field it extends on every step** (#5285). `reduce .[] as $x ({n: 0, l: []}; .l += [$x.id] | .n += 1)` ran its stages one after another on a clone of the state, so each step copied the array it extended. The stages are now applied to the moved state in turn, a later stage the in-place step declines (a padding or negative index, a failing `+`) runs on the evaluator against the state so far (it still costs time in the size of the state, 6x less than before: 14.2 s → 2.4 s at 20,000 steps, #5288), and the first stage to decline hands the untouched state back as before. Any other pipe, and a stage that could yield other than one value, keep the old route. Measured on an Apple M5 Max (release builds, interleaved, min of 5, ~20 ms process-spawn floor included, output identical to jq 1.7.1): the `reduce` above 0.22 s → 0.022 s at 5,000 records, 0.83 s → 0.028 s at 10,000, 3.15 s → 0.039 s at 20,000 (jq: 0.04 s at 5,000, 0.47 s at 20,000). A pipe whose later stage reads the state into an array operand (`.i += 1 | .a += [.i]`) is 2.4-2.5x faster (`until` at 20,000 steps, 5.38 s → 2.14 s) but still grows with the size of the state, because reading `.i` for the operand does (#5288).
- **jq: a fold step whose operand reads the state into scalars is linear** (#5288). `reduce range(N) as $k ({i:0,a:[]}; .a += [.i])` cost the size of the whole state on every step, so it was quadratic where jq is linear: the operand was evaluated on a copy of the state that was serialised and indexed again. The step now reads `.i`, `.a += [.i, .j]`'s fields, a comparison such as `.n > 3`, `not`/`type` of a field, and `+`, `-` or `*` of integers (up to 2^53, the range jq computes exactly) straight off the tree, for integers, booleans, `null` and strings. A float, a container read off the state, a division and a string concatenation take the earlier route, so their spelling and errors are unchanged. Measured on an Apple M5 Max and an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (release builds, interleaved, min of 5, output identical to jq 1.7.1): `.a += [.i]` at 10,000 / 20,000 / 40,000 steps 290 / 1,080 / 4,426 ms → 9 / 10 / 16 ms on the M5 Max and 395 / 1,564 / 6,193 ms → 5 / 9 / 16 ms on the 7950X (jq at 10,000: 120 ms); `.a += [.i + 1]` at 40,000 steps 8,055 ms → 22 ms and 11,250 ms → 21 ms; 2,000 steps beside an untouched 100,000-element field 3,394 ms → 7 ms and 3,775 ms → 7 ms; the closed-operand control `.a += [$k]` and the float row `.a += [.f + 1]` are unchanged.
- **jq: a string interpolation of plain navigation reads its `\(...)` slots at the cursor** (#5305). `.users[] | "\(.name) <\(.email)>"` ran at 0.8x jq on 100 MB while the equivalent `.name + " <" + .email + ">"` ran at 1.7x: the evaluator copied the whole ambient value into an owned one (serialised and indexed it again) to read a field of it, so every user record was rebuilt per output. An interpolation whose slots are all plain navigation (`.`, a field or index, `.[]`, `?`, parentheses and pipes of those) now reads them off the document node itself, in the streamed (`.users[] | "..."`), collected (`[.users[] | "..."]`, `map("...")`) and object-value (`{n: "..."}`) forms; any other slot (a call, `..`, `del(.x)`, a position read, `inputs`) keeps the earlier route unchanged. Measured on an Apple M4 Pro and an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (release builds, interleaved, min of 9, output identical, 2 / 10 / 100 MB `users`): `.users[] | "\(.name)"` 1.34 s → 0.42 s on 100 MB (M4 Pro) and 1.62 s → 0.48 s (7950X), `.users[] | "\(.name) <\(.email)>"` 1.65 s → 0.74 s and 1.94 s → 0.79 s, `[.users[] | "\(.name)"] | length` 1.32 s → 0.39 s and 1.57 s → 0.50 s, `.users | map("\(.name) <\(.email)>") | length` 1.59 s → 0.69 s and 1.79 s → 0.69 s; the five-slot `"\(.id): \(.name) \(.age) \(.active) \(.score)"` is 34% and 40% faster, and the ratio is flat from 2 MB to 100 MB. The concatenation and `.name` controls are unchanged on the M4 Pro (within 1.3%) and read +2-5% on the 7950X at instruction counts identical to within 650 of 791M (code layout).
- **jq: `group_by(f)` over an array keeps its groups as document nodes** (#5306). It went through the `eval.rs` bridge, which re-serialised and re-indexed the whole array, decoded every element into a `(key, element)` pair and then into groups: twice `sort_by`'s time and, with every element held decoded, more memory than jq (1,000 MB against jq's 668 MB on a 70 MB document). The keys are now read off the cursors, only the cursors are sorted and cut into groups, and a group stays on its cursors for what reads it: a printed result is written from the document, `length` counts the groups, `.[n]`, `first`, `last` and slices hand groups on undecoded, `.[]` yields them undecoded, and `map(f)` runs `f` over each group's cursors when it only reads some of them (`.[0].id`, `length`) and over the group decoded once otherwise. `map` runs to the end whatever follows it, as in jq: a failing, breaking or halting `f` stops where it does there, and a later `first` cannot skip it. yq mode, a non-array input and an alias-bearing document take the earlier route. Under `--preserve-input` the groups echo their source spelling, as `sort_by`'s elements do (a repeated key stays). Measured on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X and an Apple M4 Pro (release builds, interleaved, min of 9, output identical to the earlier build; the unchanged `sort_by(.age) | length` row stays within +1.6% on both). `.users | group_by(.id % 100)` printed in full, 1 / 10 / 70 MB: 23.7 / 245 / 2,625 ms → 11.5 / 108 / 1,144 ms (7950X) and 18.1 / 156 / 1,768 ms → 10.9 / 79 / 848 ms (M4 Pro); `| length` at 70 MB 2,278 → 989 ms and 1,375 → 732 ms; `| map({k: .[0].id, n: length})` at 70 MB 2,583 → 1,953 ms and 1,670 → 1,463 ms; `| map(.[0].id) | length` with one group per element 2,527 → 1,021 ms and 1,598 → 802 ms; `| map(.)`, which keeps every group, +3.0% on the 7950X and -14% on the M4 Pro. Peak RSS at 70 MB of the `map({k: .[0].id, n: length})` query 1,000 MB → 251 MB (7950X) and 970 MB → 251 MB (M4 Pro). A single group that holds every element is decoded whole by any stage that reads it (-4% to 0% time, 1,024 → 904 MB), and `INDEX(.id)` is unchanged.
- **perf(jq): `INDEX` no longer rebuilds a temporary document from its array** (#5306). `.users | INDEX(.id)` ran `.[]` over the array it already held as a value, which built a temporary document from the whole array and decoded every element out of it again; an array's elements are now taken directly, and a plain `.name` key is read in place from an object row. Interleaved A/B (base vs head, output identical, control run -0.7%/-0.2%): wall time on the `users` file at 100 MB falls by 34% on an M4 Pro (2.04 s to 1.33 s) and 43% on a 7950X (3.88 s to 2.22 s), 30-38% at 1 MB and 10 MB, and the `| length` form by 42% / 49%; peak RSS at 100 MB falls from 1.58 GB to 0.85 GB (M4 Pro, jq 0.85 GB) and from 1.72 GB to 0.97 GB (7950X, jq 0.76 GB). On the 7950X `INDEX` was 0.62x of jq and is now 1.09x. yq mode and a computed key expression take the previous path.
- **jq: `last(f)` holds one value at a time** (#5377). It collected every output of `f` before taking the final one, so `last(range(30000000) * 2)` was killed at 3 GB where jq stays at 2.5 MB (since #5292 lifted the `range` cap there is no limit to bound it). Unless `f` is navigation alone (`last(.[])`, `last(.a[] | select(.b))`, `last(..)`), `last(f)` now runs as the `reduce f as $x (null; $x)` jq defines it by, which streams its source: an empty `f` still answers `null`, and an error after the final value (`last(1, error("x"))`), a `break` or a `halt` is `reduce`'s own. A navigation keeps the collecting route, whose outputs are cursors into the document and not values to decode. Measured on an Apple M5 Max (release builds, min of one run): peak RSS of `last(range(3000000) * 2)` 399 MB → 102 MB (the 97 MB floor is the 70 MB document loaded beside it), `last(range(0;20000000;3))` 304 MB → 102 MB and `last(.users[] | {id})` over that document 355 MB → 97 MB; with no document, 312 MB → 15 MB and 217 MB → 14 MB. The price is `reduce`'s per-step cost: those take 0.19 s → 0.39 s, 0.14 s → 0.59 s and 0.37 s → 0.76 s, against jq 1.7.1's 0.54 s, 3.34 s and (for the first) more.
- **jq: `pick(f)` over a `recurse(g)` walk is no longer quadratic in the paths it picks** (#5390). `[pick(recurse(.[]? | .) | select(type == "number"))] | length` over 40,000 one-element arrays (80,001 nodes) took 16.5 s in a debug build, against 0.56 s for the same selection through `..`, and did not finish in 120 s at 524,289 arrays; it is now 1.5 s wall (0.32 s CPU) at 80,001 nodes, linear as `..` is. The path interpreter ran jq's own `reduce path(f) as $a (null; setpath($a; $in | getpath($a)))`, which copied the accumulated result once per pick; `pick` now folds in place, as `=` and `|=` do (#5256), except inside `path(...)` or an assignment's target, which keep jq's body.
- **jq / yq: a parenthesized pipe over computed values is linear in its stage count, not quadratic** (#5404).
  A pipe of `n` stages that runs over values the program computed (`[range(0;20000) | (. + 1 | . + 1 | ...)]`)
  rebuilt an owned `Expr::Pipe` of the rest of the pipe for every value at every stage, and each copy re-ran the
  analyses a pipe asks of itself. A pipe that a second value goes down now keeps the copy of each tail it hands on
  (pipes of up to 128 stages and tails of up to 1,024 nodes; a tail holding a `def` is kept in pieces in some pipes, #5421), and
  remembers the three syntactic facts the owned re-entry walked the whole rest for. This covers the route that
  collects a pipe's outputs (an array constructor, `add`-style consumers); a pipe driven one output at a time
  (`select`, `limit`, `first`, `reduce` over it) is covered by #5417, and a tail holding a user `def` call by #5421 in jq mode, when it holds a run of plain arithmetic stages. 20,000
  values on an Apple M5 Max, interleaved min of 3 CPU seconds, output identical: n=20 0.658 s -> 0.158 s, n=40
  1.714 s -> 0.268 s, n=80 5.444 s -> 0.451 s (the flat spelling at n=80 is 0.46 s); 200,000 values through a
  10-stage pipe 1.146 s -> 0.401 s (-65.0%), through a 3-stage pipe -19.1%, through 2 stages unchanged. A body
  rebuilt for each value (`. as $x | (...)`) is within +2.3%, and document-sourced pipes within noise. On an AMD
  Ryzen 9 7950X: n=20 0.641 s -> 0.153 s, n=40 2.206 s -> 0.306 s, n=80 8.338 s -> 0.606 s; the 10-stage pipe
  1.418 s -> 0.597 s (-57.9%), the 3-stage pipe -17.8%.
- **jq: `-C`/`--color-output` streams its output instead of building it twice** (#5415).
  `succinctly jq -C` used to materialize each result as an owned tree, render it into one
  whole `String` and color that into a second, and it left the M2 streaming route. It now
  renders through the printers uncolored output uses and colors the text a block at a time on
  its way out. `-C .` on an 84 MB document peaks at 296 MB instead of 2635 MB on an Apple M5 Max,
  the same as uncolored `.`, and its first output arrives after 0.67 s instead of 3.46 s
  (wall-clock 1.09 s instead of 3.53 s); `-C -c .` peaks at 200 MB instead of 1755 MB. Interleaved
  A/B on an 84 MB document, `-C .`: 3.31 s to 1.18 s on an Apple M4 Pro and 5.07 s to 1.35 s on an
  AMD Ryzen 9 7950X; `-C .[]` is 42% and 58% faster there. `-C -S` and `-C -a` still materialize
  each value, but color it in blocks: 595 MB instead of 2426 MB for `-C -S .` on the M5 Max, and
  within noise of the old time for `-C -S .[]` (+3% on the M4 Pro, -2% on the 7950X). Uncolored
  output is unchanged (every row within the control's range on both machines).
  The colored bytes are unchanged, as are the refusals: a document with an undecodable string
  or nesting past the limit in it, a NaN or `Infinity` word, or `--preserve-input` keeps the
  old render. One thing moves, on stderr only: a malformed `true`/`false`/`null` or number under
  `-C` now reports the message `-c` gives (`Invalid JSON text: invalid keyword 'tru' ...`) where
  it reported the materializer's (`invalid boolean`), still with exit 5 and empty stdout.
- **jq / yq: a parenthesized pipe driven one output at a time is linear in its stage count, not quadratic** (#5417).
  #5404 made the pipe an array constructor collects keep the owned copy of each tail it hands on; a pipe driven
  through the streaming drivers (`select`, `limit`, `first`, `last`, `nth`, `any`, `all`, `isempty`, a streamed
  result) built a fresh copy of its rest for every value of its first stage, at every stage, and a pipe with an
  effect before its last stage (`input_line_number`, `input`, ...) did the same through `eval_pipe`. Those drivers
  now ask the pipe that owns the rest, so the copies are the ones it already keeps (and they no longer walk the
  rest for path context at each stage). 20,000 values through a 40-stage pipe, interleaved min of 3 CPU
  seconds, output identical: `range(0;20000) | (T) | select(. == -1)` 1.96 s -> 0.35 s on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X
  (n=20 0.57 -> 0.16 s, n=80 7.36 -> 0.74 s), 1.26 s -> 0.27 s on an Apple M5 Max (n=80 4.56 -> 0.54 s);
  `last` and `[limit(...)]` match it; an effect before the last stage 2.08 s -> 0.36 s (7950X). The array
  constructor row #5404 fixed is unchanged (+2% on the 7950X, within noise on the M5 Max), and the native-stack
  recursion limit of `def f: if . >= N then . else (. + 1 | f) end; 0 | f` moves from 7144 to 7138 levels
  (-0.08%). A tail holding a `def` is handled by #5421 where it can be, and a body rebuilt for each value that reads
  its variable (`. as $x | ...`, the body of a `reduce`/`foreach`) still copies per value (#5424 links the bodies that
  do not).
- **jq: a parenthesized pipe holding a `def` call is linear in its stage count, not quadratic** (#5421).
  #5404 and #5417 keep the owned copy of each tail a pipe hands on, but refused a tail holding a `def` call (a node
  remembers what evaluation did to it, so a copy shared across values would carry that across them), so one call
  anywhere in a tail made every tail containing it copy its rest per value at every stage. A tail of at least 8
  stages holding a call is now handed on in pieces: each run of plain arithmetic, comparison or literal stages
  between its other stages is a copy the pipe keeps like any other tail, and every other stage (the call, a
  `select`, a fan-out, a navigation, a `?//` bind) is cloned afresh for the call, so the evaluator reads a pipe of
  the same stages and every route behaves as before. `succinctly yq` is unchanged and still copies such a tail per call, and so does a tail with no run of two such
  stages next to each other (`.a | f | .b | g | ...`).
  20,000 values, interleaved min of 5 CPU seconds, output identical, `[range(0;20000) | (. + 1 | ... | f)]` with
  a call at the end: n=8 0.125 s -> 0.065 s, n=14 0.375 s -> 0.117 s, n=20 0.658 s -> 0.171 s, n=40 (5,000
  values) 0.551 s -> 0.090 s on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X; n=8 0.095 s -> 0.045 s, n=14 0.221 s -> 0.080 s, n=20 0.400 s
  -> 0.114 s, n=40 0.340 s -> 0.060 s on an Apple M4 Pro. Shorter tails and the same pipe without parentheses
  are unchanged (n=6 and the flat spelling within 4%). The kept runs are held for the life of the program, up to
  1,024 nodes each in pipes of up to 128 stages, which a pipe with a call did not hold before; a pipe with more
  than one call every few stages gains little, and a body rebuilt for each value that reads its variable (`. as $x | (...)`, the
  body of a `reduce`/`foreach`) still copies its rest per value (#5424 links the bodies that do not).
- **jq: a `--no-default-features` build no longer keeps every `def` call's tree** (#5422).
  The #3148 retention scope is backed by a `thread_local!`, so a `no_std` build had none and kept the bound body
  of every call it evaluated for the node's lifetime: `def fib(n): if n < 2 then n else fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2) end; fib(24)`
  held 251 MB after one evaluation (`fib(21)`: 59 MB). A `no_std` build now declines to keep a body on a node's
  first reach and keeps it from the second, so the same program holds under 2 KB and peaks at 44 KB; a loop whose
  body calls `fib(18)` five times peaks at 37 KB where it peaked at 42 MB. A node reached twice pays one more bind
  than in a `std` build, and a hot body's own calls turn hot a reach at a time. The `std` build is unchanged.
- **jq / yq: a body rebuilt for each value that reads no variable (`. as $x | (...)`, the update of a `reduce`, the extract of a `foreach`, a destructuring bind) is linear in its stage count, not quadratic** (#5424).
  #5404 and #5421 keep the copy of each tail a pipe hands on, but a body that a substitution rebuilds for each value
  was a new pipe each time, so the tails kept for it were made once per value and used once: `n^2/2` stage copies
  and a table for a pipe that goes down once. A pipe that reads no variable is rebuilt stage for stage, so the one
  rebuilt for a value now reads the tails kept for the pipe it was rebuilt from (from the second value on; a
  substitution that happens once keeps nothing). A body that reads its variable differs from one value to the next
  and still copies its rest per value, as before, and a source pipe rebuilt twice now keeps its tails for the life of
  the program like any pipe that went down twice. 20,000 values, interleaved min of 5 CPU seconds, output identical,
  `[range(0;20000) | . as $x | (. + 1 | ... x n)] | length`: n=6 0.068 s -> 0.042 s, n=14 0.357 s -> 0.123 s, n=40
  2.205 s -> 0.384 s on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X; n=6 0.054 s -> 0.034 s, n=14 0.216 s -> 0.085 s, n=40 1.346 s ->
  0.261 s on an Apple M4 Pro. The `reduce` update (n=40 2.022 s -> 0.429 s, 1.243 s -> 0.329 s) and the `foreach`
  extract (2.019 s -> 0.434 s, 1.242 s -> 0.332 s) match it. The same pipe written without a binding (n=40 within
  1.3%), a body that reads its variable (within +2.9%), a program pipe holding a `reduce` or `as` stage, a 1,000-value
  fan-out per body and a NaN container compared by identity down a 9-stage tail are unchanged on both machines.
- **jq / yq: a body rebuilt for each value that reads its variable keeps the tails after its last reading stage, so the stages after it are linear in the pipe's length** (#5436).
  #5424 linked a pipe that a variable substitution rebuilds to the kept tails of the pipe it was rebuilt from, but only
  when the pipe reads no variable; a body that reads its variable (`. as $x | (. + $x | ...)`, a `reduce` or `foreach`
  update that mentions `$i`) still copied its rest per value per stage. A stage that reads no variable is the same in
  every rebuild, so a pipe that reads one now has a table of its own for the pipes rebuilt from it, whose runs end at a
  reading stage. A tail that starts at or before the last reading stage is copied for the value as before, and the copy
  reaches the same table at its offset, so the tails after the variable are kept however the copy was reached. The
  tails kept hold no variable, so a pipe hands them on as it does when it reads none (#5424, #5421), and a container
  keeps its storage identity (`[nan] as $a | ... | . == $a`). A variable read in the last
  stage leaves no tail to keep and is unchanged. 20,000 values, interleaved min of 7 CPU seconds, output identical:
  `[range(0;20000) | . as $x | (. + $x | . + 1 | ... x n)] | length` n=6 0.068 s -> 0.041 s, n=14 0.359 s -> 0.122 s,
  n=40 2.249 s -> 0.379 s on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (the same pipe reading no variable: 0.378 s); n=6 0.055 s -> 0.035 s,
  n=14 0.219 s -> 0.085 s, n=40 1.323 s -> 0.260 s on an Apple M4 Pro (reading none: 0.257 s). The `reduce` update
  (2.063 s -> 0.444 s, 1.246 s -> 0.333 s) and the `foreach` extract (2.090 s -> 0.449 s, 1.281 s -> 0.334 s) match it,
  and a variable read in the middle of a 40-stage pipe is 21% and 20% faster. A variable read in the last stage, in
  every stage, and a pipe that reads none are within 3% at n=14 and n=40 on both machines (the noise of the control).
- **jq: a body rebuilt for each value that reads its variable late is linear in its stage count, not quadratic** (#5441).
  #5436 keeps the tails of a rebuilt body that start after its last reading stage, so a body that reads its variable
  in its last stage (`. as $x | (. + 1 | ... | . + $x)`), second last or in the middle still copied its rest per
  value per stage. A tail of at least 8 stages that holds a reading stage is now handed on in pieces, as #5421 hands
  on one holding a `def` call: each run of plain arithmetic, comparison or literal stages between the reading stages
  is a copy the pipe keeps, and each reading stage is the rebuilt body's own. The same applies to a `reduce`/`foreach`
  update, a `|=` body, a destructuring bind and a `def f($a)` that reads `$a` late. `succinctly yq` is unchanged, and
  so is a body whose stages are not plain arithmetic (`.a`, `[.]`, a call): those still copy their tails per value.
  20,000 values, interleaved min of 9 CPU seconds, output identical, `[range(0;20000) | . as $x | (. + 1 | ... |
  . + $x)] | length`: n=14 0.372 s -> 0.120 s, n=40 2.373 s -> 0.394 s on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (the same pipe
  reading its variable first: 0.393 s); n=14 0.242 s -> 0.091 s, n=40 1.478 s -> 0.269 s on an Apple M4 Pro
  (first: 0.268 s). Read second last, in the middle, by a `reduce` / `foreach` / `|=` update, a destructuring bind,
  a `def f($a)` or over document input: 0.17x to 0.22x on the 7950X, 0.18x to 0.24x on the M4 Pro. A variable read
  in every stage, first, or not at all, n=6, and twelve record queries (`map`, `sort_by`, `group_by`, `select`,
  `to_entries`, `with_entries`, `reduce`, `paths`, `walk`, `tostring | fromjson`) are within 3% on both machines.
- **yq: the stages after a union share one rest pipe across the context list, so they are linear in the pipe's length** (#5462).
  `(., 1) | . + 1 | . + 1 | ...` ran the stages after the union once per entry of the context list, each entry with a
  rest pipe of its own over a slice nothing owned, so every entry copied the whole rest and every stage in it copied
  its rest again: quadratic in the stages after the union. One rest pipe now drives the list, and a list of several
  entries gets a pipe to own the stages, which keeps its tails once (#5404) and hands the same ones to every entry. A
  single entry runs the stages once and is unchanged. 100,000 values, interleaved min of 5 CPU seconds, output
  identical: `[range(100000)] | .[] | (., 1) | . + 1 | ... x n` n=3 0.295 s -> 0.225 s, n=8 1.120 s -> 0.614 s,
  n=20 5.967 s -> 1.661 s on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X; n=3 0.208 s -> 0.147 s, n=8 0.820 s -> 0.430 s, n=20 3.712 s ->
  1.313 s on an Apple M4 Pro. The same work with the multiplicity from `(1, 2) as $k | . | ...` (the control with the same
  output count) reads 1.689 s and 1.149 s at n=20 and is within 5% of the baseline at every n on both machines, and a
  one-stage pipe after the union (n=1) is within 2%.
- **jq: a pipe's tail copies inherit the "no" answers the pipe already holds** (#5488, first step).
  A body rebuilt for each value (`. as $x | (. + $x | . + $x | ...)`) copies the rest of its pipe once per stage, and each copy started with empty memo cells, so it re-walked its `O(rest)` stages for `needs_path_context`, `effect_before_last` and the `holds_*` questions: about 55% of a 2-second sample at 80 stages, beside the clones themselves.
  `tail_copy` and a kept copy now take every `false` the pipe has settled; a `true` is not inherited, since the stage that holds it may not be among the copy's.
  On an Apple M5 Max (release, instructions retired, `[range(0;20000) | . as $x | (<n stages>)] | length`) at n = 10 / 20 / 40 / 80: every stage reading `$x` -13% / -20% / -25% / -29%, `[.][0]` stages with the read last -17% / -25% / -31% / -34%, and the read-first controls within +1.2% to -0.9%.
  On an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (release, min of 5 wall-clock, the same rows): every stage -18% / -23% / -28% / -34% (7.22 s to 4.80 s at 80), read last -21% / -26% / -33% / -37%, the read-first `. + 1` control within +0.6% to -0.1%, and the read-first `[.][0]` control +2.1% / +1.4% / +2.2% / +2.8%.
  The cost is still quadratic in the number of stages, because the copies are; removing them is the next step of #5488.
- **jq: a body rebuilt for each value copies the rest of its pipe once, not once per stage** (#5488, second step).
  A copy of a pipe's tail now holds its stages in storage it can share, and each tail of that copy is a view of it (an offset into the same stages) instead of another copy, unless a stage of that tail holds a `def`, whose node remembers what evaluation did to it (#3148).
  A pipe of the program, or one a substitution rebuilt, still owns its stages, so a pipe that is never copied pays nothing for this.
  For one value down a pipe of `n` stages, the copies of its rest drop from `n - 1 + n - 2 + ...` stages to one copy of `n - 1` (two for `floor` stages), in jq and yq mode alike.
  Not yet covered: a rest entered through one of the owned evaluator's doors (a projection, `select`, a path) and a stage that yields several values ahead of the rest are still copied at every stage, as before.
  On an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (release, min of 7 interleaved wall-clock runs, `[range(0;20000) | . as $x | (<n stages>)] | add`) at n = 10 / 20 / 40 / 80: every stage reading `$x` -19% / -42% / -62% / -78% (4.81 s to 1.07 s at 80, now linear), `[.][0]` stages with the read last -25% / -45% / -60% / -71%, `floor` stages with the read last -9% / -22% / -33% / -42%.
  Those two read-last rows are still superlinear, which the #5488 prototype's profile attributes to a re-entry re-walking the rest of the pipe at each stage (`reentry_can_observe`), the next step of #5488.
  The read-first controls move +1% to +3% (`. + 1` stages) and +1% to +7% (`[.][0]` stages) in wall-clock at instruction counts within +1.4% to -1.1% of the base, which reads as code layout on that machine (not confirmed with a padding holdout). On an Apple M4 Pro (same method, min of 7) the same rows read -24% / -44% / -61% / -76% (every stage), -27% / -45% / -59% / -70% (`[.][0]`, read last) and -14% / -22% / -28% / -33% (`floor`, read last), with the read-first controls within ±2%, so the +1% to +7% above did not reproduce on ARM64.
  **Breaking for library callers** that edit `Expr::Pipe`'s stages: `PipeStages` now derefs to `[Expr]` rather than `Vec<Expr>`, so `push`, `insert`, `extend` and `retain` go through `make_mut()`, which returns the `Vec` (and forgets what the pipe remembered, as `DerefMut` does), and `as_slice()` is an inherent method.
- **jq: a body that reads its variable late, behind stages that are not arithmetic, is linear in its stage count** (#5488, third step).
  `. as $x | (<n - 1 stages of [.][0], floor or fabs> | . + $x)` copied nothing more than once per value after the second step, but each of the `n` tails of its pipe asked whether it holds a marker, which re-walked the stages to the last one, and each re-entry walked them again for the marker a rewrite would change: 43% of a profile at 80 stages, `n` walks of up to `n` stages per value.
  What is true of a shared storage (the position of the last marker, of the last node that can start a resolver invocation, and the markers themselves) is now worked out once and every view of it answers from that, found from the end of the storage, so a body whose last stage reads the variable answers at once.
  A pipe that holds the node in its first 8 stages pays what it did.
  At n = 10, 20, 40, 80 on an Apple M4 Pro, `[.][0]` stages read last take 0.088, 0.194, 0.454, 1.141 s and now 0.090, 0.190, 0.377, 0.778 s (2.0x per doubling, was 2.6x), `floor` 1.080 s and now 0.526 s at 80, `fabs` 1.231 s and 0.708 s, and a read in the middle of the pipe 0.805 s and 0.734 s; on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X `[.][0]` 1.763 s and 1.149 s at 80, `floor` 1.251 s and 0.755 s, `fabs` 1.519 s and 1.026 s, mid-pipe 1.171 s and 1.045 s (interleaved min of 5, output identical to jq 1.7.1).
  The read-first and `. + 1`-then-read controls, and ten shapes that do not read late (reduce, foreach, `.[] |=`, destructuring, `def f($a)`, a plain pipe, a late `def`) and eight queries over a 7 MB document, are within 0.99x-1.02x on both; the every-stage shape is within 0.99x-1.01x on the M4 Pro and 1.01x-1.03x on the 7950X, whose retired instructions are +0.5% (`[.][0]` read last: -14.3%).
- **jq: `--stream-errors` reads a string or number token without the document parser's index** (#5498, first slice).
  The `jv_parse.c` port built a `JsonIndex` for every scalar token it handed out; a string with no escape and
  valid UTF-8 is now its own bytes, and a number is read by `OwnedValue::from_number_bytes`, which keeps the
  literal's spelling. `-n 'reduce (inputs|select(length==2)) as $e (0;.+1)'` over a generated `users` document,
  interleaved A/B on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, best of 7: 10 MB (6.9 MB) 0.47 s -> 0.32 s, 50 MB (35 MB)
  2.40 s -> 1.65 s, output byte-identical on those documents; the index route (`--stream`) is the control and unchanged at 0.37 s
  and 1.68 s. Peak memory is unchanged (216 MB at 10 MB): `--stream` still holds the event list, which later
  slices of #5498 remove. Not measured on ARM.
- **jq: `--stream` and `--stream-errors` under `-n` hand `input`/`inputs` their events as the program asks, not from a list built first** (#5498).
  `--stream -n 'reduce (inputs|select(length==2)) as $e (0;.+1)'` over a generated `users` document held every event before the program ran: 207 MB for 6.9 MB of input, 1.96 GB for 69 MB (jq 2.4 MB).
  The `jv_parse.c` port (`jq_stream_errors.rs`) is now a pull-based reader that feeds jq's streaming parser one `fgets` refill at a time, and the `input` queue pulls from it through the producer seam (#5842), so the program holds the input's bytes and the parser's state: 17 MB and 78 MB at those sizes on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, 13 MB and 74 MB on an Apple M4 Pro.
  `--stream` also stops being slower than jq there: interleaved min of 11 against the merge-base, 0 output differences, on the 7950X the `reduce` is 47% faster at 6.9 MB and 41% faster at 69 MB, and `first(inputs)` takes 4.4 ms and 29.5 ms (was 233 ms and 2.39 s); on the M4 Pro the `reduce` is 13% and 14% faster and `first(inputs)` takes 3.2 ms and 8.7 ms (was 114 ms and 1.11 s).
  `--stream-errors` reads the same way: 40% faster `reduce` and 98% faster `first(inputs)` on the 7950X, 8-9% and 97-99% on the M4 Pro.
  The other `--stream` routes (a program that reads `.`, `-s`, no `-n`) are unchanged here; slices 4 and 5 moved them.
- **jq: a `--stream` walk that reads `.` holds no document and no event list, and answers as jq's streaming parser does** (#5498, slice 4).
  A program without `-n` or `-s` walked the events of a document that had been built whole first, so a
  70 MB `users` document peaked at 664 MB on an Apple M4 Pro (785 MB on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X), against jq's 2 MB.
  It now reads through the stream reader of the `-n` route (#5894), which the driver loop pops one event at a time:
  72 MB and 76 MB, the input's bytes and the parser's state. `select(length==2)|empty` takes 1.50 s (was 1.95 s) on the
  M4 Pro and 1.87 s (was 2.63 s) on the 7950X over that document, `length` 1.15 s (1.60 s) and 1.44 s (2.18 s), printing every
  event `.` 1.66 s (2.10 s) and 1.96 s (2.66 s), and `if length==2 then .[1] else empty end` the least, 4.17 s (4.67 s) and 5.61 s
  (6.38 s); interleaved min of 3 (7 on a 7 MB document, 0.66x to 0.89x there too), output identical.
  What the plain walk now does as jq does: a document nested past 256 levels is read (257 and 1000 levels give jq's 257 and
  1,000 events), each event carries the line jq had read when it yielded it, a repeated key is emitted every time, and a
  fault prints jq's own `jq: parse error: <message>` with no location after the events before it, at exit 5, where it
  read `Invalid JSON text` at `(at <file>:<line>)`. A 1,980-row differential run (22 streams, 15 programs, 3 flag sets, a file and stdin) answers
  exactly as jq 1.7.1 on stdout, stderr and status, where 1,272 rows did before, and 1,264 of those rows are pinned. `--seq` and `--stream-errors`
  without `-n` keep their routes and their differences (`-s` followed in slice 5).
- **jq: `--stream` reads a file or stdin a chunk at a time, so it holds neither the input nor the events** (#5498, slice 6).
  The stream reader took the whole file (or stdin) first and read its events out of that buffer, so a plain `--stream` walk and `--stream -n` with `inputs` still peaked at the size of the input (110 MB on a 107 MB document) where jq's 4 KB reads peak at 2 MB.
  It now makes jq's refills (a line, or 4095 bytes) from a buffered reader per file and from stdin, with the same refills as before: an empty file, a BOM at the front of the first file that has bytes, and a token that continues in the next file read as they did.
  `--validate`, `-s` and `--stream-errors` without `-n` keep the whole read.
  Equivalence is pinned by a test that reads 19 streams through both sources, cut into reads of 1 to 100,000 bytes and buffers of 1 to 8,192, and by `tests/jq_cli/i5498_chunked.rs` over a 170 KB line, multi-byte characters across chunks, lines of exactly 4095 and 4096 bytes, a BOM and 20,000 short lines, over a file and over stdin.
- **jq: `$var.field` in a `reduce`/`foreach` update no longer rebuilds the whole object** (#5499). Each loop element was converted to a literal tree, converted back to a value, and only then asked for one field. The field is now spliced in directly when the object holds it. Interleaved A/B on `users` documents of 2, 10 and 70 MB, identical output: `reduce .users[] as $u (0; .+$u.score)` -34% on an M4 Pro and on a 7950X (70 MB: 1.22 s to 0.80 s and 1.39 s to 0.90 s; jq 1.7.1 was 0.74 s on an M5 Max, where this was 0.58x and is now 0.97x), `reduce .users[] as $u ({}; .[$u.name] = $u.score)` -43% to -47%, and a `foreach` update -32% to -35%. A lookup of a field the object lacks is about 1% slower. jq mode only; a longer pipe, an absent field, a non-object, EXTRACT and path-position reads keep their old route and error text.
- **yq: an error that ends a collected walk no longer converts the outputs delivered before it** (#5505). A yq document answers all or nothing, so nothing reads them, but a walk such as `recurse(.[]?; cond)` whose `cond` raises late (`--jq-extensions`) turned each node it had delivered into an owned copy of its whole subtree to carry as a partial prefix. Over 60,000 integers nested 120 levels deep, `[recurse(.[]?; if . == 59999 then error("x") else true end) | 1] | length` takes 63 ms in 15 MB instead of 578 ms in 136 MB on an Apple M4 Pro (9.2x; 40 levels 4.4x, 80 levels 7.1x) and 80 ms in 19 MB instead of 842 ms in 140 MB on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (10.5x; 4.9x and 8.0x), and 240,000 integers 9.2x and 10.7x, the cost no longer growing with the depth. The same walk that does not raise is unchanged (30.6 ms and 38.7 ms), and so is every answer, including those of `first`, `limit`, `isempty`, `any` and `all` over a walk that raises after their last output and of a `try` or `?` that reads the outputs before the raise. A `break` or `halt` keeps the prefix, and so does jq mode (`jq` prints what came before an error), which the walk reaches by another route.
- **jq: a `reduce`/`foreach` whose update reads its loop variable only as `$u.field` converts just those members of each element** (#5519). Each element was converted whole (every member hashed into a map and allocated) for a body that read one of them; the element is now an object holding only the fields the update and extract read (at most 8; more converts it whole), found in one checked pass over its members. Interleaved A/B on `users` documents of 1.4, 7 and 51 MB, identical output, against the tip of `main`: `reduce .users[] as $u (0; .+$u.score)` -28% to -36% on an M4 Pro and a 7950X (51 MB: 570 ms to 363 ms and 650 ms to 439 ms), a loop variable nothing reads (`.+1`) -61% to -74%, `reduce ... .[$u.name] = $u.score` -18% to -23%, a `foreach` update -29% to -36%, `. + ($u.score | floor)` -22% to -31%. On 20-member records, reading 1, 5 and 8 fields is -44%, -33% and -26% on the 7950X and -49%, -30% and -21% on the M4 Pro. A fold that reads `$u` whole (`[$u]`, `$u | length`), one naming more than 8 fields, a scalar source and a non-fold query are within about 2% of a same-binary control, apart from one row on the M4 Pro that runs no new code. jq mode over JSON only. **A member the fold does not read is no longer decoded**, so an undecodable one (`[{"a":"\ud800","b":5}]`) that jq refuses at parse time no longer fails `reduce .[] as $u (0; .+$u.b)`; `.[] as $x | $x.b` and `.[] | .b` already answered the same. For a fold that reads a member, the object's own frame (keys, delimiters, tail) is still checked, so a malformed element fails the fold as before; a loop variable nothing reads checks nothing, as `.[] as $x | 1` does. Recorded in `docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`.
- **jq: the regex builtins compile a pattern once, not once per input value** (#5531). `test`, `match`, `capture`, `sub`, `gsub`, `scan`, `split` and `splits` built their regex again for every value, and `regex::Regex::new` dominated a short-string match. A pattern seen a second time now has its compiled form kept, per thread, for the last 16 `(mode, pattern, flags)` (errors too, so a refused pattern is not translated and compiled again per input; `fancy-regex` patterns too; a pattern over 1 KiB is never kept). Over a 20,000-element array of short strings (user time, interleaved A/B, output identical): `test("[a-z]+[0-9]{2,}x?")` 860 ms to 7 ms on a Ryzen 9 7950X and 762 ms to 9 ms on an Apple M5 Max; a literal `test("item5")` 38 ms to 7 ms and 40 ms to 9 ms; `sub("[0-9]+";"#")` 414 ms to 13 ms and 380 ms to 14 ms. A pattern that is different for every input (7,919 distinct) costs 1.02x on both: it is only kept on its second sighting, because keeping every one cost 6% on the 7950X.
- **jq: a `reduce`/`foreach` that destructures its loop variable with literal object keys converts only the members the pattern names** (#5544, item 1 of #5519's follow-ups). `reduce .users[] as {score: $s} (0; . + $s)` converted each element whole (every member hashed into a map and allocated) before the pattern picked one; an object pattern whose keys are all literal (`{score: $s}`, `{$score}`, `{id: $i, name: $n}`) now takes the same projection as `$u.field` (#5519): the element becomes an object holding only the named members (at most 8; more converts it whole). Interleaved A/B on `users` documents of 1.4, 7 and 51 MB, identical output, against the tip of `main`: `reduce .users[] as {score: $s} (0; . + $s)` -30% to -32% on a 7950X and -31% to -34% on an M4 Pro, a two-key pattern -20% / -21%, the `{$score}` shorthand -31%, a `foreach` -27% to -34%; the M5 Max reads -19% to -34% across the same rows. A pattern naming a computed key, an array pattern, a `?//` alternative, one naming more than 8 keys, a whole-element loop variable (`$u`) and a non-fold query are within about 1% of a same-binary control. jq mode over JSON only. **A member the pattern does not name is no longer decoded**, so an undecodable one (`[{"a":"\ud800","b":5}]`) that jq refuses at parse time no longer fails `reduce .[] as {b: $b} (0; . + $b)`, as with #5519. A malformed element still fails the fold. Recorded in `docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`.
- **jq: a `reduce`/`foreach` loop variable read through a parenthesis (`($u).score`, `(($u)).score`, `($u)["score"]`) converts only the members it reads** (#5544, item 1B). The test for "reads `$u` only as the head of a field chain" looked for a bare `$u` followed by `.k`, so a parenthesis around the variable counted as a read of the whole element and each element was converted whole. A parenthesis only groups, so it is now seen through there; one around the field stage (`$u | (.b)`) projects the same way (#5957). `reduce .users[] as $u (0; .+($u).score)` over a 35 MB document takes 344 ms instead of 442 ms on an Apple M5 Max (interleaved min of 7, output identical; `$u.score`, which already projected, is 256 ms either way, so the parenthesised spelling still pays for what it does to the arithmetic around it), and on a document with a member that does not decode and that nothing reads (`[{"a":"\ud800","b":5}]`) it answers `5` as `$u.b` does, where it raised. A bare `$u`, `[$u]`, `($u | length)` and a read of the member itself still decode. x86_64 and ARM64 chips other than the M5 Max were not measured.
- **jq: `tojson`/`tostring` write their text in one pass, and a `del` of a static path no longer round-trips through JSON** (#5549).
  `tojson`, `tostring`, string interpolation and `@json` built a `String` per node and joined them, so every level of nesting copied everything below it again;
  they now append to one buffer, and `.users | map(tostring)` over a 7 MB document is 21% faster on a 7950X and 31% on an M4 Pro.
  A `del(.users[0])` (a path of field names and literal indices) used to write the whole document out as JSON and index it again to hand the builtin a cursor;
  it now deletes from the document it already holds (a program that binds a variable to a node of the document, `. as $x | ...`, keeps the old route).
  `del(.users[0]) | .users | length` over 7 / 73 MB went from 93 / 922 ms to 75 / 738 ms on an Apple M4 Pro (jq 1.7.1: 70 / 746 ms) and from 153 / 1555 ms to 123 / 1253 ms on a 7950X;
  `tojson | fromjson | .users | length` from 259 / 2608 ms to 208 / 2085 ms (M4 Pro; jq 1.7.1: 195 / 1986 ms) and from 352 / 3807 ms to 308 / 3159 ms (7950X).
  Release builds, interleaved, min of 11, output identical on all 27 configurations; the rows this change cannot reach read within the control run's noise (`.users | length` and a `select` over the records).
  What is left of the gap to jq on `.users[0].name = "x" | .users | length` (about 1.10x on an M4 Pro) is the cost of building the owned document, the same for every query that has to.
- **macOS: `sjq`/`syq`/`succinctly` start about 0.8 ms faster and use about 4.5 MB less memory** (#5551).
  The `cli` feature no longer pulls in `ctrlc`, which on Apple targets brought `objc2` and linked
  Foundation, CoreFoundation and `libobjc` into every process. `succinctly jq -n 1` now starts in 2.36 ms
  instead of 3.18 ms and peaks at 4.8 MB instead of 9.4 MB on an Apple M4 Pro, level with jq 1.7.1's
  2.36 ms. `dev bench {jq,yq,dsv,utf8}` still catch Ctrl+C to write the results gathered so far: on Unix
  through a plain `SIGINT` handler over the `libc` the CLI already uses; a Windows build without
  `bench-runner` has no handler, and Ctrl+C ends the run at once.
- **jq: a global `l` regex search is linear in the matches, not quadratic** (#5563). An `l` search returns the longest match anywhere at or after its start, so it reads the rest of the text, and `match`, `scan`, `sub`, `gsub` and `splits` with `g` ran one per match. One forward pass over the starts now serves every search of the same text (the longest match among the starts from there on, the earliest of equals), and a pattern with `\G`, which ties a match to where its search began, keeps the search per match. `[match("a|ab+";"gl")] | length` on `"ab "` repeated 5,000, 10,000 and 20,000 times (release builds, interleaved, min of 3, output identical to jq's) went from 0.97 s, 3.79 s and 15.3 s to 7 ms, 9 ms and 14 ms on an Apple M5 Max; jq 1.7.1 takes 0.21 s, 0.93 s and 3.5 s. The pass keeps a 24-byte entry per start that matches, for the length of one call.
- **jq: `floor`, `ceil`, `round`, `trunc`, `sqrt` and `fabs` of a document number no longer write it out and index it again** (#5593).
  Each was a text round trip and an index build per number to make one libm call. They now read the number's double the way the
  evaluator does and answer from it; a string, a computed double, a non-finite literal and yq mode keep the old route, so errors
  and every answer are unchanged. `[.numbers[]|floor]|add` over a generated `numbers` document is 1.56x-1.83x faster than before
  (0.85x-0.90x of jq 1.7.1 before, 1.45x-1.61x after; 1/10/100 MB, interleaved min, Apple M5 Max), `[.numbers[]|floor]|length`
  2.0x-2.6x faster, and `.numbers|map(ceil)|length` 1.9x-2.3x faster. A step after the builtin (`floor|.+1`) is still 0.87x-0.89x of jq.
- **jq: a materialized document builds and prints with fewer allocations** (#5594).
  In jq mode, an object in an array now makes room up front for the member count the two objects before it agreed on, instead of growing its map from empty, until a guess overshoots.
  `tojson` and the other JSON writers append a parsed number literal (and a NaN) to the output instead of building a `String` for it; a computed float still formats through one.
  A JSON string is scanned once for its end and its escapes.
  On the `users` pattern at 7.1 MB (Apple M5 Max, instructions retired, output identical), `del(.users[0]) | .users | length` is -8.7% instructions and -5.8% peak RSS, `.users[0].name = "x" | .users | length` -8.9% and -5.6%, and `tojson | length` -10.9% (-15.6% on a float-heavy 8 MB document).
  An array that alternates wide and narrow records is unchanged, and yq mode keeps growing its maps from empty.
  The object map keeps its per-process-seeded SipHash: an unseeded Fx hash would have saved at most 2.6%.
- **jq: `add` over an array no longer converts it twice and indexes it again** (#5595).
  `add` had no native arm, so the generic fallback converted the whole array, wrote it out as JSON, indexed that, and had `builtin_add` convert every element a second time from the new cursor;
  62% of `.numbers | add` over a 0.9 MB document was that detour.
  The array's elements are now converted once from the document's own cursor and folded with the same addition, in jq mode and while no variable is bound to a node of the document (an object, a scalar and `succinctly yq` keep the old route).
  `.numbers | add` over a 10 / 105 MB document of numbers went from 244 / 2429 ms to 87 / 846 ms on a 7950X and from 196 / 1863 ms to 79 / 727 ms on an Apple M4 Pro (jq 1.7.1 built from source: 181 / 1719 ms on the M4 Pro, where `succinctly jq` was 10% behind it before and is 2.3x ahead now);
  `.strings | add` over 9 MB went from 96 to 43 ms (7950X) and from 51 to 28 ms (M4 Pro).
  Release builds, interleaved, min of 11, output identical on all 16 configurations on each machine; `.numbers | max`, `.numbers | length` and `[.numbers[] | floor] | add` read within the control run's noise.
  An undecodable element is still reported ahead of an addition that fails earlier in the array, as before.
- **jq: the stage after a computed number no longer writes the number out and indexes it again** (#5601, #5593 follow-up).
  `[.numbers[]|.+1|.*2]` wrote each `.+1` result out as JSON and indexed it to run `.*2`. A computed `Int` or `Float` (not a NaN, not a
  document's literal) now meets an arithmetic stage, `type`, a comparison, `and`/`or`/`not` and `tostring` directly, and `floor`, `ceil`,
  `round`, `trunc`, `sqrt` and `fabs` of any owned number, including the `$x|floor` a `reduce` or `foreach` binds, are one libm call.
  Over a generated `numbers` document (Apple M5 Max, interleaved min, 1 and 10 MB, jq 1.7.1): `[.numbers[]|.+1|.*2]` 0.55x -> 1.08x of jq,
  `.*2|floor` 0.55x -> 1.13x, `.+1|type` 0.65x -> 1.07x, `.+1|floor|.+1|floor` 0.41x -> 1.11x, `floor|.+1` 0.90x -> 1.80x, and
  `reduce .numbers[] as $x (0; .+($x|floor))` 0.63x -> 0.87x. A `select`, `if`, `[...]` or `as` after a computed number still bridges.
- **jq: `select`, `if` and `tojson` after a computed number no longer write the number out and index it again** (#5602, #5601 follow-up).
  `[.numbers[]|.+1|select(.>10)]` wrote each `.+1` result out as JSON and indexed it to run the `select`. For a computed `Int` or `Float`
  (not a NaN, not a document's literal) the condition is now settled from the number, as `owned_select_door` does on the sink route, `if`
  takes its branch from the same verdict, `else empty` yields nothing, and `tojson` is the number's `tostring`. A condition outside the
  pure grammar (a generator, a path) bridges as before. Over a generated `numbers` document (Apple M5 Max, interleaved min, 1 and 10 MB,
  jq 1.7.1, against a build with #5601): `.+1|select(.>10)` 0.61x -> 1.39x of jq, `.+1|if .>10 then 1 else 0 end` 0.58x -> 1.27x,
  `.*2|select(.>10 and .<500000)|.+1` 0.64x -> 1.55x, `floor|select(.>10)` 0.91x -> 2.56x and `.+1|tojson` 0.72x -> 1.18x.
  An array constructor or an `as` binding after a computed number still bridges.
- **jq: an array constructor, an object construction and an `as` binding after a computed number no longer write the number out and index it again** (#5606, #5602 follow-up).
  `[.numbers[]|.+1|[.]]` wrote each `.+1` result out as JSON and indexed it to build `[.]`. For a computed `Int` or `Float` (not a NaN, not a document's literal)
  `[e]` is now the one-element array of `e`'s answer, `{k: e}` the object of its entries' answers, and `. as $x | body` binds `$x` to the number as the evaluator's own bind does and
  answers the body from the number, for the element, entry values and body the owned routes answer (the operators, `$x`, `.`, literals, constructors, nested `as`). Anything else
  (a generator element, a computed key, a destructuring bind, a body that calls a function) bridges as before. Over a generated `numbers` document (Apple M5 Max, interleaved
  min, 10 MB, jq 1.7.1, against a build with #5602): `.+1|[.]` 0.67x -> 1.18x of jq, `.+1|. as $x|$x` 0.50x -> 1.03x, `floor|. as $x|$x*2` 0.61x -> 1.40x,
  `.+1|{a:.}` 0.60x -> 1.13x and `.+1|[.+1]` 0.61x -> 1.17x; instructions retired fall to 0.43-0.56 of the base build, and the same rows on an Apple M4 Pro read 0.66x -> 1.20x, 0.53x -> 1.11x, 0.73x -> 1.46x, 0.65x -> 1.19x and 0.64x -> 1.29x.
- **jq: `--stream` input is validated without building a discarded tree and without walking each document twice** (#5608).
  The strict pass deserialized every value of the input into a `serde_json::Value` it then threw away, and each accepted span was then converted through a check that walked its delimiters again, though `serde_json` had just accepted that very span.
  The pass now deserializes into `IgnoredAny` and skips the second walk for a span `serde_json` accepted; the splitter's fallback spans, which it has not seen, keep the walk.
  `IgnoredAny` also takes a number outside `f64` (`1e999`) and a lone trailing surrogate escape, which the tree had refused and sent to that fallback, and it has no recursion limit, so the nesting ceiling is now the materializer's own check; the values and the errors are the same (a document past 256 levels is still a clean error).
  `--stream -n '[inputs] | length'` over 0.7 / 7 / 74 MB of records went from 24.0 / 209 / 2111 ms to 19.4 / 166 / 1648 ms on an Apple M4 Pro and from 43.1 / 443 / 4488 ms to 36.7 / 389 / 3734 ms on a 7950X, `--stream -c .` by 6.7% to 8.6% (M4 Pro) and 10.3% to 14.8% (7950X), and peak memory of `--stream -n '[inputs] | length'` over 7 MB fell 19% (332 to 271 MB, Apple M5 Max).
  Release builds, interleaved, min of 11, output identical on every configuration; `--slurp` and the rows this cannot reach read within the control run's noise.
  On the M4 Pro `--stream` is now at about 0.8x of jq 1.7.1's speed (`reduce (inputs | select(length == 2)) as $e (0; . + 1)`: 27.9 / 250 / 2481 ms against jq's 22.3 / 197 / 1909 ms), up from 0.7x; what remains is converting each document to an owned value and one owned array per event.
- **jq: `--stream` takes each document apart into its events instead of copying it** (#5611).
  When the program reads the events with `inputs`, `-n` or `--slurp`, each input document is turned into its `[path, leaf]` events and then dropped, but the events were built by a borrowed walk that cloned every leaf and cloned every key of a leaf's path again for each event beneath it.
  The walk now moves a leaf and its own key into its event and shares a container's key once, so the events under it clone a reference count; the events and their order are unchanged.
  `--stream -n '[inputs] | length'` over 0.7 / 7 / 74 MB of records went from 20.5 / 171.5 / 1748 ms to 17.5 / 145.0 / 1442 ms on an Apple M4 Pro and from 36.9 / 402 / 3842 ms to 30.0 / 352 / 2818 ms on a 7950X, `--stream -s 'length'` by 11% to 14% (M4 Pro) and 20% to 23% (7950X), and the `reduce (inputs | select(length == 2)) as $e (0; . + 1)` form by 10% to 12% (M4 Pro) and 8% to 20% (7950X); retired instructions over 7 MB fell 20% (4.03G to 3.22G, Apple M5 Max).
  Release builds, interleaved, min of 11, output identical on every configuration. A plain `--stream .`, which prints each event and does not hold them, is unchanged (printing dominates it), and so are the rows this cannot reach (`.users | length` retires the same 281.7M instructions on a 7950X; its wall-clock read 5% slower at 7 and 74 MB there with the instruction count flat, which is code placement).
- **jq: `--stream` builds the events it keeps from the document's index instead of from a converted value** (#5618).
  When the program reads the events with `inputs`, `-n` or `--slurp`, each input document was converted to a value and then taken apart into its `[path, leaf]` events; the events are now walked from the document's index, so only the leaves are converted and the document is never built or dropped.
  The events and their order are unchanged, and a document with a repeated key (compared after decoding) still goes through the converted value, which keeps the key's first position and last value as before.
  On a 7950X, `--stream -n '[inputs] | length'` over 0.7 / 7 / 74 MB of records went from 29.7 / 355.6 / 2822 ms to 26.1 / 278.1 / 2494 ms, the `reduce (inputs | select(length == 2)) as $e (0; . + 1)` form by 8% / 16% / 10% and `--stream -s 'length'` by 6% to 10%; retired instructions over 7 MB fell 17.6% (3.30G to 2.72G).
  Release builds, interleaved, min of 11, output identical on every configuration, against a control run within 1.5%. A plain `--stream .`, which walks each converted document one event at a time, is not changed (its instructions are equal to within 0.001%; its wall-clock read up to 2.5% slower, which is code placement), and neither are queries without `--stream`.
- **jq: the filter `.` over a `--stream` event, a `--seq` record or a DSV row no longer writes the value out, indexes the text and converts it back** (#5624).
  An input that is already a value (anything but a document read from a file) was evaluated by writing it as JSON, indexing that text and running the filter against the new cursor, so even `.` paid it: about 9,000 instructions for a 35-byte `--stream` event.
  A program that is `.`, `(.)` or a pipe of them now prints the value as it is, under every output option (`-S`, `--tab`, `--indent`, `-a`, `-r`, `-j`, `-C`, `-e`); `--preserve-input` keeps the old route.
  `--stream -c .` retires 62% fewer instructions over 7 MB of records (15.3G to 5.8G, Apple M5 Max; jq 1.7.1 retires 10.8G) and `--input-dsv , -c .` 53% fewer; the wall-clock figures from the interleaved A/B on an Apple M4 Pro and a 7950X are in the pull request.
- **jq: the stage after an object or array the filter built, or `fromjson` parsed, no longer writes it out and indexes it again** (#5652, #5606 follow-up).
  `[.users[]|{a:.age,b:.name}|.a]` wrote each object out as JSON and indexed it to read one key. A computed array or object (not with the embed table active) now meets
  `.a`, `.[0]`, `select(cond)`, `if`, `tojson`, `has("k")` and `keys` from the owned tree, the way a computed number has since #5601. A stage outside that grammar
  (arithmetic on a read, a comma, a nested `.b.c`, a generator condition) bridges as before. Over a generated `users` document (Apple M5 Max, interleaved min, 10 MB,
  jq 1.7.1, against a build with #5606): `{a:.age,b:.name}|.a` 1.39x faster, `|select(.a>30)` 1.64x, `|keys` 1.56x, `|has("a")` 1.40x, `[.age,.name]|.[0]` 1.33x,
  `tojson|fromjson|.age` 1.49x (0.63x -> 0.94x of jq) and `tojson|fromjson|select(.age>30)` 1.47x; instructions retired fall to 0.58-0.69 of the base build, and an Apple M4 Pro reads the same rows 1.37x, 1.51x, 1.47x, 1.40x, 1.30x, 1.42x and 1.42x faster.
- **jq: `-n` with `input`/`inputs` converts each document when the program reads it, not all of them up front** (#5661). `first(inputs)` over a 56 MB NDJSON file parsed and held all 1.6 million documents before the filter ran (1.7 s, 952 MB peak, jq 4 ms and 2.5 MB).
