A clean single-source plain-JSON stream (strict JSON `serde_json` accepts, no BOM, documents nested no deeper than 64) now queues each document's byte range and converts it, and counts its line, on the read that pops it, so a program that stops early (`first(inputs)`, `limit(n; inputs)`, `input` in a counted loop) converts only what it reads and holds the text and those ranges: on the 56 MB file `first(inputs)` takes 0.36 s and 205 MB (was 4.0 s and 952 MB), and on a 7 MB file 57 ms (was 428 ms), measured on an Apple M5 Max (interleaved min of 5, a loaded box, so read the ratios). A program that reads every document costs what it did. A stream with a BOM, `-s`, `--stream` or `--seq` keeps the up-front route and its error placement, and one with a parse error keeps its clean start lazy and the up-front route for the rest (#5853, below); jq 1.7.1 agrees on 2,624 stream-by-program rows.
That route also no longer makes two more whole-stream passes before the filter runs: the end-of-stream marker (#4303) is read off the document ranges it already found instead of a strict re-scan, and each document's line is counted when it is read, with nothing kept per unread document. On an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (interleaved min of 7, a loaded box) `first(inputs)` on a 77 MB NDJSON file takes 229 ms and 117 MB (was 578 ms and 194 MB) and on 9.7 MB 35 ms (was 79 ms), and `reduce inputs` is 5-7% faster with a third less peak memory.
On an Apple M4 Pro (interleaved min of 7) the same change takes `first(inputs)` on a 63 MB NDJSON file to 125 ms and 104 MB (was 286 ms and 204 MB) and on 7.9 MB to 19 ms (was 38 ms), and programs that read every document are 9-10% faster with peak memory halved.
The same route (#5854) now builds one index per run of consecutive documents (16 KiB of text for the first run, doubling to 1 MiB) and converts each document from its root in that index, instead of building and dropping an index for every document. `reduce inputs`, `last(inputs)` and the like over an NDJSON file of small records are 13.5-15.8% faster on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X and 7.2-8.6% faster on an Apple M4 Pro (interleaved min of 11, 8 MB and 64 MB; 0 output differences; peak memory unchanged), and `first(inputs)` is unchanged within noise (+0.6% to +1.7% on the 7950X, -0.6% to +0.4% on the M4 Pro) because its first run is small.
A program that reads `input`/`inputs` without `-n` takes the same route (#5855), since its driver loop already pops its documents from the queue the program's own `input` draws from, and the strict end-of-stream scan is skipped for it as well. `jq -c '[., input_line_number] | halt'` on a 64 MB NDJSON file takes 0.12 s (was 0.82 s) on an Apple M4 Pro and 0.12 s (was 1.41 s) on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, and a program that reads every document is 4-8% faster on the M4 Pro (`[., input] | length` 1.37 s against 1.46 s) and 19-36% faster on the 7950X (`[., input] | length` 1.66 s against 2.60 s, `input_line_number` 2.31 s against 3.20 s); interleaved min of 7, output identical, and the same programs under `-n` do not move. A stream the route turns down (one that is malformed from its first quarter, or begins with a BOM), `-s` and `--stream` keep the up-front route. None of 4,840 rows (22 programs, 22 streams, 5 flag sets, a file and stdin) answers differently from the build before the change, and 1,622 rows that jq 1.7.1 answers the same are pinned.
A stream that turns malformed after a clean start keeps that start lazy too (#5853): the documents before the first fault are converted when the program reads them, the eager route reads the stream from the end of the last of them, and a number or literal directly before the fault is left to it, since jq never reads one the fault's own byte completes. `-nc 'first(inputs)|.id'` over a 64 MB NDJSON file with a stray `}` on its last line takes 236 ms and 133 MB on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (was 3.89 s and 1,078 MB) and 220 ms and 130 MB on an Apple M4 Pro (was 2.67 s and 896 MB); with the `}` in the middle 1.14 s and 606 MB (was 3.04 s and 1,027 MB) and 713 ms and 560 MB (was 1.92 s and 961 MB), and with it 30% in 1.53 s and 786 MB (was 2.78 s and 1,070 MB) and 901 ms and 733 MB (was 1.63 s and 918 MB) (interleaved min of 7 to 11, 0 output differences). The start is kept only when it covers a quarter of the stream: a fault within the first quarter of the file takes the eager route as before, because keeping the text alive for next to no lazy work held 2% to 9% more memory (a program that reads every document after a fault has the same peak, +0.6% to -4% across the faulted files; `[inputs]|length` at a 30% fault is 1,071 MB before and 1,025 MB after on the 7950X). Clean streams are unchanged.
A clean stream of several files takes the route too (#5857): one source per file, each with its own source tag and line count, so a token that runs on from one file into the next (#4316), an empty file and the end-of-stream marker read from the last file are all as before. A file the route turns down, a file that is not UTF-8 or `--validate` sends the whole stream to the up-front route. `-nc 'first(inputs)|.id'` over four NDJSON files (8, 32 and 64 MB in all) takes 25.3, 96.3 and 189.4 ms on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (was 194.2, 906.9 and 1,803.7 ms; peak memory 24, 56 and 99 MB, was 99, 366 and 720 MB) and 23.0, 86.0 and 172.4 ms on an Apple M4 Pro (was 114.4, 452.0 and 914.6 ms; 17, 51 and 105 MB, was 90, 347 and 695 MB). The driver loop without `-n` (`[., input_line_number] | halt`) moves the same (-87% to -89% on the 7950X, -80% to -81% on the M4 Pro), `reduce inputs` and `last(inputs)` are 11-13% faster on the M4 Pro and 44-47% faster on the 7950X with a fifth of the memory, and two and eight files read as four do. A single file does not move in time (-1.7% on the 7950X, +0.3% on the M4 Pro); its peak memory is +4.4% (2.3 MB of 53 MB) on the 7950X and unchanged on the M4 Pro. Interleaved min of 11, 0 output differences against the build before the change and against jq 1.7.1 on 16 rows per chip, the control run (the build before the change against itself) within -1.4% to +2.4% on the 7950X and -0.3% to +1.4% on the M4 Pro.
`-R` takes the route as well (#5857): the files are handed to the queue's producer, which finds the next newline when the program asks, joins a line one file leaves open with the next, and places each line where the up-front route did (in the file holding its newline, at that file's newline count, and a final line without one in the last file), so no string or location is built for a line the program does not read. `-nRc 'first(inputs)|length'` over four NDJSON files (8, 32 and 64 MB in all) takes 4.6, 17.3 and 31.8 ms on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (was 29.2, 119.1 and 218.6 ms; peak memory 21, 46 and 78 MB, was 42, 147 and 285 MB) and 3.4, 6.1 and 9.8 ms on an Apple M4 Pro (was 13.5, 46.0 and 90.2 ms; 14, 38 and 70 MB, was 43, 151 and 293 MB); one file and eight read as four do. The driver loop without `-n` moves the same (-82% to -86% on the 7950X, -75% to -89% on the M4 Pro), and a program that reads every line (`reduce`, `last`) is 28-43% faster on the 7950X and 8-16% faster on the M4 Pro with 49-76% less memory. Interleaved min of 11, 0 output differences against the build before the change and against jq 1.7.1 on 16 rows per chip, the control run within -2.1% to +0.8% on the 7950X and -0.6% to +1.3% on the M4 Pro.
The scan that decides which documents of a single file are lazy no longer runs over the whole stream before the first input is read (#5856): it covers a chunk of text at a time (64 KiB for the first, doubling to 512 KiB), the two parsers are checked against each other over each chunk alone, and the producer scans the next chunk when it has read the last, forgetting the byte ranges of the documents it has read, so a program that stops early pays for the chunks it read. A fault met by a later chunk is read eagerly from the end of the last lazy document, as one the first chunk meets is, and the end of the stream is settled when the scan reaches it; the documents the eager reader finds after a fault are handed out as they are read, where they were copied into a second queue beside the vector they came from. `-nc 'first(inputs)|.id'` over a 63 MB NDJSON file takes 10.1 ms on an Apple M5 (was 128.5 ms) and 28.5 ms on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (was 119.0 ms), and over a 7.5 MB file 3.4 ms (was 16.4 ms) and 5.0 ms (was 14.4 ms). With a stray `}` at the 10% mark of the 63 MB file it takes 10.7 ms (was 1,298 ms) and 30.2 ms (was 2,499 ms), in the middle 9.1 ms (was 755 ms) and 29.0 ms (was 1,356 ms), and on its last line 10.1 ms (was 223 ms) and 28.1 ms (was 241 ms) (interleaved min of 7, 0 output differences in every configuration). A program that reads every document of such a stream is 13% faster on the M5 and 14% faster on the 7950X when the `}` is at 10%, since the first tenth is no longer read eagerly (`reduce inputs as $r (0; .+1)` 1,172 ms against 1,353 ms, and 2,202 ms against 2,565 ms). The peak memory of `first(inputs)` over the 63 MB file is 74 MB (was 119 MB; 1,113 MB with the `}` at 10%), of `reduce inputs as $r (0; .+1)` 76 MB (was 120 MB), and of the same program over a stream with a `}` at 10% 965 MB (was 1,113 MB), on an Apple M5. Programs that read every document of a clean stream cost what they did within 2% on the M5 and 1.5% more on the 7950X (`reduce` 1,320 ms against 1,300 ms, with the instruction count unchanged within 0.5%); over a stream with a fault, 2.1-3.0% more on the M5 and 0.7-5.2% more on the 7950X for a fault on the last line or in the middle.
- **jq: `log`, `log2`, `log10`, `exp`, `exp2`, `exp10`, `sin`, `cos`, `tan`, `asin`, `acos`, `atan`, `sinh`, `cosh`, `tanh`, `asinh`, `acosh` and `atanh` of a number no longer write it out and index it again** (#5669, #5593 follow-up). `floor`, `ceil`, `round`, `trunc`, `sqrt` and `fabs` were answered from the number since #5593 and #5601; the other eighteen libm builtins still met each number through the reindex bridge. They are now the same libm call the builtin makes (`src/jq/math.rs`), for a document number and for one the filter computed, so no digit moves on any platform. A value that is not a number, a non-finite one and yq mode keep the evaluator's route. Over a generated `numbers` document (Apple M4 Pro, interleaved min of 7, 10 MB, jq 1.7.1): `[.numbers[]|log]|add` 0.65x -> 0.99x of jq, `sin` 0.64x -> 0.95x, `atan` 0.66x -> 1.00x, `log2` 0.65x -> 0.98x, `exp` 0.58x -> 0.92x, `tanh` 0.85x -> 1.57x and `log|floor` 0.95x -> 1.80x; on an Apple M5 Max `log` 0.53x -> 0.97x. `pow` and `atan2` take two operands and are not covered.
- **jq: `del` of several static paths, and `delpaths` of an array literal of paths, are answered on the value instead of writing it out and indexing it again** (#5670, #5549 follow-up). `del(.a)` and `del(.a) | del(.b)` were deleted from the value itself since #5549; `del(.a, .b)`, `del((.a, .b), .c)` and `del(.[0], .[1])` still wrote each value out as JSON, indexed it and deleted from that. A comma of field names and literal indices now takes the same route (the builtin's own body, which collects every path before it deletes any, so the order written does not matter); a computed key, an iteration, a condition, a `?` and yq mode keep the bridge. A comma of distinct plain field names (`del(.a, .b, .c)`) deletes independent keys, so it is applied name by name, each the cheap single-path delete rather than a path set merged into a trie. Over a generated `users` document (Apple M5 Max, interleaved min of 7, 10 MB, jq 1.7.1): `.users|map(del(.email,.score))|length` 0.66x -> 1.54x of jq (instructions retired 4.90 G -> 1.90 G), `del(.email,.score,.age)` 0.67x -> 1.76x, `del(.email,.score)|tojson` 0.78x -> 1.74x, `del(.email,.score)|keys` 0.66x -> 1.48x and `[.id,.name,.age]|del(.[0],.[2])` 1.02x -> 1.24x; `del(.email)` is unchanged at 1.36x. `delpaths([["email"],["score"]])` (a literal list of arrays of string and integer literals, the same shape of delete) takes the same route: `.users|map(delpaths([["email"],["score"]]))|length` 0.62x -> 0.99x of jq (161 -> 102 ms, instructions retired 3.89 G -> 2.27 G, -37% wall at 10 MB; -33% at 0.7 MB and -39% at 35 MB), and the three-path and `|tojson` forms move the same way. x86_64 and the M4 Pro were not measured.
- **jq: `--slurpfile` and `--argjson` values cost less to hand to the program** (#5673). `$ARGS` is substituted into every program, and it went after a container named argument, whose literal copy it then walked in full; it goes first now, and the named arguments are no longer freed when the process is about to end. `-n --slurpfile d users.json '$d[0].users|length'` over 1 / 10 / 100 MB on an M4 Pro: -15% / -16% / -18% (20.0 → 17.1, 176.6 → 147.9, 1772 → 1461 ms); NDJSON (`$d|length`) -14% / -16% at 1 / 10 MB; a 63 KB `--argjson` -8%. A primary-input run and startup are unchanged (+1.0% and -1.2% median), and output is identical on all ten rows. Still about 2.6x jq 1.7.1's 56 ms at 10 MB: the value is built as a literal expression and then again when the program runs (#5673).
- **jq: `--seq` input is read as a plain JSON stream when it is clean** (#5674).
  A stream with one source, valid UTF-8, no byte-order mark, no diagnostic from jq's reader and nothing but
  whitespace and RS between its values is read the way NDJSON is, instead of indexing and converting every
  record on its own; any other stream takes the route it always did, with the same warnings. The reader's
  walk over the stream also takes a run of ordinary string bytes at once. On an Apple M5 Max,
  `--seq -r .name` takes 109 ms instead of 268 ms on a 10 MB stream and 1.02 s instead of 2.65 s on 100 MB
  (jq 1.7.1: 116 ms and 1.10 s), `--seq -s -c 'map(.score)|add'` 114 ms instead of 251 ms and 1.08 s
  instead of 2.42 s (jq: 133 ms and 1.26 s), and `--seq .` 167 ms instead of 256 ms and 1.56 s instead of
  2.52 s. Peak memory for `--seq -r .name` on 100 MB falls from 1.05 GB to 156 MB (jq: 2.5 MB).
- **jq: `fromjson` reads plain JSON in one pass** (#5675). `fromjson` ran a validation pass, built a semi-index and walked it into a value, three passes and half a dozen allocations for a 90-byte record. Text that is plain RFC 8259 (no `nan`, leading zero, repeated key, surrogate escape or nesting past 64 levels) is now read straight into the value, and every other text, with every error and its message, still takes the old route. Over a generated NDJSON file (`-R 'fromjson|.id'`, Apple M-series, interleaved min, output identical to jq's): 1 MB 32.4 -> 23.6 ms (-27%), 10 MB 300 -> 224 ms (-25%), 50 MB 1.47 -> 1.09 s (-26%), which moves jq's lead from 1.8x to 1.3x; a 400,000-call `fromjson` loop over one record is -40%. A surrogate pair (`\ud83d\ude00`) is decoded in the same pass. The rest of the gap is the per-line cost of `-R` itself. `tonumber` and every other filter are within noise. Measured on one machine; x86_64 was not.
- **jq: `-R` hands each line to the filter as the string it is** (#5675). A `-R` line was written out as JSON text, indexed and decoded again for every line before the filter saw it, the route `--stream` events left in #5681. The filter now reads the line where it is, and `length` of a string in a `select` condition is counted from it. Over generated NDJSON on an Apple M5 Max (interleaved min of 3-11 against `main` at `8bbd3df3e`, output identical on 13,712 program, flag and input combinations): `-R length` at 1 MB / 10 MB / 50 MB 14.1 / 86.3 / 530 ms -> 7.1 / 26.5 / 147 ms (jq 1.7.1 10.5 / 70.1 / 415 ms), `select(length>50)` 20.8 / 148 / 944 -> 10.6 / 59.3 / 368 ms (jq 38 / 307 / 2,078 ms), `test("User1")` 20.3 / 167 / 984 -> 14.1 / 99.3 / 547 ms, `ascii_downcase` 25.7 / 189 / 1,305 -> 17.9 / 128 / 948 ms, and `fromjson|.id` 28.5 / 240 / 1,226 -> 20.9 / 178 / 888 ms (jq 21.5 / 182 / 880 ms). `-R .` is unchanged. x86_64 was not measured, and the box was loaded, so the ratios are the evidence and the absolute times are not quiet-machine times.
- **jq: `utf8bytelength` and `contains("lit")` of a string are answered from the string** (#5675). `-R 'utf8bytelength'` and `-R 'contains("lit")'` wrote each line out as JSON text, indexed it and decoded it again, about 0.5 us a line, because #5691's string door answered only `length`, `startswith` and `endswith`. Both now join that door, so a `select` or `until`/`while` condition reaches them too. `contains` answers only a string in a string; every other pair, any container and a non-literal or fan-out argument still take the general route and keep its error text. Interleaved min of 9 against `main` at `f62dd98f6` on generated NDJSON, output identical to the old route's: on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X `-R utf8bytelength` at 1 MB / 10 MB / 50 MB 10.6 / 90.4 / 440 ms -> 4.8 / 37.1 / 178 ms, `-R 'contains("User1")'` 10.9 / 97.2 / 474 ms -> 4.9 / 39.4 / 191 ms, `-R 'select(contains("User1"))'` 11.7 / 104 / 525 ms -> 5.7 / 44.6 / 229 ms; on an Apple M4 Pro `utf8bytelength` 12.3 / 86.5 / 394 ms -> 5.5 / 22.7 / 98.5 ms, `contains("User1")` 13.0 / 85.9 / 402 ms -> 6.1 / 23.3 / 99.8 ms, `select(contains("User1"))` 14.2 / 94.3 / 464 ms -> 6.8 / 29.8 / 143 ms. The `-R length` control moves by under 4% on both (7950X 37.9 -> 37.5 ms and M4 Pro 24.6 -> 23.6 ms at 10 MB). On the 10 MB file this takes the three programs from 0.6x-1.0x of jq 1.7.1 on an Apple M5 Max to 2.1x-2.9x ahead of it. Output (stdout, stderr, exit status) is identical to the old route on 2,245 program, flag and input combinations in jq and yq mode.
- **jq: a string is written by copying its escape-free text whole** (#5675; `-a` still writes character by character). `write_json_body_jq`, the writer under the re-index bridge, the lazy printer and the stream path, wrote one `char` at a time (an encode and a capacity check each) to escape a string that almost always holds nothing to escape. It now scans bytes for the four things jq escapes (a quote, a backslash, a C0 control and DEL) and copies the text between two hits as one span, as the yq writer already did. Output is byte-identical. Interleaved min of 9 on an Apple M4 Pro against `main` at `b409cb2b3`, 10 MB inputs: `-R tojson` over 200-byte plain lines 122.0 -> 72.3 ms (-41%) and over NDJSON records 137.9 -> 122.6 ms (-11%), `-R '[.,1]|length'` over the plain lines 75.9 -> 57.8 ms and over the records 96.2 -> 89.9 ms, `-R '{a:.}'` 131.1 -> 119.9 ms, `-R .` 47.3 -> 40.5 ms and `tojson` over a 7 MB users document 92.9 -> 85.0 ms; lines of 1-6 characters are flat (671 -> 660 ms), and text that is half escapes (quotes, backslashes and tabs) costs 1% to 3% (358.7 -> 366.2 ms). The Apple M5 Max reads the same (`-R tojson` over plain lines 116.5 -> 69.1 ms). x86_64 was not measured, and the boxes were shared, so the ratios are the evidence and the absolute times are not quiet-machine times.
- **jq: `-R 'split("lit") | length'` counts a line's pieces from the line** (#5675). A `-R` line is already the
  string the filter reads, but `split(sep) | length` still wrote it out as JSON, indexed it and split the decoded
  copy, then counted the array. Over 10 MB of NDJSON on an Apple M-series (interleaved, min of 11, output
  identical) `split(",")|length` takes 29.9 ms instead of 108.7 ms (jq 1.7.1: 89.8 ms) and `split("")|length`
  23.8 ms instead of 229.8 ms; x86_64 not measured. The pieces are counted without building them, by the same
  rules as `split` (an empty line has none, an empty separator counts characters).
- **jq: `-R '(.|length) as $n | $n * 2'` and a body that never reads `.` no longer write the line out and index it** (#5675). A binding whose source is a count the string or container door answers is substituted into the body as a literal, and an expression that is one value whatever the input is (`$n * 2` once `$n` is a literal, `1 + 2`) is answered without the input. Over 10 MB of NDJSON on an Apple M-series (interleaved, min of 11, output identical to jq 1.7.1): `(.|length) as $n|$n*2` 117.0 -> 36.8 ms (jq: 70.6 ms), `120*2` 61.2 -> 25.4 ms. x86_64 not measured.
- **jq: `pow` and `atan2` of a number whose operands are `.` or a literal no longer write it out and index it again** (#5680, #5669 follow-up). `[.numbers[]|pow(.;2)]` took the general two-operand call for every number, including the reindex bridge. When both operands are `.` or a literal (one value each, so there is no fan-out), the call is now the builtin's own libm call on those numbers, for a document number and for one the filter computed, with the operands read as the builtins read them (a `-0` keeps its sign). A generator operand (`pow(.; (1, 2))`), a computed operand (`pow(2; ./1e6)`), a value that is not a number, a non-finite one and yq mode keep the evaluator. Over a generated `numbers` document (Apple M5 Max, interleaved min of 7, 10 MB, jq 1.7.1): `pow(.;2)` 0.55x -> 0.88x of jq, `pow(.;0.5)` 0.56x -> 0.91x, `atan2(.;1)` 0.56x -> 0.93x and `.+1|pow(.;2)` 0.48x -> 0.76x.
- **jq: `--stream` with a filter that reads each event runs about 2x faster** (#5681). A `--stream` event is a `[path, leaf]` array, and the filter used to receive it as JSON text that was written out, indexed and read back for every leaf. The filter now reads the event where it is and re-indexes only the stages the owned evaluator declines. On an Apple M5 Max, over 7 MB and 35 MB of records, `-c --stream 'select(length==2 and .[0][2]=="age")|.[1]'` takes 292 ms instead of 658 ms and 1.38 s instead of 3.14 s (jq 1.7.1: 306 ms and 1.47 s, so 0.48x becomes 1.05x of jq), `select(length==2)|.[1]` 0.44x-0.49x of the old time, `.[0]|length` 0.40x-0.51x, and `select(.[1]|type=="number")|.[1]+1` 0.71x; `.` is unchanged. On an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X the same rows read 0.38x, 0.45x, 0.49x and 0.68x of the old time (jq 1.7.1 was not measured there). Output is byte-identical to the old route on 4,480 program, flag and input combinations. Streams with a parse error, `--slurp` and programs that call `input`/`inputs` still take the old route.
- **jq: `split` of a string takes its pieces straight off the text** (#5682). `split(",")` of a value read from a document or a `-R` line materialized the string, wrote it out as JSON, indexed that and had `split` read it back; the writing cost as much as the split. A literal string separator now splits the value's own text; a non-string, a computed separator, the two-argument form and a string that does not decode keep the old route and its wording. `-R 'split(",")|.[2]'` over generated lines, interleaved A/B, min of 11, output identical: 1 MB / 3 MB / 10 MB are -34.8% / -35.8% / -36.0% on a 7950X and -32.5% / -35.5% / -36.2% on an M4 Pro, which takes jq's lead (0.7x of jq before) to parity; `split(",")|.[2]|tonumber` is -25% to -29% on both, and `-R length` is within the harness's noise.
- **jq: `min` and `max` over an array walk it once and read a plain integer without decoding it** (#5683). `min`/`max` collected a cursor for every element, then keyed every element with its decoded value into a second vector, then compared; a comma of the two paid that twice. They now keep the running winner as they walk (the first of equal minima and the last of equal maxima, as before, so `1`, `1.0` and `1.00` are still told apart by their spelling), and an element that is a plain integer of up to 18 digits is compared as an `i64` instead of being built as an owned number. Everything else (a fraction, an exponent, `-0`, a longer run, a non-number) takes the general decode. Over a 700,000-number array (Apple M-series, interleaved min, output identical to jq's): `[.numbers|min,max]` 115.6 -> 35.9 ms (-69%), `[.numbers|min]` 66.3 -> 23.1 ms (-65%); at 5,000,000 numbers 826 -> 230 ms (-72%) and 451 -> 140 ms (-69%). jq / succinctly goes from 0.71x to 2.3x on the comma and from 1.02x to 2.9x on `min` alone. Only the walk's error order changed: an array with two faults reports the one first in the text. Measured on one machine; x86_64 was not.
- **jq: a program that only reads a container named argument gets it as one shared value, not a literal tree rebuilt at every `$name`** (#5690). `-n --slurpfile d users.json '$d[0].users|length'` is 58% to 66% faster on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (10 MB: 379 ms to 127 ms; 100 MB: 3.53 s to 1.31 s) and 55% to 57% faster on an Apple M4 Pro (100 MB: 1.68 s to 0.72 s); `[$d[0].users[]|select(.age>40)]|length` is 48% to 60% faster; `--argjson` and `$ARGS` likewise. A program with an assignment, a fold, a path expression (`path`, `paths`, `del`, `pick`, a `getpath` or `setpath` target) or a definition keeps the literal, as before (within noise), so a write through the value and a dynamic path target answer as they did.
- **jq: `length`, `startswith` and `endswith` of a lone last-stage string no longer write the string out and index it again** (#5691).
  `--rawfile s big '$s|length'` took the string through the re-index bridge: an escape pass over every byte to write its JSON text, an index over that text, and a second UTF-8 validation to read it back, only to count it or compare its first bytes. The string is now answered from directly when the call is the last (or only) stage; a document string and a `-R` line are served the same way. A composed use (`$s|length|tostring`, a `select` condition) is covered separately (#5712). On a 84 MB `--rawfile` on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, `$s|length`, `$s|startswith("zzz")` and `$s|endswith("zzz")` take 131-133 ms instead of 382-385 ms (2.9x), peak memory 337 MB instead of 528 MB; 10 MB: 18 ms instead of 49 ms, 1 MB: 3.1 ms instead of 6.1 ms. Output is identical in both modes. Measured on one machine (x86_64); ARM64 was not.
- **jq: a string's `length` and `startswith`/`endswith` are answered from the string in more composed positions** (#5712, #5691 follow-up).
  #5710 answered them only as a lone last stage. A leading `length` or `startswith`/`endswith` that a later stage runs on (`$s|length|tostring`, also inside a parenthesised pipe) and a `select` or `until`/`while` condition (`select(length>3)`) now take the same route instead of writing the string out and indexing it again once per crossing. On a 6.6 MB `--rawfile` on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X: `$s|length|tostring` 33 ms to 13 ms, `$s|select(length>3)|length` 44 ms to 13 ms, `$s|startswith("a")|not` 32 ms to 12 ms.
  A loop condition was read through the bridge once per round (`"" | until(length >= N; . + "x") | length`: N+2 reindexes, 271 ms at N=20,000 and 1,054 ms at N=40,000); it is now one crossing, 8 ms and 25 ms. The loop is still quadratic in jq mode, because each round's `length` counts codepoints in an O(n) pass (330 ms at N=160,000); in yq mode `length` is a byte count and the loop is linear.
  A condition over a value nested deeper than 384 levels, such as `select(tostring|length>5)`, is now answered as jq answers it instead of refused with `nesting depth exceeds limit of 384`. Output is otherwise identical in both modes.
  Measured on one machine (x86_64); ARM64 was not.
  The shapes #5718 left on the bridge take the same route: a comparison or boolean of the length outside a condition (`$s|length>5`), `try length` and `length?`, a `length` inside a per-element `range` body, a `reduce` or a `def`, and a `select` over a string inside `[...]`, `//` or an object value (and an `if` inside `[...]`). On a 7 MB `--rawfile` on an Apple M-series laptop, min of 5 (one crossing is about 18 ms): `$s|length>5` 41 ms to 25 ms, `$s|try length` 40 ms to 24 ms, `[range(9)|($s|length)]` 156 ms to 26 ms, `$s|reduce range(3) as $i (0; . + ($s|length))` 80 ms to 41 ms, `[$s|select(length>3)]|length` 46 ms to 25 ms. Output is identical to the previous build in both modes on 400 comparisons run for it.
  Still through the bridge: the `length` of a string in yq mode inside a `range` body, `reduce` or `def` (that route is jq mode only), and an `if` over a string inside an object value or a `//` operand.
- **jq: a stage that reads only a bound computed string or array is answered once per round, not through the reindex bridge each round** (#5712).
  `. as $t | [range(25) | ($t | length)]` after a computed stage (`.s | ascii_downcase | . as $t | ...`) wrote `$t` out as JSON text and indexed it again for every round, because the eager owned route had no answer for an expression that never reads `.` (its lazy twin did). It now takes the same closed-expression route, and a closed pipe answers a comparison, boolean or `try` over a string's length (`$t | length > 3`) and its prefix tests from the string.
  A closed pipe also reads a marker head in place instead of cloning it; a string marker's clone is a copy of the whole string, which a declined stage paid for nothing.
  On an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (jq mode, min of 11 interleaved runs, output identical on all 18 configurations), over a computed string of 1 / 8 / 32 MB of text: `[range(25) | ($t | length)] | add` 281 / 2047 / 9484 ms to 40 / 308 / 1473 ms; `[range(25) | ($t | length > 3)] | length` 281 / 2006 / 9416 ms to 40 / 304 / 1472 ms; the same over a computed array 167 / 1298 / 5522 ms to 33 / 245 / 967 ms; `reduce range(25) as $i (0; . + ($t | length))` 41 / 308 / 1470 ms to 40 / 294 / 1165 ms. A shape the route does not answer (`$t | length + 1`) is unchanged within noise (-0.1% / -1.4% / -1.0%), and so is a lone `length` (+0.3% / -0.6% / -0.3%). yq mode is unchanged.
  Measured on x86_64 only; ARM64 was not.
- **jq and yq: an `if`, an array, an object, an arithmetic or a `//` built from a string's `length` is answered from the string** (#5712).
  `if length > 5 then 1 else 2 end`, `[length]`, `{a: length}`, `length + 1`, `(length > 3) // 7` and what nests in them (a literal, or another such answer) over an owned string wrote the string out as JSON text and indexed it again, once per crossing; the string door of #5712's earlier steps answered a lone `length`, a comparison, `try` and the prefix tests but stopped at these. It now answers them, in both modes with that mode's `length` (codepoints in jq, bytes in yq), and a shape that raises (`length / 0`), fans out, computes a key or reads the input back (`if length > 3 then . else 0 end`) keeps the bridge and its error.
  On an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (jq mode, min of 15 interleaved runs, output identical on all 18 rows), over a computed string of 1 / 8 / 32 MB of text, each of the five shapes went from 36 / 279 / 1100 ms to 28 / 209 / 821 ms (-23% / -25% / -25%): one crossing less. A lone `length` after the same stage, which this does not touch, read +3.1% / +0.8% / +1.6% at identical instruction counts (1,954,880,268 against 1,954,880,565 at 8 MB), code placement; the base binary against itself read within +-0.2%.
  Measured in jq mode on x86_64 only; yq mode takes the same door (its answers are pinned against the bridge) and ARM64 was not measured.
- **jq: the `$ARGS` object is built only for a program that uses `$ARGS`** (#5713). It holds a copy of every named argument and was built and spliced for every run, so a large `--rawfile`, `--arg` or `--slurpfile` was copied into it even when the program never read it. A program that uses `$ARGS` anywhere, or calls a builtin a `def` shadows at another arity, builds it as before. `-n --rawfile s <35 MB file> 1` peaks at 38.5 MiB instead of 72.2 MiB (0.53x) and runs 16.8 -> 13.2 ms; `$s|length` and `$s|startswith("zzz")` over the same file peak at 106 MiB instead of 140 MiB (0.76x) and run 12-13% faster (Apple M5 Max, interleaved min of 7, output identical); a program that reads `$ARGS.named.s` over a `--rawfile` string now shares it too (see the second entry). The `$ARGS` object of `succinctly yq` is still built as before. x86_64 and the M4 Pro were not measured.
- **jq: a named string argument is shared, not copied at each `$s` read** (#5713). `--arg`, `--rawfile` and a string `--argjson` were written into the expression as a literal, then copied again at each evaluation, so a program that read an 84 MB `--rawfile` twenty times held twenty copies. `succinctly jq` now promotes the string to shared storage once when it reads the arguments, and the literal, a `def` parameter and the `$ARGS` object hold a refcount to it. Against `main` at `f62dd98f6` plus the first #5713 entry, on a Ryzen 9 7950X (interleaved min of 5, output identical): an 84 MB `$s|length` runs 130 -> 60 ms and peaks at 91 MB instead of 250 MB; `[range(20)|$s|startswith("a")]` runs 750 -> 50 ms (1770 -> 95 MB); `def f($x): [$x,$x]|length; f($s)` runs 220 -> 50 ms (490 -> 92 MB); `-n --rawfile s <48 MB file> '$ARGS.named.s|length'` peaks at 74 MB instead of 312 MB; `$s|test("zzzz")` runs 380 -> 270 ms. Only a top-level string is shared: a string inside a `--slurpfile` or `--argjson` container, a JSON data module binding, builtins that take ownership of the string (`ltrimstr`, `ascii_downcase`, `sub`, `tojson`) and `succinctly yq` still copy. Appending to a short named string (`$t + "x"`) costs no more than before. ARM64 was not measured. **Library users:** `Literal::String` now holds a `SharableString` instead of a `String`; it dereferences to `str` and converts with `From`/`.into()` (`into_string()` gives the `String` back), and `Literal::string` takes `impl Into<SharableString>`. `succinctly yq`'s own `build_args_var` and the `-R`/`-Rs` input bridge are still built as before.
- **jq: a fold step that writes under an interpolated key no longer serialises its accumulator** (#5733).
  `reduce range(0;N) as $i ({}; .["k\($i)"] = $s)` evaluated its key through the re-index bridge, which
  rendered the whole accumulator as JSON and indexed it again to answer a key that never reads it, so the
  loop was quadratic in N when `$s` was long: 44 s at N=2000 with a 5000-byte value on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X
  (jq 1.7.1: 0.00 s). A key whose `\(...)` slots are all closed is now answered from the slots, as a
  `"k" + ($i|tostring)` key already was; N=500 to 8000 takes 0.02 s on an Apple M-series.
- **jq: `--stream -s` evaluates the slurped event array where it is** (#5744). The array of `tostream` events was
  written out as JSON text, indexed and read back before the program ran: 31% of the instructions of
  `--stream -s 'length'`. It is now handed to the owned evaluator as the tree it already is. On an Apple
  M-series (interleaved, min of 7, output identical) over a 30 MB `users` file: `length` 0.66x of the old time,
  `fromstream(.[])` 0.50x, `.[0:3]` 0.44x, `tojson|length` 0.46x, `map(length)|add` 0.86x. Programs whose stages the
  owned evaluator declines re-index the array as before, and two of them read slower: `[limit(5;.[])]` 1.18x and
  `[.[]|select(length==2)]|length` 1.05x of the old time at 30 MB (x86_64 not measured).
- **jq: `reduce`/`foreach` whose UPDATE or EXTRACT reads no loop variable run it as written instead of as a copy rebuilt for every step** (#5745). Over `--stream` events, `reduce inputs as $e (0; .+1)`, `foreach inputs as $e (0; .+1; .)` and `reduce (inputs|select(length==2)) as $e (0; .+1)` are 5% to 9% faster on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X and 11% to 16% faster on an Apple M4 Pro at 10 MB and 100 MB (interleaved, output identical); `[inputs]|length`, which never rebuilds a body, is unchanged. Outside `--stream`, `reduce range(2000000) as $i (0; .+1)` is 40% faster and `reduce .users[] as $u (0; .+1)` 20% faster on an Apple M5 Max, while a body that reads the loop variable is unchanged. A body that reads a loop variable, binds the same name, or holds a definition or call keeps the per-step copy, as before.
- **jq: a slurped `--stream` array is evaluated where it is only for a program the owned evaluator answers** (#5764).
  #5744 handed the array to the owned evaluator for every program, and a program none of its doors answers
  crossed the reindex bridge, which spells the array as reindex text, registers it for storage sharing and runs
  `eval.rs`'s evaluator over the index, where the old route read the same text with the lazier `eval_generic`
  one. Such a program now reads the array's own index, as before #5744. On an Apple M5 Max laptop (interleaved,
  min of 15, output identical, a control copy of the old binary at +0.5% and -2.2%) over a 21 MB `users` file,
  `--stream -c -s`, against the old route: `[limit(5;.[])]` 1.14x -> 0.99x, `[.[]|select(length==2)]|length`
  1.08x -> 0.99x, `map(select(.[1]!=null))|length` 1.01x -> 1.00x. The answered programs keep #5744's win
  (`length` 0.72x, `.[1000]` 0.72x of the old time). The price is the wins #5744 had on programs that bridge:
  `map(length)|add` 0.84x -> 1.00x and `map(.[0][0])|unique` 0.85x -> 0.96x of the old time. x86_64 and the
  M4 Pro were not measured (both boxes were loaded by other sessions' builds).
- **jq: a `reduce`/`foreach` body that reads through a container named argument no longer rebuilds the whole value on every step** (#5774). `-n --slurpfile d users.json 'reduce range(50) as $i (0; . + $d[0].users[$i].age)'` is 97% faster on an Apple M5 Max at 1 MB (372 ms to 11 ms; jq 1.7.1 is 9 ms), and 98% faster at 10 MB (3.63 s to 72 ms) and 100 MB (37.3 s to 656 ms), so the cost no longer grows with steps times the argument's size; `[foreach range(200) as $i (0; . + $d[0].users[$i].score; .)]` goes from 1.63 s to 13 ms. A `$d` that is read through (`$d[0]`, `$d.k`, `$d[$i]`, `$d[1:]`, `$d[]`, `$d | length`, `keys`, `has(k)`) is one shared value in a fold; a bare `$d` (an operand of `+`, an element of `[...]`, a fold's initial value) and any fold with an assignment, path expression or definition keep the literal, as before (within noise). `closed_expr_to_owned` now answers a computed index `$r.items[$k]` and a container's `length` from the owned value, for every fold, not only a named argument.
- **jq: a `reduce`/`foreach` that stores a value read through a container named argument no longer rebuilds the whole value on every step** (#5803). `-n --slurpfile d users.json 'reduce range(200) as $i ({}; .[$i|tostring] = $d[0].users[$i].age)'` is 99% faster on an Apple M5 Max at 1 MB (880 ms to 11 ms), and a store of a record from a 4000-record lookup table (`.[$i|tostring] = $d[0][$i]`, 4000 steps) goes from 11.7 s to 12 ms. A read on the value side of `=`, `|=`, `op=` and `//=` is shared as #5774 does for a read; the target of a store, and anything before it, keeps the literal, as before. A container read through the shared value is stored in the accumulator as one handle, as jq's `reduce` stores the `jv`, so `reduce range(2000) as $i ([]; . + [$d[0][$i]])` is 97% faster (285 ms to 9 ms) and no longer quadratic over the accumulator.
- **jq: `test`, `index`, `rindex` and `inside` of a string literal are answered from a string input without writing it out and decoding it again** (#5816). `-Rs 'test("zzz")'` over an 18 MB file is 87% faster on an Apple M5 Max (56.8 ms to 7.7 ms, jq 1.7.1 is 30 ms), `index("zzz")` 84%, `rindex("id")` 87% and `inside("x")` 87% faster, `-n --rawfile s F '$s|test("zzz")'` 90% faster (54.2 ms to 5.6 ms), and `-R 'test("9")'` per line over 200k lines 41% faster. The same shapes inside `[...]`, `select`, `and`/`or` and `if` conditions are answered too: `[.users[]|.name|test("a")]` over a JSON document is 23% faster. A pattern or flags that is not a string literal, a pattern that does not compile and every error keep the evaluator's route and text. A program that reads the string more than once through a composite (`[test("a"), test("b")]`) still decodes it once per read, as before.
- **jq: `ltrimstr`, `rtrimstr`, `tostring` and `. + "lit"` of a string input are answered from the string, alone and at the head of a pipe** (#5816). `-Rs 'ltrimstr("x")|length'` over an 18 MB file is 86% faster on an Apple M5 Max (55.6 ms to 7.9 ms; jq 1.7.1 is 60 ms), `tostring|length` 86%, `. + "x"|length` 84%, `ltrimstr("{")|startswith("\"")` 87% and `-n --rawfile s F '$s|ltrimstr("x")|length'` 89% faster; `-R 'ltrimstr("{")|length'` per line over 200k lines is 24% faster. A pattern that is not a string literal, a non-string input and every other operator keep the evaluator's route, and a string stage in path position (`path(ltrimstr("x"))`) is unchanged. Closes the #5816 table: every row now runs at or below the cost of `length`.
- **jq: `empty`, `error(...)?`, `select` spelled as an `if`, and `.k // empty` no longer take the reindex bridge under `--stream` and `-R`** (#5840).
  Each input was written out as JSON, indexed and read back for a program holding one of them, about 340 ns per event that `select(c)` did not pay.
  They are now answered from the input itself. Over a 40 MB `users` file with `--stream`, `empty` takes 0.58 s instead of 1.21 s on an Apple M4 Pro and 0.78 s instead of 1.53 s on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, `if length==2 then . else empty end` 0.97 s instead of 1.85 s (M4 Pro) and 1.24 s instead of 2.55 s (7950X), and `.[1] // empty` 0.73 s instead of 1.53 s (M4 Pro) and 0.95 s instead of 2.10 s (7950X).
  `-R` over 50 MB of lines is 45-65% faster on `empty`, `error("x")?` and the `if` spelling on both chips.
  Output is identical to before and to jq 1.7.1, and `select(c)` itself is unchanged within noise.
- **jq: the path-mode interpreter parses a prelude definition when a program first calls it, not all ~110 up front** (#5858).
  Without the `std` feature nothing cached the parsed prelude, so every `eval` of a program the interpreter takes
  (a non-static `path`, `del`, `pick` or assignment target) re-parsed all of it first: 0.8-1.0 ms per eval on a
  5-element document (Apple M5 Max, release build), 200 times the evaluation itself. It now costs 7-16 µs there.
  With `std` the first such program on a thread no longer pays the ~0.7-1.3 ms parse either; hot interpreter
  loops (20,000-element `|=` and `setpath` reductions) are unchanged and print identical output.
- **jq: `..` and `recurse` through the library `eval` entry are linear in nesting depth** (#5869).
  Listing a container's elements checks the text after its last element, and for a last element
  that is itself a container that check counted the closers from the nest's innermost leaf every
  time, so `..` over a linear nest `[[[...1...]]]` cost the sum of the depths. The closers a check
  has read are now kept on the index, so each container on the same run of closers is answered
  from the one asked before it. `last(..)` over 80,000 levels takes 0.05 s instead of 1.4 s, and
  `[..] | length` 0.04 s instead of 1.6 s (Apple M5 Max, release); 20,000 to 320,000 levels, walked in document order or from the innermost level out, now
  take 0.009 s to 0.21 s, where each doubling used to cost 4x. The CLI refuses a document past 256
  levels at parse time and so never reached this; library callers did, and the 100,000-level
  library test took 200-256 s of every `cargo test` CI leg and now takes under a second.
- **jq: a body rebuilt for each value that reads its variable in every stage and ends in a `def` call is linear in its stage count** (#5871).
  A tail that holds a `def` call cannot be a view of its pipe's shared storage (#3148), so every tail of the
  copy was copied again: `n - 1`, `n - 2`, ... stage clones per value. The stages ahead of the call are now one
  link whose own tails are views, and only the call is cloned again.
  `def f: . + 1; [range(0;20000) | . as $x | (<n-1 stages of . + $x> | f)] | add` at n = 10, 20, 40, 80
  took 0.14 s, 0.38 s, 1.17 s, 4.03 s and now takes 0.12 s, 0.23 s, 0.47 s, 0.96 s on an Apple M5 Max, and
  0.18 s, 0.59 s, 1.79 s, 6.20 s and now 0.14 s, 0.35 s, 0.70 s, 1.42 s on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (release,
  interleaved minimum of 3, output identical to jq 1.7.1). The same pipe with the call inlined, and with
  `. + 1` stages, did not move (0.99x to 1.02x on both). jq mode only: yq keeps its copies, since its first-stage
  rule for a failing generator reads the first stage of a pipe.
- **jq: a fold whose step is `[.]`, `[., <closed>…]` or `{k: .}` is linear in the number of steps** (#5875).
  The step used to write the whole accumulator out as JSON and index it again every time, so a fold that
  nested past 384 levels (#5832) was quadratic: `reduce range(40000) as $i (0; [.]) | length` took 16.7 s
  where jq takes 0.03 s. The new container is now built around the moved accumulator, and the same program
  runs in 0.09 s (an Apple M-series chip, release build; the time is flat from 5,000 to 400,000 steps, and
  10,000,000 steps take 1.2 s in 774 MB, where jq has long since crashed). Output is unchanged, byte for
  byte against jq 1.7.1 on the programs in `tests/jq_cli/i5875.rs`. `succinctly yq` is unchanged.
- **jq: a constructor fold step that reads a scalar off the accumulator is linear too** (#5893).
  `[., length]`, `[., (.|type)]`, `{a: ., n: length}` and `{(.s): .}` as a fold's step used to take the
  re-index bridge every step, like `[.]` did before #5875: `reduce range(40000) as $i (0; [., (.|type)])`
  took 31.7 s. The members that read scalars off the accumulator (`length`, `type`, a field, integer arithmetic
  such as `.n + 1`) are now settled before it moves into the new container, and that fold runs in 0.1 s (an Apple M-series chip, release build; 400,000 steps take
  0.14 s). A member that reads a container (`[., .a]`), a float (`.n / 2`) or `tojson` is still answered from a
  rebuilt copy of the accumulator and is still quadratic. Output is unchanged, byte for byte against jq 1.7.1 on the
  programs in `tests/jq_cli/i5893.rs`.
- **jq: a parenthesised read of a bound variable (`($x).k`, `$x | (.k)`, `$x | (.k)?`) defers the bind under a repeated ambient as `$x.k` does** (#5957). The deferred bind's walk tested the head of a field chain with a bare `$x` and accepted `.k` and `.k?` as field stages, so `. as $x | .users[] | ($x).limit` kept the bind eager and decoded the whole bound node although only one member is read; a parenthesis only groups. One definition of "the variable" and of "a field read", both seeing through parentheses, now serves the deferred bind's walk, the fold's projection and `is_field_read`. On the Apple M5 Max (interleaved min of 11, output identical, control within +-0.8%), `. as $x | [.users[] | select(.n > ($x).limit)] | length` over a 1 MB, 10 MB and 100 MB document takes 17.7 ms, 164 ms and 2.66 s instead of 28.2 ms, 271 ms and 3.76 s (-37%, -40%, -29%), `$x | (.limit)` -46%, -46% and -29%, and the bare `$x.limit` spelling, which already deferred, is unchanged (-0.9% to -0.3%). On an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X the same rows are -53%, -53% and -40% for the `select` form, -60%, -60% and -42% for `$x | (.limit)`, and the bare spelling is within the control's noise (+2.6% against a control of +2.0%). The M4 Pro was not measured.
- **jq: `--slurpfile` and `inputs` read plain JSON in one pass** (#6110). A stream of plain RFC 8259 values
  separated by white space (`--slurpfile d FILE`, `reduce inputs as $u (...)` over ndjson) is read straight into values by the
  reader `fromjson` already used (#5675), not validated by `serde_json`, semi-indexed and walked again; anything
  else (a leniency such as `007` or `nan`, a repeated key, a lone surrogate, nesting past 64 levels, a fault)
  takes the route it took before, so every error and its position are unchanged. On 10 MB inputs on an AMD
  Ryzen 9 7950X `--slurpfile` over ndjson goes from 0.71x to 1.24x of jq 1.7.1, `--slurpfile` over a users
  document from 0.77x to 1.25x, and `reduce inputs` over ndjson from 0.72x to 1.20x.
- **jq: a path-free `|=` update no longer materializes the document twice, and `map(.field)` is read off the owned copy** (#6122). `.users |= .` and `.users[0].name |= "x"` took the wildcard bridge, which wrote an owned copy of the whole document out as text and indexed it again before running the update. They now go through the same owned door as `=`, `+=` and `//=`, on the one copy, and answer as before (43 update shapes, variables and definitions among them, pinned against jq 1.7.1 stdout and exit status). On a 100 MB `users` document, min of 11 interleaved runs against the commit before: 1.73 s to 1.50 s on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (0.93x to 1.07x of jq 1.7.1) and 1.09 s to 0.95 s on an Apple M4 Pro (1.90x to 2.18x of jq 1.7.1-apple), -13% on both; `.users[].age |= .+1` and `.users[0].name = "x"` are within ±1% at 100 MB.

  `.users |= map(.age)`, the shape the issue opened with, still took the bridge for its right side: `map(.age)` was not a stage the owned evaluator answered, so the array was written out as text and indexed again to read one field of each element, and the update then ran over the whole document written out as text once more. `map` of a chain of static `.name` / `.[n]` steps over an owned array is now answered from the array itself, and the owned update step takes it as a right side (an object, a scalar, an element a step would raise on, yq mode and a node a binding shares keep the bridge). On the same 100 MB document (74 MB on disk), min of 11 interleaved runs against the commit before: `.users |= map(.age)` goes from 1.58 s to 0.99 s on the 7950X (0.80x to 1.28x of jq 1.7.1) and from 0.82 s to 0.42 s on the M4 Pro (0.92x to 1.79x of jq 1.7.1-apple), and `.users |= (map(.age) | length)` from 0.76x to 1.21x and from 0.90x to 1.77x; `.users |= .` and a base-against-base control read within ±1%. The same `map` is answered from the tree wherever an owned value is the input, so a slurped `--stream` array's `map(.[1])` builds no index document either.
- **jq: a write on a large document builds its value in one pass** (#6125). Materializing a container of
  plain RFC 8259 JSON (the first step of an assignment, `del`, `|=`, `tojson` and every other stage that
  needs an owned value) now reads the container's own text directly, not through a rank and a select per node;
  a leniency, a repeated key, a lone surrogate, invalid UTF-8 or nesting past 64 levels still takes the walk, and
  yq mode and a node a binding shares are untouched. On a 10 MB `users` document, `.users[0].name = "x" | .users | length`
  goes from 0.76x to 1.05x of jq 1.7.1 on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X and from 0.82x to 1.34x on an Apple M4 Pro,
  and `del(.users[0]) | .users | length` from 0.81x to 1.11x and from 0.88x to 1.44x. Peak memory is unchanged
  (788 MB at 100 MB).
- **jq: `path |= f` of a static path into a large JSON document runs `f` on the document instead of on a copy of all of it** (#6199).
  The update copied every node of the document into one owned value before it ran. When the path reaches at least half of a
  document of 65 536 nodes or more (about 1 MB) and `f` starts by reducing the target (`map(..)` of a projection, `length`, `add`,
  `first`, `last`, `limit`, `first(..)` of navigation, an index or a slice), the target is checked by one scan, `f` runs on it in the
  document, and the containers on the path are rebuilt around its output, so what `f` does not keep is never built. On a 100 MB
  `users` document, `.users |= length` takes 134 ms instead of 390 ms on an Apple M4 Pro and 185 ms instead of 864 ms on an AMD
  Ryzen 9 7950X, `|= first` 122 ms instead of 649 ms (169 instead of 1301), `|= map(.age)` 377 ms instead of 857 (453 instead of
  1555), `|= map(.age + 1)` 480 ms instead of 914 (562 instead of 1614), `|= (map(.age) | add)` 411 ms instead of 890 (523 instead of 1626),
  and `|= .[:10]` 629 ms instead of 706 (1267 instead of 1457); the same updates are 42-82% faster at 1 MB and 10 MB. Peak memory
  on the M4 Pro falls from 624 MB to 92 MB for `|= length`, from 798 MB to 92 MB for `|= first` and from 830 MB to 152 MB for
  `|= map(.age)`. The answers are the ones the copy gave: a filter that answers nothing or raises, a `?//` retry, a `map` under
  a consumer that stops early, a document that is malformed anywhere, a repeated key on the path and a path that does not land
  all take the route they took before, and a filter that keeps most of the target (`.`, `sort_by`, `reverse`, `map(select(..))`) is
  not taken (within 1.5% either way). An update inside a per-record loop whose filter is one of these reducers
  (`[.users[] | .name |= length]`) pays for the look, about 1% and at most 2% at 10 MB and 100 MB on both machines.
- **jq: a slice of a large array, `.users | .[:10]`, reads the slice's elements by index instead of the whole array** (#6231). A literal-bound slice other than the full range was answered by materializing the array and indexing it again, so keeping ten elements cost what reading all of them cost; it is read as `E[S:T]` has been since #4287. On a 74 MB `users` document it falls from 595 ms to 108 ms (-82%) on an Apple M4 Pro and from 1,331 ms to 161 ms (-88%) on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X; at 7 MB it is -79% and -87%, and at 0.7 MB -58% and -78% (interleaved, min of 11, output identical on all 21 configurations on both). `.[5:]`, which keeps almost everything, gains 12-15% from 7 MB. `.users | length` is unchanged.
- **jq: a literal-bound slice of a variable or other owned array is cut in place** (#6258).
  `. as $a | [range(100) | $a[:2] | add] | length` wrote the whole array out as JSON, indexed it and decoded the kept part on every call.
  Over 200,000 integers it took 1.9 s (min of 7) and 1.2 GB; it is now 15 ms and 15 MB, 129x faster, and 133x faster over 1,000,000 integers (10.6 s to 80 ms), since the cost no longer grows with the array.
  Apple M4 Pro under a busy machine, CPU time, interleaved.
  Answers are unchanged: the bridge's number spelling (`1` read back as a literal) prints the same.
  `path()` of a literal slice and a literal slice of a string cursor are #6265's.
- **jq: a literal-bound slice of a string read from the document is cut where it stands** (#6265).
  `.text | .[:10]` on a 20 MB string copied the whole string through the evaluator's bridge before cutting it; the text is now borrowed and cut.
  CPU time on a 20 MB string, Apple M4 Pro, min of 7 interleaved runs: 36.7 ms to 24.6 ms, against an 18 ms floor for reading the file, so the slice itself went from about 19 ms to 7 ms (about 2.8x).
  Answers are identical to the previous build and to jq 1.7.1 over 195 string and malformed-string cases, DSV input included; yq mode is unchanged.
  `path()` of a literal slice is the following entry.
- **jq: `path()` of a narrow literal slice no longer copies the document** (#6265).
  `path(.users[:10])` materialized the whole input to name one path component. A literal slice whose bounds alone keep it
  to 4096 elements or fewer (`[:10]`, `[10:20]`, `[-10:]`) now walks with cursors; a wider range, or one that depends on the
  array's length (`[1:]`, `[:-1]`), is unchanged, because reading it element by element costs more than the one copy.
  CPU time on a 36 MB file, min of 11 interleaved runs: 521 ms to 83 ms and 378 MB to 53 MB on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, 202 ms to
  56 ms and 316 MB to 49 MB on an Apple M4 Pro. A slice of a whole array that is most of the document gains less: 41 MB, 1102 ms
  to 412 ms and 386 ms to 338 ms. The one slower row is `path(.[:4096][].id)` on a 731 KB file on the M4 Pro, 7.7 ms to 8.8 ms
  (9.5 ms from 12.8 ms on the 7950X).
  Outputs are identical on every measured row and to jq 1.7.1 on well-formed documents. On a malformed one, a narrow slice now
  validates what `.a[s:e]` validates, so a fault outside the range no longer raises, as `path(.a[0])` already did; see the jq
  limitations page. A full-range literal slice validates through the cursor, which also rejects a nested `[,]`
  (`[.[0:3]] | length` on `[[,],2,3]`) that it used to answer, as jq rejects it.
- **jq, yq: `select(cond)` answers a simple condition without copying the node** (#6350). `select` over `true`/`false`/`null`, `.`, `not`, `and`/`or` and a comparison of `.` or `type` with a literal (`select(. == null)`, `select(. != null)`, `select(type == "string")`) now reads the node in place, as `recurse(.[]?; cond)` has since #4095, instead of running the condition through the fan-out and copying the node to compare it. `[.. | select(. == null)]` over a 50 MB document: 2.41 s to 1.10 s on an Apple M4 Pro (2.19x), `. != null` 2.50 s to 1.16 s, `. == true` 2.49 s to 1.13 s, `select(type=="string")` 1.70 s to 1.12 s (1.51x); flat from 1 to 50 MB, interleaved, min of 7, the control `[.. | strings]` 1.00x. On an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X the same programs are 2.39x (`== null`), 2.26x (`!= null`), 2.39x (`== true`) and 1.61x (`type=="string"`) at 50 MB. The answers are unchanged, with one exception: a container compared with a literal (`select(. != null)` over `[[1,tru],2]`) is decided by being one and is no longer decoded, so malformed JSON nested inside it is not reported there, as it already was not for `select(type == "array")` or `select(.)`.
- **jq: `nulls`, `strings`, `objects` and the other type selectors in path position run natively** (#6359), `succinctly yq` under `--jq-extensions` too. `path(..|nulls)`, `del(..|nulls)`, `(..|numbers) |= f`, targets built on `booleans`, `numbers`, `strings`, `arrays`, `objects`, `iterables`, `scalars` and `values` went through the path-program interpreter (a function lookup and call per node) while the `select(type == "...")` spelling of the same filter was already resolved natively; they are now static path targets too. Over a 50 MB document on an Apple M4 Pro: `[path(..|nulls)]` 2.10x, `del(..|nulls)` 1.93x, `[path(..|objects)]` 2.32x, `(..|numbers) |= . + 1` 1.50x; on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X 2.30x, 2.15x, 2.47x and 1.59x; flat from 1 to 50 MB, interleaved, min of 7, with the controls `select(type=="null")` and `[.. | strings]` at 0.99-1.01x. The answers are unchanged, errors included (`path(..|nulls|tostring)` still raises `Invalid path expression`).
- **jq: `-R` makes each line a string when the program gets to it** (#6437).
  A `-R` program that reads no `input` built every line's string before it ran, holding about 3.5
  times the input: `-R length` on a 95 MB file peaked at 331 MB. Lines now come from the producer
  `input` already reads them through, so the run holds the file and the line being read: 95 MB, the
  JSON route's share (jq 1.7.1: 2 MB). On an Apple M5, `-R length` went from 152 to 123 ms and
  `-r -R .` from 148 to 118 ms at 95 MB (jq: 473 and 348 ms); `-R fromjson|.id` is 1.09 to 1.06 s
  (jq: 1.21 s). Output, locations and `input_filename` are unchanged.
- **The CLI allocates from glibc's main arena on Linux** (#6437).
  All the work runs on the evaluation thread, and glibc gave that thread a secondary arena, which grows its heap one
  4 KiB `mprotect` at a time: about 1,500 system calls for a 667 KB file. With `M_ARENA_MAX` set to 1 the heap grows
  through `brk` in 128 KiB steps. On an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, at 10 MB, `.users[0].name="x"|.users|length` takes
  73.4 ms instead of 91.0 ms (1.24x faster; jq 1.7.1 takes 91.8 ms), `del(...)` is 1.22x faster, `tostream` 1.30x and
  `walk` 1.18x. An interleaved run of all 190 rows of the jq comparison's performance queries, plus yq, printed the
  same output before and after, with peak memory unchanged. The rows that allocate little are within noise. macOS
  and other allocators are unaffected.
- **`-R 'fromjson | ...'` parses each line in place** (#6437). Each raw line was written out as JSON text, indexed, and decoded back out of the index before `fromjson` parsed it, about a fifth of the instructions of the run. A line that parses now goes straight to the parser; one that does not still takes the old route, which words the error. On a 7950X against 0286e9ddd (jq 1.7.1, interleaved, identical output) `ndjson_raw_fromjson` at 10 MB goes from 149.7 ms (0.89x of jq) to 95.8 ms (1.40x), at 1 MB from 16.6 ms (0.91x) to 11.0 ms (1.37x).
- **`-n` with `input`/`first(inputs)` over several files scans the last file a chunk at a time** (#6450). The last file was split, re-parsed with `serde_json` and line-counted whole before the first value. It now gets the 64 KiB-and-doubling scan a lone file has, so a program that stops early reads little of it. On an Apple M4 Pro, `-n 'first(inputs)|.id' one-line.json big.ndjson` went from 5.3 to 3.1 ms at 1 MB, 24.5 to 5.2 ms at 8.7 MB and 220 to 20 ms at 87 MB (jq 1.7.1: 2.4-3.0 ms); a program that reads every input is unchanged. The earlier files are still scanned whole (#6455), and the whole-file read and UTF-8 check are #6451.
- **jq: `-n 'input'` and `first(inputs)` on one large file or stdin start on the front of it** (#6451).
  The lazy route used to read the whole source and check that it is UTF-8 before the first document;
  it now reads the first 256 KiB, starts the program on the documents there, and reads the rest when
  the program asks for more. On a 95 MB NDJSON file `-n 'input|.id'` takes 2.9 ms instead of
  12.3 ms (jq 1.7.1: 2.3 ms) and peaks at 6 MB instead of 101 MB (170 MB from stdin), on an Apple M5.
  A program that reads every document takes as long as before, and a source that turns out not to be
  UTF-8, or malformed, past the front reads as it did.
- **jq: `-n` with `input`/`first(inputs)` over several files scans every file a chunk at a time** (#6455).
  #6450 did this for the last file; every file before it was still split, re-parsed with `serde_json` and
  checked for a token left open at its end before the first value. Now only the first file's first
  chunk is scanned before the program starts, and each later file when the program reaches it. A fault
  in a file, or a number or literal ending one before the last, hands the rest of the stream to the
  eager reader, so a stream that is not clean reads as before. On an Apple M5,
  `-n 'first(inputs)|.id' big.ndjson one-line.json` went from 279 to 13.8 ms at 95 MB and from 29.7 to
  3.7 ms at 9.3 MB, and two 95 MB files from 291 to 24 ms (jq 1.7.1: 2.2-2.4 ms). What is left is each
  file's whole read and UTF-8 check. A program that reads every input is unchanged.
- **jq: a `--seq` stream with one malformed record no longer holds ten times the stream in memory** (#6500).
  A stream with any diagnostic built an owned value for every record before the program ran; it now converts each record when the `input` queue is read, as `-R`'s lines are, so the values of the whole stream are never held. On an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, a 100 MB stream whose last record is malformed peaks at 156 MB instead of 1,172 MB (jq 1.7.1: 3 MB) and runs in 3,281 ms instead of 4,089 ms (-20%; the 1 MB and 10 MB streams are -18% and -22%), and a clean 100 MB stream is unchanged (831 ms against 840 ms).
  That is still 0.29-0.33x of jq 1.7.1's speed on such a stream, because the walk runs twice and each record is indexed again (#6620). The M4 Pro was not idle for the measurement, so ARM is not measured.
- **jq: a clean `--seq` stream is proved clean by a record check instead of the whole-stream walk** (#6501, #6437 follow-up).
  `--seq` input takes the NDJSON route when jq's reader would read it without a diagnostic (#5674), and to decide that it ran a byte-at-a-time model of jq's reader over the whole stream (about 200 MB/s) before the route scanned every document again. A stream that is RFC 7464's own framing, every record `RS value LF` with the value one RFC 8259 document, now skips the walk: the strict validator (about 1 GB/s) reads each record, last record first, and three guards (the stream starts on an RS, ends on a newline, and every record ends on a newline) close the ways valid records can still leave the stream unclean. Any other stream takes the walk exactly as before. A fuzz holds the check to the walk under both `-s` values (3,000,000 streams, 6,000,000 checks, 0 unsound) and drops each guard in turn to show it is needed.
  On an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (jq mode, min of 21 interleaved runs, `json generate -p json-seq --seed 6437`, output identical on every row), 1 / 10 / 100 MB: `--seq -r .name` 12.8 / 115.7 / 1150 ms to 9.7 / 84.6 / 817 ms (-24% / -27% / -29%); `--seq -s -c length` 10 / 100 MB 81.3 / 816 ms to 50.0 / 490 ms (-39% / -40%). A stream the check cannot vouch for pays about nothing when it fails at its last record (a truncated tail: 450 / 4348 ms to 449 / 4321 ms; a last record that is not RFC 8259, such as `nan`: 116 / 1151 ms to 116 / 1142 ms). A stream that fails earlier costs the records before the failure, read at the validator's speed, and plain NDJSON, which this does not touch, read -1.6% / -2.0%.
- **jq: `implode` of an array a stage built no longer takes the reindex bridge** (#6523). `explode | implode`, `explode | map(. + 1) | implode` and `[.[] | explode | reverse | implode]` wrote the array out as JSON text, indexed it and read each number back; the array is now read in place and the string written once (a codepoint `char::from_u32` rejects is still U+FFFD, a fractional or non-number element still takes the bridge). `.strings | map(explode | implode)` over generated string files, against jq 1.7.1, interleaved on a Ryzen 9 7950X: 122 to 14 ms at 1 MB, 1204 to 119 ms at 10 MB and 12164 to 1171 ms at 100 MB (jq: 32, 311, 3142 ms, so 0.2x became 2.4x to 2.7x); on an Apple M5, 10 MB: 918 to 71 ms (jq 186 ms).
- **jq: `add`, `min` and `max` of an array that an earlier stage built out of numbers no longer go through the reindex bridge** (#6527). `.numbers | map(. * 2) | add`, `| max` and `| min` (and `[.numbers[] | . * 2] | add`) wrote the array out as JSON text (a shortest-round-trip float each), indexed it, and parsed every number back, 150 to 160 ms over 800,000 floats that jq 1.7.1 does not spend (0.64x to 0.75x of it on an Apple M5). The array is now folded where it stands, with the bridged builtins' own `arith_add`, `jq_min_by` and `jq_max_by`, so the answers are the same, including which of `1` and `1.0` a `max` keeps. An array holding anything but integers and finite floats (a NaN, an infinity, a number copied from the document, a string) still takes the bridge, as do an empty array, an object, yq mode and a run with a bound node in scope. Interleaved A/B (min of 11, output identity gated on all 27 configurations) over 1, 10 and 100 MB: `.numbers | map(. * 2) | add`, `| max` and `| min` are 38-40% faster on a Ryzen 9 7950X (10 MB: 421 to 255 ms) and 39-43% faster on an Apple M4 Pro (10 MB: 392 to 231 ms), `[.numbers[] | . * 2] | add` 37-38% and 40-43%, and the `length` and `sort | length` controls move by under 2%. A differential of 870 program-by-array rows against `/usr/bin/jq` is clean before and after.
- **jq: a `reduce`/`foreach` step that builds its next state with a constructor is 2.2-2.7x faster** (#6528).
  A step such as `[.[0] + $x, .[1] + 1]` or `{s: (.s + $x), n: (.n + 1)}`, with no bare `.` member, now
  builds the new state from the old one directly when every member reads only numbers, strings or
  booleans off it. Before, it went through the general evaluator and re-indexed the state for every
  `.[0]` it read. Over 800k floats on an Apple M5 these folds went from
  0.35x-0.49x of jq 1.7.1 to 0.90x-1.24x, the same at 1, 10 and 100 MB: `reduce .[] as $x ([0, 0];
  [.[0] + $x, .[1] + 1])` takes 3.2 s at 100 MB instead of 8.1 s (jq 3.7 s). A fold-step operand that
  reads a finite float off the state, or does arithmetic or division on one (`.a += [.f + 1]`), is now
  read off the tree as integers already were, so that fold is linear: 10,000 steps take 6 ms instead
  of 2.7 s, and 160,000 take 60 ms (jq 1.7.1: 93 ms and 18 s).
- **yq: a string's `length` inside a loop body is read off the string instead of being written out and indexed again every round** (#6534).
  With `--jq-extensions`, `"abcd" * 1750000 | . as $t | [range(100) | . as $w | ($t | length)]` took the reindex bridge
  once per round, as jq mode did before #6508 and #6532; the owned stage now answers a string's `length` from the
  string (bytes in yq, as before), so a bound computed string is no longer serialised each round. A 7 MB string over 100 rounds
  takes 29 ms instead of 577 ms on an Apple M4 Pro (20.0x; 1 MB 12.2x, 10 MB 19.4x) and 464 ms instead of 1070 ms on an
  AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (2.3x at every size: the per-round copy of the bound string that the pipe makes before the stage runs
  remains, and is dearer under WSL2, #6832). The output is unchanged.
- **jq: a `select` or `if` condition that does arithmetic on a computed value no longer takes the reindex bridge** (#6536). `select(. % 3 == 0)`, `if . % 2 == 0 then . else empty end` and `select(.a % 2 == 0)` over a number a stage produced (or a field of an object one built) wrote the value out as JSON text, indexed it and read it back for every element, because the owned-value condition grammar had no arithmetic; `select(. > 10)` never did. Both operands are now settled in place and combined with the evaluator's own `arith_combine`; an operator that raises (`. % 0`, `{} - 1`) still takes the bridge so jq's message and order are kept. `[range(3000000) | select(. % 3 == 0)] | length`, against jq 1.7.1 interleaved on a Ryzen 9 7950X: 1490 to 322 ms (jq 992 ms, so 0.67x became 3.1x); the `if ... else empty end` form 1464 to 375 ms (jq 872 ms, 0.60x became 2.3x); the same at 300000 elements: 149 to 35 ms and 151 to 41 ms.
- **jq: a `reduce`/`foreach` step that rebuilds its state with a constructor extending one of its lists is linear** (#6538).
  A step such as `{a: (.a + [$i]), n: (.n + 1)}`, `{a: ((.a // []) + [$i])}`, `[.[0] + [$i], .[1] + 1]` or
  `{a: .b, b: (.a + [$i])}` now moves each field or index it reads out of the old state and extends it
  in place, as `.a += [$i]` already did. Before, it re-indexed the whole state every step, so the fold was quadratic: on an Apple M5,
  `reduce range(8000) as $i ({a: [], n: 0}; {a: (.a + [$i]), n: (.n + 1)})` takes 9 ms instead of 888 ms
  (jq 1.7.1: 52 ms), and 32,000 steps take 25 ms (jq: 734 ms). Strings and objects grow the same way.
- **jq: `map(body)` of an array a stage computed out of numbers no longer takes the reindex bridge** (#6539). `[range(n) | . * 1.5] | map(. + 1) | map(. + 1) | add` wrote each `map`'s whole input array out as JSON text, indexed it and parsed it back; an array whose elements are all plain finite numbers (an `Int` or a finite `Float`) is now mapped number by number when each element's answer is one plain value (`. + c`, `. * c`, a comparison, `floor`, `sqrt`, `tostring`, `[.]`, `{a: .}`, `. as $x | ...`). A body that raises, fans out or answers a NaN, an infinity or a literal still takes the bridge, so jq's messages and its reading of an overflow are kept. The same program, interleaved against jq 1.7.1 on a Ryzen 9 7950X at 3,000,000 elements: 2208 to 729 ms (jq 1913 ms, so 0.87x became 2.6x); `map(. * 2) | map(. - 3) | length` 2149 to 658 ms (jq 1527 ms); `[range(n)] | map(. * 2) | add` 787 to 297 ms (jq 1202 ms). On an Apple M4 Pro the first of those is 1789 to 424 ms (jq 1452 ms, 0.81x became 3.4x) and the third 596 to 170 ms (jq 944 ms). A `map` over a number array read from the document (`.numbers | map(. + 1) | map(. + 1)`) is a lazy sequence that never took the bridge and is unchanged.
- **jq: more constructor fold steps that extend part of their state are linear** (#6549).
  After #6538, a step that rebuilt its state with a constructor was linear only for a field or index one
  step down. It now also extends a slot further down, as in `{a: {b: (.a.b + [$i])}}` (nested or not),
  through a `+` chain such as `.a + [$i] + [0]`, and beside a member that counts it, such as
  `{a: (.a + [$i]), n: (.a | length)}`. `length` of a container in a fold step's operand no longer
  re-indexes the state either. On an Apple M5 these folds took 0.9-1.6 s at 8,000 steps and now take
  8-13 ms (jq 1.7.1: 51-110 ms); at 32,000 steps they take 23-40 ms, where jq takes 0.73-1.7 s.
- **jq: `$ENV` and `env` read the environment once per thread, where they built the whole object again on every evaluation** (#6560). Every name and value was copied, inserted into a new map and allocated for each record, so `$ENV.HOME` over 100 MB of NDJSON (about 850,000 records) cost more the bigger the shell's environment, and `select(.name == $ENV.HOME)` was several times slower than jq. The CLI now calls `snapshot_environment()` at startup, so the object is built on a thread's first use and each later `$ENV` is a clone of it; a library caller keeps reading the current environment unless it opts in. Against jq 1.7.1, interleaved, on a Ryzen 9 7950X (100 MB, 14 variables): `$ENV.HOME` 2046 to 701 ms (jq 1178 ms, so 0.58x became 1.7x); with 94 variables 8193 to 709 ms (jq 1167 ms, 0.14x became 1.6x); `select(.name == $ENV.HOME) | .id` with 94 variables 9841 to 1172 ms (jq 1243 ms). On an Apple M4 Pro (93 variables) `$ENV.HOME` 7273 to 485 ms (jq 1374 ms, 0.19x became 2.8x). jq's own `env.HOME` rebuilds the object per call, so it is now 16x to 24x ahead of jq with 93 variables.
- **jq: a fold step that reads its state through a computed key or a `//` default no longer re-indexes the state every step** (#6567). `reduce .[] as $x ({}; .[$k] = (.[$k] // 0) + 1)`, the counting idiom, and `.b = (.a // 0) + 1` went to the evaluator for the whole assignment, which wrote the state out as JSON text and indexed it again at every step, so the cost per step grew with the state (0.20x of jq 1.7.1 at a hundred keys, minutes at ten thousand). The pure operand grammar now reads `.[K]` for a string or integer key (a key that reads nothing of the state, such as `($i % 100 | tostring)`, is computed once) and `a // b` of pure operands, as operands only, and a read that raises still takes the evaluator's route so jq's messages are kept. Against jq 1.7.1, interleaved, on a Ryzen 9 7950X: 400,000 steps over 100 keys 4827 to 391 ms (jq 873 ms, so 0.18x became 2.2x), over 1,000 keys 37,582 to 390 ms (jq 3146 ms), and 40,000 steps over 10,000 keys 32,473 to 42 ms (jq 2779 ms). On an Apple M4 Pro the same three rows are 3587 to 276 ms (jq 713 ms), 29,074 to 286 ms (jq 2695 ms) and 25,076 to 33 ms (jq 2795 ms). The `|=` and `+=` spellings of the same fold were already fast and are unchanged.
- **jq: a fold step that is an `if` choosing `.` or a closed value is 1.9-3.0x faster** (#6569).
  A `reduce`, `foreach`, `until` or `while` step such as `if $x > . then $x else . end` (a running max)
  or `if C then 1 else 2 end` now answers from the chosen branch. Before, the whole `if` ran on the
  evaluator's general route every step. On an Apple M5 over 4,000,000 `reduce` steps, the running max takes
  743 ms instead of 1,550 ms (jq 1.7.1: 659 ms), and `if 3 > 5 then . else . end` takes 373 ms instead
  of 1,126 ms (jq: 448 ms).
- **jq: a fold step whose operand is an `if` over the loop variable is 2.1-2.5x faster, and up to 370x where it builds a string** (#6574).
  A `reduce`, `foreach`, `until` or `while` step such as `. + (if $i % 2 == 0 then 1 else 0 end)`, or
  `.n += (if ... end)`, now answers from the branch the condition picks. Before, the whole step ran on the
  evaluator's general route every round, and where it built a string, array or object each round that route
  copied the accumulator: quadratic. On an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (jq 1.7.1 in brackets), 4,000,000 numeric steps
  take 1,720 ms instead of 4,102 ms (1,463 ms); 400,000 steps that append a string take 177 ms instead of
  65,529 ms (158 ms), an array 187 ms instead of 2,933 ms (151 ms), and an object 202 ms instead of 4,257 ms
  (173 ms). Apple silicon was not measured.
- **jq: a fold step that is a pipe of stages is 1.9-4.8x faster** (#6575).
  A `reduce`, `foreach`, `until` or `while` step such as `. + [$x] | .[-5:]` (a sliding window),
  `. + $x | . % 1000` or `[., $x] | max` now applies its stages to the state one after another.
  Before, the whole pipe ran on a re-indexed copy of the state every step unless every stage was an
  assignment. On an Apple M5 over 4,000,000 `reduce` steps the sliding window takes 832 ms
  instead of 3,189 ms (jq 1.7.1: 1,869 ms), and `[., $x] | max` takes 831 ms instead of 1,594 ms
  (jq: 907 ms).
- **jq: a `foreach` whose EXTRACT is an array holding the state is 1.9x faster, and 4-12x where the state grows** (#6581).
  `[foreach range(n) as $i (0; . + $i; [$i, .])]` now builds the EXTRACT's array on the owned tree, as an UPDATE
  of that shape already did. It is taken for a constructor with exactly one `.` member whose other members are
  closed or read off the state. Before, every step ran it on the evaluator's general route and re-indexed the
  state for each `.` it read. 400,000 steps take 109 ms instead of 208 ms on an Apple M4 Pro and 157 ms instead
  of 289 ms on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (measured before #6608 landed); a state that grows by `. + [$i]` while only the last output is kept takes
  561 ms instead of 6,656 ms at 20,000 steps on the M4 Pro (1,590 ms instead of 7,558 ms on the 7950X; still
  quadratic: the output shares the state, so the next append copies it). An object EXTRACT (`{i: $i, s: .}`)
  was already answered off the tree by #6608, so it does not change here (0.99x on the M4 Pro). A constructor the
  arm does not take runs as before, within 0-5% of the old time. Output is identical to jq 1.7.1's.
- **jq: a fold step that binds a scalar read off its state with `as` is 1.4-3.0x faster** (#6582).
  A `reduce`, `foreach`, `until` or `while` step such as `. as $s | $s + $x`, `(. + $x) as $t | $t` or
  `.n as $n | .n = $n + 1` now binds the value and answers the body on the state. Before, the whole
  binding ran on a re-indexed copy of the state every step. On an Apple M5 over 4,000,000 `reduce`
  steps, `.n as $n | .n = $n + 1` takes 1,054 ms instead of 3,156 ms (jq 1.7.1: 2,564 ms), and
  `. as $s | $s + $x` takes 928 ms instead of 1,799 ms (jq: 646 ms). An `if` body
  (`(. + $x) as $t | if $t > 1000 then 0 else $t end`) gains least: 1,849 ms instead of 2,584 ms.
- **jq: `recurse(.children[]?)` reads each node's children off the tree instead of re-indexing the node** (#6595).
  A static path ending in `.[]?` (`.children[]?`, `.[]?`, `.a.b[]?`) used to write every visited node, and so
  its whole subtree, out as JSON text and index it again, once per ancestor, so the walk grew with depth at a
  fixed node count. Over 1 million nodes in chains 10, 30 and 60 deep, `[.[] | recurse(.children[]?)] | length`
  went from 3.56, 4.98 and 8.01 s to 1.65, 1.44 and 2.04 s (jq 1.7.1: 1.2-1.3 s), and `| .name` from 2.79, 4.38
  and 7.76 s to 1.00, 0.94 and 1.50 s, which is 1.3-1.4x faster than jq on the shallower chains (AMD Ryzen 9
  7950X, interleaved, median of 5). A step that would raise (`1 | .children[]?` raises in jq: its `?` guards only
  the iteration) still takes the old route, so every error and every output is unchanged. A `recurse` whose
  later stage builds a value (`{id, name}`) is still slower than jq and still grows with depth.
- **jq: a constructor of static reads, `{id, name}`, `[.id]` or `{a: .b.c, k: "lit"}`, is built from the tree instead of re-indexing the value it reads** (#6608).
  After `recurse(.children[]?)`, each visited node was written out as JSON text and indexed again to read two
  fields, so the walk grew with depth at a fixed node count. `[.[] | recurse(.children[]?) | {id, name}] | length`
  over 1 million nodes in chains 10, 30 and 60 deep went from 3.00, 4.07 and 6.17 s to 1.51, 1.39 and 1.91 s
  (jq 1.7.1: 1.71-1.76 s, so 1.2-1.3x faster than jq on the first two), and `| [.id]` from 2.25, 3.36 and 5.59 s
  to 1.09, 1.01 and 1.52 s (AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, interleaved, median of 5). A computed key, a generator, a variable,
  or a step that would raise (`.id` on a number) still takes the old route, so every output and every error is
  unchanged. A walk more than about 40 levels deep is still slower than jq.
- **jq: a document nested 41 to 64 levels deeper than a record is no longer read twice as slowly as a shallower one** (#6614).
  The conversion of a document into a value tries a one-pass text reader on every child of a container, and
  that reader gave up at 64 levels after descending all the way to the limit, so the walk paid for the failed
  attempt again one level further down at every level above the 64th. It now reads to the validator's 128
  levels. Over 1 million nodes in chains 40, 50 and 60 nodes deep (80 to 120 levels),
