  `[.[] | recurse(.children[]?)] | length` went from 1.83, 1.82 and 1.76 s to 1.17, 1.15 and 1.14 s
  (jq 1.7.1: 1.18-1.23 s, so from 0.65x to 1.03-1.05x of it) and `[.[] | tojson | length] | add` from 1.01 s to
  0.46 s (jq: 1.58 s; AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, interleaved, median of 5). Documents up to 30 nodes deep (60 levels)
  and `map(.id)` are unchanged. A document nested more than 128 levels (the pinned jq 1.7.1 reads 140 and refuses 180)
  reads 6-8% slower than before: the reader's failed attempts now go deeper before they stop, and the
  walk stops trying it at depth 128 instead of 192.
- **jq: a `--seq` stream with a diagnostic reads its plain records in one pass** (#6620).
  One truncated record sends a `--seq` run down the route that converts each record as the queue is read, and
  52% of its time on a 100 MB stream was building each record through the checked materializer (an index, a
  delimiter walk, a cursor conversion). A record of plain RFC 8259 text is now read directly, as `fromjson`
  and `--slurpfile` read it; anything the one-pass reader declines (jq's leniencies, a repeated key, nesting
  past 128 levels, a grammar error) is decided by the materializer as before. `--seq -r .name` over 100 MB with
  one truncated record went from 3.33 s to 2.39 s (first record) and 3.37 s to 2.43 s (last), and `--seq -c .`
  from 2.96 s to 1.88 s and 3.03 s to 1.92 s, which is 1.14-1.17x of jq 1.7.1 (2.19 s); `.name` and `.id`
  stay at 0.45-0.48x of it (jq: 1.10 s) (AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, interleaved, median of 5). A clean stream is
  unchanged (0.99-1.01x).
- **jq: a `--seq` stream with a diagnostic reads each record where it is for the programs that can** (#6620).
  The records of such a stream reach the main loop as owned values, which it wrote back out as text, indexed and read through a cursor before the program ran. A record is now handed to the owned evaluator's own doors, as a `--stream` event is, and a program none of them answers (`[.id,.name]`, `keys`, one that reads `input`) reads the record's index as before; a run of four such records closes the door for 64 records, and it asks again after that, so a stream whose records change shape gets it back. `--seq -r` over a 100 MB stream whose last record is truncated, before and after, interleaved, median of 9: `.name` 2.27 s to 1.50 s (-34%) and `{id,name}` 2.95 s to 1.94 s (-34%) on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, `.name` 2.06 s to 1.37 s (-34%) and `{id,name}` 2.65 s to 1.80 s (-32%) on an Apple M4 Pro (a truncated first record, and 1 MB and 10 MB streams: -29% to -36%). That is 0.70x of jq 1.7.1 on `.name` and 0.85x on `{id,name}` on the 7950X (from 0.46x and 0.56x), and 0.89x and 1.24x on the M4 Pro (from 0.59x and 0.85x). The programs the door declines are not faster: on the M4 Pro they read -4.4% to +1.7% (control -1.7% to +1.6%), and on the 7950X +1% to +3% with one 1 MB row at +5% (control -1.1% to +1.3%; a build with the door forced off reads +0.9% at the median against the same baseline, so about half of that is code layout). Output is identical to the old route's on every configuration and to jq 1.7.1's on a 10,000-case program-by-stream differential of the final code (`scripts/jq-seq-door-sweep.py`), and peak memory is unchanged (159 MB on the M4 Pro, 157 MB on the 7950X, against jq's 3 MB). The walks that run twice over such a stream stay with #6620.
- **jq: a `--seq` stream with a diagnostic is walked once** (#6620).
  The clean check that sends a `--seq` run down the lazy route walks the whole stream with jq's reader, and when a record is truncated it threw that walk away and the route that reads such a stream walked the same bytes again (and read a named file a second time). The route now takes the check's walk, with the faults it queues, for a stream read from stdin or one file, and places the values' locations from it without a second pass over the reader; a slurp, several files and a file that did not open keep the walk they made. `--seq -r` over a 100 MB stream whose last record is truncated, before and after, interleaved, median of 9: `.name` 1.50 s to 1.07 s (-28%), `{id,name}` 1.94 s to 1.50 s (-23%) and `select(.age>30)|.name` 1.68 s to 1.24 s (-26%) on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, `.name` 1.31 s to 0.98 s (-25%), `{id,name}` 1.70 s to 1.36 s (-20%) and `select(.age>30)|.name` 1.41 s to 1.07 s (-24%) on an Apple M4 Pro (1 MB and 10 MB: -15% to -29%). The programs the owned evaluator declines gain too, `[.id,.name]` and `keys` -14% on the 7950X and -12% to -14% on the M4 Pro, and a program that reads `input` does not change (within -1.6% to +2.3%). Against jq 1.7.1 that is `.name` at 0.98x (from 0.69x) and `{id,name}` at 1.12x (from 0.86x) on the 7950X, and 1.20x (from 0.90x) and 1.56x (from 1.26x) on the M4 Pro. Output is identical on all 36 configurations of each A/B and to jq 1.7.1's on a program-by-stream differential over stdin and over a named file, and peak memory is unchanged (158 MB to 150 MB on the 7950X, 159 MB on the M4 Pro; jq: 3 MB).
- **jq: `[.a, .b]`, `keys` and `has(K)` of an owned record are answered from the tree** (#6620).
  The owned evaluator's doors answered `[.a]` and `{id, name}` (#6608) but read an array of two or more static reads, `keys` and `has(K)` through the re-index bridge: the record written out as JSON, indexed and read back for two fields or its field names. An array of operands that are literals, static reads or containers built from them now builds from the tree, one element per operand in order (`[(.id, .name)]` collects as the bare comma does, and a generator, an optional or an arithmetic operand keeps the bridge), and `keys` and `has` of an owned object or array are a fresh array or boolean, in jq mode (yq lists a mapping's keys in document order and keeps its own). Every owned input reads these, not `--seq` alone: a `--stream` event, a `-R` line, a `--stream -s` array and a `recurse` walk. `--seq -r` over a 100 MB stream whose last record is truncated, before and after, interleaved, median of 9: `[.id,.name]` 2.50 s to 1.36 s (-46%) and `keys` 2.54 s to 1.50 s (-41%) on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, `[.id,.name]` 2.05 s to 1.22 s (-40%) and `keys` 2.20 s to 1.39 s (-37%) on an Apple M4 Pro (a truncated first record, and 1 MB and 10 MB streams: -35% to -46%). Against jq 1.7.1 that is `[.id,.name]` at 1.08x (from 0.59x) and `keys` at 1.22x (from 0.72x) on the 7950X, and 1.47x (from 0.88x) and 1.76x (from 1.11x) on the M4 Pro. The programs the doors already answered, and a program that reads `input`, do not move (-2.0% to +2.1% on the 7950X, -1.2% to +1.9% on the M4 Pro). Output is identical on all 36 configurations of each A/B and to the re-index bridge's over a value-by-program matrix, and to jq 1.7.1's on a program-by-stream differential over stdin and a named file.
- **jq: a `foreach` whose EXTRACT is an array of reads of the state is 1.7-3.7x faster** (#6629).
  `[foreach range(n) as $i ({a: 1, b: 2}; .a += 1; [.a, .b])]` now builds the EXTRACT's array on the owned
  tree, as one holding the state itself already did (#6581); before, every step ran it on the evaluator's
  general route. 400,000 steps take 161 ms instead of 362 ms on an Apple M4 Pro and 200 ms instead of 494 ms
  on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X; over a ten-key state 0.27x of the old time on both, and `[.a, .n]` moving an array
  slot out of the state 0.58x on the M4 Pro and 0.47x on the 7950X. Whether an EXTRACT is such a constructor
  is decided once per fold instead of walked for every step, and a fork stops offering a shape the state never
  fits (`[.a, .a]`) after four declines in a row; a shape the fold never takes, or one that declines, is within 0-3% of
  the old time (interleaved, median of 11, with a base-against-base control). An object EXTRACT with no `.`
  member is unchanged: the evaluator already answers it off the tree (#6608), and the step was 1.03x on the
  7950X and 0.93-0.95x on the M4 Pro. Output is identical to jq 1.7.1's.
- **jq: a slice of a built array is a view, not a copy, so a loop that peels one element per step is linear** (#6659).
  `.[a:b]` of an array the program built (or a loop carries) copied the range; it is now a refcount bump on the
  same storage, as jq's slice is (ADR-0029), an append to such a view writes in place, and `def`'s tail loop
  settles a `length > 10`-style condition without writing the array out as JSON. On `[range(50000)]`,
  `def f: if length>10 then .[1:]|f else length end; f` went from 62.9 s to the 68 ms floor of a bare `length` on an
  AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (54.3 s to 89 ms on an Apple M4 Pro), and stays there at 100,000; `[while(length>10; .[1:])]`
  at 25,000 elements peaked at 9.78 GB on the 7950X and now peaks at 13 MB (22.7 MB at 100,000). A queue loop
  (`.[1:] | . + [$i]` per round) went from 685 ms to the floor at 50,000. Array reads that never slice are
  unchanged on both machines (median -1.0% and -0.5% on the 7950X, -0.1% and -0.1% on the M4 Pro, all inside an
  A/A control's band). Output is unchanged, and a slice now has jq's identity: `[1,nan,2] as $a | $a[1:] ==
  $a[1:]` is `true`, as in jq, where it was `false`.
- **jq: a loop that reads an array or object the program built (by index, narrow slice, `length`, `has` or key) is no longer quadratic** (#6666).
  `[range(N)] | [range(0; length; 2) as $i | .[$i:$i+2]]`, `.users | map(.id) | [range(0; length; 2) as $i | .[$i]]` and
  their `.[3:5]` and `limit`/`first` forms walked the whole array on every read: the reindex bridge's document had no
  element index, and the slice arm collected and decoded every element before taking its range. The bridge's document now
  gets the same per-document memos as a document read, and the slice reads only its range. On an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X
  (jq 1.7.1 beside, same output): `.[$i]` over 20,000 elements 3,105 ms to 8 ms (jq 9 ms), `.[$i:$i+2]` 13,524 ms to 14 ms
  (jq 12 ms) and over 200,000 elements 104 ms (jq 107 ms); over a 6.9 MB `users` document
  `.users | map(.id) | [range(0; length; 2) as $i | .[$i:$i+2]]` went from an allocation abort after 43 s to 85 ms (jq
  150 ms; `[range(0; length; 2) as $i | length]` over 50,000 elements 18,510 ms to 20 ms, and a loop of 25,000 `.[$k]` reads of a
  50,000-key object built by `from_entries` from over 30 s to about 55 ms, jq 105 ms); a loop that streams its reads (`range(...) as $i | .[$i]` with no `[...]` around it) is linear too (10,000
  elements 781 ms to 12 ms, 20,000 elements `last(... .[$i:$i+2][0])` 28,919 ms to 23 ms, jq 22 ms). Reads that were
  already fast are unchanged (`.users[4242]`, `.[100:200]`, `del(.[0:100])` within 1-2%). The
  front slice of an owned array in a loop that keeps or recurses over its tails is a separate cost (#6659). The M4 Pro was not
  measured.
- **jq: a loop that reads the tail of a built array is no longer quadratic** (#6692). `[range(0; N; 2) as $i | .[$i:][0]]` (and `.[$i:][-1]`, `.[$i:] | length`, `.[$i:][:2]`, also inside `first`, `select`, `limit` and `try`) built each tail, `N - $i` elements decoded and copied, before reading one element or two of it. `eval.rs`'s two pipe drivers now answer the slice and the read from the slice's resolved range, as the generic evaluator already did (#4195, #4288), and a second literal slice (`.[a:b][c:d]`) is composed onto the first's range for both evaluators. At N = 20,000, `.[$i:][0]` takes 8 ms where it took 6.0 s on a Ryzen 9 7950X (4.8 s to 7 ms on an M4 Pro), and `.[$i:] | length` 8 ms where it took 10.4 s; at N = 160,000 it takes 51 ms (36 ms). Output is unchanged: 0 of 23,096 differential rows differ from jq 1.7.1.
- **yq, jq: a computed result is printed as JSON into one buffer instead of keeping a `String` per node alive** (#6814).
  `format_json` (the printer behind `succinctly yq -o json` for any result the cursor streamers do not
  print, and behind `succinctly jq`'s `-S`, `-a`, `-C` and `-s`) built a `String` for every value, a
  `Vec<String>` of them for every array and object, and a `join` per level, which was 42-51% of the live
  heap at the peak of a whole-document write. Arrays and objects now append straight into one buffer (a scalar or key still
  builds its own short-lived text); the output is byte-identical. A 100 MB `.zzz = 1` with `-o json` peaks at 1059 MB instead of 1260 MB
  (`-I0`) and 1454 MB (indented) on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, and at 1174 MB instead of 1505 MB and 1730 MB
  on an Apple M4 Pro, and finishes 10-45% sooner; across the `users`, `navigation`, `comprehensive` and
  `nested` patterns peak RSS falls 9-47% and time 10-45% (up to 3-12% and 6-24% for a result that is
  only a part of the document). Indented output now peaks where compact output does.
- **yq: a write with YAML output peaks at 36-49% less memory on record and nested documents** (#6815).
  A node of the tree that carries comments, styles and anchors to the output was 224 bytes whether or
  not it had any, and a write builds it twice (the document's, then the result's). It is now 32 bytes:
  the node's metadata is boxed only when it says something, and an object's field and key maps sit
  behind a pointer each. `.zzz = 1` with `-o yaml` on a 100 MiB `users` file peaks at 2897 MiB instead of
  4902 MiB on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X and 2886 MiB instead of 5036 MiB on an Apple M4 Pro, in 14.2% and
  4.8% less time; `navigation`, `comprehensive` and `nested` fall 41-45% the same way, and `-P`,
  `del()` and copying writes 36-49%. The output is byte for byte the same, and the JSON-output write and the
  fast path are unchanged.
- **A bound string of 4 KiB or more is held behind a refcount in its marker, so a loop that reads it no longer copies it every round** (#6832). A string is stored inline, and the marker that stands for a bound variable was cloned once per pipe step (`rewrite_markers`, at every re-entry of the evaluator), so `"abcd" * 1750000 | . as $t | [range(100) | . as $w | ($t | length)]` copied the 7 MB string 100 times (`memmove` was the whole profile). Those clones are now pointer bumps: in `succinctly yq --jq-extensions` that loop takes 25 ms instead of 565 ms on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (22x; 1 MB 12.8x, 10 MB 23x, and 7 MB over 400 rounds 84x, the cost no longer growing with the rounds) and 12.4 ms instead of 29.0 ms on an Apple M4 Pro (2.3x; 400 rounds 5.7x), where macOS's allocator hid most of the copy; with a stage that works on the string every round (`ascii_upcase | length`) it is 1.6x on the 7950X, and in `succinctly jq` the same loop is 1.8x there and level on the M4 Pro. A string below 4 KiB stays inline (3 KB over 20,000 rounds: 0.99x and 1.01x), and so does one nothing binds (a string-building `reduce`: 0.98x and 1.04x). The output is unchanged.
- **yq: a call to a `def` whose body is a string's `length` is read off the string in a loop body instead of being written out and indexed again every round** (#6833).
  With `--jq-extensions`, `def f: length; "abcd" * 1750000 | . as $t | [range(100) | . as $w | ($t | f)]` took the reindex bridge once per call,
  as the inline `length` did before #6534; the owned stage now answers a parameterless `def` call whose body is exactly `length` from the string, as `succinctly jq` and both modes' `reduce` step already did (#6841).
  A 7 MB string over 100 rounds takes 32 ms instead of 541 ms on an Apple M4 Pro (16.9x; 1 MB 12.0x, 10 MB 17.9x) and 566 ms instead of 1120 ms on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (2.0x, where the pipe's per-round copy of the bound string remains, #6832).
  The output is unchanged.
- **yq: an update over a list of merging mappings or aliases is linear, not quadratic** (#6839). `.list[] |= (.x = 7)` over N mappings that each merge one source (`<<: *base`), or N aliases of it (`- *base`), took time that grew about fourfold per doubling of N: each nested write walked the whole table of merged members and aliases, whose paths are the document's and not the body's, each path prefix looked for its anchor among every alias, and the propagation after the write rebuilt the document around each alias slot. The table is now off inside an update body with a target below the root, alias positions are found through a hash, and a slot is replaced in place. Release builds, interleaved A/B, output identical on every row (`ab-cli.py`, 5 repetitions, medians): on a 7950X the merge rows at 2,000/4,000/8,000 mappings read 505/1,945/8,429 ms before and 28/56/115 ms after, the alias rows at 4,000/8,000/16,000 read 577/2,289/9,027 ms before and 20/39/78 ms after; on an M4 Pro 277/1,058/4,166 ms before and 22/41/81 ms after for the merge rows, 386/1,496/5,909 ms before and 16/29/55 ms after for the aliases. After, the time doubles with N out to 64,000 mappings (1.06 s on the 7950X) and 32,000 aliases (155 ms). A document with no aliases or merges is unchanged on the M4 Pro (-0.3% median over three update rows); on the 7950X its update rows read +1.2%, and so do read-only rows that never touch this code (`.items | length`, `select`), which is the binary's layout and not this change. The same gate corrects a write: with `a: &x {p: 1}` and `b: *x` at the top and an element `{a: {p: 1}, b: {p: 1}}`, `.items[] |= (.b.p = 9)` wrote the element's `a.p` (the body's `.b` was matched against the document's alias position `b`) and now writes its `b.p`, as yq does.
- **yq: a write through N aliases of N different anchors is linear, not quadratic** (#6869). `.m[].p += 1` over `l: [&a0 {p: 0}, &a1 {p: 1}, ...]` / `m: [*a0, *a1, ...]` grew about fourfold per doubling of N: the alias table's redirect bound, asked for every path component of every fanned-out path, summed the alias count of every group on each call (a single anchor with N aliases, as in #6839, made that sum one term). The bound is now computed once where the table is built. Release builds, interleaved A/B, output identical on every row (`ab-cli.py`, 5 repetitions, medians; an unrelated single-core `rustc` build was running on each box, aggregate CPU 89-97% idle, and a base-against-itself control read within ±1%): on a 7950X `.m[].p += 1` at 2,000/4,000/8,000 anchors reads 27/72/221 ms before and 17/34/71 ms after, `.m[] |= (.p += 1)` reads 20/50/141 ms before and 15/30/63 ms after; on an M4 Pro 19/66/241 ms before and 15/26/49 ms after for the first, 15/43/138 ms before and 12/22/42 ms after for the second. After, the time doubles with N out to 64,000 anchors (621 ms on the 7950X, 367 ms on the M4 Pro). A 30,000-element plain document is unchanged on both (`.items[] |= (.b = 7)`: -0.5% and +0.2%).
- **yq: a write with YAML output peaks at 20-49% less memory on a document with plain, comment-free parts, and runs 8-17% faster, 25% with `-P`** (#6880).
  A write builds the presentation tree (comments, styles, anchors) of the document and then a second
  one for its result, a node for every node of the document even where there is nothing to carry. The
  snapshot now holds one word in place of each subtree that says nothing, and the result's tree is
  not walked over it. `.zzz = 1` with `-o yaml` on a 100 MiB `users` file peaks at 1760 MiB instead of
  2899 MiB on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (39% less, 8.52 s instead of 10.32 s) and at 1966 MiB instead of 3061
  MiB on an Apple M4 Pro; `-P` on 20 MiB falls 49% (718 to 365 MiB, 7950X), `.users[0].name |= "X"`
  39%, `del(.users[0])` 20%, and `comprehensive` and `nested` 31-36% at 100 MiB. A document that carries a quoted
  string or a comment in every record (`navigation`: a quoted timestamp each) saves almost nothing
  (3%), and one with an alias, a metadata write (`style =`, `head_comment =`, `tag =`) or a plain `=`
  from a read (`.c = .a`) builds the full tree as before. The output is byte for byte the same.
- **yq: a parenthesised `..` write over many aliases of different anchors is linear, not quadratic** (#6883). `(.. | select(tag == "!!int")) |= . + 1` over `l: [&a0 {p: 0}, &a1 {p: 1}, ...]` / `m: [*a0, *a1, ...]` grew about threefold per doubling of N: the descent's paths that lie below an alias position (yq's `..` does not go into an alias) were removed from the resolved list with a scan and a shift per path, each step a deep expression comparison. They are removed in one pass now, matched by a byte key counted in a multiset (one entry per mention, as the scan did). Release builds, interleaved A/B, output identical on every row (`ab-cli.py`, 5 repetitions, medians; a base-against-itself control read within ±1.2%; the 7950X was idle, a Chrome renderer held one core of the M4 Pro): on a 7950X the rows at 2,000/4,000/8,000 anchors read 52/156/528 ms before and 28/56/111 ms after; on an M4 Pro 45/135/460 ms before and 22/40/75 ms after. After, the time doubles with N out to 64,000 anchors (979 ms on the 7950X, 598 ms on the M4 Pro). A 30,000-element plain document is unchanged on the M4 Pro (-0.1% median over three update and read rows) and reads +1.0% on the 7950X, where `.items | length`, which never reaches this code, reads +2.4%: the binary's layout, not this change.
- **jq: a plain filter over one regular file reads it a window at a time, so its peak memory no longer grows with the file** (#6920). `jq -c .`, `jq -r .name` and `jq 'select(...)'` (no `-n`, no `input`) over a regular file of 4 MiB or more used to read it whole and split every document into a span first: 127 to 129 MiB at 100 MiB of NDJSON on x86_64 and 122 to 123 on aarch64, where jq's stays at a few MB. They now hold a 1 MiB window and the document being run, 10 to 12 MiB on x86_64 and 13 on aarch64 (that machine's floor for any process), flat from 10 MiB to 100 MiB. Output, error wording, exit status and the `(at file:N)` lines are the whole-file route's, checked against it on faults at several positions, an unterminated last document, a BOM, invalid UTF-8, pretty-printed and one-line streams, a document larger than a window, a named pipe, `/dev/stdin` and depth refusals. Time at 100 MiB on a 7950X: `.` −3.5%, `.name` −3.9%, `select` −5.4%, `keys` −5.1%; neutral on an M4 Pro; a file that is one document (single-line or pretty-printed) reads as before, within 2%. Standard input, a pipe, several files, programs that call `input`/`inputs`, `-R`, `--seq`, `-s` and `--validate` still read the input whole.
- **yq: a run of `---` markers on one line is read in linear time** (#6963). `--- --- --- ... a` cost the length of the line for every marker, because `yq`'s header preprocessing copied the rest of the line out for each one: 80,000 markers took 9.4 s on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X and 4.2 s on an Apple M4 Pro, 160,000 took 39.3 s and 16.8 s, and 320,000 did not finish in a minute. A marker followed by text is now settled from the bytes around it, and the rest of the line is an offset, not a copy: 1,280,000 markers (5 MB) read in the same 0.07 s (7950X) and 0.09 s (M4 Pro) as 5,000, which is the floor of the memory-capped harness. The output is the same, checked over all 402,234 short header inputs against the copying implementation and 16,000 end-to-end runs against an older build.
- **jq: `-n` programs that read `input`/`inputs`, and `-R`, read a regular file a window at a time, so their peak memory no longer grows with the file** (#7023, slice 2 of #6920). `jq -n 'reduce inputs as $x (...)'` and `jq -R length` over a file used to hold all of it: 107 MiB (aarch64) and 115 MiB (x86_64) at 100 MiB of NDJSON, where jq's stays at a few MB. They now hold about a 1 MiB window and the line or document being run, 11 to 16 MiB on both machines, flat from 10 MiB to 100 MiB. The `inputs` route also takes standard input this way. `-R` takes a regular file of 4 MiB or more; a file that is smaller, several files, and standard input under `-R` are read whole as before. Output, error wording, exit status, `input_line_number` and the `(at file:N)` marker after the last input are the whole-file route's, checked against it and against jq 1.7.1 on faults at several positions, an unterminated last document, a BOM, invalid UTF-8, documents that run across lines, a last line with no line break and a document larger than a window. Time on a 7950X at 100 MiB: `reduce inputs` −2.7%, `-R` with a filter −6.0%, `-nR` with `reduce inputs` −54%; on an M4 Pro +0.4%, −2.0% and −60%. At 1 MiB `reduce inputs` reads +5% slower on the 7950X (0.5 ms) and +1% on the M4 Pro.
- **jq: a regular file on standard input (`jq -c . < file`) is read a window at a time like a path is, so its peak memory no longer grows with the file** (#7024, #6920). A plain filter (no `-n`, no `input`, no `--slurp`, `--validate` or `--seq`) over a redirected regular file of 4 MiB or more used to read it whole and split every document into a span first, as it does a pipe; it now holds a 1 MiB window and the document being run (14 MiB at 60 MiB of NDJSON against 84 MiB through a pipe). Output, error wording, exit status and the `(at <stdin>:N)` lines are the pipe's, checked on faults at several positions, an unterminated last document, a BOM, invalid UTF-8 and a stdin that starts at an offset a parent has read to. A pipe and a terminal on standard input, and a stdin under 4 MiB, still read the input whole.
- **jq: a plain filter over several regular files reads them a window at a time, so its peak memory no longer grows with the files** (#7024, #6920). `jq -c . a.json b.json` (up to 32 regular files, 4 MiB or more between them; no `-n`, no `input`, no `--slurp`, `--validate` or `--seq`) read every file whole and split every document into a span first: 225 MiB for one 100 MiB file named twice on x86_64 and 255 on aarch64, where jq holds 3. It now holds one 1 MiB window and the document being run, 10.2 MiB on x86_64 and 6.7 on aarch64, flat from 10 MiB to 100 MiB, and reads 8% to 12% faster on x86_64 and 2% to 5% on aarch64 (a control run read within 1%). The files are read as the one stream jq reads them as: a token open where a file ends continues at the front of the next, and the file `input_filename` and a diagnostic name, the line a runtime error names and the wording of the first fault are the whole-file route's, checked on over 2,000 random streams cut into 1 to 32 files with BOMs, invalid UTF-8 and faults. A pipe on standard input, more than 32 files, a list with a path that is not a regular file and `-R` or `input`/`inputs` over several files still read the input whole. A regular file that is also standard output or error (`jq . f 1<>f`), alone or among several, is read whole now, as a standard input of that kind already was, since its output would land where the next window is read from; a file whose `stat` size is 0 and which has content (`/proc`) is read to its end.
- **jq: a plain filter over a pipe on standard input reads it a window at a time, so its peak memory no longer grows with the stream** (#7024, #6920). `cat log.ndjson | jq -c .` (a pipe or socket holding 4 MiB or more; no `-n`, no `input`, no `--slurp`, `--validate` or `--seq`) read the whole stream and split every document into a span first, about 124 MiB at 100 MiB of NDJSON on x86_64, because a regular file words its first fault by reading itself again and a pipe cannot. Each window is now certified before it is dropped: a document the strict validator accepts is one jq's parser reads without a fault, and only a document it turns down is read by jq's parser model over the bytes as read. So the first fault is worded as the whole stream words it, even where it sits in a document the filter never read and the window that held it is gone (checked against the same pipe read whole by unit tests over random streams at six window sizes, CLI tests and `scripts/jq-windowed-file-fuzz.py --pipe`). A pipe under 4 MiB, a terminal, `-R` over a pipe and `--seq` over a pipe still read the input whole, and a run that stops early now leaves the rest of the pipe unread, as jq does. The windows are certified on a thread of their own (#7106), over a copy of each, so the filter does not wait for the validator: measured interleaved at 100 MiB with an A/A control (which moved 0.4% at most), peak RSS falls from 125 to 23-26 MiB on a Ryzen 9 7950X and from 123 to 19 MiB on an M4 Pro, while `-c .` is 5.9% and 2.3% faster than the route that read the pipe whole, `-r .name` 5.0% and 3.0%, and `select(.score>50)` 2.7% and 2.4% (certifying on the filter's thread cost 3% to 17% instead). A window over 8 MiB, which holds a document bigger than a few windows, is certified without a copy. A regular file, several files and a pipe under 4 MiB start no thread.
- **jq: `-R` over standard input reads it a window at a time, so its peak memory no longer grows with the stream** (#7024, #7023). `cat log | jq -R .` (a pipe or socket holding 4 MiB or more) and `jq -R . < log` (a regular file with 4 MiB or more left from where it stands) read the whole stream first, as `-R` over a file named on the command line did before #7023; they are now read by that route's `LineWindows`, a regular file from its offset and a pipe after a probe of its first 4 MiB. A stream of lines has no fault to word, so nothing is read again or certified. Measured interleaved at 100 MiB of NDJSON against the route that read it whole, with an A/A control (within 3.6%) and outputs identical, on idle machines: peak RSS falls from 111 to 115 MiB to 14 to 20 MiB on a Ryzen 9 7950X and from 107 to 108 MiB to 8 to 13 MiB on an M4 Pro, and the run is faster on a pipe, `-R .` by 7.5% and 5.4%, `-nR 'reduce inputs as $l (0; .+1)'` by 15.8% and 6.8% and `-R 'select(endswith("9}"))'` by 11.8% and 6.7%, and redirected by 0.9% to 16.3%. A standard input not opened for reading (`jq . 0>>file`) reads as empty at every size again, on this route and on the plain filter's pipe and redirected-file routes, which had reported `EBADF` at 4 MiB or more. A pipe under 4 MiB, a terminal, `--slurp`, `--stream`, `--seq` and `--validate` still read the input whole, and a run that stops early now leaves the rest of the pipe unread (and a redirected file at the offset its last window ended), as jq does.
- **jq: a plain filter over more than 32 regular files reads them a window at a time too** (#7024). `jq -c . logs/*.json` over a list of more than 32 files read every file whole, since the several-files route held each file open for the second read that words a fault and capped the list to keep the descriptor table under 64 slots. Such a list is now judged a file at a time and closed, and each file is opened again as the run reaches it, as jq opens it. A run over hundreds of files holds one of them open at a time, as jq does, and its peak memory stays flat: `-c .` over 100 MiB of NDJSON in 64 or 256 files peaks at 9.6 to 10.6 MiB against 109 to 110 MiB before on x86_64 and at 6.4 to 6.8 MiB against 107 on aarch64, flat from 10 MiB, and reads 7.6% to 8.5% faster on x86_64 and 5.0% on aarch64 (`select` 2.1% to 3.0%, against an A/A control within 1.4% at 100 MiB). A path removed or replaced after the run starts is read as jq reads it when it gets there: a file that will not open is reported in jq's words once the reader is past it, and the run ends after the next value with exit 2.
- **jq: `-R` over several regular files reads them a window at a time** (#7024). `jq -R . a.log b.log` (up to 32 regular files, 4 MiB or more between them) read every file whole, where one file has been read a window at a time since #7023. Each file is now read a window at a time and in turn, as the one stream of lines jq reads: a file's last line without a line break runs on into the next file's first and is read in the later file, `input_line_number` counts each file's own lines, and each file's bytes are decoded on their own, as jq 1.7.1 does. At 100 MiB of NDJSON in 4 or 16 files peak RSS falls from 108.5-111.7 MiB to 11.7-14.7 on x86_64 and from 105.4-107.0 to 8.2-12.5 on aarch64, flat from 10 MiB; `-R .`, `-R length` and a `select` read 4.3% to 6.7% faster on x86_64 and within the control's range on aarch64, and `-nR 'reduce inputs as $l (0; .+1)'` 65% to 73% faster on both.
- **jq: `-R` over more than 32 regular files reads them a window at a time** (#7024). `jq -R . logs/*.log` over a list of more than 32 files, 4 MiB or more between them, read every file whole, since the several-files route held each file open and stopped at 32 to keep the descriptor table small. Such a list is now judged by `stat`, and each file is opened when the run reaches it and closed after its lines, as jq opens them, so the run holds one file at a time. At 100 MiB of NDJSON in 64 or 256 files peak RSS for `-R .` falls from 108.5-108.7 MiB to 11.2-12.8 on x86_64 and from 105.8-106.1 to 5.8-6.6 on aarch64, flat from 10 MiB; `-nR 'reduce inputs as $l (0; . + ($l | length))'` reads 50% to 61% faster on both, and `-R .` and `select` read within the control's range on aarch64 at 100 MiB and 6% to 22% faster on x86_64 (the unchanged 16-file route read 5% to 9% faster in the same build, so part of that is layout). A file that will not open when the run reaches it (removed, made a directory, or without read permission since the run started) is reported in jq's words once its reader is past it, and the run ends after the next line with exit 2, as the whole-file route reports it.
- **jq: `input`/`inputs` over several regular files reads them a window at a time** (#7024). `jq -n 'reduce inputs as $x (...)' a.json b.json` (up to 32 regular files, 4 MiB or more between them, each of them UTF-8) read every file whole, and before the program started ran jq's parser model over all of them, where one file has been read a window at a time since #7023. Each file is now a lazy source of its own, read a window at a time and in turn; a fault, a document or number a file ends inside, or a document nested deeper than 64 levels hands the rest to the eager reader there, which words it as before and holds what is left, as the old route did. At 100 MiB of NDJSON in 4 or 16 files peak RSS falls from 111 MiB to 13-17 MiB on x86_64 and from 106-108 MiB to 8-19 MiB on aarch64, flat from 10 MiB, and the runs read 24% to 53% faster (`first(inputs)` 98.6%), against an A/A control within 2.2%.

It now holds about a 1 MiB window and the record being run, 11.2 and 6.8 MiB, flat from 10 MiB. A prepass reads the file once by position to check the framing with the checker the whole-file route uses, then the plain route's windows read it with each RS as a space. Output, error wording, exit status and the `(at file:N)` lines are the whole-file route's, checked against the base binary over 1,680 random-stream runs and against jq 1.7.1. A stream that is not that framing (a fault, a truncated tail, bytes before the first RS, a BOM, invalid UTF-8), a pipe, several files, `-s`, `--validate` and `-n` are read whole as before. - **`succinctly yq`** (#7108). A `reduce`/`ireduce` (and the fold `with(PATH; SRC as $v | WRITES)` is) whose UPDATE is a plain `=` of a scalar onto a field of the object it updates, alone, in a pipe or behind `SOURCE as $v`, is answered on the owned tree and no longer re-indexes the whole state at every step: `.k |= (.x[] as $v ireduce (.; .y = $v))` over 10,000 elements took 14 s and takes 0.04 s (3 s to 0.01 s at 5,000), and `with(.k; .x[] as $v | .y += $v)` the same. A glob or `<<` key, a container value and every other shape stay on the evaluator, with unchanged output.
- **`succinctly yq`** (#7108). A `reduce`/`ireduce` (and the fold `with(PATH; SRC as $v | WRITES)` is) whose UPDATE is `|= . + N` (or `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`) of a number field by a number is answered on the owned tree, as `+=` is, and no longer re-indexes the whole state every step: `.k |= (.x[] as $v ireduce (.; .z |= . + $v))` over 5,000 elements took 3 s and takes 0.01 s. A missing key, a non-number and every other shape stay on the evaluator, with unchanged output.
- **jq: a fold whose UPDATE is a slice with literal bounds plus a closed operand (`.[1:] + [$i]`, a sliding queue) is linear** (#7109).
  `reduce range(N) as $i (.; .[1:] + [$i])` wrote the whole state out as JSON and indexed it again on every step, so
  it was quadratic: 35.3 s at N=20,000 on an Apple M4 Pro and 37.7 s on a Ryzen 9 7950X, against jq 1.7.1's 0.05 s.
  The step now cuts the owned state and combines it with the operand, as the piped form `.[1:] | . + [$i]` already
  did, and the same row takes 9.6 ms on both (5,000 and 10,000 steps: 1.97 s and 7.77 s on the M4 Pro, 2.24 s and
  9.06 s on the 7950X, before; 4.7 ms and 6.4 ms, 3.9 ms and 5.9 ms after). Measured interleaved with an A/A control
  (7 repetitions, 3 at 20,000; the control moved 3.6% at most), output identical, and the piped form and
  `. + [$i]` rows do not move.
  A slice with a computed bound, a slice on the right of the `+`, and a right operand that reads the state
  (`[.[0]]`) still take the slower route.

Arithmetic over a container's count and number literals (`length - 5`, `2 * length`, `(length - 1) * (length + 1)`) is now answered from the owned container, as `($a | length) - 5` already was; an operation that raises (`length / 0`) or reads a non-count still goes through the evaluator, which keeps its error.
- **jq: `first`, `last`, `nth(n)`, `has(k)`, `keys` and a comparison or boolean over a count, as a stage over a bound array, are answered from the value** (#7132, part). In a loop over a bound array (`. as $a | [range(n) | $a | first]`) each of these wrote `$a` out as text and indexed it again, 6 to 25 ms per call over 100,000 elements where jq takes 0.08; `eval_owned_input`, the entry a stage after an owned value takes, lacked the single-value doors its lazy twin has, and `first`/`last`/`nth` had none anywhere. The stage is now answered right after the fast path, before the embed-table scans (the witness walk was O(input)): 0.07 to 0.10 ms per call, jq's own speed. `first`, `last` and `nth` are the `.[0]`, `.[-1]` and `.[n]` they are defined as (a negative or computed `nth`, an element an owned `Int` cannot spell as the bridge does, and a container while the embed table is live stay the bridge's), and a read that raises declines, so the error text is jq's. Output, errors and their text are jq 1.7.1's (328 programs pinned in `tests/jq_cli/i7132.rs`, captured from `/usr/bin/jq`). Stages that are a comma, a pipe of stages, an `as` bind or a construction over reads (`(length | tostring)`, `[.[0], .[1]]`, `.[0] + .[1]`, `if length > 5 ...`) still take the bridge.

A pipe is answered only when every stage is (a door, or `tostring`), a bind only when its source is a count the count door answers and its body is then a door answer or a closed value, and an `if` only when its condition a door settles and the chosen branch is a literal, `.`, a door answer or a closed value; anything that raises, fans out or reads a navigated value stays the bridge's, so errors and their text are jq 1.7.1's (304 programs pinned in `tests/jq_cli/i7132_chains.rs`, captured from `/usr/bin/jq`). Index reads in a construction and arithmetic of reads stay refused while the #2889 embed table is live, as before.
- **jq: the stages of #7132 over a value bound from the input document (`. as $a | ... | $a | has(5)`, `.items as $a | ... | $a | length > 5`) are answered from the value too** (#7132, part three). It now calls `eval_owned_value_doors`, the one set of doors the eager entry already has (a key list, a comparison over a count, `first`/`last`/`nth`, a pipe of those, an `as`-bound count, an `if` over one), so `has`, `length`, a comparison, a bind, an `if` and a chain are 0.06 to 0.22 ms (jq's own speed). A container answer of `first`/`last`/`nth` still takes the bridge while the #2889 embed table is live, which a bound document node makes it (the table witnesses the node's identity). Output, errors and their text are jq 1.7.1's (400 programs pinned in `tests/jq_cli/i7132_documents.rs`, captured from `/usr/bin/jq`).

A slice with literal bounds, with bounds the loop puts in (`.[$i:]`), under `?`, and followed by a read (`.[5:][0]`) is now cut from the value, 0.012 to 0.020 ms per call on an M4 Pro and a Ryzen 9 7950X. The lazy entry a fold's stage takes (`reduce range(n) as $i (0; $a | nth(5))`) lacked the doors parts one to three added, `first`/`last`/`nth`, a comparison over a read, a pipe of doors, an `as`-bound count and an `if` over one: 3.9 to 4.0 ms per call there, now 0.013 to 0.019. Stages that answer nothing from the value are unchanged (six control programs within 1.5% on both machines). Output, errors and their text are jq 1.7.1's (369 programs pinned in `tests/jq_cli/i7132_slices.rs`, captured from `/usr/bin/jq`).
- **jq: arithmetic, a comparison and `//` over reads of a bound value are answered from the value** (#7132, part five). `$a | .[0] + .[1]`, `first + 1`, `first > 1`, `first // 0` and `.[$i] + 1` over an array the filter built (`[range(n)] as $a | [range(m) | $a | .[0] + .[1]]`) wrote `$a` out as text and indexed it again on every call: 2.9 to 5.8 ms per call over 100,000 elements on a Ryzen 9 7950X and 2.8 to 5.1 on an M4 Pro, where jq takes 0.04. The operand grammar read arithmetic and `//` only as operands, and had no arm for `first`/`last`/`nth`; such a stage is now answered from the value whenever its answer is one the bridge's copy would print, compare and compute as, 0.018 to 0.021 ms per call on the 7950X and 0.012 to 0.013 on the M4 Pro, in a loop and in a fold alike. Stages that answer nothing from the value are unchanged (eight control programs, four of them per-element arithmetic, `//` and `select`, within 2% on both machines). Output, errors and their text are jq 1.7.1's (390 programs pinned in `tests/jq_cli/i7132_operands.rs`, captured from `/usr/bin/jq`).
- **jq: a comma of stages, `first`/`last`/`nth`/`limit`/`isempty` of `.[]`, `$__loc__` and `input_line_number` over a bound value are answered from the value** (#7132, part six). `$a | first, last`, `.[0], .[1]`, `first(.[])`, `limit(1; .[])`, `isempty(.[])`, `nth(1; .[])`, `$__loc__` and `input_line_number` over an array the filter built (`[range(n)] as $a | [range(m) | $a | first(.[])]`) wrote `$a` out as text and indexed it again on every call: 2.6 to 6.5 ms per call over 100,000 elements on a Ryzen 9 7950X and 2.8 to 6.2 on an M4 Pro, where jq takes 0.04. They are now answered from the value, 0.016 to 0.021 ms per call on the 7950X and 0.011 to 0.013 on the M4 Pro, in a loop, in a fold and inside an array constructor, with jq 1.7.1's own counts (`last` of nothing is `null`, `nth` past the end is empty, `limit(0; f)` never evaluates `f`, a negative limit is all of `f`). (. + ($a | length > 5 | if . then 1 else 0 end))`, which bridged in both forms; all three are answered from the value now.   Help, version, bad flags, missing values, usage errors and runs give the same stdout, stderr and exit status as before (79 argument vectors compared against the previous binary).

- **jq: `--seq` over several regular files is read a window at a time, so its peak memory no longer grows with the input** (#7218, part of the remainder of #6920). `jq --seq -c . a.seq b.seq ...` read every file whole: 248 MiB at 100 MiB of RFC 7464 records split into 8 files on a Ryzen 9 7950X and 255 MiB on an M4 Pro. A run is now windowed when every file is, on its own, plain records (`RS value LF`, the check of one file, #7082) ending in an LF, since the join of two such files is framed as each is; the 8-file case reads in 8.3 MiB on an M4 Pro. Any other list (a file that does not start on an RS, ends mid-record or without a final LF, is empty, or is opened by its path past 32 files, which stays whole) is read whole by the route that walks jq's reader across the seam, as before. Checked against the same files read as descriptors by `scripts/jq-windowed-file-fuzz.py --seq --files K`, which cuts the stream at record starts and anywhere else.
- **jq: `--seq` over more than 32 regular files is read a window at a time too** (#7221, the remainder of #7218). `jq --seq -c . part-*.seq` over a list of more than 32 files read every file whole, since such a list is opened by path as the run reaches each file and no prepass could vouch for what the run would then read. Each file is now judged (plain `RS value LF` records ending in an LF) on the handle the run opened when it reached it; at the first that is not, the windows end and that file and the ones after it go to the route that reads them whole, which reads them as jq's reader does after the files before (a parse warning names the line counted over every file, a runtime error the line in its own file, a byte-order mark there is not the stream's front). Over 100 MiB of RFC 7464 records in 100 files, peak RSS falls from 248.8 MiB to 11.3 on a Ryzen 9 7950X and from 255.9 to 8.9 on an M4 Pro, flat from 10 MiB; with file 50 of the 100 not plain it is 132.6 and 135.6 MiB (the files from there are held), and with every file plain the run took about half the time on the idle 7950X (714 against 1,435 ms, three interleaved runs, no control). Output and exit status are main's in every row, and `scripts/jq-windowed-file-fuzz.py --seq --files K`, which now takes K up to 512, found no difference against the same files read as descriptors over 610 streams cut into 33 to 300 files.
- **yq: a chain of merges that each name the previous source twice is read in linear time** (#7224). `m0: &m0 {k: 0}` followed by `mN: &mN {<<: [*m(N-1), *m(N-1)], iN: N}` took twice as long for every level, so `.m14` (58 s in a debug build) and `.m14.k` (40 s) ran for hours a few levels deeper, from a few hundred bytes of YAML. The kind of a `<<` source is now read off the index, as `--yaml-fix-merge-anchor-to-spec` already did, and a key lookup remembers what each source answered; a chain 60 deep answers in 3 ms in a release build. The output is unchanged.
- **jq: `-sR` moves a single input into its string instead of copying it** (#7260).
  The run held the text twice, as read and as the string; now it holds it once. `-sR length` on 100 MB of
  NDJSON peaks at 112 MB instead of 214 MB on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, against jq 1.7.1's 142 MB, and at 106 MB
  instead of 209 MB on an Apple M4 Pro, against 244 MB. It is also 45% and 22% faster (96.6 -> 53.0 ms and
  22.9 -> 17.7 ms). Several inputs are joined into the first one's buffer, reserved once.
- **jq: `walk(f)` and a plain assignment write the materialized document in place** (#7260).
  `walk` no longer writes its input out as JSON and indexes it again, and it rewrites an unshared tree in
  its own storage instead of building a second one. An assignment like `.users[0].name = "x"` writes into
  the document instead of first copying every container on its path. `walk(.)|.users|length` on 10 MB of
  `users` now peaks at 83 MB instead of 156 MB on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, against jq 1.7.1's 90 MB, and runs
  in 84 ms instead of 165 ms (jq: 782 ms). On an Apple M4 Pro it peaks at 75 MB instead of 129 MB (jq:
  96 MB), and runs in 60 ms instead of 95 ms. The assignment row is 2-5% faster and holds 2-21 MB less at
  10-100 MB.
- **The release binary puts the functions a run executes first, so far less of it is resident** (#7260).
  One codegen unit with fat LTO scattered the 1-2 MB a query runs over 12-15 MB of machine code, and every
  page a run touched stayed resident: `succinctly jq -n 1` had 5.0 MB of its own text resident on Linux
  (a file fault maps 64 KB or a whole large folio) against jq 1.7.1's 0.3 MB. The release builds for x86_64
  Linux and Apple silicon now link the functions in `scripts/link-order/symbols.txt` first. Peak RSS drops by
  a median 5.8 MB per row on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X and 1.1 MB on an Apple M4 Pro over every benchmark query
  at 1 MB (`startup` 10.1 -> 4.5 MB and 3.8 -> 2.8 MB, against jq's 3.5 and 2.7 MB), and startup-bound runs
  are 4-6% and 2-3% faster. Output is unchanged, and 100 MB rows move by -0.7% to +1.4%.
- **jq: `map_values` and `to_entries` walk a wide object's fields in place instead of listing them** (#7260).
  Both built a list of every field with its key and value decoded (144 bytes each) before doing any work;
  over one object of 82,210 fields that list was 18 MiB. When the object is well formed and no key repeats,
  the fields are now walked in place; any other object takes the old route, with its errors and
  duplicate-key rule unchanged. `to_entries` also sizes each entry object and the result exactly.
  `to_entries|length` on a 10 MB object peaks at 360 MB instead of 512 MB on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (jq
  1.7.1: 435 MB) and is 13% faster; `map_values(.+1)` peaks at 219 MB instead of 324 MB and is 7% faster.
  On an Apple M4 Pro they peak at 295 MB instead of 447 MB (jq: 513 MB) and 213 MB instead of 315 MB, and
  are 2-3% faster. `with_entries` is 3-5% faster on both.
- **jq: `tostream` and `paths` share each path's keys instead of copying them into every path** (#7260).
  A key above a container is now held once per visit and shared by every path beneath it, where each path
  carried its own copies; and `tostream` consumes the document it materializes instead of writing it out,
  indexing it again and copying every leaf. `[tostream]|length` on 10 MB of the `comprehensive` input peaks
  at 444 MB instead of 615 MB on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (jq 1.7.1: 359 MB) and runs in 390 ms instead of 527 ms
  (jq: 1688 ms); `[paths]|length` peaks at 264 MB instead of 326 MB (jq: 271 MB) and is 17% faster. On an
  Apple M4 Pro the same rows peak at 435 MB instead of 511 MB and 249 MB instead of 279 MB (jq: 362 and
  292 MB), 27% and 18% faster.
- **jq: `[..|f]` runs each node through `f` as the walk reaches it, and `sort` over document numbers sorts their parsed values** (#7260).
  A pipe that starts with `..` (or `recurse`) collected every node, then every intermediate result, before
  the rest of the pipe ran: two vectors the size of the document. `[..|numbers]|length` on 10 MB of the
  `comprehensive` input peaks at 61 MB instead of 212 MB on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (jq 1.7.1: 149 MB) and runs
  in 185 ms instead of 277 ms (jq: 598 ms); on an Apple M4 Pro 62 MB instead of 251 MB (jq: 163 MB), 10% faster.
  `sort`, `sort_by(.)`, `unique`, `unique_by(.)` and `group_by(.)` over an array of document numbers now sort a
  24-byte (value, index) pair instead of a decoded copy of every number with its cursor plus a merge buffer;
  every number keeps its spelling. `.numbers|sort|.[0]` on 10 MB peaks at 59 MB instead of 108 MB on the 7950X
  (jq: 97 MB) and is 46% faster; 57 MB instead of 95 MB on the M4 Pro (jq: 104 MB), 34% faster. `group_by(.)`
  is 2.2-4.5x faster.
- **jq: field lookups, `@tsv`, `--stream` and `inputs` over NDJSON cost less per record** (#7260).
  A field lookup compares an unescaped key's bytes with the name instead of decoding every key, twice;
  `inputs` over a run of plain documents checks each one in a single non-allocating pass instead of
  splitting it and then validating it again; `@tsv` writes each row in one pass; and `--stream` hands
  events to the program as it makes them, sharing each path's keys. At 10 MB, on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X
  and an Apple M4 Pro: `[.id,.name,.score]|@tsv` is 16% and 23% faster, `reduce inputs as $u (0;.+$u.score)`
  18% and 23%, `select(.score>500)|.id` 9% and 16%, `-r .name` 10% and 14%, `.users[].name` 9% and 18%, and
  the `--stream` reduce 6% and 3%.
- **jq: startup on macOS binds 44 fewer imports, and `--arg`-heavy command lines parse once** (#7260).
  A macOS 12 binary binds every import at launch, and each one is searched for through libSystem's
  re-exported libraries; the libm functions only the math builtins call (all but `fmod`) are now looked up on their first
  call instead. The named-flag order is read off clap's own matches instead of building and running a second
  `jq` command definition. On an Apple M4 Pro, `-n 1` and the other startup-bound runs take ~6% less time
  (`-n 1` 1.58 -> 1.48 ms, against jq 1.7.1's 1.73 ms), and eleven `--arg`/`--argjson` flags 1.67 -> 1.58 ms
  (jq: 1.76 ms); on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X the `--arg` row is 3% faster and the rest unchanged.
- **jq: a lone `--seq` file is read in windows from 64 KiB, and an array of field reads walks its object once** (#7260).
  A `--seq` file under 4 MiB whose records are not all plain took the whole-file route, which turns every record
  into an owned value; it now takes the windowed route from 64 KiB. `[.a, .b]`-style arrays of field reads find all
  their fields in one walk of the object, and `keys` over an object whose keys have no escapes sorts without the
  probe that collapses a repeated key. `--seq -c .name` over 1 MB with a malformed record is 18% faster on an AMD
  Ryzen 9 7950X (11.2 -> 9.1 ms, against jq 1.7.1's 11.4 ms) and 26-27% faster on an Apple M4 Pro (12.6 -> 9.3 ms,
  jq 13.5 ms); `[.id,.name]` over NDJSON or `--seq` is 6-20% faster and `keys` 1-9% faster.
- **jq: an object of up to 16 fields is a plain field list, and records share the keys they repeat** (#7260).
  An object was an `IndexMap` behind a refcount: an entries block, a separate hash-table block and an 88-byte
  box, so a six-field record cost three allocations beyond its strings. An object of up to 16 fields is now
  a plain list of its fields scanned in place, with a hash index only past 16, behind a 40-byte box; the JSON
  reader shares a key with the same key of the record before it, and `to_entries` builds every entry from two
  shared keys. At 10 MB of the `users` input, `.users[0].name="x"` peaks at 56 MB instead of 83 MB on an AMD
  Ryzen 9 7950X (jq 1.7.1: 65 MB) and 56 MB instead of 72 MB on an Apple M4 Pro (jq: 67 MB), 30% and 22%
  faster; `with_entries(.value+=1)` over a 10 MB object peaks at 480 MB instead of 828 MB (jq: 711 MB) and
  421 MB instead of 688 MB (jq: 898 MB), 32% and 20% faster; `--slurpfile` of 10 MB of NDJSON 38% and 37%
  faster. Library users: `OwnedValue::as_object()` now returns `Option<&FieldMap<OwnedValue>>` instead of an `IndexMap`; `FieldMap` keeps `IndexMap`'s order
  and duplicate-key behaviour.
- **jq: streaming input holds less: a `--seq` file with no RS is scanned, not held, and a pipe's windows are shared, not copied** (#7260).
  A lone `--seq` file that does not open with an RS was read whole just to print jq's one "Unfinished abandoned
  text at EOF" warning; it is now scanned 64 KiB at a time with jq's own read rules. A pipe's certifying thread
  reads each window's buffer through a shared handle instead of a copy, the probe is read and freed in 1 MiB
  blocks, the lazy `inputs` route reads every window onto its text, and a resumed `--seq` tail carries its line
  count instead of a line break per line. `--seq -c '.users[]|.id'` over 100 MB with no RS peaks at 5.3 MB
  instead of 76 MB on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X and 3.5 MB instead of 74 MB on an Apple M4 Pro (jq 1.7.1: 3.6 and
  2.8 MB), 79% and 40% faster; `-r .name` on a 100 MB NDJSON pipe peaks at 7.5 MB instead of 10.7 MB and 6.3 MB
  instead of 10.7 MB, and `reduce inputs` 1-1.2 MB less.
- **jq: an array's elements live in one refcounted block** (#7260).
  An array was an `Rc<Vec<_>>`: a refcount box and a separate element buffer, two allocations per array, which
  `tostream` and `paths` pay for every path they emit. The count, length and elements now share one block, and a
  large `Vec` becomes an array without being copied. At 10 MB of the `comprehensive` input, `[tostream]` peaks at
  368 MB instead of 440 MB on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (jq 1.7.1: 359 MB) and 395 MB instead of 433 MB on an Apple M4
  Pro (jq: 362 MB), and at 100 MB below jq on the 7950X (3580 MB, jq: 3696 MB); `[paths]` peaks at 223 MB instead
  of 260 MB (jq: 271 MB) and 230 MB instead of 248 MB (jq: 292 MB), 16% and 12% faster. Library users: the guard `ArrayVecMut`
  that `ArrayOf::make_vec` returns no longer derefs to `Vec`; it has the `Vec` methods callers use and derefs to a slice.
- **jq: bare `min` and `max` take their single walk again** (#7261). #5683's walk, which keeps only the running winner, had been unreachable since the commit that tidied it: its dispatch sat in the `sort`/`unique` arm, so `min`/`max` still collected every element's cursor and decoded value before comparing. The walk also now decodes a plain integer when the element it is compared with is not one, so two document numbers compare as jq 1.7.1 compares their literals (`[123456789012345679,123456789012345678.9] | min` is the fraction). Over `.numbers|max` on the `numbers` pattern, interleaved, output identical to jq's: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X 14.5 -> 10.2 ms at 1 MB, 123 -> 81 ms at 10 MB, 1191 -> 789 ms at 100 MB (jq 1.7.1: 13.9, 125, 1305 ms), peak RSS at 100 MB 999 -> 126 MB (jq 548 MB); Apple M4 Pro 12.6 -> 11.8, 92 -> 84, 891 -> 795 ms (jq 13.4, 103, 992 ms), 909 -> 125 MB (jq 806 MB). `min` moves the same way; `add`, `[.[]|floor]|add`, `sort` and `max_by(.)` are unchanged.
- **jq: a `--seq` file with one bad record is read a window at a time up to that record** (#7262).
  One regular file of 4 MiB or more (named, or redirected onto standard input) that holds a record
  other than `RS value LF` was read whole wherever that record stood. It is now read as a `--seq`
  pipe is (#7164): windowed up to its first record that is not plain, and only the rest is held,
  once. `--seq -r .name` over 100 MiB whose last record is cut short (`seq_field_bad_last`) went
  from 1066.5 to 766.4 ms (-28.1%) and 146.1 to 10.7 MiB peak RSS on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, and
  from 1004.1 to 695.3 ms (-30.8%) and 152.2 to 7.4 MiB on an Apple M4 Pro; a bad record half way
  through holds 79-80 MiB where the whole read held 146-152. The hand-off no longer copies the rest
  of the stream either, which also helps a `--seq` pipe that turns early: one whose bad record is
  1% in went from 208.6 to 145.1 MiB (7950X) and 255.4 to 156.3 MiB (M4 Pro). Output is identical.
  A bad first record still costs the whole file, and so does a bad record in any of several files.
- **jq: `--seq` reads past the text before a stream's first RS a run at a time** (#7263).
  jq's reader discards every byte before the first RS, so a `--seq` stream with no RS at all (the
  `users_seq_output` comparison row, whose input is one plain JSON document) prints only
  `Unfinished abandoned text at EOF`; `succinctly jq` used to walk those bytes twice, one at a time, at
  about 80 instructions a byte against jq's 17-28. The walk now takes the run up to the next RS at once,
  the end-of-stream position is counted a file at a time, and the newline that ends each `fgets` chunk
  is found a block at a time. `--seq -c '.users[]|.id'` over a 10 MB `users` document takes 4.4 ms
  instead of 23.6 ms on an Apple M4 Pro (67.7M instructions instead of 551.7M) and 6.2 ms instead of
  21.7 ms on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, and 22.7 ms instead of 226 ms (M4 Pro) and 55 ms instead of 206 ms
  (7950X) at 100 MB. A stream with a malformed record, whose walk counts the same chunks, is 4-8% faster
  (`--seq -r .name` over a 100 MB stream whose last record is cut short: 917 ms instead of 995 ms on the
  M4 Pro, 977 ms instead of 1056 ms on the 7950X). The output is unchanged.
- **jq: `first(inputs)` over a file no longer scans 64 KiB before it hands out the first record** (#7264, refs #7260). The lazy input scan started on a 64 KiB first chunk and a 256 KiB read of the file, each document checked by two parsers against each other (about 3,600 instructions per 85-byte record): 2.9 M of the 3.9 M instructions of `-n 'first(inputs)|.id'`, where `-n 1` is 1.1 M. The first chunk is now 4 KiB and doubles to the unchanged 512 KiB cap, and a file longer than the 256 KiB front is first read on 16 KiB (reading on to the front when the first chunk does not fit, and the rest of the front as the first window, read onto the text's own buffer so no page is touched twice). `-n 'first(inputs)|.id'` over an NDJSON file takes 1.035 ms against 1.242 ms on a Ryzen 9 7950X at 10 MB (-17%; jq 1.7.1 1.071 ms; about 1.35 M instructions against 3.94 M, callgrind) and 1.923 ms against 2.025 ms on an Apple M4 Pro (-5%; jq 1.643 ms), flat from 1 MB to 100 MB, and `-n 'input|.id'` 1.004 ms against 1.232 ms (7950X) and 1.962 ms against 2.073 ms (M4 Pro). Which files try the lazy start (those longer than 256 KiB) does not change, but a stream whose first fault or invalid UTF-8 lies past the first 4 KiB chunk now takes the lazy route and meets it in a later chunk or window, where it used to be read whole by the eager route; the output is the same (29,640 differential runs against the previous binary, byte for byte). On the 7950X `reduce inputs` and `[inputs]|length` read 1-3% slower than the base's default layout and 0.1% faster to 0.3% slower than the base laid out differently (`-align-all-functions=6`); an independent placement test of 12 layouts per source judged it code placement (about 80-85% sure), and the M4 Pro rows do not move.
- **jq: a pipe of line-delimited JSON on standard input holds about 6 MiB less** (#7266).
  The plain route's pipe reader handed out the 4 MiB its probe read as one window with a block read onto it,
  which grew the buffer to 8 MiB and gave the certifying thread a 5 MiB copy; the probe is now handed out a
  block at a time from the buffer it was read into. `cat ndjson-100mb.json | succinctly jq -r .name` peaks
  at 17.2 MiB instead of 23.3 MiB on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (private memory 6.2 MiB instead of 12.5 MiB) and
  at 11.8 MiB instead of 18.2 MiB on an Apple M4 Pro, the same at 10 MB and 1 GB and for `-c .` and `@tsv`
  over a pipe, with run times and output unchanged. A document over several lines that does not end within
  a block of the probe is read as before.
- **jq: an array of values computed per element of a document array holds a third to a half less memory** (#7267).
  `[.xs[] | f]` kept every element's result as an 80-byte evaluator result until the end of the walk, beside a
  second vector of the values that it grew by doubling, so it held 112-144 bytes per element where jq holds 16.
  Once the first 64 elements of a walk of at least 128 have each yielded one computed value or nothing, the values
  now go straight into one vector sized for the walk, which is the result; a shorter walk, or one that meets another
  kind of result first (a cursor, an inner generator's values, a failure), carries on exactly as before. At 100 MB, `[.numbers[]|floor]|add` peaks
  at 547 MiB instead of 1,081 MiB on an Apple M4 Pro and at 554 MiB instead of 874 MiB on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X,
  now below jq 1.7.1 on both, and runs 6% faster on the M4 Pro; `[.strings[]|length]|add` peaks at 158 MiB
  instead of 215 MiB (M4 Pro) and 164 MiB instead of 199 MiB (7950X), and `[.users[] | {name, s: (.score + 1)}]`
  at 349 MiB instead of 402 MiB (M4 Pro) and 408 MiB instead of 440 MiB (7950X). The output is unchanged.
- **jq: pretty-printed output of a compact document streams, in about half the memory and up to 2.7x faster** (#7271).
  `succinctly jq .` rendered the whole result into memory before writing any of it, so that a document that turns
  out malformed late prints nothing, as in jq; it held the input plus the full output. When the canonical scan the
  compact path already uses certifies the document, the indented render cannot fail, so it is now written out
  64 KiB at a time, and written by re-indenting the certified bytes instead of walking the tree. At 100 MB,
  `jq .` over `users` peaks at 89 MiB instead of 197 MiB and takes 199 ms instead of 532 ms on an Apple M4 Pro
  (92 MiB instead of 200 MiB, 253 ms instead of 666 ms on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X); over `numbers` 119 MiB instead
  of 245 MiB and 315 ms instead of 446 ms (121 instead of 249 MiB, 339 instead of 520 ms), and over `strings`
  111 MiB instead of 203 MiB, below jq 1.7.1's 130-159 MB (113 instead of 206 MiB), with `--tab`, `--indent n`,
  `-C` and piped input the same. Pretty-printed input, `-S` and any document the scan declines (a number spelling
  jq rewrites, a repeated key, a fault anywhere) keep the buffer and print exactly what they printed before, and
  a document with a late fault still prints nothing.
- **jq: a `--seq` pipe on standard input holds about 1.6 MiB less** (#7277).
  Its reader read a block onto the 4 MiB its probe read before ending its first window, which grew the
  buffer to 8 MiB and made a window of 5 MiB; the probe is now handed out a block of records at a time, as
  the plain pipe's has been since #7266. `cat jsonseq-100mb.json | succinctly jq --seq -c .` peaks at 4.97
  MiB of private memory instead of 6.61 MiB on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (peak RSS 16.3 MiB instead of
  18.2 MiB) and at a 6.28 MiB footprint instead of 7.94 MiB on an Apple M4 Pro (9.30 MiB peak RSS instead
  of 10.97 MiB), the same at 10 MB and 1 GB, with run times and output unchanged.
- **jq: `add` and `min`/`max` over a document array read each number's value without copying its spelling** (#7278). Both folds built every element as an owned number literal, with a heap copy of its text that they dropped unread. `add` computes a new number, and `min`/`max` print only the winner, which they take from the document. `add` now adds each number after the first as its value alone; the first still keeps its spelling, so `[1.0] | add` prints `1.0`. `min`/`max` key each number by its literal's double and integer and read two spellings off the document only when the doubles tie, as jq's exact literal comparison does. Over the `numbers` pattern, interleaved with an A/A control and output identical to jq 1.7.1's: `.numbers|add` on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X 12.1 -> 10.5 ms at 1 MB, 99 -> 83 ms at 10 MB, 960 -> 803 ms at 100 MB, and on an Apple M4 Pro 12.5 -> 11.1, 89 -> 78, 847 -> 736 ms; `.numbers|max` 10.5 -> 8.2, 84 -> 62, 815 -> 597 ms (7950X) and 11.8 -> 9.9, 84 -> 69, 791 -> 647 ms (M4 Pro); `[.numbers|min,max]` 1462 -> 1041 ms (7950X) and 1398 -> 1087 ms (M4 Pro) at 100 MB, now ahead of jq's 1581 and 1161 ms. Instructions at 10 MB fall 12-23% on the 7950X and 20-31% on the M4 Pro; `sort`, `[.[]|floor]|add` and identity are unchanged in instructions.
- **jq: `--seq` over 2 to 32 files reads the files before a bad one a window at a time** (#7279).
  A `--seq` run over several regular files (4 MiB or more between them, held open by the run) was
  read whole, every file of it, if any one file was not plain `RS value LF` records ending in an LF.
  The files before the first that is not are now read a window at a time, and only that file and
  the ones after it are read whole, as a list of more than 32 files already was (#7221). Over
  100 MiB of records in 8 files, `--seq -r .name` with a bad record in the last file went from
  1249 to 803 ms (-35.7%) and 245.9 to 41.4 MiB peak RSS on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, and from 1068 to
  727 ms (-31.9%) and 252.6 to 38.0 MiB on an Apple M4 Pro; in the fourth file, 245.7 to 158.5 MiB
  and 252.6 to 167.3 MiB. A bad record in the first file costs what it did. Output is identical.
- **jq: `group_by(f) | map({k: .[0].k, n: length})` builds each group's object from the group's nodes** (#7280).
  An array or object construction of literals and one-value reads of a group (`length`, `first`, `last`, `.[n]`,
  optionally followed by `.name`/`.[n]` steps) no longer decodes every group and writes it out and indexes it
  again: `corpus_tabular_group` runs 6.84 M instructions instead of 12.22 M on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (jq 1.7.1:
  18.69 M) and takes 1.36 ms instead of 1.77 ms (jq 1.595 ms), and 2.14 ms instead of 2.46 ms on an Apple M4 Pro
  (jq 2.23 ms). `.users | group_by(.age) | map({age: .[0].age, n: length})` over 10 MB takes 91.0 ms instead of
  182.7 ms on the 7950X and 64.5 ms instead of 138.9 ms on the M4 Pro (jq 217.8 ms and 152.3 ms); output
  unchanged.
- **jq: `[group_by(f)[] | length]` runs the rest of the pipe on each group's nodes** (#7282).
  A `.[]` over `group_by`'s groups with more of the pipe after it (`group_by(f)[] | g` or `group_by(f) | .[] | g`)
  no longer decodes every group before `g` reads it, as the streaming route already did. Over 10 MB of 500 groups,
  `[group_by(.a)[] | length]` takes 165.2 ms instead of 386.9 ms on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (289.5 M instructions
  instead of 552.1 M at 1 MB) and 125.0 ms instead of 254.1 ms on an Apple M4 Pro, `[group_by(.a)[] | .[0].id]`
  165.6 ms instead of 401.5 ms and 124.4 ms instead of 282.8 ms, and `[group_by(.a)[] | map(.score) | add]`
  241.5 ms instead of 411.7 ms and 193.7 ms instead of 279.5 ms. `[group_by(.a)[]]`, which keeps every group, runs
  the same instructions as before; a `map(f)` read by `first` or `.[0]` keeps raising on a later element's error,
  as jq does; output unchanged.
- **jq: a document number's decode no longer tries an integer parse that fails on every fraction, nor re-checks UTF-8 that its grammar already proved** (#7287). The shared number parse ran `i64`'s `FromStr` first, which builds an error at the `.` of every fraction; an exact equivalent now stops at the first byte that is not a digit. The JSON cursor ran `str::from_utf8` on a number token just accepted as RFC 8259 number text, whose grammar admits only ASCII; the token's text is now taken straight from that check. Over the `numbers` pattern at 10 MB, instructions on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (cachegrind) fall 6.7% for `.numbers|add` (1.525G -> 1.423G), 7.3% for `.numbers|max` (1.389G -> 1.287G) and 1.5% for `.numbers|sort` and `.numbers|map(.+1)`; identity and `[.numbers[]|floor]` are unchanged. Every output is unchanged, yq mode included.
- **jq: `.[]` over an object no longer keeps a 144-byte field record per field, and `[.[]] | add` adds the array's elements without decoding it first** (#7290). `.[]`'s object arm built the duplicate-key-aware field list (key and value decoded, both cursors) and took the value cursors from it with an in-place collect, so the 32-byte cursors kept the whole list's buffer alive for as long as the result lived. It now walks the object keeping one value cursor per field and its key hash, on the stack for an object of up to eight fields and hashed 64 at a time past that, and collapses a repeated key (first position, last value, as jq 1.7.1 does) over those cursors in place, finding each key's slot by its own hash and confirming it against the key's text. `[.[]] | add`, and any array built of document nodes followed by `add` (`[.xs[] | select(f)] | add`), reached the decoding fallback, which built every element as an owned value with a copy of each number's spelling before the sum ran; it now takes the document array's streaming sum, which reads each number after the first as its value alone. `any`/`all` over an object take the same walk. Over one `wide` object (about 82,000 keys per MB), interleaved with an A/A control, output identical to jq 1.7.1's, `[.[]]|add` on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X: 34.9 -> 15.8 ms and 27.2 -> 13.9 MiB at 1 MB, 306 -> 125 ms and 174 -> 53 MiB at 10 MB, 2698 -> 1158 ms and 1546 -> 405 MiB at 100 MB (jq 1.7.1: 4896 ms, 1331 MiB); on an Apple M4 Pro 22.6 -> 13.1 ms and 26.2 -> 8.6 MiB, 173 -> 89 ms and 202 -> 67 MiB, 1606 -> 819 ms and 1848 -> 433 MiB (jq 1.7.1: 3220 ms, 1452 MiB), with instructions halved. At 100 MB on the M4 Pro, `[.numbers[]]|add` falls from 2233 to 706 ms and 1085 to 330 MiB, an object repeating a key every 1,000 keys from 2262 to 1397 ms and 2796 to 963 MiB, and `[.[] | [.[]] | add]` over 1.7 M six-key objects from 4114 to 1768 ms; objects of 0 to 8 fields iterated by the million are at or below base on both chips.
- **jq: `.` and `-c .` over an object of more than 786,432 keys print it from its text, 2.2-3.6x fewer instructions** (#7293).
  The canonical scan that lets a document be echoed (`-c`) or re-indented (pretty) gave up on an object wider than
  the key-hash table's ceiling after hashing 786,432 of its keys, and the walk that then printed it hashed and sorted
  every key again; since #7271 that made pretty `.` over the 100 MB `wide` object (7.1 M keys) about 3% slower
  than before. The scan now settles such an object's keys with the same sort, so one without a repeated key is
  printed from its text. On that object `jq .` retires 9,294 M instructions instead of 20,526 M and `jq -c .`
  6,824 M instead of 19,971 M (AMD Ryzen 9 7950X); on an Apple M4 Pro they take 360 ms instead of 788 ms and
  265 ms instead of 761 ms, in 186 MiB instead of 320 MiB and 293 MiB, file or stdin.
  An object that wide which the scan declines now pays the scan up to the reason before it is declined, where
  the scan used to stop at 786,432 keys: a repeated key, wherever it sits, is found only at the object's end
  (+8% instructions and +3-4% wall on the 100 MB object), any other non-canonical text past the first
  786,432 keys costs the scan up to it (+7% instructions, +5% wall for a non-canonical last member), +3% at
  1.6 M keys and about 1% just past the ceiling.
- **jq: one big document piped on standard input is no longer validated whole before it runs** (#7294).
  A pipe of 4 MiB or more is read a window at a time and each window is certified by the strict validator,
  so that a fault in it can still be worded once its text is dropped (#7024). The last window is never
  dropped, so it is now certified only when the run asks for a fault, over its own buffer, which it shares
  with the certifier instead of copying. One big document is that one window, and a run over it that
  meets no fault reads as the same file read by name does: `.users[0]` over a 70 MB document piped on
  stdin takes 107 ms instead of 170 ms on an Apple M4 Pro (the file: 101 ms) and 189 ms instead of 249 ms
  on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, `-c .` over a 100 MB one-line object 770 ms instead of 861 ms (M4 Pro), and the
  same programs over a 7 MB document hold 10.2 MB of private memory instead of 17.0 MB (M4 Pro; 9.0 MB
  instead of 15.0 MB on the 7950X). NDJSON on a pipe, whose windows are dropped and keep being certified
  on their thread, is unchanged. Output, fault wording and exit status are unchanged.
- **x86_64: the JSON index is built by a branch-free kernel, faster on every input measured and much less sensitive to code placement** (#7299).
  The AVX2 standard-cursor kernel ran a per-byte `match` with about three data-dependent branches and kept both bit writers' state in memory, and on a Ryzen 9 7950X its speed moved by up to 10% with where unrelated changes placed it in the binary.
  It now steps a compile-time table of the state machine with one load and one shift per byte, pulls each 32-byte block's bits out with `movemask`, and skips blocks that lie wholly inside a string.
  The kernel alone is 1.2x faster on its weakest input (strings that are all backslash escapes), 1.7-2x on record-shaped JSON, and up to about 50x on long strings.
  On the 7950X, 100 MB `users`: `.users[0]` 155.1 -> 119.4 ms, `-c .` 235.6 -> 197.4 ms, `[.users[]]|length` 173.4 -> 134.2 ms; `strings` `-c .` 258.7 -> 173.3 ms, `nested` `-c .` 286.3 -> 179.8 ms; NDJSON of 48-byte documents -7% to -9% at 1, 10 and 100 MB; every timed row is as fast or faster.
  Inert padding that moved the old kernel through four positions mod 64 spread `.users[0].name` over 143.5-154.5 ms (min), a 7.7% band; the new kernel's band is 1-4% across the rows swept, and its slowest position is faster than the old kernel's fastest.
  Anonymous memory is unchanged: with both binaries copied at the same moment and a same-source control pair, 100 MB `users` `-c .` holds 89,604 kB of `RssAnon` before and after, and the tiny and 10 MB NDJSON rows differ by 4 kB or less.
  An early measurement read the peak 0.5-1.0 MB higher; that was file-backed pages (`RssFile` moves by 24-72 kB between two copies of the same binary, and the text section grew by 996 bytes), not an allocation (#7319).
  Apple silicon builds the index with NEON and is unchanged.
- **x86_64: the SSE2 JSON index builder runs the AVX2 builder's branch-free kernel, and both are faster** (#7305).
  The SSE2 standard-cursor builder, which runs on x86_64 CPUs without AVX2 and in every `no_std` x86_64 build, still had the per-byte branch tree that #7299 removed from AVX2, and was no faster than the scalar PFSM builder.
  The two builders now share one block loop; each instruction set answers only which bytes of a block are a quote or backslash, and the three bit masks of the block's stored steps.
  Both read those masks as two 16-byte halves, which on a Ryzen 9 7950X made the AVX2 kernel 15-20% faster than one 32-byte `movemask` per mask, and a run of blocks inside a string is now skipped with one write.
  Kernel alone on the 7950X: the SSE2 builder is 1.25x (strings made only of escapes) to 38x (long strings) faster, about 2x on record-shaped JSON (100 MB `users` 81.5 -> 41.2 ms); the AVX2 builder is 9-18% faster on every generated pattern and size (100 MB `users` 44.1 -> 37.6 ms).
  End to end with AVX2, 100 MB `users`: `.users[0].name` 117.3 -> 110.1 ms, `-c .` 138.7 -> 129.9 ms, `length` 100.4 -> 93.2 ms (medians); no row is slower beyond the A/A noise.
  With the SSE2 builder forced on the same machine (a stand-in for a CPU without AVX2; nothing else in the binary changes path), the same rows run 24-36% faster at 10 and 100 MB (`.users[0].name` 157.9 -> 113.0 ms), `nested` `-c .` 56-59% faster, and NDJSON of small records 3-11% faster.
  Apple silicon builds the index with NEON and is unchanged.
- **jq: `min_by(f)`, `max_by(f)` and `add` keep only what they need as they walk an array** (#7306). `min_by`/`max_by` collected every element's cursor and then every element's `[f]` key before comparing any, and `add` collected every cursor before its fold only to check every gap first; all three now take one walk that checks each gap inline and keeps the winner and its key (or the running sum), with jq 1.7.1's tie rules (first of equal minima, last of equal maxima, the NaN order of #6008) and error order unchanged. The full evaluator's `min_by`/`max_by`, which a computed array (`[.[]]`, `map(.)`, a slice) reaches, keeps only the winner too. Over the `numbers` pattern, interleaved, output identical to jq's: `.numbers|max_by(.)` on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X 2006 -> 1044 ms and 1987 -> 130 MB peak RSS at 100 MB (jq 1.7.1: 3200 ms, 985 MB); Apple M4 Pro 1175 -> 971 ms and 1810 -> 126 MB (jq 2316 ms, 1142 MB). `.numbers|add` at 100 MB: 7950X 706 -> 556 ms, 346 -> 128 MB; M4 Pro 630 -> 563 ms, 350 -> 125 MB. `.users|max_by(.score)` at 100 MB: 284 -> 99 MB (7950X), 264 -> 94 MB (M4 Pro). Over a computed array, `[.numbers[]]|max_by(.)` at 100 MB: 7950X 2980 -> 2389 ms and 1939 -> 784 MB (jq 3855 ms, 985 MB); M4 Pro 1870 -> 806 MB (jq 1142 MB). Bare `min`/`max`, `sort`, `sort_by`, `group_by` and `unique_by` are unchanged.
- **jq: `.` and `-c .` over a wide object that repeats a key take 20-29% less time** (#7310).
  The canonical scan that lets a document be printed from its text settles a wide object's key hashes at its
  closing brace, after every member is certified, so a repeated key is all it has left to decline, and it has
  hashed every key on the way. The printer then walked the keys again to hash and sort them before collapsing the
  repeat (#7311). It now takes the hashes the scan found repeated and skips that walk. On the 100 MB `wide` object
  (7.1 M keys) with one repeated key, `jq .` takes 0.96 s instead of 1.34 s and `jq -c .` 0.94 s instead of
  1.32 s on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, and 0.75 s instead of 1.02 s for both on an Apple M4 Pro, which retires
  17,500 M instructions instead of 23,277 M (`.`) and 16,905 M instead of 22,682 M (`-c .`) and peaks at 313 MiB
  instead of 370 MiB. The saving is 20-22% at 10 MB, and where the repeat sits does not matter.
- **jq: an object that repeats a key no longer holds every field and every key to collapse it** (#7311).
  jq's rule (a repeated key keeps its first position and takes its last value) was applied by
  materializing the object's fields and owning each key in a map. Only the keys whose hash another key
  shares are decoded now, and the other fields stream as before. On a 100 MB object of 7.1 M keys with
  one repeated key, `.` takes 1.36 s instead of 3.90 s and peaks at 261 MB instead of 2,648 MB on an AMD
