  Ryzen 9 7950X (1.08 s instead of 1.76 s, and 311 MB instead of 2,852 MB, on an Apple M4 Pro). That peak
  is what the same object takes without the repeat when its text cannot be echoed. `-c .` and `-C .` gain
  the same, `map(.) | length` takes 1.60 s instead of 4.06 s (351 MB instead of 2,649 MB), `.[]` 1.77 s
  instead of 3.19 s and `select(true)` 1.64 s instead of 2.64 s (7950X). The saving grows with the
  object: `.` is 53%, 61% and 65% faster at 1, 10 and 100 MB on the 7950X. Objects that repeat no key
  time as before.
- **jq: a `--seq` file that does not open with an RS holds a megabyte less** (#7312). A lone regular
  file with no RS byte (or text, a BOM or white space before the first one) is handed on to the
  whole-stream route at its first byte, but the windowed start of #7262 first read a 1 MiB window of
  it, found it to be all tail and freed it, and the allocator kept that block resident beside the
  file. The first read is now a page when the first byte is not an RS (judged where the run reads
  from, so a file on standard input counts from its offset). Output is identical, and a stream that
  opens with an RS is read as before. `--seq .` over a 7.1 MB users file (peak memory footprint,
  11 interleaved runs) went from 9,776 to 8,752 KB on an Apple M4 Pro, the figure before #7262
  (8,736 KB), and over 70 MB from 74,784 to 73,792 KB. On an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X peak RSS went
  from 16,964 to 15,988 KB at 7.1 MB (41 runs; 15,596 KB before #7262) and is unchanged at 70 MB.
  Time is unchanged within the noise on both.
- **jq: a math builtin of a document number no longer decodes the number's text three times** (#7315).
  `floor`, `ceil`, `round`, `sqrt`, `fabs`, `log`, `sin` and the other unary math builtins, and `pow`/`atan2`,
  read each number's source span as UTF-8 once to check it, once more to read it, and a third time inside
  the reader, 12.5% of `[.numbers[] | floor]`'s instructions. They now validate it as a number and as text
  in one pass and read the double from that text. `[.numbers[]|floor]|add` on the 100 MB `numbers` document
  takes 769 ms instead of 921 ms on an Apple M4 Pro (-16.5%, 13.3% fewer instructions at 10 MB) and
  1222 ms instead of 1356 ms on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (-9.9%, 16.4% fewer instructions); `sqrt` and
  `map(floor)` gain about as much, `pow(.;2)` 2-6%. Output is unchanged.
- **jq: `.numbers | sort` retires 6% fewer instructions** (#7316).
  The `SpelledScalar` arm that #7251 added to `jq_kind` called `jq_kind` again on `kind.canonical()`, and a function that calls itself is not inlined, so the kind of each value became an out-of-line call inside every comparison of the sort (399 M of the 6,421 M instructions of `.numbers | sort` on the 10 MB `numbers` document).
  The arm now maps the kind directly and output is unchanged. `sort_by`, `min`, `max`, `unique` and `group_by` compare through the same `sort_rank`; only `.numbers | sort` was measured.
  Instructions, #7251's merge against the same merge with this change: 6,421 M to 6,037 M on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (cachegrind; 6,024 M before #7251), 5,957 M to 5,429 M on an Apple M4 Pro (`time -l`; 5,385 M before #7251).
  Wall-clock, min of 15 interleaved runs: 372.3 ms to 358.0 ms on the 7950X (356.7 ms before #7251) and 248.9 ms to 242.2 ms on the M4 Pro (239.0 ms before #7251).
- **jq: macOS startup is 3.3% faster** (#7321). A 12.0 deployment target makes the linker emit chained fixups, which
  replace 22,214 rebase opcodes into 103 `__DATA_CONST` pages (a copy-on-write fault each, at every start). `jq -n 1`
  on an Apple M4 Pro, interleaved with an A/A control, 40 rounds of 100 spawns per build: 2.0434 ms to 1.9753 ms for
  the stripped binary (2.0546 ms to 1.9851 ms unstripped, -3.4%); the control pair, one binary at two paths, differed
  by 0.4%. The same builds' `/usr/bin/jq` 1.7.1 reads 1.8299 ms in this driver, so jq is still about 8% faster at
  startup on this chip; the remaining gap is clap and the loader's work on the image (not addressed here).
- **jq: a `--seq` stream is read a window at a time past a bad record** (#7322). A `--seq` file of
  4 MiB or more (or a pipe) was windowed only up to its first record other than `RS value LF`, and
  the rest was held whole, so a bad first record cost the whole file. The windows now carry on when
  plain records follow the bad one: the stretch between is read as jq's reader reads it, its
  values run and its warnings are printed where jq prints them. `--seq -r .name` over 100 MiB whose
  first record is cut short (`seq_field_bad_first`) went from 979.4 to 703.0 ms (-28.2%) and 145.9
  to 10.1 MiB peak RSS on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, and from 908.1 to 683.8 ms (-24.7%) and 152.3 to
  6.6 MiB on an Apple M4 Pro; at 10 MiB it is -27.9% and -24.0%, and at 1 MiB (under the 4 MiB the
  windows start at) unchanged. A cut record every 1000 records reads the same (146.8 to 10.1 MiB
  and -31.0% on the 7950X, 152.6 to 6.7 MiB and -24.9% on the M4 Pro), as does the same stream on
  a pipe (146.3 to 13.2 MiB, 151.7 to 9.4 MiB). Output is identical, and identical to jq 1.7.1's.
  The rest of the stream is still held from a record the windows cannot carry on after: one jq
  reads a value from that is not RFC 8259 (`nan`, a control character in a string), a stretch of
  4 MiB or more or with over 1024 warnings, the stream's last record, and a bad record in any of
  several files.
- **jq: `-R` holds half the memory it did, over a pipe and over a file** (#7323).
  Over a pipe, the 4 MiB probe was copied whole to make the first window while the probe was still held
  (since #7264), and every window was read while the text of the one before was still held, so `-R` over a
  file held two 1 MiB windows at once. The probe is now the first window's own buffer, and a window's text
  is dropped before the next is read. `cat ndjson-100mb.json | succinctly jq -R length` peaks at 4.02 MiB
  of heap in DHAT instead of 8.02 MiB on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (peak RSS 12.2 MiB instead of 15.9 MiB), and
  the same file named on the command line at 1.02 MiB instead of 2.02 MiB (9.5 MiB RSS instead of 11.6
  MiB), the same at 16 MB and 100 MB, with wall-clock time unchanged. What is left over a pipe is the probe
  itself, which the route reads to decide whether to window the stream.
- **jq: a run keeps its last value's index instead of freeing it first** (#7332). The process ends
  after the last value, and `free` of the index's buffers is the first large block glibc sees go
  back once the program has dropped a big array of small strings: when those buffers join one another
  past 64 KiB, it first sweeps every small chunk in its fast bins (`malloc_consolidate`), 54 M
  instructions and 3.2 M extra L1 misses for the million number spellings of `.numbers | sort |
  .[0]`. Whether the buffers sit side by side decided it, and #7151, which only changed the
  start-up allocations, flipped it: 331 to 355 ms at flat instructions. On a 7950X (min of 11
  interleaved runs, output identical) `.numbers | sort | .[0]` on `numbers-10mb` reads 339.9 to
  319.1 ms (-6.1%) and is 6.1 to 7.5% faster with the heap start moved by 24 and 56 bytes; 1 MB
  reads 28.4 to 26.6 ms and 100 MB 4,405 to 3,632 ms (-17.5%); instructions fall 1.1% (5,056 M to
  5,002 M). The run holds one index more than it did, the last value's (of a window, for a windowed
  file, given back when the next arrives), and every other value's is freed at its end, so NDJSON
  reads as before (58.6 and 59.6 ms, 10 MB). On an M4 Pro (macOS malloc) the row is unchanged.
- **jq: `--seq` windows carry on past more of the stretches that are not plain records** (#7341).
  A `--seq` stream from one file of 4 MiB or more, or a pipe, used to hold the rest of the stream from a stretch
  holding a value jq reads and RFC 8259 does not (`nan`, `012`, nesting past 128 levels, invalid UTF-8 in a
  string), from one over 4 MiB or that drew over 1024 warnings, and from one that ran to the stream's end. Such
  values are now read where they are. A long stretch is read in 64 KiB pieces, each cut at an RS that starts a
  line, and one that runs to the end is handed on from its last such RS. A window ends once 65536 warnings wait
  for it. At 100 MiB a stream of `nan` records holds 14.4 MiB instead of 257.0 on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X and 10.4
  instead of 290.8 on an Apple M4 Pro, and runs 55% and 46% shorter. One whose first record is `nan`, or draws
  3000 warnings, holds 11.8-12.4 MiB instead of 234 on the 7950X and 7.1-8.1 instead of 259 on the M4 Pro, 10-14%
  shorter. A 10 MB stream with 5 MB of lines that only warn holds 34-36 MiB instead of 1059-1101, and a 5 MB one
  that warns once a byte 21-23 instead of 171-200. Over several files, one that is not plain records and opens
  with an RS is read by a gate of its own, where it and every file after it were read whole: at 100 MiB in four
  files, a bad first, middle or last file holds 11 MiB instead of 99-340 on the 7950X and 7 instead of 105-366 on
  the M4 Pro, 5-21% shorter. Output unchanged.
- **jq: a wide object that repeats a key is printed from its text** (#7346).
  An object whose only fault is a repeated key has every member already in jq's spelling, so under `.`,
  `-c .`, `--indent n` and `--tab` the runs of members jq's duplicate-key rule leaves alone are now copied
  (`-c`) or re-indented from the text, and each repeated key is written in its first place with its last
  value. It used to be walked and re-rendered member by member. That holds for the object printed whole,
  for one inside the printed value (#7366) and for one that repeats an early key (#7355). On a 100 MB
  object of 7.1 M keys with one repeated key, `.` takes 0.64 s instead of 0.96 s and `-c .` 0.54 s
  instead of 0.94 s on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (0.48 s instead of 0.76 s, and 0.40 s instead of 0.75 s, on
  an Apple M4 Pro), and the same object one level in reads the same. Each now peaks where the same object
  without the repeat does, 196 MB on the 7950X and 192 MB on the M4 Pro, instead of 244-287 MB and
  297-340 MB. The saving grows with the object: `-c .` is 37%, 41% and 43% faster at 1, 10 and 100 MB on
  the 7950X. An object whose fields are mostly occurrences of repeated keys keeps the walk, which is the
  faster route for it, at 4-5% more time than before for recording spans it then gives up.
- **jq: a wide object that repeats a key finds its repeats from its text** (#7350).
  When the only reason the canonical scan declines an object is a repeated key, the printer used to walk every
  field through the index to find the few that repeat before printing the object from its text (#7346). It now
  cuts the members out of the certified text and hashes each key the way the scan did, and leaves only objects
  of long members (over 256 bytes each on average) to the walk, which costs the same per member whatever its
  length. On a 100 MB object of 7.1 M keys with one repeated key, `.` takes 0.47 s instead of 0.64 s and `-c .`
  0.38 s instead of 0.54 s on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (0.40 s instead of 0.49 s, and 0.31 s instead of 0.40 s, on an
  Apple M4 Pro, which retires 9,579 M instructions instead of 11,195 M for `.`). The saving grows with the
  object: `-c .` is 17%, 24% and 30% faster at 1, 10 and 100 MB on the 7950X. A repeat-declined object inside a
  larger value gains as much, and peak memory is unchanged.
- **jq: a wide object that repeats a key among its first 16 is printed from its text, as one that repeats a later key already was** (#7355). `.` and `-c .` over a 17.9 MB object of 1 M keys whose second key repeats the first took 164.6 ms on a 7950X against 134.7 ms for the same repeat at the end; they now take 135.0 ms (0.82x), and 400,000 NDJSON records that each repeat an early key 0.90x. Every other shape measured is within noise with the same output, and a repeat inside a nested object still walks the object, as before.
- **jq: an indented echo no longer holds a long string token twice** (#7356). `.` over an 80 MB object holding one 50 MiB string peaked at 149.6 MB on a 7950X and now peaks 53 MB lower (96.2 MB), 20% faster in wall-clock; a write of 64 KiB or more now goes to the writer as it is instead of being gathered into the chunk buffer first, and every smaller write is chunked as before. Other shapes (`users`, `numbers`, `wide` at 10 and 100 MB) time 1.00x-1.02x of before (an A/A control reads 0.99x-1.01x) with the same output, and 0.5% fewer instructions.
- **jq: a document holding one object that repeats a key is printed from its text around that object** (#7366). The canonical scan stopped at such an object unless it was the whole value, so `{"data": <1 M keys, the second repeating the first>}` (17.9 MB) and an array of 400,000 records one of which repeats a key walked and re-rendered every member. The scan now records the first such object below the value and goes on past it, and the printer writes the text before it, the object by its keys, and the text after it. On a 7950X, `-c .` over the 17.9 MB object takes 141.7 ms against 165.4 ms (0.86x; with the repeat at the last key 0.79x), and over the records 61.4 ms against 253.0 ms (0.24x); `.` reads 0.86x, 0.79x and 0.40x. Output and peak memory are unchanged and documents without a nested repeat are within noise; a document with two such objects still walks, and one whose nested repeat is followed by a byte jq would respell now scans to that byte before walking (+9% on 400,000 records).
- **The release binary is 22% smaller: the CLI is compiled as part of the library, not as its own crate** (#7384).
  As a separate crate the CLI instantiated every generic evaluator function it reached a second time, and fat LTO
  does not merge identical functions, so the binary carried two copies of most of the evaluator. Stripped, as the
  release archive ships it, `succinctly` goes from 19.92 MB to 15.61 MB on an Apple M4 Pro and from 24.77 MB to
  19.34 MB on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X. Over the 225 rows of `succinctly dev compare jq --full`, against jq 1.7.1 timed
  in the same runs, wall-clock is -1.5% on the 7950X (-2.6% at 1 MB, -9% at startup) and -0.3% on the M4 Pro,
  and peak RSS is -10.5% and -6.7%. `.numbers|add` on 100 MB is -18.7% (559.2 ms -> 454.7 ms) and -11.0%
  (577.7 ms -> 514.3 ms), because a document float is now added to a float sum in place. Three object-building
  rows regress on the M4 Pro only, `wide_map_values` by up to 8.5% (#7392), and `wide_keys` by up to 6.8%
  (507.6 ms -> 542.5 ms at 100 MB) on the 7950X only. yq is 0.5% to 0.7% faster on both chips (median of 45
  rows, JSON and YAML output; an A/A control of identical binaries reads within 0.11% of zero), with no row
  slower by more than 2.1%.
- **yq: `map_values` holds its field list once, and `to_entries` skips an unused key census** (#7406). yq mode's `map_values` re-collected the mapping's field list into a second copy, alive at the same time as the first; on an Apple M4 Pro `map_values(. + 1) | length` now peaks at 346.9 MiB instead of 433.3 MiB over a 9.9 MB wide YAML mapping (-19.9%; -19.4% at 1 MB, -20.7% over 10.5 MB of JSON with `-p json`), and on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, where that copy is less often the peak, 268.1 MiB instead of 280.5 MiB (-4.4%). yq mode's `to_entries` hashed every key for a census that only chose between two identical walks: `to_entries | length` over a wide mapping is 3.6-4.5% faster on the M4 Pro and 4.3-4.7% on the 7950X (3.5-4.1% fewer instructions), and `[.users[] | to_entries] | length` 6.2% and 10.3% faster. Output is unchanged (8,357 jq and yq programs compared against the previous build). Measured with interleaved runs against an A/A control on both machines.
- **jq: `[.[] | f]` over a document's array no longer holds every element's cursor beside every value** (#7412).
  Once a long run of elements has each yielded one computed value, the fold now writes those values over the
  32-byte cursors it has already read, in the cursors' own buffer, instead of into a second vector of the
  same size. Peak RSS at 100 MB, on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X and an Apple M4 Pro: `[.numbers[] | floor] | add`
  545 -> 332 MB on both, `[.strings[] | length] | add` 156 -> 133 MB, `[.strings[] | ascii_upcase] | length`
  247 -> 225 MB, and `[.users[] | .name | ascii_downcase] | length` 153 -> 132 MB and 143 -> 122 MB. At 10 MB
  the `strings_*` rows drop 2.0-2.3 MB, which puts their private memory below jq 1.7.1's (13.9 against
  15.8 MB on the 7950X). `[.numbers[] | floor] | add` is also 8% faster on the 7950X.
- **jq: streaming input reads 256 KiB windows instead of 1 MiB, so a stream holds about 1-2 MiB less** (#7412).
  The plain, `--seq`, `-R` and `inputs` routes read their source a window at a time, and the window was most of
  the private memory a streaming run held: `-r .name` over a 100 MB NDJSON file held 2.0 MiB of anonymous memory
  on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X where jq 1.7.1 holds 0.8, the same over a pipe 3.2 (two windows in flight with the
  thread that certifies them), and `reduce inputs` 2.7. The window is now 256 KiB, a file is read in windows from
  1 MiB (4 MiB before) and a pipe from 512 KiB, and a file under 4 MiB that is one long document is read on to
  its end at once, as it was read whole before. Peak RSS at 100 MB: `-r .name` 6.5 to 5.6 MiB on the 7950X and
  4.8 to 3.8 MiB on an Apple M4 Pro (jq 1.7.1: 3.4 and 2.8), over a pipe 7.8 to 5.8 and 6.1 to 4.3, `reduce inputs`
  7.3 to 6.1 and 5.9 to 4.5; three 1 MB files 7.8 to 5.7 and 6.4 to 3.7. Times are unchanged within an A/A
  control on both machines from 1 MB to 1 GB, and the 1 MB rows are 2-11% faster on the 7950X.
- **jq: `map_values(f)` over an object in the document reads its fields where they stand** (#7412).
  It wrote the object out as JSON, indexed that copy and ran over it, with the copy, its text and the
  result all live at once; it now runs `f` on the document's own fields, and the check that every value
  decodes (so that one `f` never reads still raises jq's parse error first) is a walk that builds nothing.
  `map_values(.+1)|length` on a 10 MB object peaks at 92 MiB instead of 202 MiB on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X
  (jq 1.7.1: 169 MiB) and is 18% faster; on an Apple M4 Pro it peaks at 87 MiB instead of 197 MiB (jq:
  206 MiB) and is 1-2% faster. At 1 MB it peaks at 16 MiB instead of 27 MiB (jq: 22 MiB) and 12 MiB
  instead of 22 MiB (jq: 27 MiB). `[.users[]|map_values(tostring)]` over 10 MB of `users` is 14-16% faster
  on both.
- **jq/yq on Linux: 0.5-1 MB less resident binary in every run** (#7412).
  Three things kept pages of the executable itself in the RSS of every run. The relocation table
  (`.rela.dyn`, 429 KiB), which the loader reads once before `main`, stayed mapped to the end; it is
  now unmapped first thing in `main` (`MADV_DONTNEED` on its whole pages, which are clean pages of
  the read-only segment). The C runtime's `_start` and `crtbeginS.o` functions were left out of the
  link order, 2 MB past the ordered block, and on Linux 6.18 the page they share kept a large folio of
  text resident; the linker wrapper now puts them first. And the functions the windowed stream routes
  run were unordered, because the order was traced at 1 MB and those routes start at 4 MiB; the 60 of
  them are now at the end of the list. Peak RSS on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X: `jq -n 1` 4.31 to 3.77 MiB,
  `.` over the npm corpus file 4.82 to 4.29, `-r .name` over 100 MB of NDJSON 5.72 to 4.81, `--seq -r
  .name` 5.82 to 5.03, and about 0.9 MiB less on every 100 MB row. On an Apple M4 Pro only the stream
  rows change, by 0.05-0.1 MiB. Times are unchanged within an A/A control and the spread that inert
  padding alone produces, on both machines.
- **jq: `-R` over a pipe holds one 256 KiB window instead of a 1 MiB probe** (#7412).
  A pipe's length is not known, so `-R` read its first four windows (1 MiB) to decide whether to read
  it a window at a time, and held them as its first window: `cat log | jq -R ...` held 1.68 MiB of
  anonymous memory on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X at every size from 1 MB to 100 MB, where the same lines read
  from a file held 0.91 and jq 1.7.1 holds 0.84. The probe is now one window, so a pipe holds what a file
  does. Peak RSS of `-R length`, `-R 'fromjson|.id'` and `-nR 'reduce inputs ...'` over a pipe falls by
  0.7-0.8 MiB at 1, 10 and 100 MB on the 7950X (7.2-7.5 to 6.4-6.7 MiB) and on an Apple M4 Pro (4.2-4.7
  to 3.5-4.0 MiB). Times are unchanged within an A/A control on both machines, and 2-8% faster at 1 MB.
- **jq: a fold step that appends or stores a container built by a builtin or a pipe is linear** (#7451).
  `reduce range(n) as $t ([]; . + [$t|tostring|split("")])`, `.[$t] = [range(3)]`, `. + [[$t]|sort]`,
  `.a += [[$t]|sort]` and their `foreach`, `+=`, `|=`, `setpath` and constructor (`[.[0] + [[$t]|sort], .[1] + 1]`)
  forms copied the whole accumulator on every step, because the in-place fold step had no stage for the builtin
  that built the operand and handed the step to the evaluator, whose `+` or write on a state the fold still held
  copied it: the time grew with the square of the step count where jq 1.7.1 is linear. An operand that reads no
  input and has no effect is now evaluated once on `null` and the step writes in place; one that reads `.`, has
  an effect, raises or yields other than once keeps the evaluator's route, and the answers are unchanged.
- **jq: refusing a deeply nested document is linear on the routes that read past a parse fault** (#7470).
  On `-n input`, `inputs` and `input_line_number`, a document past jq's parse-depth limit (`{"a":` 400,000
  levels deep, 2.4 MB) did work in the square of the depth where jq 1.7.1's is linear: after each fault jq drops the
  rest of its read and parses on from the next, and every such read that opened another refused container was
  split, indexed and validated to the end of the text, which made the refusal quadratic in the depth. A read
  past a fault is now parsed only through the bracket jq refuses: doubling the depth now doubles the work where
  it quadrupled it, and the output is unchanged.
- **jq: a long chain of `E as $x |` bindings is linear** (#7471).
  Each bind substituted its value into a copy of the whole rest of the chain, read or not, and held the copy while
  the rest ran, so `1 as $x0 | 1 as $x1 | ... | $x0` cost memory and time in the square of the chain's length
  (4,000 bindings: 1,750 MiB peak RSS on an Apple M4 Pro), where jq 1.7.1 runs it in a few MB. A body that does
  not read the bound variable is now evaluated as it is, and a chain answers that question for all of its links in
  one walk: 4,000 bindings take 30 MiB (Apple M4 Pro), and doubling the chain doubles the work and the memory. A chain whose
  every variable is read at its end still copies the rest of the chain per bind, as before.
- **jq: an `until`/`while` loop that keys its state by a value read off it is linear** (#7473).
  `{i:0,p:{}} | until(.i>=4000; .p["k\(.i)"]=1 | .i += 1)`, the same in `while`, and
  `(.i|tostring) as $cs | .p[$cs] = .i` as the round, re-indexed and rebuilt the whole state every round, so
  the time grew with the square of the round count where jq 1.7.1 is linear (28x slower at 4,000 rounds on an Apple M4 Pro, 58x on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X). The
  loop's in-place step now reads such a key off the state: a string interpolation whose slots are scalars, and
  `.i | tostring`; a slot that is a container, raises or yields other than once keeps the evaluator's route, and
  the answers are unchanged.
  `last(while ...)` over the same round is not changed and stays quadratic.
- **jq: a recursive `def` that threads a state through its calls no longer copies the state at each call** (#7483, #7473).
  `def f($n): if $n == 0 then .a = 1 else f($n - 1) | f($n - 1) | .a += 1 end; {x: [range(k)]} | f(12)`
  wrote the whole state out as JSON and indexed it again at every call, so its time grew with the size of `x`,
  a member the program never touches: 2.86 s at k = 32,000 on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, where jq 1.7.1 takes
  17 ms; it is now 22 ms at every k. A call, a definition, a pipe a call or an assignment leads, an `if` whose
  condition reads the state and a `$`-parameter's binding run on the built value itself, which each assignment
  they reach writes in place. A recursive `def` that loops in place, `def f: if .i >= n then . else
  (.p["k\(.i)"] = 1 | .i += 1 | f) end`, copied the growing `p` every round and was quadratic in its rounds
  (5.66 s at 16,000); its writes now land in place too, and it takes 11 ms (jq 1.7.1 49 ms). The answers are
  unchanged.
- **jq: a path-mode run that cannot hand an object key out keeps the document's keys as read** (#7489). #7401 gave every object key its own identity in the path-mode interpreter (the route for path expressions that do more than navigate), one or two allocations per key, but a key's identity is only asked of a key handed out as a value, by `.[]` on an object, `..`, `keys`, `keys_unsorted` or a jq-defined builtin built on them (`to_entries`, `paths`, `map`, ...). The interpreter now decides once per run whether the program can reach one, and leaves the keys alone when it cannot; answers are unchanged. Peak RSS of `. as $d | path($d)` (interleaved with an A/A copy of the base): over the generator's `users` pattern -31 to -33% at 10-100 MB on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (968 to about 649 MiB at 100 MB) and -28 to -30% on an Apple M4 Pro (858 to about 601 MiB), and -7% over `comprehensive`, about the 8% #7401 added. Programs that can hand a key out keep the identities and are unchanged.
- **jq: a fold that writes an array slot by a negative index, or by one that pads, is linear** (#7563, #7452).
  `reduce range(1;n) as $i ([range(n)]; .[-$i] = $i)` (and `|=`, `+=`, `//=`, a constant `.[-1]`, inside
  `foreach`), and a fold that grows null-padded rows such as `reduce range(n) as $t ([]; .[$t][799] = 1)` or
  `.[$t][$t] = 1`, re-indexed and rebuilt the whole accumulator on every step, so the time grew with the square
  of the step count where jq 1.7.1 is linear. Both indexes now take the in-place fold write, through the same
  `set_index` the evaluator writes with, and a `-$i` key no longer evaluates on a rebuilt copy of the state; an
  index still negative after counting back from the end keeps jq's `Out of bounds negative array index`, and the
  answers are unchanged.
- **`add` and `flatten` stay linear in a program that holds a path target the shipped evaluator cannot take** (#7564). Such a program (`1 |= 1`, `del(1)`, `path(1)`, `path(tostream .[0])`, even in a branch that never runs) runs through the path-mode interpreter, whose `reduce` copied its array state on every `. + $x` step, so `add` and `flatten` of an array of arrays were quadratic in the result. `[range(1600)|[range(1600)|0]] | if false then (1 |= 1) else . end | add | length` was quadratic in the size of the result where jq 1.7.1 is linear, and is now linear. A step that only appends to an array state now appends in place, as jq's `f_plus` does.
- **`succinctly jq --stream` and `--stream-errors` are linear in a document's depth, as jq is** (#7567). Each event carried a copy of the path as it stood, so the closing events of a document nested `n` deep cost `O(n^2)` (`[`*10000 + `]`*10000, 20 KB, `-n --stream '[inputs] | length'`, took 205.6 ms on an Apple M4 Pro and 921.0 ms on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X where jq 1.7.1 takes 16.8 ms and 4.6 ms); from 64 levels deep an event now takes a window on a path the parser keeps for its events, as jq's do, so the cost is linear in the depth; a shallower path is copied per event as before, so ordinary record streams run the instructions they did (within 0.2% on x86_64). A `--stream-errors` event, and the array `-s` slurps them into, is also read where it is now, as a `--stream` event is, instead of being written out as JSON and indexed again, which cost each event its path's length too. On an Apple M4 Pro the user CPU of every such route grew with exponent 2 in the depth (2,500 to 20,000 levels) and now grows with exponent 1, as jq's does (100,000 to 800,000 levels).
- **A plain `succinctly jq --stream-errors` walk reads its events as the program asks for them** (#7571). Without `-n` it read every event of the input into a list before the program ran, a large multiple of the input at its peak (where jq 1.7.1 stays flat); it now takes the route a plain `--stream` walk has taken since #5498, the stream reader behind the input queue, reading its files a chunk at a time. Peak RSS of the plain `--stream-errors` walk is now flat in the input's size (3.7 to 3.8 MiB at 1, 10 and 100 MB of `--stream-errors -c .` on an Apple M4 Pro, and 15.3 MiB, the benchmark driver's own size before exec, on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X), the output unchanged and equal to jq's.
- **`add` of objects or strings, and `reduce ... (. + {(k): v})` or `(. + "s")`, stay linear in a program that holds a path target the shipped evaluator cannot take** (#7610). Such a program (`1 |= 1`, `del(1)`, `path(1)`, even in a branch that never runs) runs through the path-mode interpreter, whose `reduce` copied an object or a string state on every `. + $x` step, as it did an array state before #7564: user CPU grew four times per doubling of the input (`[range(n) | {("k\(.)"): .}] | if false then (1|=1) else . end | add` and string `add` alike). An object or a string state that nothing else shares now grows in place, as jq's `f_plus` lets `jv_object_merge` and `jv_string_concat` do, and the cost is linear in the number of steps.
- **jq: reading past a parse fault into a deeply nested remainder is linear** (#7611).
  On `-n input`, `inputs` and `input_line_number`, a text whose first fault is not a depth refusal and which
  goes on into a deep remainder (`[x[x[x...` with its closers at the end, 1.6 million levels) took seconds where
  jq 1.7.1 reports the fault at once: after each fault jq drops the rest of its read and parses on from the next,
  and every such read was split, indexed and validated to the end of the text. #7470 cut that work at a depth
  refusal; a read past a fault is now parsed only through the next fault of any kind, so doubling the remainder
  doubles the work where it quadrupled it, and the output is unchanged.
- **jq: a program the path-mode interpreter runs no longer takes the last document's tree apart** (#7697).
  `[path(.data[] | .name // empty)] | length` freed every member of the document but `.data` as it read
  `.data`, millions of small blocks, and on glibc a later free swept them all again
  (`malloc_consolidate`). The last value's document is now kept to the end of the run and forgotten, as
  its index already was (#7332), when it is 64 KiB or more and the program cannot walk it with `..`
  (such a walk frees the tree as it goes, and keeping it would raise the peak). At 100 MB, wall clock on
  an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X / an Apple M4 Pro: that row -26.2% / -30.1% (1773.9 -> 1308.9 ms /
  858.4 -> 600.1 ms), `(.data[] | .name // empty) |= 1 | .data | length` -27.0% / -30.1%,
  `[path(.users[] | .name // empty)] | length` on users -10.2% / -25.9%; peak memory unchanged, output
  identical.
- **jq: `jq . /dev/stdin < big.json` reads a window at a time on Linux** (#7698).
  A lone regular file named by a path whose `stat` is the file standard input is open on (Linux's
  `/dev/stdin`, `/dev/fd/0` and `/proc/self/fd/0`, or the file's own name with the same file on standard
  input, on every platform) was read whole before the program ran, so the run held the whole file where
  `jq . < big.json` holds a window of it. The plain, `-R` and `--seq` routes now read such a path a window
  at a time wherever a new open of it does not share standard input's offset, as on Linux, where it opens
  the file again from its start. Output, errors, exit status and where standard input is left are
  unchanged, as jq 1.7.1 gives them; macOS's `/dev/stdin` and `/dev/fd/0` were already read a window at
  a time (#7446).
- **`succinctly jq` copies a recursive `def`'s body once fewer per call when there is nothing to substitute into it** (#7699). A call to a `def` with `$` parameters copied the body to substitute the parameters' bare names into it even when the body never reads them, before binding the `$` names with their `as` wrappers; a recursion copies the body on every call, since each level's call nodes are new. The copy is now skipped when no parameter is read by its bare name and no argument is a literal: 19-25% less time on the recursions #7460 named (`def f($n): ... f($n - 1) | f($n - 1) ...; 0 | f(16)` 281.6 -> 227.8 ms on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, 251.5 -> 189.0 ms on an Apple M4 Pro; jq 1.7.1 44-46 ms), `f($n - 1) + f($n - 1)`, `fib($n)`, `[f, f] | add` and three piped calls alike (-23.5 to -25.7% instructions), output identical; a body that reads a bare parameter, a literal argument and a call whose bound body is cached are unchanged. The rest of the gap to jq (3-6x on these shapes) is the copies that remain, recorded in #7699.
- **jq: a fold or loop step whose update calls a `def` no longer copies the state at each step** (#7702).
  `def f($v): .a = $v; {x: [range(k)]} | reduce range(400) as $i (.; f($i))`, and the same update in `foreach`
  (EXTRACT included, a call there too), `until`, `while`, `recurse`, `limit(n; recurse(..))` and a pipe of a call
  and a write, wrote the whole state out as JSON and indexed it again at every step, so the run's time grew with
  the size of `x`, a member the steps never touch, where jq 1.7.1's does not. The step now hands the state to
  the owned evaluator's door for a call (#7483), which writes in place: on an x86_64 box under cachegrind the
  `reduce` at k = 100,000 retires 78 million instructions where it retired 22.3 billion, and every shape above is
  now flat in `k`. The answers are unchanged.
- **jq: `getpath` of a bound container reads one element, not the whole container** (#7721).
  `[range(n)] as $a | reduce range(n) as $i (0; . + ($a|getpath([$i])))`, its `foreach`, `until`, `limit` and
  `[range(n) as $i | $a|getpath([$i])]` forms, `$o|getpath(["k",$i])`, and the same reads of a document, an
  `input` or a `--slurpfile` value wrote the bound container out and indexed it again for every read, because
  neither the in-place fold step nor the owned evaluator's doors had a `getpath` stage: the time grew with the
  container's size times the number of reads, quadratic where jq 1.7.1 is linear. A `getpath` whose path never
  reads `.` now walks the bound value in place, with the walk the evaluator's own `getpath` takes; a path that
  raises or is not an array keeps the evaluator's route and its message, and the answers are unchanged.
- **jq: under `--seq`, a program that stops early reads only the records it consumes** (#7775).
  `--seq -n 'first(inputs)'` read and walked the whole stream before its first record ran, so it cost as much as
  `[inputs]` and grew with the input, where jq reads a line at a time and stops at the records the program takes.
  A program that calls `input`/`inputs` now walks the stream as it reads it, a block at a time, from named files
  or a pipe, so `first(inputs)`, `limit(n; inputs)`, `input | halt` and `first(inputs | select(...))` stop after
  the blocks their records are in, and answer while a pipe is still open, as jq does. Each named file is opened
  only when the walk reaches it, as jq's reader opens it, so a run that stops early never opens the files after
  its records (a named pipe with no writer among them). Each record is let go once the program has it, so
  `-n 'reduce inputs as $x (0; .+1)'` over a pipe holds a few reads however long the stream (its peak is the same
  at 1 GB as at 100 MB), where it held the whole stream and grew with it. A main loop that can halt (`.id, halt`) no longer reads a file whole to vouch for it before its
  first record: it is read a window at a time from the start; over a pipe it is walked as it is read too, so it
  answers at the record it halts on where it waited for 4 MiB or the pipe's end, and one that never halts stays
  as small. None reads past the records it consumes, so a fault later in the stream is not met, as jq never
  meets it, and every answer is unchanged. Instruction counts (cachegrind, the AMD Ryzen 9 7950X box): `--seq -n
  'first(inputs)'` is 6.6 million at 10 MB and at 100 MB, where it was 817 million and 8.08 billion; `--seq -c
  '.id, halt'` over a 10 MB file is 12.1 million, where it was 326 million.
- **jq: `contains` of a bound container searches it in place** (#7785).
  `[range(n)] as $a | reduce range(k) as $i (0; if $a|contains([$i]) then . + 1 else . end)`, its `foreach`,
  `until`, `limit` and `[range(k) as $i | $a|contains([$i])]` forms, `$o|contains({k: [$i]})`, a bound string's
  `contains("\($i)")`, and the same calls over a document, an `input` or a `--argjson` value wrote the bound
  container out and indexed it again for every call, because neither the in-place fold step nor the owned
  evaluator's doors had a `contains` stage for a needle other than a string literal: the time grew with the
  container's size on every call, where jq searches the value in place and stops at the first match. A
  `contains` whose needle never reads `.` now asks the evaluator's own search of the bound value; a needle of
  another kind keeps the evaluator's route and its containment error, and the answers are unchanged.
- **jq: `del(.. | f)` and `delpaths([path(f)])` hold less memory** (#7789).
  A stage after a descent (`.. | .pad?`, `.. | strings`, `.. | select(. == null)`) rebuilt each result's whole path
  chain rather than sharing the chain of the node it extends, so the paths held memory proportional to their total
  length, quadratic in the depth of a deeply nested document, where they now share it: linear in the nodes the paths
  name. The delete trie keeps a leaf in a few words and a node's few edges in a short list, releases each path once it
  is inserted, and a jq-mode `del` drops its resolved branches before the trie grows. `delpaths([path(f)])` builds its
  path list as `[path(f)] as $p | delpaths($p)` does rather than holding it three times over. Output is unchanged, and
  a stage whose results cannot share a chain (`del(.users[] | select(.score < 100))`) and yq mode build their paths as
  before. Peak RSS on an 18 MB array of 201,000 small records, on the AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (Apple M4 Pro): `del(.. |
  .pad?)` 1724 -> 870 MiB (1718 -> 1141), `del(..|strings)` 1061 -> 748 MiB (1121 -> 849), `del(.. | select(. ==
  null))` 918 -> 744 MiB (991 -> 832) and `delpaths([path(.. | .pad?)])` 1155 -> 695 MiB (1265 -> 641), where jq 1.7.1
  takes 570 / 485 / 450 / 570 MiB (611 / 534 / 493 / 611). On 300 chains of 120 nested objects, `del(.. | .n?)` falls
  from 490 to 43 MiB (426 to 58), below jq's 74 (85).
- **One JSON value spread over many input files is read once, not again at every file boundary** (#7792). The stitch that carries a token a file ends inside onto the next file scanned, validated and copied the whole value so far at each boundary, so the cost grew with the number of files times the size: `length` over a 10 MB array cut into 40 files took 4.83 G instructions where one file takes 0.26 G (cachegrind on the x86_64 box), and on the AMD Ryzen 9 7950X box a 100 MB array in 40 files took 2.8 s where jq 1.7.1 takes 1.4 s. jq's parser state now goes on with the carry and each file is read from where it stopped; the same 10 MB array takes 0.42-0.53 G instructions in 2, 8, 40 or 200 files.
- **jq: a `--rawfile` file that is UTF-8 throughout becomes its string without a second copy** (#7814).
  Since #7436, `--rawfile`, `-f` and `import ... {raw: true}` decoded every file one 4,096-byte read at a time
  into a new string, so the file's bytes and its text were held at once and every byte was copied again. A
  file that is valid UTF-8 now becomes the string in place, and only a file with a byte that is not UTF-8
  takes the per-read walk, starting at the read that holds the first such byte, with the same answers as
  before. Modules and `~/.jq` no longer copy a valid file either. `-n --rawfile s F '$s|length'` over the
  100 MB users input is back to the instruction count it had before #7436 (88.9M -> 80.2M; cachegrind on
  the AMD Ryzen 9 7950X box; 10 MB: 9.65M -> 8.81M).
- **jq: a `--rawfile` or large `--arg` value is no longer read for `__jq` on every run** (#7880). Since #7719 the walk that decides which evaluator runs a program looked for `__jq`, the key of jq's label value, in every string of the program, and a named argument's value is substituted into the program as one, so `-n --rawfile s FILE '$s|length'` paid two passes over the file. Whether the run spells `__jq` is now decided from the program as written, before the arguments are substituted, and an argument's value is read for it only by a program that holds an `error`, the one way to raise a value that is not a string; the refusal check and the route decision also share one walk instead of two. Cachegrind instruction counts on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X box (valgrind 3.18.1, `--cache-sim=no`): `-n --rawfile s users-10mb.json '$s|length'` 91.41M to 8.85M (8.84M before #7719) and 9.92M to 1.92M over the 1 MB file (1.90M before); `--arg` with a 120 KB value 4.25M to 2.81M; `-n 1` 1,135,403 to 1,133,237. A program that does raise (`try error($s|length) catch .` over the 10 MB file) reads the value once: 91.42M to 13.06M.
- **jq: an `--argjson` text and a `--jsonargs` word are parsed once, not twice** (#7881). Since #7743 (option errors in argv order, #7712) the walk over argv parsed each `--argjson` text and each `--jsonargs` word to check it where jq's option loop checks it, dropped the value, and the run parsed the same text again to bind it. The walk now keeps the value it built, under the word's place in argv, and the run binds that value when the text it is asked for is that word's; a name an earlier flag bound is still skipped unread, and every option error is reported where it was. Cachegrind instruction counts on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X box (Linux, valgrind 3.18.1, `--cache-sim=no`, stripped release builds with `--features cli`) for `-n --argjson v VALUE 1`, the commit before #7743 in brackets: a 100 KB array of small objects 81.17M to 39.65M (39.62M), a 100 KB array of numbers 73.58M to 36.17M (36.18M), one 100 KB string 10.59M to 6.44M (6.36M); at 10 KB 9.35M to 5.07M (5.06M), 8.62M to 4.78M (4.77M) and 2.10M to 1.68M (1.65M). The same 100 KB values as a `--jsonargs` word: 80.75M to 39.23M, 73.18M to 35.61M and 10.16M to 6.02M. `-n 1` is 1,102,295 before and 1,101,749 after (1,077,583 at the commit before #7743, so about 24,000 of each bracketed difference is start-up cost that other changes added since). The CI perf guard gains a row for an `--argjson` value (`argjson_objects`), which no row covered.
- **jq: an `--argjson` value and a `--jsonargs` word of plain JSON are read in one pass** (#7881). Such a text now goes first to the one-pass reader a `--slurpfile` file is read by (#6110), which builds the same value, number spellings included (`1.000`, `1e1000`, `100000000000000000000`). Text that reader declines (a leniency such as a leading zero, a repeated key, a lone surrogate escape, `nan`, nesting past 128 levels, or text that is not JSON) takes the route every text took before: the validator, the index and the walk over it, which still decides every refusal. Cachegrind instruction counts on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X box (Linux, valgrind 3.18.1, `--cache-sim=no`, stripped release builds with `--features cli`) for `-n --argjson v VALUE 1`, on top of the single parse above, with jq 1.7.1 on the same box in brackets: a 100 KB array of small objects 39.65M to 9.87M (31.97M), a 100 KB array of numbers 36.17M to 12.15M (33.36M), one 100 KB string 6.44M to 3.48M (17.97M); at 1 KB 1.54M to 1.22M, 1.50M to 1.24M and 1.18M to 1.14M. The same bytes through `--slurpfile` cost 8.69M, 11.09M and 2.28M.
- **jq: the outputs of a recursive generator reach their consumer from where they are produced, not through every level of the recursion** (#7893).
  `def f: if . > 0 then (. - 1 | f), . else . end; [N | f] | length` handed each output of a level back up through every level above it, N²/2 calls for its N outputs, where jq hands each straight to the consumer.
  Two things stood between a level's call and the sink its caller was given.
  Since #7856 every call to a def that may recurse wrapped its sink in a check of the native stack, even where the sink was already such a check: that was the whole cost of `def f($n): if $n > 0 then f($n - 1), $n else $n end; [f(N)]`, in `succinctly yq --jq-extensions` too.
  And since #7702 a def that threads its count through `.` ran its `,` and its `. - 1 | f` on the owned evaluator's re-index bridge, whose own sink the call was given.
  A call whose sink is the check of the call that handed it on is no longer wrapped again (each output is still checked, once), and a `,` or a pipe that ends in the recursive call runs on the owned tree with the sink it was given.
  Under cachegrind on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (x86_64 Linux, release build) the first program retires 35.8 / 70.3 / 139.5 million instructions at N = 1,500 / 3,000 / 6,000 where it retired 126.7 / 416.3 / 1,488.7 million, and the second 40.4 / 79.6 / 158.0 million where it retired 68.6 / 192.2 / 608.2 million; `reduce`, `foreach`, `first`, `last`, `limit` and `select` as the consumer scale the same way.
  The answers are unchanged, and so is every refusal #7856 added: a recursion whose outputs climb through a consumer at each level is checked at each level, as before.
- **The release binary's link-order list is regenerated, and a stale one now fails CI** (#7894, #7826).
  `scripts/link-order/symbols.txt` had drifted until 8.0% of its names no longer resolved, so functions renamed or
  added on hot paths sat outside the ordered block and each kept a page of text resident per run. Regenerated from
  `a9da4e814`, peak RSS on the 231 rows of the #7412 memory run drops by a median 1.40 MB on rows under 60 MB on an
  AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (rows above jq 1.7.1: 92 -> 86, geomean ratio 0.720 -> 0.626, `jq -n 1` 5.10 -> 3.63 MB) and
  by 0.35 MB on an Apple M4 Pro (79 -> 76, 0.578 -> 0.553, 3.25 -> 2.88 MB); wall-clock moves by -2.6% on 1 MB
  rows, -1.0% on 10 MB rows and -5% at startup on the 7950X and by -1.3% to +0.3% on the M4 Pro, output identical. CI's perf-guard job
  now runs `generate.py stale`, which fails when more than 5% of the listed names no longer resolve, and
  `generate.py macos` adds every platform-named function instead of claiming to sample which ones run.
- **jq: a comma with a `.[]` branch over a collected array no longer writes the array out and indexes it** (#7935).
  `.[], .`, `., .[]`, `.[]?, .` and `.[], .[]` over an array or object the program built (`[...] | .[], .`) declined
  the owned door and went through the re-index bridge, which writes the value out as JSON and indexes it again. A
  recursion that collects each level and yields `.[], .` of it (`def f: if . > 0 then [. - 1 | f] | .[], . else .
  end;`) wrote out a value whose text doubles per level, so `first(50 | f)` reached 2.6 GB in 5 s with no answer,
  where jq 1.7.1 answers `0` at once. The children of such a branch are now handed on as they are read, each still
  sharing its storage, so the sink sees the first before the rest are copied. Indicative, Apple silicon laptop, peak
  RSS and time, output identical:

  | Program                                                       | jq 1.7.1        | Before          | After           |
  |---------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------|-----------------|-----------------|
  | `first(20 \| f)`                                              | 2.6 MB, 0.00 s  | 26.5 MB, 0.07 s | 5.0 MB, 0.01 s  |
  | `first(24 \| f)`                                              | 2.6 MB, 0.00 s  | 359 MB, 0.73 s  | 5.0 MB, 0.01 s  |
  | `first(25 \| f)`                                              | 2.6 MB, 0.00 s  | 689 MB, 1.38 s  | 5.1 MB, 0.00 s  |
  | `first(50 \| f)`                                              | 2.6 MB, 0.00 s  | killed at 5 s   | 5.5 MB, 0.01 s  |
  | `first(22 \| g)`, `g` yielding `.[], .[]`                     | 150 MB, 0.26 s  | 230 MB, 0.49 s  | 130 MB, 0.07 s  |
  | `[22 \| g] \| length`                                         | 309 MB, 0.44 s  | 539 MB, 0.74 s  | 382 MB, 0.12 s  |

  A comma no door answers (`(.[] | .), .`, `(range(length) as $i | .[$i]), .`) still takes the bridge.

### Fixed

- **yq: `{...}` and `[...]` built from nodes of the document keep each node's quote style, flow style, trailing comment and anchor** (#865). `{"a": .a, "b": .b}` over `a: 'single' # ca` / `b: "double" # cb` printed `a: single` / `b: double`; it now prints both lines as yq does, and so do `[.a, .b]`, nested constructions, literals, `length` of a read and arithmetic on reads among the entries (`.a + "x"` takes its left operand's), a node reached through `.` and a construction behind a path (`.c | [.]`), at the cost of the nodes read. yq's own placement is followed: a standalone comment above a node stays with its key, and a non-empty flow mapping after the first entry of a constructed mapping prints as a block. Entries with several outputs (`(.a, .b)`, `.[]`), other computed entries, computed or repeated keys, a construction a later stage reshapes and one wrapped in a `def` print plain, as before.
- **yq: a container read into a construction no longer carries the comment after its key** (#865 follow-up). `[.d]` over `d:` / `  x: 2` / `# f` printed `- x: 2` / `# f`; the comment after the last member is the key's foot, which yq leaves with the key (`- x: 2`). A comment inside the container (`  # f`) is a foot of one of its own keys and still comes along.
- **yq: a computed `NaN`/`Infinity` prints as yq spells it, and a document `.inf`/`.NaN` keeps the bytes it was written with** (#1071). `sub("a"; 1e300*1e300)` on `abc` answered `.infbc` where yq answers `+Infbc`; `0*(1e300*1e300)` printed `.nan` (yq `NaN`), `[.a, (1e300*1e300)] | join(",")` on `a: .inf` printed `.inf,.inf` (yq `.inf,+Inf`), and `{"v": (1e300*1e300)}` printed `v: .inf` (yq `v: !!float +Inf`, the tag a nested computed non-finite carries). A document `.INF`, `+.inf` or `.NaN` read through `tostring`, `join` or a bracketed copy was folded to `.inf`/`.nan`; it now echoes its own spelling, as yq does. JSON output of a non-finite is still `null` where yq errors (#1087). Library note: `succinctly::jq::nonfinite_display_string::<YqSemantics>` now answers the computed spelling (`NaN`/`+Inf`/`-Inf`) instead of `.nan`/`.inf`/`-.inf`.
- **`@props` ends every line with a newline, the last included** (#1076). `{"a":1} | @props` was `"a = 1"`; yq's properties encoder writes `"a = 1\n"` (a bare `"x" | @props` is `"x\n"`), so the CLI printed `a = 1` and a blank line there and a single line here, and `@props | length` was one short. A value with no lines (`{}`, `[]`) is still the empty string. `@yaml` already ended this way (#1183). Over a 12-row differential against yq v4.53.3 (plain keys and values: objects, nested arrays, scalars, `null`, `1e10*2`, `4/2`) none now differ; the escaping of special characters in keys and values (`\n`, `\t`, `\\`, a leading or key space, `:`) is a separate gap (#4977). `succinctly jq` shares the format and ends its lines the same way. The float arms the issue was filed about (`1e10*2`, `2.0*1`) were fixed earlier (#2902).
- **`succinctly yq` keeps both comments of two chained anchored keys** (#1080). `a: &x # c1` followed by `b: &y # c2` dropped `c1` and `c2` entirely; they now float and attach as real yq does (`b: # c1` / `&y` / `  c: 1 # c2`), for plain and compact (sequence-item) mappings and for longer chains.
- **`succinctly yq` rejects a `-` sequence line right after an explicit `?` key at the same indent** (#1104). `? k` / `- item` is no longer read as `{"k":["item"]}`: an explicit key's value must be introduced by `:`, so it now fails with a parse error where real yq fails with "did not find expected key". A bare `?` keeps parsing as before, and `k:` / `- item` is unchanged.
- **yq: an integer too big for `i64` keeps its digits through `tostring`, string interpolation, `join`, `length` and a YAML re-emit** (#1129).
  `a: 99999999999999999999 | .a | tostring` answered `1e+20` (and `"\(.a)"` the expanded `100000000000000000000.0`, and
  `.a = .a` rewrote the untouched field to that spelling, and `-r -o=json` printed the rounded double); yq answers the digits as written, `99999999999999999999`, while its JSON
  encoder still prints the double it parsed (`100000000000000000000.0`), which `-o=json` and `@json` keep doing. The digits ride
  with the value as its literal text and every yq JSON writer asks for the rounded spelling. The `+`-signed, leading-zero and explicitly tagged `!!float` spellings follow in #4921.
- **yq: `tostring` of an array or object is its YAML, not JSON** (#1130). `[1, 2] | tostring` was `"[1,2]"`, jq's text; yq answers the YAML it would print, `"- 1\n- 2"`, with the trailing line break chomped (`{"a": [1]}` is `"a:\n  - 1"`, `[1.0 * 3]` is `"- !!float 3"`, `[]` is `"[]"`). A container the source wrote in flow style stays flow (`b: [1, 2]` gives `"[1, 2]"`). The text comes from the CLI's own YAML writer, and the owned fast paths (`select(tostring | ...)`, a `reduce` body) share one definition with the main route. jq mode still JSON-encodes. Not part of this change: a flow container nested in a block one, or rebuilt by `with_entries`, prints block; `-I` is ignored; and string interpolation of a container still JSON-encodes.
- **yq: a slice write on a mapping is a no-op, as in yq** (#1157). `succinctly yq '.a[0:1] = [99]'` over `a: {x: 1, y: 2}` failed with `Cannot index object with object`; yq leaves the document unchanged for `=`, `|=`, `+=`, `-=` and `*=` alike (a scalar right-hand side to `-=`/`*=` is still an arithmetic error, as in yq). The update filter still runs against the mapping's alternating key/value child list, the same one `.[S:E]` reads (#1102), so its own errors surface; `del` and the array/string no-ops (#1142) are unchanged, and `succinctly jq` keeps jq's error.
- **yq: `@yaml` renders block-style YAML with a trailing newline, as yq does** (#1183). `{"v": 3.0*1} | @yaml`
  printed the flow-style `{v: 3.0}`; yq answers `v: !!float 3\n`. `@yaml` had its own flow-style
  copy of the value-to-YAML renderer, which is gone: it now runs the streamer behind the CLI's YAML
  output, so containers come out as block mappings and sequences, a nested computed float carries its
  `!!float` tag, and a root string keeps its quoting (`"1" | @yaml` is `"1"`, `"a: b"` is `'a: b'`).
  `succinctly jq`'s `@yaml` extension follows, so a `@yaml "v: \(1)"` interpolation slot now carries
  the newline too. A flow-sourced container still prints block, since an owned value carries no source
  style (#739, #865), and a root computed float stays untagged (#1090).
- **`succinctly yq` reads a flow collection followed by `:` as a mapping key** (#1188). `[a, b]: value` and `{a: 1}: value` are `{"":"value"}` where they were the collection and the value as two separate results, and a sibling after them (`z: 1`) joined neither; `k:` / `  [a, b]: value` no longer loses its value. The same holds under `- `, after `? k` / `:`, behind an `&anchor` or `!tag`, and for `? [1, 2]: value` (`{"":null}`), matching yq in each case.
- **yq: a comma-grouped `del()` stops at a bare slice of the root, as yq's delete does** (#1325). `del(.a[0:1], .[2:3])` over `{"a":{"x":1,"y":2},"b":6,"c":9}` deleted `.a`; yq deletes nothing. yq walks the matches from the last to the first and returns at the first one without a parent, and a slice of the root has none, so the branches written before the bare slice are never deleted (`del(.[2:3], .a[0:1])` still deletes `.a`, `del(.b, .[2:3])` deletes nothing, `del(.a[0:1], .[2:3], .b)` deletes only `.b`). Nested groups, `?`, parentheses, a run (`.[2:3][0:1]`) and a pipe of slices all count; a tail after the run (`.[2:3][0]`) does not. 43 rows over an object and an array root match yq v4.53.3 byte for byte (the 4 that raise differ in wording only). A group whose earlier branch could create nodes while it resolves (an index past the end of an array, an index or `.[]` on `null`) keeps its earlier behaviour.
- **`paths(f)` keeps both occurrences of a duplicate YAML mapping key under `succinctly yq --jq-extensions`** (#1342). It materialized the document and re-resolved each path, so `a: 1 / a: 2` answered `paths(scalars)` with `a` once where `paths` and `to_entries` answer it twice, and `paths(. == 1)` looked up the surviving `a: 2` and found nothing. It now walks the document and runs the filter on the node each path names. `succinctly jq`, where a duplicate collapses anyway, is unchanged.
- **yq: an owned value keeps a repeated mapping key's earlier entries** (#1344, #1343, #2063, #2186, #5414). `a: 1` / `a: 2` was merged to `a: 2` by every route that materializes a document into an owned value: `-s`/`--eval-all` input, `[...]`, `as $x`, `..`, `-P`/`-C`/`-0`, `reduce`/`foreach` bindings, `group_by`, `while`/`until`, and every write. `succinctly yq` now prints what yq v4.53.3 prints on all of them (`[.]`, `[..]` and `. as $d | $d` are `{"a":1,"a":2,"b":3}`; `.a = 5` is `{"a":1,"a":5,"b":3}`; `del(.b)` is `{"a":1,"a":2}`), and `to_entries`, `with_entries`, `from_entries`, `map_values`, `omit` and `+` follow yq's rule for which entry they act on. 68 oracle rows are pinned in `tests/yq_cli/i1344.rs`. `contains`, `sort_keys` and an earlier entry's comment, anchor or style are still the collapsed answer (see `docs/compliance/yq/limitations.md`). `succinctly jq` is unchanged: jq reads the last value of a repeated key.
- **yq: `tonumber` of an integer string keeps its spelling** (#1356).
  `"0x10" | tonumber`, `"007"`, `"+5"`, `"0X10"`, `"0o17"` and `"1_000"` print as written through `tostring`, interpolation and YAML output and keep their base under arithmetic (`"0x10" | tonumber | . + 1` is `0x11`), as yq does; `-o=json` still prints the number, and the strings yq refuses (`"-0x10"`, `" 0x10"`, `"0x"`, `"0o9"`) are still refused.
  A nested `_1` carries the `!!int` tag yq gives it.
  The float spellings (`"+2.0"`, `"2."`, `".5"`) are not part of this change.
- **yq: a float written `+2.0`, `2.`, `.5`, `1.e5`, `+1e5` or `007.5` keeps its spelling** (#1356).
  A document float and `tonumber` of such a string print as written through `tostring`, string interpolation, `join` and YAML output (`a: +2.0 | .a | tostring` is `+2.0`, `.5` is `.5`, `1.e5` is `1.e5`), and `sort`, `max` and `unique` return the node with its spelling, as yq does.
  `-o=json` prints yq's `FormatFloat` of the value: `2.0`, `0.5`, and `100000.0` for `1.e5` and `+1e5`, which printed `1.0e5` and `1e5` before.
  An underscored decimal or a hex float string (`"1_0.5"`, `"0x1p3"`) still normalizes.
- **yq: a query that is a comma of document nodes (`.x, .y`) keeps the comments, style and `&anchor` marks of each result** (#1361).
  `printf 'x: &a {p: 1}\ny:\n  q: *a\n' | yq '.x, .y'` starts with `&a {p: 1}`; `succinctly yq` printed `p: 1`. `x:\n  p: 1 # note\ny:\n  q: "str"` lost `# note` and the double quotes, and a flow sequence read twice (`.l, .l` on `l: [1, 2]`) came out in block style, though each half of the comma kept all three on its own. The branches that answer nodes of the document now stay cursors, as `.[]`'s results do, so the output is byte for byte what `--arg z 1 '.[]'` prints for the same nodes. Over 38 comma queries on four YAML documents (plain and `-o json`) and two JSON documents under `jq`, 27 outputs changed, all of them plain YAML and each now showing the comments, style and anchors yq shows; `-o json` and `jq` (against `/usr/bin/jq` 1.7.1) did not change. A branch that is not a node (`.x, (.y | length)`, `.x, 1`, an absent key in `.x, .zz`) still turns the nodes before it into copies, and a comma inside a bigger expression (`[.x, .y]`, `(.x, .y) | f`) is read by that expression as before.
- **yq: `setpath` checks its path before its value, as yq does** (#1380). A path element that is not a `!!str` or an `!!int`
  (a slice descriptor, a float including `1.0`, a sequence, a boolean, a null) is refused with `SETPATH: expected either a
  !!str or !!int in the path, found <tag> instead` before anything is navigated or the value is evaluated, where
  `setpath(["a",1.5]; 5)` wrote element 1 and `setpath(["a",{"start":0,"end":1}]; [9])` spliced a slice. A path error now
  outranks a value error (`setpath([error("p")]; error("r"))` is `p`), a string or integer key through a scalar is a no-op
  (`a: 5 | setpath(["a","b"]; 5)` is unchanged) instead of `Cannot index number`, and the count, path-array and negative-index
  refusals take yq's sentences. jq mode is unchanged.
- **yq: `-=`/`*=` on an absent slice target now follow yq** (#1390). `.b[0:1] -= 5`, `.b[0:1] -= [1]` and `.b[0:1] *= [1]` on a document without `.b` raised `Cannot index null with object` where yq leaves the document alone (`b: null`), and `.b[0:1].c += 5` (any operator, with a step after the slice) raised `Cannot index array with string "c"` for the same reason. The discarded write's throwaway is now `null` once a step follows the slice, and for `-=`/`*=`, as in yq (an empty `null`-tagged sequence): `null - X` is identity, `null * [1]` is too, and `null * 5` still raises yq's arithmetic error. A plain terminal `|=`/`+=` keeps its `[]` (`length` 0, `tojson` `[]`). A non-null scalar target (`b: 5`) follows the same rule: `.b[0:1] -= [1]` and `*= [1]` leave the document alone and a scalar right side still raises, as in yq.
- **`succinctly yq` no longer evaluates an assignment's right side when its left side is all no-ops** (#1412). `5 | (.a, .b) = error("boom")`, `"a" as $k | .[$k] += error("boom")` and `select(false) = error("boom")` raised `boom`; yq answers the document unchanged, because it resolves the left side first and only runs the right side for a target that exists. `=`, `+=`, `-=` and `*=` all follow, and a dynamic left side is now resolved once instead of twice. A left side yq does not track as a path (`[.a]`, `1`, `.a | length`) still runs the right side and raises, as in yq. `succinctly jq` is unchanged: jq runs the right side first.
- **`succinctly yq -p json -o json` substitutes invalid UTF-8 as yq does** (#1616). A stray byte in a string or key becomes one U+FFFD per invalid byte (`{"a":"x�y"}`, exit 0) on every route including `--slurp`, `--eval-all` and `-i`, where it used to fail with `invalid UTF-8 in string` after printing a prefix. With YAML output the string is still refused when printed, as yq does, and a filter that never prints it still succeeds. A YAML document with a stray byte is still rejected unconditionally (#1242).
- **library: a duplicate-key collapse no longer merges two different complex YAML keys** (#1740). A YAML key
  with no scalar form (`? {}`, `? [1]`, a non-string alias) stringifies to `""`, so evaluating a `YamlValue`
  under `JqSemantics` (library API only: `sjq` reads JSON and `syq` evaluates under `YqSemantics`) treated
  `? {}: 1` / `? []: 2` as one repeated key and kept only the last. Such a key now has no identity hash, as a key
  that will not decode already did (#1385), so both entries survive.
- **yq-locate, jq-locate: a mapping key that does not decode no longer fails the locate** (#1759). On
  `a: 1` / `"b\xe4c": 2`, `yq-locate --offset 7` (the key), `--offset 12` (its value) and any descendant of
  the key failed with `Could not locate position`, hiding the real cause already warned about on stderr;
  `jq-locate` failed the same way on a JSON key. The key is now read lossily, so its invalid bytes (or an
  invalid escape's raw text) show as U+FFFD and it takes bracket form: `.[0]["b�c"]`.
- **yq: `|=` evaluates its whole update filter, so a later error aborts with no document** (#1779).
  `.x |= (1, error("boom"), 3)`, `.a |= (., error("x"))` and `.a[] |= (1, error("x"))` printed the
  document with the first output written and no error; yq raises the error and prints nothing, because
  it reads the whole filter before taking its first output. `=` and the compound assignments already
  did this; `succinctly jq` keeps jq's `_modify` reading only the first output.
- **yq: `join` writes a document `{}` element as the empty string** (#1791). `- {}` / `- x` joined with `","` printed `{},x`, where yq v4.53.3 prints `,x`, and so does a `{}` reached through `$x`, `[.[0]]` or `del`. yq writes the text `{}` only for an empty mapping the expression itself spelled `{}`; `join({})` still prints `1{}2`, but the literal element (`[{}] | join(",")`) is now `""` here and `{}` in yq, because this evaluator cannot tell it from a document one. Recorded in `docs/compliance/yq/limitations.md`.
- **yq: `del()` over a comma group with a literal target follows yq's back-to-front loop** (#1865). yq walks the targets
  of `del()` in reverse and stops at the first one with no parent, keeping what it already deleted, so `del(.a, 1)` deletes
  nothing while `del(1, .a)` deletes `.a`, and `del(.a, .c, 1)` deletes nothing. succinctly raised `Invalid path expression`
  for every such group, and for a lone literal (`del(1)`). A literal, constructor or root now ends the scan the way it does
  in yq, in objects, arrays and fan-outs alike (`del(1, .a[])` empties `.a`; `del(., 1)` keeps the document, `del(1, .)`
  empties it). A target that is a derived value or a bound variable (`del(.b | tostring)`, `del(.a, (.b as $y | $y))`)
  still refuses, and jq mode is unchanged.
- **`succinctly yq` no longer raises when a write's scalar-literal branch is followed by navigation** (#1868). `(.a, 1 | .[]) = 5`, `(.a, 1 | .b) = 5`, `(.a, "s" | .[0]) = 5`, `(.a, 1 | .[0:1]) = 5` and `del(.a, 1 | .[])` raised jq's "Invalid path expression"; real yq has no such notion, leaves the document alone for that branch and writes every other (`a: 5`, `b: 2`). `=`, `|=`, the compound operators and `del()` now match. A bound `$x`, a computed value, a literal array or object, a computed key and `..` keep the refusal (`(.a, 1 | ..) = 5`, `(.a, 1 | .[$k]) = 5` still differ from yq), and `succinctly jq` is unchanged.
- **yq: block indentation after stacked compact sequence items follows yq's round-up rule** (#1881). go-yaml opens a block child under a mapping value at the smallest multiple of `-I` above the current indent, and a compact `- ` adds a literal 2 columns, so with two stacked `- - b:` levels over `c:` the column of `c` is 6, 6, 8, 5, 6 at `-I=2..6` (not monotonic), and with three stacked levels `-I=4` and `-I=5` do not follow the pattern either. succinctly stepped from a pre-compact base instead and disagreed at `-I=3` (two levels) and `-I=4`/`-I=5` (three levels). One rounding step (`deeper_yaml_indent`) is now shared by the cursor writer, the DOM writer and the owned-value streamer; output outside a compact chain is unchanged (the indent is already a multiple of `-I` there). The "stacked compact items" entry in `docs/compliance/yq/limitations.md` is removed as no longer a divergence.
- **yq: a hyphenated name that starts with a builtin's spelling is that name, not the builtin** (#1890). In yq mode `-` followed by an identifier character continues the identifier, but the keyword matcher stopped at the hyphen, so `def sin-approx: 99; sin-approx` was rejected for using `sin` (naming a `--jq-extensions` flag that did not help) and with the flag parsed as `sin - approx` (`approx/0 is not defined`). `sin-approx`, `length-of-thing`, `not-x` and `input-foo` now parse as one identifier, through one predicate shared with the identifier scanner; a spaced `length - 1` is still subtraction and `succinctly jq` is unchanged.
- **yq: `.a[] = <rhs>` no longer evaluates the RHS when there is nothing to write into** (#1921).
  `.a[] = error("boom")` on `a: []`, `a: {}`, `a: null` and a root `null` raised `boom`; yq never runs the
  right side for zero elements and prints `{"a":[]}`, `{"a":{}}`, `{"a":[]}` and `[]`. The same holds for
  the compound assignments and a nested `.a[][] = ...`; a non-empty target still evaluates the RHS, and
  `succinctly jq` is unchanged. The comma form `(.a[], .b[]) = ...` is not covered.
- **yq: a flow mapping missing a comma is rejected instead of swallowing the next entry** (#1960).
  `{a: 1 b: 2}` read as `a: "1 b: 2"`, and `.a = 9` then wrote `{a: 9}` with exit 0, silently dropping `b: 2` from the
  file. A flow plain scalar now ends at `:` followed by a blank, a line break or end-of-input (a continuation line that
  opens with `: ` included), so the parser reports `expected ',' or '}'` as yq does. A `:` before a flow indicator or
  inside a word is still content (`{a: 1:, b: 2}`, `{a: x:y}`), matching yq v4.53.3.
  A plain flow key now ends only at `:` followed by a blank, a line break, end-of-input or a flow indicator, so `[a:\n 1]`,
  `[x:y: 1]` and `{a:1}` (a key `a:1`) read as yq reads them.
- **yq: `-0`/`--nul-output` no longer implies `-r` for JSON output** (#1996). `yq -o=json -0 '.a'` on
  `a: hello` printed `hello` and on `a: "b\0c"` failed with `can't serialise value because it contains
  NUL char`; yq prints `"hello"` and `"b\u0000c"` (JSON's default unwrap-scalar setting is false, only
  YAML's is true) and so does `succinctly yq` now. `-o=json -r -0` and YAML `-0` still refuse a NUL.
  `-j`/`--join-output` still implies `-r`; its reshaping is #1731.
- **yq `sort`, `sort_by`, `reverse` and `shuffle` on a non-array** (#1998). They raised jq-style wording (`number (5) cannot be sorted, as it is not an array`, `Cannot index number with number`, `shuffle requires array, got number`); they now raise yq's `node at path [] is not an array or map (it's a !!int)` with the node's tag. The path is always `[]`, so the text matches yq for a root or literal input; after a navigation (`.a | sort`) yq names the node's path.
- **yq: `--colors -0` writes the clean results before a NUL-bearing one, as yq does** (#2004). `succinctly yq --colors -0 '.[]'` over `["hello", "wor\0ld", "x"]` printed nothing and failed on the NUL, where yq prints `hello\0` and then fails (exit 1, same message); the colored render was scanned whole before anything was written, so one NUL discarded every earlier result. The results that end before the first NUL are now colorized and written, then the run stops with the same error. Output without a NUL, and the memory cost of coloring, are unchanged.
- **yq: `fromjson` rejects every surrogate `\u` escape, as go-yaml's scanner does** (#2018). `"😀"` (a valid pair)
  decoded to the emoji, and `["😀"]` to a one-element array, where yq fails with `yaml: while scanning a quoted
  scalar at line 1: line 1, column 5: found invalid Unicode character escape code`. A lone high or lone low surrogate
  already errored, but under jq's `Invalid numeric literal` wording. All three now take yq's message, with the quoted
  scalar's line and column and the escape's, counted in characters across `\n`. jq mode is unchanged.
- **yq: a slice bound that yields several values is yq's `expected to find 1 number` error** (#2056). `del(.[(0,1):2])` on `{"a":1}` answered `{"a":1}`, reads fanned the bound out (`.[(0,1):2]` printed two slices) and `.[(0,1):2] = 5` raised an unrelated `Cannot index object with object`; yq v4.53.3 raises `expected to find 1 number, got 2 instead` (the count, `got N`) for all of them, on every target kind including `null` and scalars, with `?` not suppressing it. The error is now raised once the target produced a node, after any error the target raised, so `5 | .a[select(false):2]` also prints nothing as in yq instead of #4197's empty-bound error. `succinctly jq` is unchanged.
- **yq: `sort` and `sort_by(f)` on a mapping reorder its entries instead of raising jq's pairing error** (#2064). yq sorts a mapping by its values (or by `[f]` of each value), stably and with the comparator it uses for an array, and answers a mapping: `{"a":2,"b":1} | sort` is `{"b":1,"a":2}` and `{"a":{"x":2},"b":{"x":1},"c":{"y":9}} | sort_by(.x)` is `{"c":{"y":9},"b":{"x":1},"a":{"x":2}}`. `succinctly yq` raised `object (...) and array (...) cannot be sorted, as they are not both arrays`; `succinctly jq` still does, as jq does. The sorted mapping is an owned value, so YAML output drops its comments, flow style and anchors and writes a numeric key as a string; a mapping with a repeated key is refused rather than losing an entry (recorded in `docs/compliance/yq/limitations.md`).
- **yq: `reduce` and `foreach` now need `--jq-extensions`, as real yq's lexer rejects both** (#2065, #2447, #2605).
  `succinctly yq 'reduce .[] as $x (0; . + $x)'` ran with no flag, presenting extension surface as reference
  surface; it now fails with the same `is not part of yq's syntax; pass --jq-extensions` error as the other gated
  names (`limit`, `paths`, ...). `succinctly jq` and `--jq-extensions` runs are unchanged.
- **yq: `del()` turns a `null` behind a bracket key into the container the key implies** (#2126).
  `echo null | yq -o=json 'del(.["k0"])'` is `{}` in yq (and `del(.[(0,1)])` is `[]`, `{"a":null} | del(.a["k0"])` is
  `{"a":{}}`), where the dotted `del(.k0)` leaves the `null`; `succinctly yq` printed `null` for all of them. A `del()`
  argument in yq mode keeps a string bracket key apart from the `.k0` field step, and `del()` vivifies the first `null` a literal
  bracket key indexes. The read-side twin (`(.["k0"]) as $x | .` also prints `{}` in yq) is recorded in
  `docs/compliance/yq/limitations.md`.
- **yq: a write through an out-of-range negative index uses yq's wording** (#2335). `.a.b[-5] = 9` (and `|=`, `+=`, `*=`, a deeper path, a comma target, `setpath`, and an index reached through an auto-vivified `null`) answered jq's `Out of bounds negative array index`; yq v4.53.3 raises `index [-5] out of range, array size is 3`, the text the read side already used. `?` still does not suppress it, `.a.b[-3] = 9` still writes, and `succinctly jq` keeps jq's text.
- **yq: `del()` through a mid-path `.[]` before a slice-run and a field now raises per element, like yq** (#2344). `del(.a[][0:2].x)` on `{"a":[[1,2,3],{"y":1}]}` printed the document unchanged where yq fails with `cannot index array with 'x'`: the path was classified once from a prefix the classifier cannot walk past a `.[]`, so it always answered "no-op". It now defers to `delete_at_path`'s per-element walk, which already re-classifies each element. The call fails when any element is not a string (yq slices a mapping, int, bool, `null` or array to an empty sequence, so `.x` is parsed as an index), a string element and an empty `a` stay a no-op, `.x?` suppresses, and a comma sibling does not rescue it. Without a `.[]` the same rule now covers a mapping, int or bool target (`del(.a[0:2].x)` over `a: 5`), which was only applied to arrays and `null` (#2333).
- **yq: `first(f)` is the first child of the context for which `f` is truthy, as in yq, not jq's first output of `f`** (#2377).
  `[{"a":1},{"a":2}] | first(.a == 2)` answered `false` and `first(.a)` raised `Cannot index array with string "a"`; both now match yq (`{"a":2}`, `{"a":1}`). The result keeps the child's path, so `first(.a == 2) |= x`, `del(first(.a == 2))`, `path` and `key` follow it. A scalar or null context has no children and answers nothing. jq mode is unchanged. `--jq-extensions` does not restore jq's meaning (`limit(1; f)` is the jq spelling).
- **yq: a comma-grouped `del()` sibling that iterates a missing key and keeps going no longer raises** (#2380). `del(.missing[].x, .y)` printed `Cannot iterate over null (null)` where yq prints `{}`: the sibling pre-pass that tolerates a `null` `.[]` (#2324) only recognised a *trailing* `.[]`, so `.missing[].x` (and `.missing[].x.z[0]`, `.missing[].x[]`, `.n[].x` over a stored `null`, `.[5][].x` past the end of an array) fell through to the read-based resolver that rightly raises. It now also takes a `.[]` followed by static path, in either position of the group, and a prefix that is a scalar rather than `null` (`del(.s[], .y)` over `s: 5` raised `Cannot iterate over number (5)`; yq leaves `s` alone). A sibling with a negative or computed index still declines the whole pre-pass, as before (yq's own answer there depends on order).
- **yq: `--eval-all` folds the whole document list, so `. as $item ireduce ({}; . * $item)` merges the files** (#2427). The recipe yq's documentation gives for merging several files folded each document on its own and printed one result per document; it now reads the source and the initial value over every document of every file, as yq does, and prints the merged mapping once. `. as $i ireduce (0; . + 1)` counts the documents, the loop variable's node reads (`$i | document_index`, `file_index`, `path`, `line`, `tag`) answer from the document each node came from, and an empty `{}` is one mapping under `--eval-all` (`yq ea '{}' f1 f2` printed one `{}` per document). An `ireduce` after a navigation, and the plain route, are unchanged; an absent key read through the loop variable, a multi-output UPDATE and `{}` after a fan-out outside `--eval-all` still differ from yq (limitations).
- **yq: a numeric index that lands on a quoted mapping key names it by the string** (#2435). `.a[5] | key` and `.a[5] | path` over `a: {"5": five}` answered `5` and `["a",5]`, where yq answers `"5"` and `["a","5"]` (its tag is `!!str`); a plain number key (`7: seven`) and an index with no matching member keep the number, as before. The path component is now the matched key node's own value, the rule a name already followed (#2801). A mapping that a filter built keeps no key types, so an index into `(.a | . + {})` still answers the number. The vivification half of #2435 (`.a.b | parent` showing `{b: null}`) is unchanged.
- **`succinctly yq` field lookup through a `<<: [a, b]` merge-key sequence picks the later-listed source** (#2478). `.z.x` on `z: {<<: [*a, *b]}` answered `a`'s value; yq answers `b`'s, treating own keys, `<<` sources and their nested `<<` as one textual-order fold where the last write wins. `-o json '.z'` keeps its earlier-listed-wins output, which is what yq prints there too.
- **yq: an alias mark follows a plain `=` onto a target under a parent the write created, a comma of targets, a negative-index source and a source container that holds an alias** (#2505, #2497 residual).
  `printf 'a: &x 1\nb: *x\n' | yq '.c.d = .b'` printed `c:\n  d: 1` where yq prints `c:\n  d: *x`, and the same for `.c[0] = .b`, `(.c, .d) = .b`, `.c = .b[-1]` over `b: [0, *x]` and `.c = .b` over a block `b:\n  - *x`. The pass that copies the mark read both sides as static paths in the existing tree, so a target the write created had no node to mark, a comma target and a negative index (which needs the array's length) were not paths at all, and a container source was read only for its own mark. The target is now created for the mark, each comma branch is a target, the source is read from the comment tree, and every alias inside a copied container stays one. Values are unchanged (`-o=json` is identical), and an alias still drops when the write destroys its anchor. The other shapes #2505 lists (a constructed or computed right side, `+=`, a copied comment or flow style, the alias group) are unchanged.
