A comma, `map`, a `?` guarding a longer pipe, an iteration of an array that is itself too deep, an uncaught `error` of a deep value and the `reduce`/`foreach` accumulator rows still read the refusal until the native-stack floor below lifted it; the text stage remains the fallback past that floor.
- **jq: a value built past 384 levels is bounded by the native stack, not refused at 384** (#5554). `reduce range(500) as $i (0; [.]) | length`, `reduce range(400) as $i (0; [.]) | flatten`, `last(foreach range(500) as $i (0; [.])) | length` and, over `def f(n): if n == 0 then 0 else [f(n-1)] end;`, `f(400) | [., 1] | length`, `f(400) | sort | length`, `[f(400)] | map(tojson)`, `f(400) | error` and about 80 other consumers raised `nesting depth exceeds limit of 384` (exit 5) where jq 1.7.1 answers. Most of them refused in the re-index bridge, before the stage itself ran. In `succinctly jq`, every walk over a built value that is past 384 levels now checks ADR-0025's native-stack floor once per level instead, so it answers as jq does (byte-identical with jq on the 27 programs probed at 400 levels, comparing stdout and stderr together, and exit status). Past the floor, about 700,000 levels for the bridge on the 256 MiB release thread on Apple Silicon, it refuses with `nesting depth exceeds limit of the native stack` at exit 5, uncatchable, where jq segfaults. In a sweep of 75 consumers at 600,000 and 3,000,000 levels, every one answered or refused at exit 5. The exceptions were four path builtins at 600,000 levels: their output grows with the square of the depth, and they hit a 6 GB memory cap. A fold whose step has no owned door (`[.]`, `{a: .}`) re-indexes its accumulator every step, so past 384 levels it is now quadratic instead of refused. `succinctly yq` keeps 384.
- **jq: a malformed input document is reported with jq's parser message and position** (#5555). The default
  route, `--slurp`, and `input`/`inputs` said `Invalid JSON text` where jq prints its parser's own text, at a position
  that did not match: `printf '1 [2,' | jq -c .` now prints `jq: parse error: Unfinished JSON term at EOF at line 1,
  column 5`, and `-s` and the splitter's other faults (`Unmatched '}'`, `Unfinished string`, `Invalid numeric literal`)
  read the same, at jq's line and column, which count across the files as one stream. The fault named is the first in
  the input, including one inside a value the splitter delimits ahead of the one it stopped at. Under `input`/`inputs`
  it is `jq: error (at <file>:<line>): ...`; `-n -s` with `inputs` now names the file and line jq's parser stood on
  (`b.json:2`) where it named `a.json:0`, and `-s` with `input`/`inputs` and no `-n` is the parse error jq prints. A
  malformed member the semi-index accepts, found when the filter reads it, is worded the same way (#5576).
- **jq: `-S` and `-a` apply to the line `debug` and `debug(msg)` write to stderr** (#5558). jq 1.7.1 writes `["DEBUG:",v]` with its dump options minus the indent flags, so `jq -S 'debug'` sorts the keys of `v` and `jq -a 'debug'` escapes non-ASCII as `é`. `succinctly jq` ignored both unless `-C` was also given (#5553) and always wrote plain compact JSON. The CLI now installs its output formatter for the line under any of `-C`, `-S` and `-a`, so the bytes match jq's, number spellings (`1.50`, a literal past a double) and a NaN (`null`) included. With none of the three, under `-M` alone, and in `succinctly yq`, nothing changes. Pinned against jq 1.7.1 in `tests/jq_cli/i5558.rs`.
- **jq: `$` before a final newline picks the right match, and works after a doubled newline** (#5572). jq's `$` matches at the end of the text or just before a final `\n`; the text is searched with and without that `\n` and one match is picked. A tie went to the shorter match, so the trailing-whitespace idiom `"abc \n" | sub("\\s+$";"")` answered `"abc\n"` where jq answers `"abc"` (greedy `\s+` takes the `\n`, lazy `\s+?` does not), and a text ending in `"\n\n"` skipped the second search altogether (`"a\n\n" | [match("$";"g").offset]` was `[3]`, jq has `[2,3]`; `gsub("\\n$";"")` on `"line\n\n"` left the `\n`). A tie between two different matches is now decided by the exact engine (the `fancy-regex` route, which reads `$` as `(?=\n?\z)`), built only when it is needed, and the doubled newline is searched like a single one. A pattern with both `$` and `\z` is read by that engine alone. No change for a text that does not end in a newline. Left as they were, recorded in `limitations.md`: a pattern the exact engine refuses (a repeated empty group) and text that follows a `$` (`a$\n`).
- **jq: a malformed member found when the filter reads it is worded as jq's parser words it** (#5576).
  `succinctly jq -c . a.json b.json c.json` with `{"a":1,}` in `b.json` printed `jq: error (at b.json:2): Invalid JSON text:
  expected string key, found '}'` and went on to read `c.json`, where jq 1.7.1 prints `jq: parse error: Expected another
  key-value pair at line 4, column 8` after the values before the fault and reads nothing more. The semi-index accepts
  such a member and the evaluator finds it only when the filter reads it, so the stream is now read again from its start
  for jq's first fault when that error is reported, on the error path alone: a filter that reads no malformed member
  pays nothing. The fault is jq's text and position, which count lines across the files as one stream, and the run
  stops there with exit 5, as jq's does. `-s` over files words it the same way; `-s` from stdin keeps the evaluator's
  line, since the original bytes are gone once the values are joined.
- **jq: `l` on an alternation of multi-byte branches now gives the longest one** (#5580). `"éé" | match("é|éé"; "l")` answered `é` (length 1) where jq answers `éé` (length 2), and `"aééé" | match("aé|aéé"; "l")` stopped at `aé`. `fancy-regex`'s longest-match mode stops searching once a match is as long as the pattern's `max_size`, which it counts in characters and compares with a length in bytes, so any variable-length pattern whose shorter match is that many bytes lost its longer one, in a group or with `.` as well. A pattern whose matches differ in length now carries a branch that never matches and has no length bound, so the stop never fires; a fixed-length pattern is unchanged.
- **jq: three programs jq 1.7.1 compiles no longer fail with exit 3** (#5590). A surrogate pair in a string literal (`"\ud83d\ude00"`) is one character, `"😀"`; a lone low surrogate is U+FFFD, and a high one without its low half stays a compile error, as in jq. A keyword spelled right after the dot (`.then`, `.elif`, `.else`, `.end`, `.as`, `.catch`, `.and`, `.or`) is a field name, where `succinctly jq` read the dot as the identity and failed on the word; `. and true` and `if . then 1 end` read as before. A namespaced function name (`def a::b: 1; a::b`, `def a::b::c(x): x; a::b::c(1)`) defines and calls. `succinctly yq` is unchanged. Pinned against the jq 1.7.1 source build in `tests/jq_cli/i5590.rs`; the syntax-form probes of `dev compare jq` (#5552) stop listing the ten differences they found.
- **jq: a program with no expression of its own, and a reserved word as a `def` name, parameter or `import` namespace, are compile errors, as in jq** (#5591).
  `succinctly jq ''` (or a comment, or only whitespace, or only `def f: 1;`, or only `module`/`import`/`include` lines) ran the identity and exited 0;
  jq 1.7.1 refuses it with `jq: error: Top-level program not given (try ".")`, `jq: 1 compile error` and exit 3, and so does `succinctly jq` now, byte for byte.
  The check comes straight after the parse, so `include "missing";` reports only that, never the module, as in jq.
  `def if: 1; 2`, `def f(then): 1; 2` and `import "lib" as end; 1` ran and now exit 3 with `syntax error, unexpected if, expecting IDENT`
  (`IDENT or BINDING` for the other two); the same 17 words jq reserves (`def module import include if then else elif reduce foreach end and or as label try catch`) are refused at all three places,
  while `not`, `__loc__`, a `$if` variable or parameter, `.if` and `{if: 1}` still work.
  `succinctly yq` is unchanged. Checked against `/usr/bin/jq` 1.7.1 for 22 words at 7 positions, and the six `syntax` probes `succinctly dev compare jq` listed for these differences are off its ledger.
- **jq: a `::`-qualified name is accepted as an unquoted object key, a bare parameter name and a `label`/`break` name** (#5600). jq reads `a::b` as one identifier wherever an identifier is allowed, so `{a::b: 1}` is `{"a::b":1}`, `{a::b}` is `{"a::b":null}`, `. as {a::b: $x} | $x` binds, `def f(a::b): a::b; f(1)` is `1` and `label $a::b | break $a::b` runs; `succinctly jq` failed each with exit 3. #5590 had taught only the `def` name and a call. A reserved word before the `::` (`{if::x: 1}`) is part of the name, and a `::` with a gap or no name after it (`{a:: 1}`, `{a::1: 1}`) stays a compile error, as in jq. `succinctly yq` is unchanged. Pinned against the jq 1.7.1 source build in `tests/jq_cli/i5600.rs`; syntax-form probes of `dev compare jq` (#5552) cover them.
- **jq: a `.field`, `[i]` or `[]` after `first`, `last`, `limit`, `range`, `repeat`, `until`, `while`, `error` or `JOIN` no longer fails with exit 3** (#5612). `first(.a[]).id`, `last[0]`, `[limit(2; .[]).x]`, `range(3)[0]` and `try error("x").y catch .` compile and run as in jq 1.7.1; these nine were the only builtins the parser refused a postfix after (a sweep of every builtin name against every postfix form, 1688 probes plus the `JOIN`/`IN`/`INDEX` family, now reports no difference). `succinctly yq` takes one after `first`, `error`, `filter`, `collect`, `with` and `explode`, as yq 4.53.3 does, and still refuses it after the names yq's lexer rejects (they follow jq under `--jq-extensions`). Pinned against jq 1.7.1 in `tests/jq_cli/i5612.rs` and `tests/yq_cli/i5612.rs`.
- **jq: a program is split into tokens on space, tab and newline only** (#5613). jq 1.7.1's lexer
  skips `[ \n\t]+` and `#` comments; CR, form feed, vertical tab, NBSP and U+2028 are
  `INVALID_CHARACTER` (exit 3), so a program saved with CRLF line endings is refused at its first
  `\r`. `succinctly jq` skipped everything `char::is_whitespace` accepts, and read a `-f` program file
  through `trim()`, so `1\r+ 1` printed `2` and a `-f` file ending in `\r\n` ran. A CR inside a
  comment is still part of the comment. `succinctly yq` is narrowed the same way (#5616).
- **jq: a number literal with an empty fraction and an exponent keeps its decNumber spelling** (#5614). `1.e1` is the decNumber `1e1`, so jq prints `1E+1` (and `10.e1` as `1.0E+2`, `0.e5` as `0E+5`, `1.e1000` as `1E+1000`); `succinctly jq` collapsed the spelling to the double and printed `10`, `100`, `0` and `1.7976931348623157e+308`. A trailing dot with no exponent (`123456789012345678901234567890.`, `9007199254740993.`) keeps its digits the same way, where it printed the rounded double. The spelling now goes through the same literal path as `1e1`, in a program, `tojson` and string interpolation alike; arithmetic and comparison still see the value. `succinctly yq` is unchanged. Pinned against the jq 1.7.1 source build in `tests/jq_cli/i5614.rs`.
- **jq: a number literal with leading zeros keeps its decNumber spelling, and `1..e1` indexes the number** (#5615).
  `00e1`, `007e1` and `007.50` read as the double (`0`, `70`, `7.5`) because RFC 8259 forbids the leading zeros and the spelling failed the validity check; jq drops the redundant zeros and prints `0E+1`, `7E+1` and `7.50`.
  jq's lexer also takes the longest number match, so `1..e1` is `1.` followed by `.e1` (a runtime `Cannot index number with string "e1"`, exit 5, also under a unary minus: `-1..e1`), where `succinctly jq` stopped the number before the `..` and refused the program at compile time.
  `succinctly yq` is unchanged.
- **yq: an expression is split into tokens on space, tab and newline only** (#5616). yq v4.53.3's
  lexer refuses CR, form feed, vertical tab, NBSP, U+0085, U+2028 and U+3000 between tokens with
  `lexer: invalid input text`; `succinctly yq` skipped everything `char::is_whitespace` accepts, so
  `1<NBSP>+ 1` printed `2`. Three of yq's token regexes take Go's `\s*` and so accept a CR or form
  feed beside them: the `:` of an object entry, the six comparison operators and
  `comments=` / `comments|=`; those stay accepted and nothing else does. `--from-file` now reads
  the file as yq does, with each CRLF turned into LF (inside a string literal too) and a lone CR
  left in place, where `succinctly yq` used to accept a lone CR as whitespace. A CR inside a
  comment is still part of the comment.
- **yq: a chain of comparisons is parsed right-associatively** (#5629). yq gives `==`, `!=`, `<`,
  `<=`, `>` and `>=` one precedence (40) and its operator stack pops only a strictly higher one, so
  `1 == 1 == true` is `1 == (1 == true)` and prints `false`; `succinctly yq` stopped at the second
  operator with a parse error. A chain longer than the expression-nesting limit is an error here
  where yq takes any length. `succinctly jq` still refuses a chain, as jq 1.7.1 does.
- **yq: `+ - * / % //` fold from the right, as in yq** (#5630). yq gives the six operators one precedence and its operator stack pops only a strictly higher one, so `2 * 3 + 4` is `2 * (3 + 4)` (`14`, was `10`), `10 - 3 - 2` is `10 - (3 - 2)` (`9`, was `5`), `100 / 10 / 5` is `50` (was `2`), and `//` ties with them, so `1 // 2 == 2` is `(1 // 2) == 2`. The comparisons and the assignments are one level too (`.a = 5 == 5` is unchanged; `x == y = z` is `x == (y = z)`). Output differs from earlier releases for any yq program that mixed these operators without parentheses; `succinctly jq` keeps jq's grammar.
- **yq: an ordering comparison of unlike kinds, or of a bool or a container, raises as in yq** (#5631). `2 > true` printed `true` and yq stops with `!!int not yet supported for comparison`; the same for `"a" < 1` (`!!str ...`), `true > false` (`!!bool ...`), a container on the left (`arrays`/`maps not yet supported for comparison`) and a scalar against a container on the right (`!!seq () cannot be subtracted from !!int`), which includes `null` against a container. Two numbers or two strings still compare, and a `null` on either side still answers `false`. `==`/`!=` and `succinctly jq` are unchanged. Not reproduced: yq's timestamp-string and hex-against-float errors.
- **the CLI runs under a capped address space** (#5634). The evaluation thread reserves 256 MiB of stack (2 GiB in a debug build), and `ulimit -v` counts a reservation, so under a cap below that every run died with `failed to spawn the evaluation thread`, whatever its input, where jq reads the same document. The stack now starts at a quarter of the cap (never below 16 MiB, never above its full size) and halves if it still cannot be mapped; its native-stack floor follows the size it got, so deep recursion is refused rather than overflowing. A 1M-integer array and a 300,000-key object now answer under `ulimit -v` 64 MiB (jq aborts there), and a 1M-integer array under 256 MiB, where each used to fail at start. A cap of 32 MiB or less still fails to start, and a document that does not fit still aborts on the failed allocation, as jq does.
- **jq: `--stream` over a document with a syntax error part-way through prints the events before it** (#5635). `[1,2,3 x]` and `{"a":1,"b":[2,@]}` printed nothing for that document; they now print `[[0],1]` `[[1],2]` and `[["a"],1]` `[["b",0],2]`, as jq 1.7.1 does, and then raise the error (exit 5). The events come from the port of jq's streaming parser that `--stream-errors` reads with, so `input_line_number` names the line jq had read when it yielded each, and a program using `input`/`inputs` reads them before the fault it resumes after. A number or literal that the fault's own byte completes (`22]`) is no longer printed, as in jq. A stream that fails to parse is expanded to events up front, so a large input with a late syntax error holds its earlier documents' events in memory first.
- **jq: `-n --seq` with `input`/`inputs` raises `Unfinished abandoned text at EOF` on a stream with no RS byte** (#5636). jq never syncs onto text that has no leading RS, so the first read of it is an error: `printf '1\n' | jq -cen --seq '[inputs] == []'` exits 5 with `jq: error (at <stdin>:1): Unfinished abandoned text at EOF at line 2, column 0`. `succinctly jq` read it as no inputs and answered `true`, exit 0. `input` raises the error (catchable), `inputs` re-raises it, and the marker names the last source and its newline count as jq's does (`a.json b.json` reads `b.json:0`). The same stream without `-n` still only warns. `-n -s` and the reader's other parse errors under `-n` are unchanged.
- **jq: under `-n --seq`, `input`/`inputs` raise the stream reader's parse errors** (#5640). A record cut off at EOF (`\x1e[1,`), an unfinished string, a number at EOF without its RS, a stream that starts with a malformed BOM or a stray `}` between records were read as no input and exited 0, where jq raises each (`Unfinished JSON term at EOF at line 2, column 0`, `Invalid numeric literal ... (need RS to resync)`, exit 5, named `(at <stdin>:N)`, or `<unknown>` for the EOF report jq defers past the last value). Each error comes behind the values read before it and the reads after it resume, so `try input catch .` sees it; under `-s` every one is raised before the slurped array. A plain run still only warns `jq: ignoring parse error`. The stream with no RS byte at all (`1 2`) also raises `Unfinished abandoned text at EOF`.
- **jq: a junk byte right after `[`, `{` or a key's closing quote is refused instead of skipped** (#5644). `[@1]` parsed as `[1]` and `{"a":@-3}` as `{"a":-3}`, because the index reads a byte that begins no JSON token (`@`, `#`, a control byte, ...) as whitespace; jq 1.7.1 stops with `Invalid numeric literal` at the column of the byte, and so does `succinctly jq` now, with the same message and exit status. The check covers the first element of an array, the first key of an object and the value after a `:`. A form feed in those gaps is refused too, since JSON does not count it as whitespace.
- **jq: a number or literal where an object key belongs is met at the token after it, as jq does** (#5645). `printf '{1.5e3\n1"k":false' | jq -nc '[limit(6; repeat(try input catch "E"))]'` is six `"E"`s in jq, because its lexer takes `1.5e3` without complaint and meets the fault at the `"` on the next line, so the whole second line is discarded. This build resumed at the line after the number and read `1` and `"k"` as documents (`["E",1,"k","E","E","E"]`). The same holds for `true`, `false`, `null` and numbers after a comma, across any run of whitespace, and under `--stream`. A container in the same place (`{[1]`) still resumes where it did.
- **jq: a junk byte, a form feed or a glued token between a sibling and its `,` is refused instead of skipped** (#5650). `[1@,2]` printed `[1,2]`, `[1null,2]` printed `[1,2]` and `[1,2]<FF>` (a form feed before the closing bracket, or around the root: `<FF>[1]`, `[1]<FF>`, `[1,2]<FF>[3]`) were read as whitespace, because the index judged a gap by the byte it stopped on and took `is_ascii_whitespace` (which counts a form feed) for JSON's whitespace. jq 1.7.1 stops with `Invalid numeric literal` on each, and so does `succinctly jq` now, with the same message and exit status. A sibling must end on a byte a value can end on, a bare token that starts like a number must be one number (`1null`, `1true`, `1e` are refused; `1e5`, `1.`, `.5`, `+1`, `nan` and `-Infinity` still read), and the splitter and the closing-bracket gap use space, tab, LF and CR only. `succinctly yq` is unchanged. A bare token glued to a number that ends in a digit (`0x1`, `1_000`) is not checked, so the pretty printer pays one byte test per element. A byte sweep of the `stdin` route (every byte x 14 templates against jq 1.7.1) leaves four differences: a NUL between documents, which jq ignores, and `[[1]},2]`. Still open, filed apart (#5654): a junk byte after a container that is a container's last child (`[[1]@]`), a NUL inside a document (the message differs), `--slurpfile` and `--argjson` (a form feed around the value), and programs that read a document lazily (`map(.)`, `first(.[])`).
- **yq: an integer written in hex or octal against a float raises `strconv.ParseFloat`, as in yq** (#5651). `0x10 < 1.5` answered `false` and yq stops with `strconv.ParseFloat: parsing "0x10": invalid syntax`, because it compares an int with a float through `ParseFloat` of each node's text and Go's `ParseFloat` refuses a radix prefix (`0x`, `0o`). Two integers still compare as integers, a decimal spelling (`007`, `+5`, `1e3`) still parses, and `==` and `succinctly jq` are unchanged. The timestamp-string rows of the issue stay open.
- **yq: a string that parses as a timestamp is compared as a time** (#5651). On the left of `<`, `<=`, `>` or `>=`, a string that Go's `time.Parse` reads as RFC 3339 or `2006-01-02` is now an instant, and its right operand is parsed the same way: `"2001-01-01T00:00:00Z" < 1` raises `parsing time "1" as "2006-01-02": cannot parse "1" as "2006"` (it answered `false`), so does a `null`, a bool or a string in another layout, with Go's own wording (`extra text`, `month out of range`, `cannot parse "0101" as "-"`), and the same moment in two zones is equal where the strings ordered. `==`, `!=`, `sort`, `min` and `max` are unchanged. `src/jq/go_time.rs` ports the part of `time.Parse` the two layouts use, including a one-digit hour, a comma fraction and a 24-hour zone offset; `scripts/yq-time-fuzz.py` replays mutated timestamps against yq (0 differences over 2,500 strings x 4 expressions). Still different: a `!!timestamp`-tagged document value that no layout reads, and a `!!str` against a `!!timestamp`, which need a timestamp kind.
- **jq: `--argjson`, `--jsonargs` and `--slurpfile` skip only JSON whitespace around a value** (#5654). A form feed, a vertical tab or a Unicode space around the text (`--argjson x $'1\f'`, `--jsonargs ' 1'`, a `--slurpfile` file holding `1<NBSP>`) was trimmed and accepted; jq 1.7.1 refuses each (`invalid JSON text passed to --argjson`, `Bad JSON in --slurpfile`, exit 2) and so does `succinctly jq` now. `--argjson x ''` (and `' '`) is refused too, where it was `null`.
- **jq: junk after a container that is its parent's last child is refused, off the lazy routes** (#5654, #1676/#2243 residual). `[[1]@]`, `[1,[2]\f]`, `[{}@]`, `{"a":[1]@}` and `[[1]},2]` printed the document at exit 0, and so did a trailing comma after such a child (`[[1],]`, `{"a":1,"b":[1,2],}`, `length` over `{"a":[1,2],}`); jq 1.7.1 refuses each as a parse error. Only a scalar last child had the gap before the closing bracket checked, since a container's end could not be told from its start. The end now comes from the balanced parentheses, asked of the last child only. `map(f)` checks the gaps it pulls past (see the next entry); a consumer that stops early, such as `first(.[])`, still skips them. Interleaved A/B on an Apple M-series chip: `.` and `length` are within noise; `[.[]|.id]|length` over records whose last field is a container reads +7% to +13% (each lookup locates the end of that field).
- **jq: `arr | map(f)` and `obj | map(f)` refuse a bad gap they pull past** (#5654, #1641 residual). `[1@,2] | map(.)`, `[1,,2]`, `[1,2,]`, `[1 2]`, `{"a":1,"b":2,}` and `{"a":1,"b"}` answered at exit 0 because the lazy source read the elements through a cons list that ran no gap check; jq 1.7.1 refuses each as a parse error, and `succinctly jq` does now, with jq's messages. An object is checked whole, by the probe that already finds a repeated key (a repeated key included), at no extra walk. An array is checked as it is pulled, so a consumer that stops early (`first(.[])`, `map(.) | first`) never sees a bad gap after its answer, and a gap inside a child `f` never reads is not seen; matching jq there would validate the rest of the array for a filter that exists to stop early. Cost, retired instructions on an Apple M5 Max (min of 5, release, not wall-clock; x86_64 not measured): `map(.) | length` over 3M integers +6.5%, `map(.+1)` +4.2%, `map(.[0])` over short arrays +3.0%, an object of 1M members +2.1%, and `.users | map(.id)` / `map(select(...))` over 14 MB of records +2.5% / +1.2%; unrelated paths move by layout alone (`[.[]] | length` +2.3%, `.[]|select(...)` +1.5%), and `length`, `.[100]`, `first(.[])` are within 0.1%.
- **jq: a number with bytes glued on is refused wherever it is read** (#5654). `[0x1,2]`, `[12x3,2]`, `[0.0x1]` and `{"a":0x1}` read as `0`, `12` and `0.0` because the three JSON number scanners stopped at the first byte outside `[0-9.eE+-]` and dropped the rest. jq 1.7.1 reads the whole run up to the next token boundary as one token and refuses it (`Invalid numeric literal`); `succinctly jq` does now on every route that reads the element (`.`, `.[0]`, `.a`, `first(.[])`, `map(.)`, `add`, `tostring`), with jq's message and column. The check lives in the scanners, not on the comma gap, so routes that never read a number (`length` over a number array) pay nothing; such a route still answers for a digit-ending glued token that is not the last element (`[0x1,2] | length`), as `[1.5.5,2] | length` does. `succinctly yq` is unchanged.
- **jq: a container where an object key belongs is met at the token after it by the plain reader, as jq does** (#5655). `printf '{[1]\n2\n3' | jq -nc '[limit(6; repeat(try input catch "E"))]'` is `["E",3,"E","E","E","E"]` in jq, because its lexer takes `[1]` as a value and meets the fault at the `2` on the next line; this build met it at the `[` and read `2` and `3` as documents. A fault inside the container is still met first, and `--stream`, whose parser refuses the bracket itself, resumes where it did.
- **jq: under `-n --seq`, an empty record no longer drops the values behind it from `input`/`inputs`** (#5662). `\x1e\x1e[1]` read as no input at all, so `try input catch .` printed `"break"` forever and `[inputs],[inputs]` printed `[]` twice. jq's main loop stops silently at an empty record (#2998), but `input` reads through the same driver and raises `break`, the error an exhausted stream raises, and the next read scans on: `try input catch .` sees `"break"` and then `[1]`, `[inputs]` ends at the `break` (`[]`) and a second `inputs` yields `[1]`. A plain run still stops there, as jq's main loop does.
- **jq: a long chain of field or index reads over a computed value evaluates in linear memory** (#5663). `{} | .a.a.a…` re-entered the owned evaluator once per stage, and each re-entry built the owned pipe of the stages left and held it while the next ran, so a chain of `n` reads held `n` pipes of up to `n` stages: 2,000 steps took 198 MB, 5,000 took 1.4 GB and 20,000 were killed at 2 GB (jq answers 20,000 in 48 ms). The stages after the first that are plain `.field` or `.[n]` reads are now stepped in a loop, so 20,000 steps peak at 24 MB in a debug build. Reading a document from a file or stdin was never affected.
- **jq: a long pipe of computed stages (`. + 1 | . + 1 | …`, `map(.) | map(.) | …`) evaluates in linear memory** (#5679). A pipe of more than 128 stages handed each call a copy of every stage after it and held that copy while the rest ran, so `n` stages held `n` copies of up to `n` stages. A tail is now the rest of its block of 16 stages plus one link to a kept chain of the blocks after it, so a call copies at most two blocks. Peak RSS of `-n '0 | . + 1 | …'` (Apple M5 Max, release build, output identical): 750 stages 99 MB to 11 MB, 1,500 358 MB to 17 MB, 3,000 1.37 GB to 28 MB, and 24,000 stages 183 MB (the old build's growth extrapolates to about 90 GB there; it was not run); `[1] | map(.) | …` 3,000 stages 874 MB to 29 MB. Interleaved A/B, min of 15: 3,000 stages 416 ms to 14 ms (`. + 1`) and 228 ms to 14 ms (`map(.)`); pipes of up to 128 stages do not reach the new code. jq mode only; a pipe holding a `def` stage, or a marker and a node that can read it, is copied as before. x86_64 and the M4 Pro were not measured.
- **jq: `fromjson` reads to jq's parse-depth ceiling** (#5688). `fromjson` refused a text nested more than 128 levels deep with an `Invalid numeric literal` error, where jq reads 256 nested arrays and refuses the 257th (`Exceeds depth limit for parsing`). It now takes jq's ceiling, counted jq's way (an object is two entries of it, so 128 nested objects read and 129 do not), and words the refusal as jq does. `tonumber`'s probe, which shares the check, follows. A text nested 128 levels or less is read exactly as before.
- **jq: a path through a container named argument is the argument's own** (#5692). `--argjson d '{"a":1}' '$d | path($d)'` is `[]`, `'$d | del($d)'` is `null` and `'$d | path($d.a)'` is `["a"]`, as in jq 1.7.1; all three were refused with `Invalid path expression`. A program with a path expression (`path`, `paths`, `del`, `pick`, `getpath`, `walk`) now gets a container `--argjson`/`--slurpfile` argument as the one shared value #5690 gave read-only programs, which also makes `--slurpfile` programs that delete or list paths faster (over a 4.7 MB file, min of 5 release runs: `del` 182 to 78 ms, `paths` 262 to 146 ms, and 20 records each reading it 920 to 600 ms; Apple M5 Max). An assignment to the argument itself, `$ARGS.named.d | path($d)` and a scalar argument are still refused (`docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`).
- **yq: a NUL ends a JSON input, and an explicit `-p=json` makes `-o auto` YAML** (#5721). `printf '\0' | yq -p=json -o=json .` was refused and is now `null` (the empty document), `1<NUL>2` is `1`, as in yq; `-p=json -o auto .` over `{"a":1}` printed JSON and now prints `a: 1`, as yq does. The `filename`, `select(. == null)` and `--eval-all` rows of the issue are still open.
- **yq: `filename` is empty over the empty document, and `select`, `(.)` and `..` over a comment-only or empty document print no extra blank line** (#5721). `printf '' | yq filename` and `yq filename empty.yaml` printed `-` and the file's name where yq prints an empty line (`file_index` and `document_index` stay `0`; a file holding a line break is a document of its own and is still named). `printf '# c\n' | yq 'select(true)'` printed `# c` and a blank line, and an empty input two blank lines, where yq prints the document once.
- **yq: `-0` writes the NUL in place of the line break a comment-only or empty document ends in** (#5721). `printf '# c\n' | yq -0 .` printed `# c`, a line break and no NUL, and `select`, `(.)` and `..` printed the line break and then the NUL; an empty input printed a line break. yq writes `# c<NUL>` (a lone NUL for an empty input, `---<NUL>` for a bare `---`); `succinctly yq` now does, on the streamed and the `-P` routes, and a result that follows it in the same document (`select(. == null), 1`) still gets its own NUL. With `--colors` a comment's span keeps its break (`ESC[90m# c<LF>ESC[0m<NUL>`), as yq's does.
- **jq: a long pipe with a few `def` calls in it evaluates in linear memory** (#5722). A pipe of more than 128 stages that held a stage with evaluation state (a call of a user `def`) was copied whole per call, so it kept the quadratic memory #5679 removed for stateless pipes. The chain now links each run of blocks with no such stage and clones only the blocks that hold one, so a call copies the stateful blocks plus a link per run. Peak RSS of `-n 'def f: . + 1; 0 | . + 1 | … | f | …'` (AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, release build, output identical), one `f` in 200 stages: 1,500 stages 411 MB to 17 MB, 3,000 stages 1.59 GB to 23 MB (1.5 s to 0.01 s); one in 1,000: 3,000 stages 1.59 GB to 23 MB. A pipe with an `f` in every block of 16 stages, or in every stage, is copied as before (3,000 stages of `f`: 468 MB, unchanged). jq mode only. Apple silicon was not measured.
- **jq: `JQ_COLORS` is parsed as jq's `jq_set_colors` does** (#5750, #5751). A field longer than 12 bytes (jq's 16-byte colour buffer less `ESC [ m` and the NUL) now rejects the whole variable (`Failed to set $JQ_COLORS`, defaults kept), where the long field used to be applied (`JQ_COLORS='1;2;3;4;5;6;7;8;9'`). The field loop ends when the text left after a `:` is empty, so `JQ_COLORS=` keeps every default colour (it used to blank the null colour) and `JQ_COLORS=:::` leaves the number colour at `0;39` (it used to blank it); `1:` sets only the null colour. Output is byte-identical to jq 1.7.1 on every spec tried. Four `to-triage` ledger entries are gone.
- **jq: `strptime`'s `%b`, `%B` and `%h` take a month's full name or its three-letter abbreviation, and no more** (#5752). The parser read every letter that followed and accepted any word that began with a month's first three, so `"05 Mart 2015" | strptime("%d %B %Y")` was March where jq 1.7.1 rejects it (`date ... does not match format`); `Marx`, `Marc`, `Marchx`, `Septembe` and `Sept` were accepted the same way, while `Ma` was rejected. The input now matches a full month name if it starts with one and its abbreviation otherwise, in any letter case, and the letters after the match belong to the rest of the format, so they have to match it. `05Mar2015` with `%d%b%Y` and `05 March 2015` with `%d %b %Y` still parse. Across 495 name, format and input combinations (every month's full and abbreviated spelling in three cases, one- and two-letter prefixes, trailing letters, digits and punctuation, and eleven format shapes) the rows differing from jq 1.7.1 went from 199 to 23, none introduced; the 23 left are the weekday of a format that sets no date (#5753) and `Mar-`/`Mar 2015` before a `%Y` with no separator, where jq's libc hands back the unparsed rest of the text.
- **`succinctly jq` `strptime` reads `%E`/`%O` modifiers, `%k` and `%l`, and refuses what the libc does not know** (#5754). `"03/05/15" | strptime("%Ex")`, `"2015" | strptime("%EY")` and `"9:30 PM" | strptime("%l:%M %p")` parse as in jq 1.7.1, where each was an error. A specifier jq's libc does not know (`%Q`, `%P`) and a `%` that ends the format are now a mismatch (`"x" | strptime("%Q")` is an error, as in jq) instead of matching the literal text.
- **`succinctly jq` `strftime`/`strflocaltime` take the `_`, `-` and `0` padding flags and fail on an empty or oversized result** (#5754). `1420167845 | strftime("%_d|%-d|%0e")` is `" 2|2|02"`, as in jq 1.7.1, where the format used to come back unchanged. `%+` and `%v` are read, `%E`/`%O` pass every specifier through (`%-Ed` is `2`), a NUL ends the format, a character that follows `%` and names nothing is printed bare (`%Q` is `Q`), and a result that is empty or `strlen(fmt) + 100` bytes or longer is `strftime/1: unknown system failure` (`0 | strftime("")`, `%p` under `de_DE`), where it was returned as it stood.
- **`strptime` reads `%U`, `%W` and `%V`** (#5754). With a year read, the week number places the date as jq's libc does: `%U` counts from the year's first Sunday, `%W` from its first Monday and `%V` from the Monday of ISO week 1, and a weekday read with `%w`, `%u` or `%a` picks the day within the week (`"2015 09" | strptime("%Y %U")` is `[2015,2,1,0,0,0,0,59]`). A day of week 0 that falls before 1 January is no match, and one of week 53 past 31 December rolls into the next year. `%w` now refuses 7 and up and `%u` refuses 0 and 8 up, as jq does.
- **`strptime`'s `%Z` reads only `GMT` and the local zone's names, and `GMT` and `%s` convert to local time last** (#5754). `%Z` took any run of letters; it now takes a run of capital letters naming `GMT` or one of the local zone's `tzname` names (its latest standard and daylight-time names, `AEST` and `AEDT` in Sydney, renamed by each later conversion to local time as jq's libc does), and anything else is no match, as in jq. `GMT`, like `%s`, makes the fields a UTC instant that becomes local time once the whole format is read, so `"2015-03-05 10:00 GMT" | strptime("%F %R %Z")` is 21:00 in Sydney and a field read after `%s` is a UTC one. An instant before 1900 is 1969-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, as jq's `timegm` gives it.
- **`succinctly jq` `strptime` reads a `%` specifier after a width, and refuses it straight after a `+` flag** (#5754). `"%" | strptime("%E4%")`, `"%" | strptime("%O5%")` and `"%" | strptime("%E+0%")` now read the `%`, and `"%" | strptime("%+%")` is no match, as in jq 1.7.1: the libc refuses a `%` specifier whose prefix ends in a modifier or a `+` flag (`%+%`, `%E%`, `%E+%`, `%4E%`) and reads it when digits end the prefix (`%5%`, `%+0%`). Found by a 2,925-format grid of flag, modifier and width prefixes against `/usr/bin/jq`, which also confirmed that a layout holding a `_` or `-` flag matches jq (both are no match), so that item of #5754 needed no change.
- **jq: a `JQ_COLORS` value that is not UTF-8 warns** (#5760). `JQ_COLORS=$'\xff' succinctly jq -C .` ignored the variable silently; jq prints `Failed to set $JQ_COLORS` on stderr and keeps the default colours, and so does `succinctly jq` now. stdout is unchanged.
- **jq: a slice assigned onto `null`, a `del` that names nothing and `.[5] |= empty` build a new array** (#5761).
  `[nan] as $a | null | .[1:] = $a | . == $a`, `$a | del(.[5]) == $a` (also `.[-5]`, `.[-0.5]`, `.[5]?`, a computed index, `del(.[0][5])`) and `$a | (.[5] |= empty) == $a` handed back the array they were given, so `==` (which short-circuits on `jv_identical` in jq, while `[nan] == [nan]` is `false`) answered `true` where jq 1.7.1 answers `false`.
  The array is now split from any other handle that holds it, which costs a copy only when the array is shared; a path that runs through something absent (`del(.[5].x)`) keeps its identity, as in jq.
  A fold step that stores its loop variable through either no longer keeps the literal operand, so the fold shares the element there too. `succinctly yq` is unchanged.
- **jq: a fold that adds or defaults its loop element onto a `null` start keeps the element** (#5761). `[nan] as $a | reduce $a as $v (null; . += $v) | . == $a`, `. //= $v` over a `null` or `false` start, and the `foreach` spellings of both are `true` in jq (`null + x` is `x` itself, and jq's own `add` is `reduce .[] as $x (null; . + $x)`) and were `false` here, because the owned fold step only combined two values of one kind and handed everything else to the evaluator, which rebuilt the element. The step now stores the operand as the state; a truthy state is left alone by `//=`, a second element still adds into a new container, and `succinctly yq` is unchanged. `(.x, .y) += $v`, `(.x += $v)?`, `.x = $r.items` and a trailing identity stage after the store (`. += $v | .`) still rebuild it.
- **jq: the right-hand side of `op=` and `//=` keeps the operand's storage** (#5761).
  `[nan] as $a | null | . += $a | . == $a`, `{x:null} | .x += $a | .x == $a`, `(.x, .y) += $v` and `(.x += $v)?` over a fold, `. += $v | .` and `. //= $v | .` are `true` in jq, where the operand is stored as itself, and were `false` here: the per-path filter rebuilt a container operand from literals.
  A container operand now rides a by-value marker, as a fold's loop variable already does; a scalar stays a literal and `succinctly yq` is unchanged.
  The marker is by-value on purpose: a plain untracked one took `. + <operand>` off the owned fast path (`.[] += [0]` measured +64% in a prototype).
  Measured interleaved A/B on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, min of 9, output identical: `.[] += [0]` over 150,000 pairs -1.0%, `map(. += [0])` -6.0%, `[.[] | .meta += {c:1}]` -4.3%, `.tags += [1]` over 60,000 records -0.3%, `//=` -2.4%.
  Not measured on ARM.
- **jq: a container read off a fold's loop variable keeps its storage when stored** (#5761).
  `[{"items":[nan]}] as $in | reduce $in[] as $r ({}; .a = $r.items) | .a == $in[0].items` is `true` in jq, where the stored member is the element's own array, and was `false` here: only a whole-variable read (`.a = $r`) carried the fold's marker, so a field read (`.a = $r.items`, `.a += $r.items`, `. + $r.items`, `.[$r.n] = $r.items`) rebuilt the container.
  The gate that decides whether a fold step marks its loop variable now counts any read of it on the right-hand side of an assignment or in arithmetic; the in-place step is unchanged and still takes the marker as one `Rc` clone.
  `succinctly yq` is unchanged.
  Measured interleaved A/B on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X over 300,000 records, min of 7, output identical: `.[$r.name] = $r.tags` -6.2% time, `.[$r.name] = $r.meta` -2.8%, `. + $r.tags` -5.1%, `.x[$r.name] += $r.score` +1.6%, `.[$r.name] += ($r.score|floor)` -0.7%.
  Peak RSS is unchanged (within 1%) except `.[$r.name] = $r.meta`, which keeps each record's `meta` object alive: 206 MB to 225 MB (+9.2%).
  Not measured on ARM.
- **jq: dropping a value built millions of levels deep no longer aborts the process** (#5782). `succinctly jq -n 'reduce range(10000000) as $i ([]; .[0] = .) | length'` overflowed the native stack in `OwnedValue`'s drop glue (exit 134) and now prints `1`, as does the object form (`.a = .`). jq 1.7.1 segfaults on the same program from a few hundred thousand levels (between 150,000 and 200,000 on macOS with an 8 MB stack), so there is nothing to match (ADR-0018). A per-thread count of nested container drops lets a shallow value drop through the ordinary glue as before; once 256 are running, the rest of the value goes onto a heap worklist, so a drop needs at most about 54 KB of native stack. As first written (#5815), the count cost about 1% of instructions on queries that build and drop millions of small containers (`[.users[] | [[[.id]]]]`) and -0.4% to +2.2% wall-clock on a 7950X over 10 and 100 MB inputs. Releasing the container's storage inside the count instead (#5868) cut the registers `OwnedValue`'s drop glue saves from ten to six (four before #5782); on the 7950X that removes about half of the count's extra instructions on the container-heavy queries (`Ir` against the code before #5782: `[.users[] | [[[.id]]]]` +0.90% to +0.50%, `[.users[] | {a: ., b: [.]}]` +1.05% to +0.45%), and wall-clock is within the control's spread (median row +0.85% against the code before #5782, +0.6% against #5815, where an identical binary measured -0.5%). On an M4 Pro the median row is then -0.3% against the code before #5782: rows that build and drop several containers per record are +0.3% to +3.2% (`[.users[] | [[[.id]]]]`, three arrays per record, +3.2%, where each unique container pays one macOS thread-local address lookup) and the rest are -0.9% to -2.5%.
- **jq: an error in a last-stage `map(f)` over a document file ends the input, as in jq** (#5785). `.[] | map(if .==0 then error("boom") else . end)` over `[[1],[0],[2]]` printed `[2]` after the error; jq prints `[1]` and stops, and so does `succinctly jq` now (the same for `(.[] | map(f)), "after"`, `limit(n; .[] | map(f))` and `.. | map(f)`). The exit status (5) and the one diagnostic were already right; the later outputs were the bug.
- **jq: `map_values(f)` reads only the first output of `f`, as in jq** (#5791). `[1] | map_values((1, error("x")))` raised `x`; jq prints `[1]`, because `map_values(f)` is `.[] |= f` and never runs the rest of `f`, and so does `succinctly jq` now (for arrays and objects alike). `succinctly yq` still raises, as real yq does. A side effect of a later output (`halt_error`'s stderr text, `debug`) still fires, because `f` is still run to its end; that residual is recorded in the limitations page.
- **jq: an index or slice key that is a failing `map(f)` raises `f`'s error** (#5793). `.[(.a|map(error("x")))]`, `.[(.a|map(error("x"))):]` and `.[0:(.a|map(error("x")))]` over a file or stdin printed nothing and exited 0, and `try ... catch` never saw the error, because the key was read as an empty list. They now raise `x` and exit 5, as jq does; a key that came before the failing one is still indexed first (`.[("a",(.a|map(error("x"))))]` prints `[1]` and then the error). `-n` was already right.
- **jq: `walk(f)` on an object reads one output of `f` per member, as in jq** (#5794). `{"a":1} | walk((., error("x")))` printed nothing; jq prints `{"a":1}` before raising, because `walk` rewrites an object's members with `map_values` and never runs the rest of `f` on a member. A control that `f` raises on a member after its first output (an error, a `break`) no longer replaces the parent's output; arrays, which collect every output, are unchanged. A side effect of a later output (`halt_error`'s stderr text) still fires; that residual is recorded in the limitations page. `succinctly yq --jq-extensions` follows jq, as real yq has no `walk`.
- **jq: `fromjson` and `tonumber` word a partial UTF-8 BOM as `Malformed BOM`, as jq does** (#5804). `"\ufffd" | try fromjson catch .` is `"Malformed BOM (while parsing '\ufffd')"` in jq; `succinctly jq` said `Invalid numeric literal at EOF at line 1, column 3`. Any text that opens with `EF` and then departs from `EF BB BF` is malformed to jq's parser, which covers every character from U+F000 to U+FFFF, so a string `@base64d` made of replacement characters reaches it. Both fail with exit 5 either way; only the message that `try ... catch` hands back differed. A whole BOM is still skipped. The primary input stream words the same fault as a numeric-literal fault still (`printf '\xef\xbf\xbd1' | jq .` is `Malformed BOM` in jq).
- **yq: an alias key printed as its text keeps its anchor's quoting** (#5813).
  When the soundness pass drops a key alias (`*a : 1`) because the anchor is gone (`del(.b)` on `b: &a "true"`), the key used to print bare, so the string `"true"` became the bool key `true`.
  It now takes the quoting of its anchor's node: `"true": 1`, `'1': 1`, `"12": 1` for `!!str 12`.
  Where the anchor survives the key is still `*a`, as in yq.
- **yq: a tab between a quoted or alias key and its `:` is read as yq reads it** (#5814).
  `- "k"\t: 1` was a parse error ("mapping values are not allowed in this context"), and `"k"\t: 1` in a block mapping was reported as "tab character used for indentation".
  A tab there is separation, as a space is, so both now parse (`[{"k": 1}]` and `{"k": 1}`).
  A tab that indents block structure is still an error.
- **jq: `Cannot index <type> with string` leaves the key out when it is 30 bytes or longer, as jq does** (#5817). `[1] | try .["kkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkkk"] catch .` (30 bytes) is `"Cannot index array with string"` in jq 1.7.1, which quotes the key only up to 29 bytes (and counts bytes, so 15 two-byte characters drop it); `succinctly jq` quoted it whole. It showed up when the key was a document's own text (`.[(. | tojson)]`). The message is the only difference: both fail the same way. `succinctly yq` shares the message and drops a long key's text too, but real yq's wording is different and neither matched it before (`docs/compliance/yq/limitations.md`).
- **yq: a plain `<<` value carries the `!!merge` tag yq gives it** (#5833). `printf 'a: <<\nb: [<<, x]\n' | succinctly yq '.'` printed `a: <<` / `b: [<<, x]` where yq prints `a: !!merge <<` / `b: [!!merge <<, x]`, and `.a | tag` answered `!!str` where yq answers `!!merge`: YAML resolves a plain `<<` to the merge tag wherever it sits, and only a `<<` key carried it here. Both output routes now write the tag, `tag` and `type` report it, and a computed `"<<"` (`.z = "<<"`, or a `!!str <<` whose tag `-P` drops) is written quoted, as yq writes it, rather than as a plain `<<` that reads back as the merge tag. A quoted `"<<"` and a JSON string stay `!!str`.
- **yq: string builtins refuse an input whose tag is not `!!str`, and a plain date's `tag` is `!!timestamp`** (#5836). yq's `split`, `sub`, `test`, `match`, `capture`, `upcase`, `downcase`, `trim`, `@base64`, `@uri` and `@sh` refuse a number, a bool, a null, a container, a plain date, a plain `<<` and a string with a core tag (`!!binary aGk=`), naming the tag: `printf 'a: 5\n' | succinctly yq '.a | @base64'` printed `NQ==` and `.a | upcase` raised `explode input must be a string`, where yq raises `cannot encode !!int as base64, can only operate on strings` and `cannot change case with !!int, can only operate on strings. `. succinctly now refuses a document node in yq's words, after the arguments, flags and pattern yq checks first, `tag`/`type` answer `!!timestamp` for a plain date (`2001-12-14`) as yq does, and a verbatim tag as what it spells (`!<tag:yaml.org,2002:binary>` is `!!binary`).
- **`succinctly yq` writes a top-level string as its own text from `to_yaml` and `@yaml`** (#5836). yq's encoder unwraps a scalar root while `--unwrapScalar` holds, the default, so `"<<" | @yaml` is `<<`, `"1"` is `1`, `"- x"` is `- x` and `"x\ny"` is two lines, where go-yaml would quote each of them and they printed quoted here. A string inside a collection (`["<<"] | @yaml`) is quoted as before, and so is every string under `--unwrapScalar=false` and `-o=json`. A probe of 1,820 rows against yq v4.53.3 (27 strings, 14 filters, 5 flag sets) fixed 786 and changed none that already matched; a multi-line string inside a collection (yq writes a literal block) and a string encoded twice under `--unwrapScalar=false` are not part of this fix.
- **yq: `@sh` quotes a string as yq does** (#5837). `printf 'a: hello\n' | succinctly yq '.a | @sh'` printed `'hello'`, `a b` printed `'a b'` and `it's` printed `'it'\''s'`, where yq prints `hello`, `a' b'` and `it\'s`. yq leaves a run of characters in `[A-Za-z0-9_@%+=:,./-]` bare, opens a single quote at the first character that needs one and keeps it open to the end or the next `'`, which it writes `\'`. succinctly now does the same, and refuses a non-string under `-n` in yq's `@uri` wording, as it already did for a document node. `succinctly jq`'s `@sh` is unchanged.
- **yq datetime operators** (#5863). `succinctly yq` now adds a duration to a timestamp and subtracts one from it (`.t += "3h10m"`, `.t -= "24h"`), keeping the timestamp's zone and raising Go's error for a duration that does not parse; before, `+=` concatenated the text and exited 0. `format_datetime(layout)`, `with_dtf(layout; expr)` and yq's `tz(zone)` are implemented over a port of Go's `time.Parse`, `time.Format` and `time.ParseDuration`. `now`, `from_unix`, `to_unix` and the ordering comparisons read and write timestamps as yq does, in the local zone and under the `with_dtf` layout. `OwnedValue` has no timestamp tag, so a string spelled like a timestamp stands for one: a duration added to a quoted date is added rather than appended, other text is appended (`"2026-01-01" + "T00:00:00Z"`, as in yq), and `now | type` is `!!str`; `docs/compliance/yq/limitations.md` records the rest.
- **`succinctly yq` answers a value the program builds past 384 levels, as yq does** (#5876). `.[] as $i ireduce (0; [.]) | length` over 385 or 2,000 items is `1` (it was `Error: nesting depth exceeds limit of 384`), and the value prints as YAML, `-o json` and `-P` byte for byte as yq prints it. A walk over such a value now checks the native-stack floor once per level, as `succinctly jq` has since #5554, and refuses past it with `nesting depth exceeds limit of the native stack`. A value built to 257-384 levels and read back out of a fold (`{"a": .}` folded 300 times, then `.a | length`) no longer hits the 256-level document ceiling.
- **jq: a computed object key that is not a string is rejected only once its value yields** (#5915).
  Over a computed value, `{"n":1} | {(.n): .[0]?}` raised `Cannot use number (1) as object key`
  where jq prints nothing, and `{"n":1} | {(.n): .[0]}` reported the key where jq reports the value's
  own error (`Cannot index object with number`). The streaming route checked the key as soon as it
  was produced; it now waits for the first value, as the eager and generic routes and jq do.
- **yq: `map(f)` over an empty mapping is that mapping** (#5918).
  `{} | map(.)` printed `[]` (`!!seq`) where yq v4.53.3 answers `{}` (`!!map`) without running `f`, so `map(.) | . + {"a": 1}` and `[map(.)]` differed too.
  Only an empty mapping behaves that way: a non-empty mapping, an empty sequence, `null` and a scalar already matched, and `jq` mode still answers `[]`.
- **jq: the second of two parse errors `input` raises is placed where jq places it** (#5923).
  After a fault, jq drops the rest of the read it was in and never counts the dropped bytes, so its
  parser's line and column carry on from where the first fault stopped it, and from one file to the next:
  for the input `}\n}\n[4]\n`, `[limit(3; repeat(try input catch .))]` reports `Unmatched '}' at line 1,
  column 1` and then `... at line 1, column 2`, where `succinctly jq` said `line 2, column 1`. A run of
  faults on adjacent lines (`]\n}\n]`), a fault after blank lines or after a document, and a fault in a
  second file now report jq's positions; the text and the first fault's position were already right.
- **`succinctly jq` resumes after a parse error that ends in an unterminated string, as jq does** (#5925). After a fault `input` raises, jq drops the rest of the read the fault was in and reads on. When the fault is a number a quote ends (`1e"str`, `-"x`, `1."x`), `succinctly jq` took the string the quote opens for a token to complete, and a string that never closes put the fault at the end of the input, so the stream ended there: `printf '{"a"}\n\n1e"str\n\ntrue\n\n]\n[}12 34\t' | jq -nc '[limit(14; repeat(try input catch .))]'` read the first two errors and then `break`, where jq goes on to `true`, `]` and `}`. The fault is now met at the quote.
- **yq: `*`, `/` and `%` refuse a timestamp as yq does, and `from_unix` names the tag of a non-number** (#5930). `printf 't: 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z\n' | succinctly yq '.t * 2'` printed `2026-01-01T00:00:00Z2026-01-01T00:00:00Z` and exited 0; yq v4.53.3 answers `Error: cannot multiply !!timestamp with !!int`. `/` and `%` say `!!timestamp cannot be divided by !!int` and `!!timestamp cannot modulo by !!int`, a timestamp on the right of any of the three is refused the same way (`2 * .t`: `cannot multiply !!int with !!timestamp`), and a timestamp times `null` is the timestamp. `"x" | from_unix` says `from_unix only works on numbers, found !!str instead`, not `math function requires number`. 96 filters over a document with every scalar tag, both operand positions and the write forms (`*=`, `|=`, `*?`, `//`, `[...]`) match yq; a container or `null` operand of `/` and `%` is refused with the same words but without yq's key names in parentheses. jq mode is unchanged.
- **`succinctly jq` `strptime` resolves `%C`, `%y` and `%Y` in the libc's order, and `%n`/`%t` need white space** (#5934). `"2015 20" | strptime("%Y %C")` is now year 2000 (it was 2015), `"20 85" | strptime("%C %y")` is 2085 (it was 1985), and `"2015" | strptime("%Y%n")` is a mismatch where it used to parse, as in jq 1.7.1. The `%j` next to a month and the `%z` offset still differ and are tracked on the issue.
- **`succinctly jq` `strptime` counts a `%j` beside a month from the month's start** (#5934). `"2015 03 050" | strptime("%Y %m %j")` is now `[2015,2,-9,0,0,0,4,49]` (it was `[2015,2,0,0,0,0,6,58]`, the zeroed day and the yearday of the month read), the day passing 31 or going below 1 and the year not rolling, as in jq 1.7.1. A day read beside `%j` with no month takes the month from the day of year (`"2015 19 050" | strptime("%Y %d %j")` is February 19). Where the day read disagrees with the day of year jq aborts on its own assertion, so there is no answer to match.
- **jq: a fault met in bytes that rode across two or more files is placed where jq places it** (#5936).
  A file that is only an open tail (`[1,\n` then `x<TAB>`) hands it on to the next, and jq reads each file
  in reads of its own, so a fault in those bytes drops the rest of the read that ends at that file's end.
  For the files `}\n[1,\n`, `x<TAB>` and `[1,\nx  }}[}  `, `[limit(8; repeat(try input catch .))]` now reports
  `Invalid numeric literal at line 3, column 2` as its third message, where `succinctly jq` said `line 2,
  column 4`. Against jq 1.7.1, a randomised run over 3 and 4 files (7,200 programs) changes 266 from
  different to identical and none the other way; the 127 and 160 left over all hold invalid UTF-8.
- **jq: a field read through an `as` rebind of a fold's loop variable keeps its storage when stored** (#5938).
  `[{"items":[nan]}] as $in | reduce $in[] as $r ({}; $r as $s | .a = $s.items) | .a == $in[0].items` is `true` in jq, where the stored member is the element's own array, and was `false` here: the in-place step declined an `as` rebind of the fold's marker, so the evaluator rebuilt the member as a literal.
  The step now binds the new name to the same marker, and the gate counts a read of a name rebound that way as a read of the loop variable (`.a = $s.items`, `.a += $s.items`, `.[$s.n] = $s.items`, a rebind of a rebind).
  A rebind in front of arithmetic, a pipe of writes or a destructuring pattern is unchanged and recorded in `docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`.
  `succinctly yq` is unchanged.
- **`strptime` reads an empty field and a signed year as jq does** (#5947). `%Y`, `%y`, `%M` and `%S`, and those fields inside `%R`, `%T` and `%D`, read nothing at the end of the input or before white space and succeed, so `"" | strptime("%Y")` is the zeroed time and `"10:30:" | strptime("%T")` reads, where both were no match. `%s` with no digits reads 0 and consumes nothing. `%Y`, `%y` and `%C` take a sign that uses one character of the field's width (`"-5" | strptime("%y")` is 1995, `"+" | strptime("%Y")` is year 0), and a week number in a negative year is placed with jq's libc's own arithmetic. A month outside 1-12 or a day past 31 is refused as it is read, so a later `%s` no longer hides it (`"13" | strptime("%m%s")`).
- **`strptime` reads `%z`, refuses `%p` after an hour past 12, and takes only C white space** (#5960). `%z` was skipped; it now reads a sign and four digits and, like `GMT`, makes the fields a UTC instant that becomes local time once its offset is taken off, so `"2015-03-05 10:00 +0500" | strptime("%F %R %z")` is 05:00 under `TZ=UTC`, and a later `%s` or `%Z` naming `GMT` drops the offset, as in jq. `%p` refuses an hour past 12 read before it (`"2015 13 PM" | strptime("%Y %H %p")`). White space in the format, before `%s` and at the end of the input is C's `isspace`, so other Unicode white space is text, as in jq.
- **`jq` parse-error column over invalid UTF-8** (#5964). A parse error counts its column over the bytes jq read, so `printf '\xff }'` names column 2 where `succinctly jq` named column 4: the substitution turned each invalid byte into a three-byte U+FFFD before the position was counted. The default, `-s` and `--stream` routes, a program's `input` and the main loop all count the original bytes now.
- **jq: a parse error the main loop meets reads `jq: parse error: ...`, as jq prints it, when the program uses `input`, `inputs` or `input_line_number` without `-n`** (#5965). `printf '1\n}' | jq -c input_line_number` printed `jq: error (at <stdin>:1): Unmatched '}' at line 2, column 1`, where jq prints `jq: parse error: Unmatched '}' at line 2, column 1`; stdout and the exit code (5) already matched. A fault the program's own `input` reads keeps its `(at F:N)` marker, in both.
- **jq: `strptime`'s `%d` and `%e` read the white space before the day as jq's libc does** (#5974). A white-space character stands in for the first of the day's two digits: `%d` reads `" 5"` and `"\t5"` as day 5 (they were no match) and refuses `"  5"` and `" 05"`, and `%e` skips one white-space character and then reads as `%d` does, so `"\t5"` and `"  5"` are day 5 (the first was no match) and `"   5"` is no match (it was day 5). A day above 31 is refused where it is read (`"500" | strptime("%d%d")` read 50 first and answered), and `%D`, `%F`, `%c` and `%x`, which stand for `%d`, read their day the same way. Checked against jq 1.7.1 on macOS over 93,600 rows (20 formats, every string of up to four characters from white space, digits, `-` and `/`, weekday and yearday left out): all of them match, 3,324 differed before. glibc's `strptime` skips any run of white space, so jq on Linux reads more of these than the pin does; this follows the pin.
- **`jq` parse-error column after a run jq collapses inside a string, and the fault of a read that starts inside a character** (#5975). `printf '"\xe1A" }'` names column 6 as jq does (it was 7: the lead byte takes the `A` with it, so two bytes are one U+FFFD in the text), and a character cut by the end of a file and completed by the next, with a fault before it, raises jq's own `Invalid numeric literal at line 1, column 11` where it raised `Invalid JSON text`. The same wording now holds on a single file whose 4095-byte read ends inside a character. The library's `succinctly::jq::utf8_document::substitute_invalid_utf8_jq_document_mapped` returns the substitution with the bytes each replacement covers.
- **`jq --validate`, `json validate` and `yaml validate` no longer panic on an error in a long line of multi-byte characters, and the caret stands under the right character** (#5988). The context line under a validation error was cut to 80 bytes around the error at byte offsets that can fall inside a character, so `"€€…€" 1` (40 or more `€`) died with `end byte index 80 is not a char boundary` (exit 101) instead of exit 3 (`jq`) or 1. `text validate utf8` cut the same way and printed its caret at a byte offset, so the caret sat far to the right of a multi-byte character's column. The four validators now share one cut (`error_snippet::truncate_line`) that moves each cut point down to a character boundary and counts the caret in characters. `jq --validate` also shows the last 80 bytes, marked on the left only, for an error in the last half of a long line, as the other three already did, where it showed a window with a trailing `...`.
- **`succinctly jq` `strptime` reads the `0` and `+` flags and a width between the `%` and the specifier** (#5989). `"03" | strptime("%0d")`, `"-2015" | strptime("%+5Y")` and `"201599" | strptime("%6Y")` now match as in jq 1.7.1, where they used to fail with an unknown specifier. A width is the most digits a numeric field takes (`"012" | strptime("%3m")` is month 12, `"31" | strptime("%1d")` is no match), `%s`, `%w`, `%u`, the names and the composite formats ignore it, `%c %x %X %r` accept the prefix, and `%Z` with a width reads exactly that many capitals. A second `E`/`O`, a `+` after a digit and `_`/`-` flags stay no match, as in jq.
- **jq: a raw control character in a string is refused even when an invalid UTF-8 byte comes before it** (#5990). `"\xe1\n"` read as a lone U+FFFD, because the invalid-UTF-8 drop quirk (a lead byte with too few bytes left in its string takes the rest of the string, #1743) ran before the parse; jq's lexer refuses the control character first, so it is now `Invalid string: control characters from U+0000 through U+001F must be escaped` at the newline, with jq's line and column, on every input route.
- **jq: a character cut at a file boundary that the next file does not complete** (#5990). After a parse error `input` raises, `"a\xe2` at the end of one file and `\x82" 23null` at the start of the next read `Unfinished string at EOF at line 2, column 10` where jq reads `Invalid numeric literal at line 2, column 3`: the stitch moves the open tail onto the next file, the substitution replaces the two bytes by one U+FFFD that spans the file boundary, and the read jq resumes at starts inside it, a place the text did not have. The seam now places each share of the moved bytes by the substitution of the whole file and keeps where it ended in the bytes as read, so the read is the parser's own over the original bytes from there. The same holds with the character spread over three files and with an empty file between. The stitch differential (`--pool nasty`, seeds 5, 9, 10 at 600 streams) had one differing run in each and has none, and none of 21,600 runs over seeds 1 to 12 changed against `main` except those three.
- **jq: the values after an invalid byte outside a string are read** (#5994). A lead byte outside any string took the white space after it into its U+FFFD (the short-tail rule jq applies inside a string), so in `\xe1\n"a" 1` the newline was lost and `[limit(4; repeat(try input catch .))]` read the fault and then nothing. jq substitutes nothing outside a string; each ill-formed run there is now one U+FFFD that takes no valid byte with it, and the read goes on to `"a"` and `1`, as in jq.
- **jq: `strptime`'s `%s` skips leading zeros before it counts digits** (#5996). `%s` read at most 19 characters, so `"00000000000000000001"` left a `1` behind and was no match, where jq's libc reads the whole run with `strtol`: it is `[1970,0,1,0,0,1,...]`, as are `"0000000000000000000000000042"` (42 seconds), `"-000000000000000000001"` (the second before the epoch) and a signed run (`"+0000000000000000000001"`). The 19-digit limit is now on the significant digits, so `"99999999999999999999"` and `"9223372036854775808"` stay no match, as in jq. Checked against jq 1.7.1 on macOS over 2,808 rows (three signs, 0 to 25 leading zeros, twelve values, three formats): 346 differed before and 52 now, all one value, `67768036191676799`, where jq's `tm_year` wraps to `-2147481748` and this answers no match as before.
- **jq: a fault `input` raises in bytes moved across several files names the file jq read them in** (#6004, item 1).
  A file that is only an open tail hands it on to the next, so a fault in those bytes was named after the later file they now sit in. For the files `[`, `\xe1\n` and `]`, `jq -nc '[inputs]'` says `jq: error (at b:1): Invalid numeric literal at line 2, column 0` as jq does, where `succinctly jq` said `(at c:1)`. Each file's share of the moved bytes now records the file it came from.
  Over 3 and 4 files (4,800 programs each, nasty pool) the multi-file differential changes 177 runs from different to identical and none the other way; the two items of #6004 that remain (`<unknown>` after a number run into `[`, and `-s .` printing `[1]`) are untouched.
- **`succinctly jq` treats a bare number or literal before a stream's last opener as a value, as jq does** (#6004). When the input ends in a number, `true`, `false` or `null` straight before one last `[` or `{` (`1[`, `true{`), jq's parser has completed that token when it meets the end of input. `printf '1[' | jq -cs .` now prints `[1]` before the parse error, as jq does (it printed nothing), and an `input`/`inputs` read that meets the fault names `(at <unknown>)` instead of the file. Only that exact shape: `1 [`, `"a"[` and `[1][` are unchanged.
- **jq: `-n -s --stream` raises a fault in the stream from `input`, as jq does** (#6005). The whole stream was read before the program ran, so a fault ended the run at exit 5 even for a program that never calls `input`. jq reads on the first `input`: `printf '1 2 }' | jq -nc --stream -s 'try input catch "E"'` prints `"E"`, `input_line_number` prints `0`, and the call after the fault returns the array of the events (`[[[],1],[[],2]]`, with the ones that follow the fault too). A fault at the end of the stream comes after the array. 8,235 stream-by-program runs over one to three files (495 hand-picked, the rest random token soup) matched `/usr/bin/jq` 1.7.1 on stdout, stderr and exit status.
- **jq: a `--stream` walk stops one event past a file that did not open, as jq does** (#6006). jq's main loop reads no further input once its reader has moved past a missing file, after processing the input that took it there, so `jq -c --stream . missing a.json` over `[3]` prints `[[0],3]` and exits 2; succinctly printed every event of the files after it. `--stream -s` over only files that do not open is `[]` and exit 2, where it panicked. `-R` and `--stream-errors` still read on (`docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`).
- **jq: `sort`, `unique`, `group_by`, `min` and `max` leave NaN ties in jq's order** (#6008).
  jq orders a NaN before every number and before another NaN, and settles the tie by input position; `succinctly jq` reversed such ties, so `[{"a":nan,"b":1},{"a":nan,"b":2}] | sort` came out `b:2` first, `[3,1,2] | sort_by(nan)` was `[2,1,3]`, and `[3,1,2] | min_by(nan), max_by(nan)` was `3` and `2` where jq answers `2` and `3`.
  `sort`, `sort_by`, `unique`, `unique_by` and `group_by` now keep NaN-keyed items in input order, `min`/`min_by` take the last of a run of NaNs and `max`/`max_by` the first, in both evaluators and in path mode.
  A grid of 13 arrays by 16 builtins differed from jq in 65 of 208 probes and matches in all 208; the scan for a NaN that gates the tie rule is one pass over the keys of a sort.
- **jq: `delpaths` over a string or a `null` words its error as jq does for a path of two or more components** (#6012). jq reads the first key of such a path with `jv_get` before it reaches the next one. On a string an object key is a slice descriptor, so `"abc" | delpaths([[{"a":1},0]])` is `Array/string slice indices must be integers` (it was `Cannot index string with object`), and a descriptor that is valid (`{"start":1,"end":2}`) names a substring the rest of the path cannot delete from, `Cannot delete fields from string`. On a `null` root a `null`, boolean or array key is `Cannot index null with <kind>`, where this answered `null`; a `null` child is still skipped before jq descends, so `[null,[1]] | delpaths([[0,[1],0]])` is unchanged. Checked against jq 1.7.1 over 429 rows (29 paths, 13 inputs of every kind): all match, 44 differed before. yq is unchanged.
- **`succinctly jq` reads `--indent` as C's `atoi` does, and accepts `-L ""`** (#6017). `--indent -1` is a tab, `--indent " 2"` and `--indent 3x` are 2 and 3, and a value that does not start with a digit (`""`, `abc`) is 0, where each was a usage error (exit 2). Values outside -1 to 7 are still refused. `-L ""` is an empty search-path element, as in jq 1.7.1, not a missing value. Checked against `/usr/bin/jq` on 30 values and 17 option combinations.
- **jq: `-n -s` raises a fault in the stream from `input`, as jq does** (#6019). A stream with a fault was read in full before the program ran, so the fault ended the run at exit 5 even for a program that never calls `input`. jq reads on the first `input`: `printf '1 2 }' | jq -nc -s 'try input catch "E"'` prints `"E"`, `input_line_number` prints `0`, and the call after the fault returns the array of every value read (`[1,2]`, with the ones that follow the fault too). Every fault is one call, all of them before the array, the one at the end of the stream included. 17,000 stream-by-program runs over one to three files matched `/usr/bin/jq` 1.7.1 on stdout, stderr and exit status, but for the rows #6004 tracks (the file a stitched fault names, a bare token ended by a bracket at the end of the stream).
- **`succinctly jq` reads standard input for an input file named `-`** (#6023). `echo '{"a":1}' | jq . -` and `jq . a.json - b.json` fail with `Could not open file -` (exit 2) where jq reads stdin; the same holds for `-s`, `-R`, `--stream`, `--seq` and `-n` with `input`/`inputs`. Stdin is read once, so a second `-` is empty, `input_filename` is `"<stdin>"` for it, and an error location names `<stdin>`. `--slurpfile`, `--rawfile` and `-f` with `-` still fail, as in jq. Compared with `/usr/bin/jq` over 1,120 stdin x program x file-shape cases.
- **`succinctly jq` `strftime` prints `%y` and `%C` of a negative year as jq's libc does** (#6030). `%y` is the absolute value of the year's remainder by 100 in two digits, and `%C` of a negative year of fewer than three digits is `-0`: year -5 formats `%y` as `05` (it was `-5`), `%D` and `%x` as `01/01/05` (`01/01/-5`), and `%C` as `-0` (`00`). Checked against `/usr/bin/jq` over 25,920 year, format and zone rows.
- **`succinctly jq` `isfinite` is true for a NaN** (#6041). `nan | isfinite` answered `false`; jq defines `isfinite` as `type == "number" and (isinfinite | not)`, so a NaN, which is not infinite, is finite there (`[nan, infinite, 1.5] | map(isfinite)` is `[true,false,true]`). Found by a builtin x value sweep against jq 1.7.1.
- **jq: a `-0` written as a program literal keeps its sign through path mode** (#6042). `-0 | del(empty)`, `[-0|try path(error) catch .]` and `[-0|try pick(error) catch .]` printed `0` where jq 1.7.1 prints `-0`: the path-mode literal arm rebuilt the `-0` literal as an integer zero. A `-0` read from a document, `-0.0` and a computed negative zero already kept their sign.
- **jq: `-C` no longer colors a top-level string under `-a` with `-r`, `-j` or `--raw-output0`** (#6047).
  jq writes such a string quoted and escaped through a branch that has no color flag, so
  `echo '"é"' | jq -C -r -a .` prints `"é"` with no escape sequences, for any string and not only
  a non-ASCII one. `succinctly jq` colored it. A string inside a container, a non-string, and `-C` with
  only `-a` or only `-r` are unchanged.
- **jq: a `-0` array index or slice bound is `-0` in the path jq records** (#6049). `[1,2,3] | path(.[-0])` printed `[0]` where jq 1.7.1 prints `[-0]`, and `.[-0:]`, `.[:-0]`, `.a[-0]` and a computed key (`.[-0,1]`, `.[-0|.]`) lost the sign the same way: the parser folded the literal to the integer index 0, and a computed key read its spelling as the integer. The value of the index, the writes through it and `-0.0` are unchanged, and `succinctly yq` still prints `0` as yq does.
- **yq: a `-0` expression literal prints `0` in JSON output** (#6051). In yq a `-0` literal is the integer zero: its text stays `-0` for `tostring` and YAML output, and its JSON encoder prints `0`. `succinctly yq -o json` echoed the text, so `-0`, `[-0]`, `{"a": -0}`, `.a |= -0`, `to_json` and `@json` of one printed `-0`, and `-0 | . as $i | .[$i] | path` (a `-0` index bound to a variable) printed `[-0]`. A document's `-0` is a float in both tools and still prints `-0.0`.
- **jq: a number written with a trailing dot and no fraction (`5.`, `99999999999999999.`) reads as the integer in `fromjson`, `--argjson`, `--jsonargs` and `tonumber`, and a large one is no longer rounded** (#6052). `"1." | fromjson` and `--argjson x 1.` were errors, where jq answers `1`; and `succinctly jq -c .` on `99999999999999999.` printed `100000000000000000` where jq prints `99999999999999999` (the dot sent the token to a lossy `f64` read), as did `tonumber` (`1e+17`). The dot is dropped before the literal is kept, so every spelling jq reads (`-5.`, `+5.`, `007.`, `-0.`, `[1.]`) prints as it does there, and a dot with no integer part (`.`, `1.5.`, `1..`) is still refused. yq is unchanged.
- **`succinctly jq` reads a field access written with an interpolated string** (#6053). `{"a1":5} | ."a\(1)"` is a compile error here and `5` in jq, where `.` followed by a string indexes by that string and the string may hold `\(...)`; it is `.["a\(1)"]`. The step works after another field (`.a."b\(0)"`), takes `?`, and works under `=`, `|=`, `del` and `path`. `succinctly yq` is unchanged. Found by a syntax-edge sweep against jq 1.7.1.
- **yq: a single-quoted scalar with an empty line is written back across lines, as yq writes it** (#6058). `printf "a: 'x\n\ny'\n" | yq .` kept the value `x\ny` but `succinctly yq` wrote `a: 'x` and `y'` on adjacent lines, which a YAML reader folds back to `x y`: the YAML output read back as another value. Each `\n` of the value is now written as an empty line with the text after it indented, as yq does, in block and flow position, after a write elsewhere in the document, and under `style="single"`; JSON output and the value were never affected. A flow sequence nested in a flow sequence and an explicit `? ` key still print the older spelling.
- **yq: a plain scalar in a flow collection that continues on a line starting with a tab is refused as in yq** (#6059). `a: [x⏎⇥y]` printed `a: [x y]`, where yq stops with `found a tab character that violates indentation`: go-yaml refuses a tab at a column below the enclosing block's indent plus one in the leading blanks of a continuation line (also a tab-only line, and one before a closing `]` or `,`). A collection at the document root (`[x⏎⇥y]`), a tab after enough spaces, and a tab that starts a new item after a `,` are still read, as in yq.
- **`succinctly jq -s --stream` keeps the events read before an end-of-input fault, as jq does** (#6061). jq closes the slurp array at the call that consumes the last byte, so an event that byte completes is in the array and the fault comes after it: `printf '1[' | jq -cs --stream .` prints `[[[],1]]` and then the parse error, `[1,` prints `[[[0],1]]` and `[{}` prints `[[[0],{}]]`; it printed nothing. A fault met by that call or an earlier one (`[1,2`, `1 [`) is still the whole result. Checked on 10,640 runs against jq 1.7.1.
- **yq: `--argjson` reads a number written with a bare trailing dot (`5.`, `-0.`, `007.`), as the `-p json` reader does** (#6063). `succinctly yq --argjson n 5.` was refused (`invalid JSON for --argjson n`), where yq's JSON reader answers `{"n":5}` for `{"n":5.}`. A whole-valued span is now the integer (`5.` prints `5`, not `5.0`), also for `--input-format json` under `--slurp` and `--eval-all`; `.5` stays `0.5`, and `.`, `-.`, `1.5.` and `1..` are still refused.
- **jq: `range(.; .+10)` over an integer past 2^53 emits the start unrounded** (#6064). `9007199254740993 | [limit(1;range(.;.+10))]` printed `[9007199254740992]` where jq 1.7.1 prints `[9007199254740993]`, and so did `-9007199254740993 | range(.;.+1)` and `range(.;infinite)` over `9223372036854775806`: when the upper bound is a float the range runs on doubles, and its first value started from the rounded double instead of the start's own literal. An exact-integer bound already kept it. Only that first value is affected: the values after it still step exactly past 2^53 where jq steps on doubles (the recorded `range` divergence).
- **yq: a line break after an escaped line break in a double-quoted scalar is kept, as in go-yaml** (#6067). `a: "z\` followed by an empty line and ` x"` read `z x` here and `z\nx` in yq, and two empty lines read `z\nx` where yq has `z\n\nx`: after a backslash-newline go-yaml is at the start of a line, so it keeps every break that follows instead of folding the first into a space. The same holds in the YAML and JSON writers, for CRLF and after an escaped U+0085, U+2028 or U+2029. A scalar with two escapes in a row, or an escaped backslash before a break, is unchanged. Of 28 bodies in each of two output formats, 38 differed from yq v4.53.3 before and none do now.
- **jq: a regex with `\u`, a literal brace or a `\p{..}` under `i` no longer matches differently from Oniguruma without an error** (#6068). `\u` and `\U` are not escapes in jq but the letter (`"u00e9" | test("\\u00e9")` is `true`; here `"é"` matched it and a lone `\u` was an error); `a{ 1}`, `a{1 }`, `a{1, 2}` and `a{,2}` are literal text in jq and repeated `a` here; `\p{Lu}`, `\P{Lu}` and `(?i)\p{Lu}` do not case-fold in jq (`"a" | test("\\p{Lu}"; "i")` is `false`), and a `\p` or `\P` with no brace is the letter. Of 1,512 pattern, text and flag rows, 408 differed from jq 1.7.1 before and none do now. yq's Go dialect is untouched.
- **jq: a group under a repeat whose body can match empty reports jq's last, empty iteration** (#6069). `"ab" | match("(a*)*b")` had the group at offset 0 holding `"a"`, the last non-empty iteration; jq's Oniguruma ends the loop with an empty iteration and reports `""` at offset 1, and so does succinctly now. `capture`, `scan` and `sub` read the same groups (`"aab" | capture("(?<x>a*)*b")` is `{"x":""}`). A group nested in the body keeps what an earlier iteration captured, as in jq. Patterns that go to `fancy-regex` (lookaround, backreferences, the `l` flag) keep the old captures; yq mode is unchanged, as Go's `regexp` reports the last non-empty iteration too.
- **`succinctly jq` reads Oniguruma's escapes the way jq does, and refuses what it refuses** (#6070).
