Of 2,500 random small documents compared with yq, 55 that were read here and refused by yq are now refused too, and none that yq reads is newly refused.
- **jq: a counted `{n,}` (n of 2 or more) of a capture group that has a group inside it ends at the body's empty way and sets the outer group there, as Oniguruma's does** (#6347). `"ba" | [match("((a)|b*){2,}";"g") | .captures | map(.string)]` printed `["a","a"]` for its first match; jq 1.7.1 answers `["","a"]`. The capture rewrite of #6309 now writes such a repeat as the `*` loop, which the loop rewrite of #6332 reads and whose groups it copies; it does so outside another repeat and with no flag switch inside the group, where the sweep found it changed an answer that agreed. Over two draws of 5,000 generated loops (`scripts/jq-regex-capture-loop-sweep.py`), 20 and 29 patterns that differed from jq now agree and none changed the other way; wider draws (assertions, `(?i)`, `{3,}`), nested draws (`--nest`) and counted repeats near the unrolling limit fixed 5 to 57 and broke none (`docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`).
- **yq: a block scalar header with anything after its indicators is refused, as yq refuses it** (#6348). The header holds one chomping character, one digit 1-9, blanks, a comment and the line break. `a: |  x` / `  y`, `a: |x`, `a: |-x`, `a: |"q"` and `- |  x` read `{"a":"y\n"}` (the text dropped, the lines below taken as the content) and are now `did not find expected comment or line break`, as is a second chomping character or digit (`a: |--`, `a: |-+`, `a: |22`) and a `0` (`a: |0`). A header with a comment, blanks or a tab before its break reads as before. U+0085, U+2028 and U+2029 end the header in yq and still do not here.
- **yq: a run of leading `---` lines is one document, as yq reads it** (#6349). yq's header slurp sets aside every leading blank, comment, directive and `---` line before the first content line, so `---` / `---` / `x` is the one document `"x"` where `succinctly yq` read a null document and then `x` (`---` / `---` alone was two nulls, a third marker a third document). The printed header already held every marker; the document count, `document_index`, `[.]`, `--doc` and `line` now agree with it, and a marker after content, an empty later document and the library's `YamlIndex::build` are unchanged.
- **`path()` of a static chain past 384 components answers instead of refusing** (#6356).
  `path(.a.a...)` and `.a.a... | path` exited 5 with `nesting depth exceeds limit of 384` at the 385th component where
  jq and yq answer, and the same chain with a trailing slice already did. #5554 and #5876 moved the owned walk to the
  native-stack floor and left the cursor walker on the constant. It now asks the floor too in `succinctly jq` and
  `succinctly yq`; past the floor it refuses at exit 5, and `?` and `try` do not absorb that. A library caller of
  `jq::eval`, which arms no floor, keeps 384.
- **jq: a loop with capture groups answers as Oniguruma's does beside a flag switch written in the pattern, and in a `{n,}` of a non-capturing group of several ways** (#6358, most of it). `"bab" | [match("(?:(a)?|(?i)b)*";"g") | .string]` printed `["","ab",""]` and jq 1.7.1 answers `["","a","",""]`; `"aab" | [match("(?:(a)|()){2,}") | .captures | map(.string)]` printed `["a",null]` where jq answers `["a",""]`, because the empty third iteration ends the loop and sets the second group. The loop rewrite scopes a switch over the items and ways it reaches and takes its empty way from them (a way that is only a switch too), and the capture rewrite reads a counted repeat of a group that holds several groups as the `*` loop it is. Over four draws of 5,000 generated loops with `(?i)`, `(?s)`, `(?m)` and `(?-i)` among the atoms, 297 patterns that differed from jq now agree and none changed the other way; five draws of the existing sweep fixed 52 more. A loop with capture groups inside another repeat that can run it again is written with the rest, so the repeat around it ends at the empty iteration as Oniguruma's does: `"ba" | match("((?:(b|)*|a)+)*")` printed `"ba"` and is `"b"` now, as in jq. Over five draws of 5,000 generated loops with `--nest` (one of them under the flags `gi`), 212 to 239 patterns that differed from jq agree (256 differed on the first draw, 17 still do) and none changed the other way; seven draws of 4,000 with loops beside other items in the ways of an outer repeat (`--ways`) fixed 565 to 642 and broke none. A leading assertion over a counted repeat, a lazy bounded repeat that leaves a group unset, a counted repeat large enough that the rewrite gives up (`((?:(b|)*|a)+){4,8}`), and a loop under a lookaround or backreference inside a repeat still differ (`docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`).
- **jq: a loop with one way that is only an anchor answers as Oniguruma's does** (#6358). `"bab" | [match("(?:(a)\\b|\\bb?){2,}?";"g") | .string]` printed `["b",""]` and jq 1.7.1 answers `["",""]`; `"ba" | [match("(a|\\b)*") | .string]` kept the group's last consuming iteration where jq's empty one sets it. An anchor way is a conditional exit, on both sides of the ways after it, which one star cannot write: the loop is written from what the anchor is (`\b` by its complement, `\A` at the first head, `\z` where nothing can consume), and a repeat Oniguruma counts leaves at the anchor outright. Over three draws of 3,000 loops with anchors the patterns that differ fall from 113, 115 and 137 to 69, 50 and 62 and none changed the other way. Two anchor-only ways in one body still differ.
- **jq: a lazy bounded repeat over a body that opens with a flag switch answers as Oniguruma's does** (#6358). `"bbc" | [match("((?i)|b*){2,5}?c";"g") | .captures | map(.string)]` printed `[["bb"]]` and jq 1.7.1 answers `[[""]]`: the switch hid the body from the rewrite, which is needed to make the `regex` crate leave the repeat at the empty iteration as Oniguruma does. Oniguruma never unrolls a lazy repeat with an upper bound, so the operation count that made a switch unknown does not apply to it. Over ten draws of 2,500 `--bounded` loops (`scripts/jq-regex-capture-loop-sweep.py --bounded --seed 3` to `10`) 7 to 16 patterns per draw that differed from jq agree and none changed the other way; the plain, `--nest`, `--ways` and `--assert` draws are unchanged. A lazy repeat with no upper bound, and a body with a way that is only an anchor, keep their text beside a switch.
- **jq: a lazy `{0,n}?` or `{1,n}?` over a body whose empty way is only an anchor, with a capture group around it, answers as Oniguruma does** (#6358). `"a b" | [match("(?:(\\b)|b){0,3}?\\z";"g") | .captures[0].string]` printed `["", ""]` and jq 1.7.1 answers `[null, ""]`: Oniguruma tries a lazy repeat's exit before an iteration, so the anchor's iteration only ends the loop, where the `regex` crate went on from it into the consuming way with the anchor's group kept. Over 3,000 patterns of `scripts/jq-regex-capture-loop-sweep.py --bounded` at seed 23, 13 are fixed (92 still differ before, 79 after) and no draw broke one; the other classes are unchanged.
- **yq: `from_yaml` and `from_json` apply yq's header slurp to their string** (#6363). yq reads that string through its YAML decoder, so a leading `--- text` line loses its line break (`"--- x\ny" | from_yaml` is `"xy"`, not `"x y"`) and a run of leading `---` lines is one document (`"---\n---\nx" | from_yaml` is `"x"`, which read `null`). The lost-break rule moved from the yq runner into the library (`succinctly::yaml::glue_after_leading_marker_text`) for it.
- **yq: a block scalar that holds U+0085, U+2028 or U+2029 is read as go-yaml reads it** (#6369). go-yaml ends a block scalar's line at each of the three as at `\n`, so the spaces after one are indentation (`a: |` over `  x<U+2028>  y` is `"x y\n"`, where `succinctly yq` kept the two spaces), a line left of the indent after one ends the scalar (`  x<U+2028>b: 1` is the scalar `"x "` and a key `b`, where the whole line was content), a comment, key, sequence item or `---` there is structure or an error (`  x<U+2028>y` and `  x<U+2028>- y` are refused), and U+0085 is a `\n` in the value while U+2028 and U+2029 stay and never fold in a `>` scalar. The scalar's lines, its end, its indent and its value are read that way for exactly the scalars that hold one of the three; the parser notes one on the line walk it already makes (looking at a byte only where a `0xC2` or `0xE2` lead byte shows up) and lists the scalar in the index, so the decoders never scan for them. This replaces #6287's tab-after-break check, which is a case of the same reading. Checked against yq v4.53.3 on 960 documents (four headers, the three breaks, 0-3 spaces on each side, five tails) and on 40,000 random ones (seventeen headers: `|`, `>`, `-`, `+`, explicit indents, `&anchor`, `!!str`, sequence items and a nested key; leading, trailing and empty lines made of spaces and any break, CRLF and lone CR; a dedent line or none), with no difference. The random draws put no break after a line left of the scalar's indent, since three neighbouring shapes outside a block scalar still differ: a plain key that spans a break, a comment line that ends at one, and a document-root `--- |` whose first blank line is spaces and a NEL (#6820). Time, interleaved and min of 11 (medians quoted) on a block-scalar corpus with no break at 10 and 50 MB: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X -2.0% to +0.4% on ASCII and -1.5% to +0.8% on text with U+2014 and U+00E9, 5-8% faster on text with tabs; Apple M4 Pro -1.2% to +1.3% on both (control -3.3% to +2.2%) and 1.5-9% faster on text with tabs. A rescan of the scalar for the three breaks, tried first, cost 12-18% on the non-ASCII text, which is why the walk looks at a byte only where a lead byte shows up. A scalar that does hold a break takes the slower path: 14,240 block scalars that each hold an LS index in 28.0 ms against 14.6 ms (7950X, 10 MB).
- **yaml: a block sequence at a bare `?`'s own column is the explicit key, as yq reads it** (#6370). `?` / `- a` / `: v` was `{"":["a","v"]}` (the sequence taken as the value of an empty key, the `v` joining it), `?` / `- a` / `k: w` as `{"":["a"],"k":"w"}` and `?` / `- a` as `{"":["a"]}`, where yq reads the sequence as a complex key and answers `{"":"v"}`, `{"":null,"k":"w"}` and `{"":null}`; the YAML Test Suite case 6PBE (`?` / `- a` / `- b` / `:` / `- c` / `- d`) now answers `{"":["c","d"]}` as yq does, where both sequences were merged into the value. A non-empty key still refuses a same-column sequence (`? k` / `- a`, #1104), and a sequence one column in (`?` / ` - a`) is unchanged. Checked against 11,718 YAML files on disk (none changed) and 12,000 randomized dash/key/`?` documents against yq v4.53.3: about 430 more documents match yq, and two that matched stopped matching, both an exotic nested explicit key inside the key sequence that already read wrongly with the dash on the `?` line (`? - ? a` / `   x` / `   x` is accepted where yq refuses it).
- **yaml: an explicit key's plain scalar that a comment ended takes no more lines, as in yq** (#6371). `printf '? a⏎  b # c⏎  d⏎: v⏎' | succinctly yq -o json .` printed `{"a b":"d"}`, the line after the comment read as the entry's value and the `: v` line lost; yq stops with `did not find expected key`, and so does `succinctly yq` now, for a line more indented than the `?` that follows the comment (`? a # c⏎  b⏎: v`, a comment line between, a deeper `- x` or `k: v`). A comment followed directly by the `:` line or the next key still reads. Over 3,600 generated explicit-key documents with comments and continuation lines, the 1,430 that differed from yq now agree and none changed the other way.
- **yq: a tab after an explicit indent's spaces, and after the spaces of the line that ends a block scalar, is refused as yq refuses it** (#6372). go-yaml eats a block scalar's leading spaces while the column is below the indent and raises `found a tab character where an indentation space is expected` on a tab met there; #6295 made that so for an auto-detected indent. What was left: a tab after fewer spaces than an explicit indent indicator gives (`a: |2` over ` <tab>x`, which read as an empty scalar and a stray key), and a tab after the spaces of the dedented line that ends the scalar (`a: |` over `  x` and ` <tab>y`, which read as `{"a":"x\n","y":...}`). A tab where the indent is known (`a: |2` over `  <tab>x`, or after the first content line) is still content. Checked against yq v4.53.3 on a grid of 11,340 documents (four hosts, nine headers, five leading-line shapes, 0-6 spaces), with no difference in which are refused, and on 6,000 random block-scalar documents, none newly refused here that yq reads.
- **yq: a `?` after an implicit key's colon is refused, as yq refuses it** (#6379). `c: ? w` read `{"c": "? w"}`; yq stops with `mapping keys are not allowed in this context`, because an explicit key cannot open a mapping on its parent key's line. Refused likewise in a sequence item's mapping (`- c: ? w`), nested (`x:` / `  c: ? w`), with a property between (`c: &a ? w`, `c: !!str ? w`), after a quoted or flow key (`"c": ? w`, `[a]: ? w`), as a value in a flow collection (`{c: ? w}`, `[c: ? w]`) and after the colon of an explicit pair in flow (`[? c : ? d]`). `?w` and `?? x` stay plain scalars, and an explicit key that opens an entry (`c:` / `  ? w`, `- ? w`, `[? w]`, `: ? x` after an explicit key's colon) reads as before. This is the largest single bucket (89 of 220) of the "read where yq refuses" differences a structural fuzz found.
- **yq: a property before a `?` and a tab after a `?` or an explicit `:` are refused, as in yq** (#6379). A `?` after a node property opens no key in go-yaml, so `&t ? x`, `- &t ? x`, `k:` / `  - &t ? x` and `? - &t ? x` are `mapping keys are not allowed in this context` (a property on a line of its own, and `&t ?x`, are not that); `succinctly yq` read `- &t ? x` as a key sequence and `? - &t ? x` as an empty key. go-yaml skips no tab right after those indicators, so `?⇥x`, `? ⇥x`, and `:⇥b` after an explicit key are `found character that cannot start any token`, which the top level read (the library loader keeps YAML 1.2's reading, a tab as separation); a tab whose blanks end at a `#` is its comment scanner's and is read, which #6340's nested check refused (`? ?⇥# c`). Over every stream of up to three lines from 26 explicit-key lines (18,278 streams) the baseline differs from yq on 4,441 and this build on 967, all of them streams both tools refuse (yq prints the part before its error, `succinctly yq` prints nothing); 3,474 are fixed and none changed the other way.
- **yq: a block scalar's leading blank line that is wider than its first content line ends the scalar, as it does in yq** (#6381). go-yaml takes an auto-detected block scalar's indent from the widest of the leading blank lines and the first content line, so `a: |` over a line of four spaces and then `  x` has an indent of four: the scalar is empty and `  x` is a stray line, an error in a mapping or sequence. `succinctly yq` took the indent from `  x` alone and read `{"a":"  \nx\n"}`. A blank line no wider than the content (`a: |` over a line of two spaces and `  x`), a deeper content line, and an explicit indent indicator are read as before. Checked against yq v4.53.3 on a grid of 13,824 documents (six hosts, eight headers, blank-line widths 0-7, content indents 1-6), 7,384 of them refused by yq, with no difference in which are refused; before the change 2,520 of them were read here.
- **yaml: a line after a quoted or flow explicit key, more indented than the `?`, is refused as yq refuses it** (#6382). `printf '? "a"⏎  b⏎: v⏎' | succinctly yq -o json .` printed `{"a":"b"}`, the line read as the entry's value and the `: v` line lost; yq stops with `did not find expected key`, with a comment after the key or without one, and `succinctly yq` now does too, for a quoted scalar and a flow sequence or mapping (`? [a]⏎  b⏎: v`, `? 'a' # c⏎  d⏎: v`). The `:` of the key's value, a comment line, the next key and a node still open across a line break read as before. Over 3,600 generated documents with such keys, the 961 that differed from yq now agree and none changed the other way.
- **yaml: a `key: value` line indented between a sequence item and its compact mapping is rejected as yq rejects it** (#6385). `- k: a` / ` b: 1` read as `[{"k":"a","b":1}]`, `-   a: hello` / `  b: 2` as `[{"a":"hello","b":2}]`, `- k:` / ` x` as `[{"k":null}]` (the `x` gone) and `- ? a` / ` b: 1` as `[{"a":null,"b":1}]`, where yq stops with `did not find expected '-' indicator`. This was the #885 tolerance, which read such a line as another entry of the mapping so that it was not dropped; #5086 removed its `-` counterparts (#325/#485/#900) for the same reason, and an error loses nothing silently. A line on a sequence item's own virtual indent after the item's mapping closed is refused whichever line it is. Checked against 11,718 YAML files on disk (none changed) and 9,000 randomized dash/key/`?` documents against yq v4.53.3: 540 more documents match yq, and one that matched stopped matching (a `?` / `- ? a` / `  x` stray line that the `?`-column work of #6370 already accepted, see #6377). The remaining random differences against yq fell from 25-40 per 1,500 documents to 0-1.
- **yq: a key with no value, followed by a quoted or flow-collection key, keeps its null** (#6386). `a:` / `"b": 1` read `{"a": "b", "b": 1}` (and `a:` / `[x]: 1` read `{"a": [], "": 1}`): the empty value's node was written at the start of the *next* line, and a node is decoded from its first byte, so a quote or a bracket there made the key's text its value. It happened when the next line was at the key's indent or a dedent (`x:` / `  a:` / `"b": 1`), in a sequence item's mapping (`x:` / `  - a:` / `"b": 1`) and with a property on the empty value (`- a: &x`).
- **yq: `line` and `column` of an empty value are the key's, as in yq** (#6386). `.a | line` of `a:` / `b: 1` was 2 (the next line) and is 1, `.a | column` is 3 (right after the colon, as yq says), including a value at the end of the input (`a:` was column 4) and `x:` / `  a:` / `  b: 1`'s `.x.a | line` (3, now 2).
- **yq: a block scalar header at its key's own indent is the key's value** (#6386). `a:` / `|` / `  x` is `{"a": "x\n"}` in yq: a `|` or `>` line cannot be a key. It read correctly only by accident of where the empty value was written, and `a:` / `|-` / `  x` / `b: 1` read `{"a": "x", "x": "b"}`; in a sequence item's mapping (`- a:` / `  |` / `    t`) it read `{"a": null}`. All read as yq reads them now.
- **yq: a block scalar header at the indent of an empty `:`, `-` or property-carrying key is that node's value** (#6390, #6386 follow-up). `? a` / `:` / `|` / `  t` read `{"a": null}` and yq reads `{"a": "t\n"}`; `a:` / `  -` / `  |` / `    t` read `{"a": [null, "t\n"]}` (a second, extra item) where yq reads `{"a": ["t\n"]}`; `a:` / `  b: &y` / `  |` / `    t` read `{"a": {"b": null}}`. A `|` or `>` line cannot be a key or an item, so at the indent of the empty node above it is that node's value, as a block sequence is for a key. Four places that tell a null value from one on the next line each had their own test (the explicit value after `:`, a bare dash and a dash with properties, and a key with an anchor or tag); they now share one helper, `Parser::header_at_indent`, with a test that the lookaheads agree. The `-` and `:` owners, with no property, `&y`, `!!str` or both, and `|`, `>`, `|-` or `>+`, 128 documents across 8 owners, agree with yq v4.53.3 on value and verdict, and a sweep of 2,640 documents around them (header indent below, at and above the owner's; with and without a following key or item) fixed 470 and changed none the other way.
- **yaml: a single-quoted key holding an escaped quote and ` # ` no longer makes a block sequence on the next line "follow a completed mapping entry"** (#6392). `- 'a ''b'' # c':` / `  - cell` was refused with `a sequence cannot follow a completed mapping entry` where yq reads `[{"a 'b' # c":["cell"]}]`: the text scan that decides whether the previous line's key still waits for its value took the first `'` of the `''` pair for the closing quote and the ` #` after it for a comment. Found on Playwright MCP accessibility snapshots (`.playwright-mcp/*.yml`), which quote a row's text this way; one such file in about 1,200 of the YAML files on a development machine was refused. Checked against 10,507 YAML files on disk for an accept/reject difference from yq.
- **yq: a line of spaces wider than a block scalar's indent is content, as it is in yq** (#6393). go-yaml eats a block scalar line's spaces only up to the indent column, so a line of spaces alone with more of them than the indent has the extra spaces as its text. `a: |` over `  line1` and a four-space line (the kind an editor leaves behind) is `"line1\n  \n"` in yq; `succinctly yq` called that line blank and answered `"line1\n"`, and `|-` lost the line, `>` and `>-` likewise; the same line first under an explicit indent (`a: |3` over four spaces) was dropped too. A line no wider than the indent is still blank, and `|+` already kept both. The range finder and the folded decoder in `light.rs` now read it so, and its indent detection takes the widest leading blank line as the parser does (#6381), which also fixes a scalar whose widest blank line precedes a `# c` line. Checked against yq v4.53.3 on 3,344 documents (three hosts, eleven headers, eleven trailing-line shapes, explicit indents, end of input and the document root) with no difference, and on 5,500 random block-scalar documents, where the documents that differed in value fell from 116 per 1,500 to 0.
- **yq: a whitespace-only line in the head of a stream prints as a comment, and a head that ends mid-line gets its line break** (#6401). yq hands go-yaml a line of only blanks in the head of the first document, which reads it as a comment and writes `# ` plus the line (`⇥` is `# ⇥`, wherever it sits between comments, a `---` or a `%YAML` line), where `succinctly yq` printed nothing for it; a line of blanks after the first node is dropped by both. A head with no final line break (`%YAML 1.2`, `# c`) is written with one, and a `---` that ends it is followed by an empty line, kept under `-N` where the marker is not. Pinned against yq v4.53.3 in `tests/yq_cli/i6401.rs`; the `-P` route still does not reproduce the `---` and `%YAML` lines of the header.
- **yq: a `%` directive line inside a document, and a `%`, `@` or backtick that starts a plain scalar, are refused as yq refuses them** (#6402). `printf 'a: 1\n%TAG ! x:\n' | succinctly yq .` printed `{"a":1,"%TAG ! x":null}` and yq stops with `did not find expected <document start>`; `!!str` / `%YAML 1.2` read as the string `%YAML 1.2` where yq refuses it, and `a: %x`, `- @x`, `[a, %x]` and a key `%k:` were content too (go-yaml starts no plain scalar on `%`, `@` or a backtick, and reads a `%` at column 0 as a directive wherever it stands). A `%` that continues a plain scalar or stands in a quoted or block scalar is still content, as in yq. Over four draws of 1,500 to 2,000 generated streams, 760 that differed from yq in whether they are refused now agree and none changed the other way. The indented `%YAML` of a stream's head and a directive after a `...` marker still differ (`docs/compliance/yq/limitations.md`).
- **yq: an indented `%YAML` directive before any content is yq's header, not content** (#6408). yq's header slurp trims a line before it looks for `%YA`, so ` %YAML 1.2` (a space or tab before the `%`), in the head of a stream or after its leading `---`, is set aside as a column-0 one is: the stream is a null document, `  %YAML 1.2` / `a: 1` is `{"a":1}`, and the line prints back as a comment, `# ` and the line with its indent (`#  %YAML 1.2`). `succinctly yq` read it as the string `%YAML 1.2` (an error since #6402). Every stream of a 40-row matrix, as JSON and as YAML, now prints what yq prints; a write or `-P` still prints the head's `%YAML` line differently from yq, for a column-0 line as for an indented one (`docs/compliance/yq/limitations.md`), and any other indented directive (`%TAG`, a misspelt `%YAML`) and a `...` after the head are still refused, as in yq.
- **yq: a directive before the first `---` that go-yaml refuses is refused: an unknown or empty name, a malformed or repeated `%TAG`** (#6412). yq's header slurp sets aside only a line that starts `%YAML`; every other directive reaches go-yaml, which wants the name `YAML` or `TAG` and, for `%TAG`, a handle, a prefix and at most a `#` comment, with no handle given twice. `succinctly yq` skipped them all, so `%FOO`, `%`, `%TAG`, `%TAG ! x: y` and a second `%TAG !` before `---` read as a document where yq stops with an error; they are refused now, and `%YAM` and `%YA` (not yq's header) with them. Pinned against yq v4.53.3 in `tests/yq_cli/i6412.rs`, and by `scripts/yq-directive-name-sweep.py` (12,000 random directive streams: none that the build before read as yq does is refused now). The library loader keeps skipping every directive.
- **yq: a properties-only line with no owner, and a `- ` in a flow collection, are refused as yq refuses them** (#6413). A line of node properties (`!!map`, `&a`) in the place of a sibling, level with the keys or items of a block mapping or sequence, was accepted and attached to nothing: `printf 'a: 1\n!!str\n' | succinctly yq .` printed `{"a":1}` where yq stops, and so did `k: |` / `!!map`, `k: !!str` / `&a` and `- a` / `&a`. A `-` followed by a blank inside a flow collection (`[- x]`, `[a, - x]`, `{a: - x}`) was read as the text `- x`; go-yaml refuses it as a block sequence indicator. The properties of a document, of a value and of a key on its own line are read as before. Over five draws of 2,000 generated streams, 474 that differed from yq in whether they are refused now agree and none changed the other way; three YAML Test Suite cases that are invalid YAML (`G9HC`, `GT5M`, `H7J7`) are refused now and leave the known-failures list.
- **yq: a property in front of a block sequence `-` on its line, and a tab after the `-`, are refused as yq refuses them** (#6414, #6379 follow-up). `&t - x`, `- &t - x`, `a: &t - x`, `- !!seq - x` and `? &t - x` are `block sequence entries are not allowed in this context` in yq and were the sequence `["x"]` here (`&t - a: b` was `{"- a": "b"}`, the key `- a`); `-⇥x`, `- ⇥x` and `-⇥# c` are `found character that cannot start any token`, where go-yaml skips no tab in the place of a simple key, and were read as the item. A property on a line of its own above the `-` is read as before, and so is a tab after the item's content. Both checks are made in yq mode only (the library loader reads YAML 1.2's way, and `key: - a` with no property still reads as the sequence, #6355), through one helper that the explicit-key site shares with `parse_sequence_item`. Over 518 generated documents the 409 that differed from yq in whether they are refused now agree, and a sweep of 2,308 valid documents near the rules changed none the other way.
- **yq: a `%YAML` directive outside the head is checked, and a directive after a document's content ends the document** (#6419). yq's header slurp takes a `%YAML` line only in the head of the stream, before any other directive; every other one reaches go-yaml, which accepts `1.1` alone (`found incompatible YAML document` for `1.2`), once for a document, with only blanks and a `#` comment after it, and `succinctly yq` skipped them all. A directive at column 0 where a node would start is not an error either: it closes the document as a `...` does, whatever it held (`!!str` is the empty string, `a:` a null value, a block scalar its text), so `a: 1` / `%TAG !e! w` / `---` / `b: 2` is two documents, as in yq, where #6402's refusal read it as an error; a `---` has to follow, and one is also wanted after a directive that ends the stream after a `...`. 42 streams are pinned against yq v4.53.3 in `tests/yq_cli/i6419.rs`, and `scripts/yq-directive-name-sweep.py` (21,000 random streams) broke none that the build before read as yq does.
- **A regex compile error is worded as in jq** (#6423). `succinctly jq` said `invalid regex: <message>` where jq says `Regex failure: <message>`, which `try test("[") catch .` puts on stdout; the prefix is jq's now. A refusal the `regex` crate's parser makes is given Oniguruma's message instead of the crate's multi-line parse error: an unclosed or unopened group, a reversed repeat range, a group header or name cut short, `\k<name>`/`\g<name>` to a name no group has, and an unknown property name. A repeat count past Oniguruma's 100000 (`x{100001}`) is `too big number for repeat range`, where it was matched, or refused for the crate's size limit. `succinctly yq` keeps Go's wording, as yq does.
- **jq: a loop body with a second exit after its first answers as Oniguruma's does when no way follows it** (#6424). `"bab" | [match("(\\A|a|\\B)+";"g") | .captures[0].string]` printed `["","a",""]` and jq 1.7.1 answers `["","",""]`; `"ba" | [match("(\\B|(?:a|b*)){2,}";"g") | .string]` printed `["ba",""]` and jq answers `["b","",""]`. Oniguruma tries what follows the loop once at a head, at the first exit that holds there, so a second anchor-only way (or a way that matches nothing) with no consuming way after it is the exit every loop ends with, except that it sets the group around the body: the loop now writes it back last among each head's ways, and the first exit only where its anchor holds. The same anchor again (or `\A` and `^`) is never the first to hold and is dropped. Over three draws of 1,500 loops with anchors (`--assert`, seeds 3, 4 and 5) the patterns that differ fall from 91 to 55 and none changed the other way; 433 of 3,744 generated two-anchor loops that differed agree, and none changed. A second exit with a consuming way after it still differs.
- **jq: a loop with a `$` way under `(?m)` answers as Oniguruma's does, and so does one with a `^` way when no way ends a line** (#6425). `"a\nb" | [match("(?m)($|a|\\n|b)*";"g") | .string]` printed `["a\nb",""]` and jq 1.7.1 answers `["a","","b",""]`: under `(?m)` `$` holds before every newline, so the empty iteration that ends Oniguruma's loop was dropped by the `regex` crate, which went on to consume the newline. A way that starts with a newline runs only where `$` holds and any other only where it does not, which tells the two kinds of head apart without a complement of the anchor: the loop is written as the second kind, greedy, then the first, lazy, each leaving through the empty way. A `^` holds again after a newline a way ends with, so only a body no way of which ends one is written, as `\A` is. A way that may start either way (`\s`, `[^b]`), a `^` beside a way that ends a line, a `(?m)` that something switches, and the `n` flag keep their text and differ. Over three draws of 3,000 loops under `(?m)` the patterns that differ fall from 273, 260 and 255 to 235, 229 and 219 and two in all changed the other way, each on a subject that ends with a newline, where `(?m)^` holds here and not in jq (#6456).
- **jq: a loop with capture groups beside a lookaround, an atomic group or a comment answers as Oniguruma's does** (#6426). `"ba" | [match("(?=b)((a|b)|){2,}";"g") | .captures | map(.string)]` printed `[["a","a"]]` and jq 1.7.1 answers `[["","a"]]`, and `"ba" | [match("(?=b|a)((?:(b|)*|a)+)*";"g") | .string]` printed `["ba"]` where jq answers `["b",""]`. The loop and capture rewrites now read such a pattern through the plain copy of it, keep the construct as written, and run the result on `fancy-regex`; a text with a lazy repeat between two greedy repeats of one expression (`b+a*?b*`) is kept off it, because `fancy-regex` 0.20 makes the lazy repeat greedy. Over three draws of 4,000 generated patterns of `scripts/jq-regex-capture-loop-sweep.py --fancy`, 353 patterns that differed from jq now agree (363 differed on seed 3, 10 still do) and none changed the other way; the plain, `--nest`, `--ways`, `--assert`, `--bounded`, `--newlines` and `--flags gx` draws broke none.
- **jq: a lazy `*?` or `+?` over a body with a group, and a loop with groups inside one, answers as Oniguruma does** (#6427). `"bab" | [match("(?:(?:a|(b))+?(?:(a*)|b)+|b)+?";"g") | .string]` printed `["bab"]` and jq 1.7.1 answers `["ba","b"]`: an empty iteration leaves `*?`, and `+?` over a short body is `X X*?`, whose first copy has no empty check. Loops inside a lazy `{0,n}?` or `{1,n}?` follow. Over 4,000 patterns at each of seeds 3 to 6 of `scripts/jq-regex-capture-loop-sweep.py --ways`, 67 to 97 are fixed, 3 to 9 still differ where 69 to 106 did, and no draw broke one.
- **jq: a lazy `{0,n}?` or `{1,n}?` unsets the group of an empty iteration that failed, as Oniguruma does** (#6428). `"ab" | [match("(?:(b*)|a){0,2}?b") | .captures[0].string]` printed `[""]` and jq 1.7.1 answers `[null]`: Oniguruma counts a lazy bounded repeat, and an iteration that matches nothing leaves the count. Over 4,000 patterns at each of seeds 3, 4 and 5 of `scripts/jq-regex-capture-loop-sweep.py`, the new `--bounded` draw fixed 109 to 121 and the `--ways` draw 5 to 7, and no draw broke one.
- **jq: a loop with capture groups answers as Oniguruma's does in a pattern that uses a group name twice** (#6430, part of #6358). `"ba" | [match("(?:(?<n>a)|(?<n>a)|())*";"g")] | .[1].captures | map(.string)` printed `["a",null,null]` and jq 1.7.1 answers `["a",null,""]`: `regex-syntax` refuses a repeated name, so both loop rewrites left the pattern as written and the loop kept the crate's last iteration instead of the empty one. The rewrites now read the pattern with each later use of a name renamed, and report the names as written. Over eight draws of 5,000 generated loops (plain, `--nest`, `--ways`, `--assert`, `--fancy`, and `gx` and `gi`) 18 patterns that differed from jq agree and none changed the other way.
- **Regex refusals #6423 left in the crate's words are now jq's** (#6433). A repeat count past 100000 is `too big number for repeat range` wherever its brace stands, as Oniguruma lexes it: inside a look-around or an atomic group (`(?=a{100001})` was answered `false`), in a brace that never closes (`x{100001`) and with nothing before it (`{100001}`), while an error before the brace still comes first. A call `\g<n>` to a missing group is `undefined group <n> reference`, `\g<0>` and `\g<-1>` before any group `never ending recursion`, and an error after `(?'name'…)` or a reference to a group the pattern has is found (`(?<x>a)\k<x>(` is `end pattern with unmatched parenthesis`). Over 7,500 generated patterns, about a third moved to jq's answer and none moved away from it.
- **An error message whose value preview cuts a multi-byte character writes U+FFFD, as jq does** (#6434). jq cuts the embedded value at 11 bytes (26 for `path()`'s message) and its message then holds one U+FFFD where the partial character was; `succinctly jq` dropped the partial character, so `try (.[]) catch .` on `"abc😀😀😀"` printed `"Cannot iterate over string (\"abc😀...)"` where jq prints `(\"abc😀�...)`. The `succinctly yq` messages that embed a cut value use jq's convention and get it too.
- **jq: a loop with capture groups answers as Oniguruma's does under the `x` flag and a leading `(?x)`** (#6442, part of #6358). `"bab" | [match("(()(?:a|)|(b*))*";"gx") | .string]` printed `["","ab",""]` and jq 1.7.1 answers `["","a","",""]`: the group-copy rewrite stood down for any switch that names `x`, so every such loop kept the `regex` crate's last iteration. The switch now stays in the pattern, which is read from its start with the blanks skipped; a pattern with a `#` keeps its text. Over nine draws of 5,000 loops under `gx` (plain, `--nest`, `--ways`, `--assert`, `--fancy` and `--blanks`, which `scripts/jq-regex-capture-loop-sweep.py` has for this), 95 to 892 patterns that differed from jq agree and none changed the other way; a loop under `x` differs on as many patterns as the same loop without it.
- **yq: an empty plain key is written single-quoted on the streaming route** (#6443). A key that is an empty plain scalar (`&a : 1`, `!!str : 1`, `? ` / `: 1`, `- &a:` as in the Google Cloud SDK's `resources.yaml`) printed as `"": 1` with `.`, where yq writes `'': 1` (go-yaml's emitter cannot leave a simple key empty) and a write already did; an empty plain value (`a: !!str`) and a key the source quoted are unchanged. Found by a differential sweep over 7,398 real YAML files, where it was 4 of the 114 files that differed from yq. Pinned against yq v4.53.3 in `tests/yq_cli/i6443.rs`.
- **yq: a folded scalar that starts with blank lines is written with the blank lines it had** (#6446). The streaming route (`.`) widened the run of breaks a `>` scalar starts with, one empty line too many, which changed the value when read back (`a: >` / blank / blank / `  x`, the value `"\n\nx\n"`, came out with a third blank line), and a `>+` of nothing but blank lines gained a trailing one. go-yaml's folded writer widens nothing for a string that starts with a break and adds no trailing extra to a value of only breaks; the write route (`.zzkey = 1`, `-P`, `-i`) already agreed with yq. Over a fuzz of random folded scalars every document whose yq output reads back as the same value is now byte-identical to yq on `.`. A break beside a more-indented line keeps the lossless spelling ADR-0018 and #836 chose, where yq adds an empty line that changes the value. Pinned against yq v4.53.3 in `tests/yq_cli/i6446.rs`.
- **jq: after a depth-limit refusal inside an object, the next parse error `input` raises is placed where jq places it** (#6454).
  For `{` followed by 300 `[`, a newline and `"k": 1}`, `try ([inputs]|length) catch .` reported the
  second fault `at line 3, column 4`, counting the rest of the refused line and its newline, which jq
  drops without counting; it now reports jq 1.7.1's `at line 2, column 261`. The refusal itself, and a
  refusal outside an object, were already right.
- **jq: a fault a later chunk meets at the very end of the input is placed as jq places it** (#6455).
  Where the stream's last file ran past its first 64 KiB and ended in a number straight before an
  opener (`... 5[`), `input`/`inputs` reported `(at file:N)` for the `Unfinished JSON term at EOF`
  error; jq 1.7.1 reports `(at <unknown>)`, since that number completes in the read that reaches the
  end (#6004). The lazy route's handoff to the eager reader now knows the file ends the stream.
- **jq: a `^` under `(?m)` does not hold at the end of a text that ends with a newline, as in Oniguruma** (#6456). `"a\n" | [match("(?m)^";"g") | .offset]` printed `[0,2]` and jq 1.7.1 answers `[0]`; `"a\nb\n" | gsub("(?m)^";"> ")` ended with a stray `"> "`; `"a\n" | test("(?m)\n^")` was `true` and is `false`. The `regex` crate's `^` holds after any newline. A match of the crate that ends at the end of such a text is now asked of `fancy-regex`, with each multi-line `^` written as `(?:\A|^(?!\z))`; a match that ends before the end of the text cannot have used it and is kept. Of 333 subject and pattern pairs 159 differed before and none do.
- **jq: a lazy repeat between two greedy repeats of one expression stays lazy on the `fancy-regex` route** (#6460). `"bab" | [match("(?=b)b+a*?b*";"g") | .string]` printed `["bab"]` and jq 1.7.1 answers `["b","b"]`: `fancy-regex` 0.20 merges `X+ M*? X*` into `X+(?:M+?X*)?`, which makes the lazy repeat greedy. A lazy repeat that can match nothing is written as `(?:M*?|(?!))` there, which the optimizer does not merge and which means the same. Only the lazy repeat in the shape is written so, and the extended mode is read when the leading switches turn it on. Over 3,584 generated patterns of that shape (`scripts/jq-regex-capture-loop-sweep.py --lazyrun`: `+`/`*` on both sides, 4 lazy forms, 7 atoms, under a lookaround, a repeat or a group), 1,675 that differed from jq agree, under `g` and `gx`, and none changed the other way.
- **jq: `-n` with `input_line_number` no longer opens the input files** (#6464). `jq -n input_line_number missing.json` printed `jq: error: Could not open file missing.json` and exited 2 where jq 1.7.1 prints `0` and exits 0: only `input` and `inputs` ask jq for a file, and `input_line_number` reads the position of whatever was read. `-n` with `input`/`inputs` is unchanged.
- **jq: `-R` stops after the first line past a missing file, as jq's main loop does** (#6464). `jq -R . missing.txt lines.txt` printed every line of `lines.txt` and jq 1.7.1 prints the first (`"line1"`), the same rule JSON documents already followed (#5472): once the reader has read from a file past one that did not open, the value that took it there is processed and the loop ends. `jq -R . lines.txt missing.txt lines.txt` prints up to the first line of the second `lines.txt`, joined to the last line of the first as jq does.
- **jq: a depth-limit refusal after an invalid UTF-8 byte is placed at jq's column** (#6465).
  For `{"\xff":` followed by 300 `[`, a newline and `}`, `succinctly jq` named the refusal at column
  262, counting each invalid byte as the three bytes of the U+FFFD it is replaced by; it now names
  jq 1.7.1's column 260, under `input`/`inputs` and in the main loop alike, and the fault after it
  under `input` is placed from there as #6454 places it. An invalid byte in an earlier document on
  the same line is counted the same way.
- **jq: a lazy repeat that keeps its text no longer costs the pattern's other lazy repeats their write-out** (#6469). A pattern is read again at the next reading only for the lazy repeat it gave up inside, so `"aac" | [match("(?:^x*|(?:(y*)|x)+(?:(y)|x?){0,2})*?(?:(?:(b*)|a){0,2}?)*?c";"g") | .captures | map(.string)]` is `[[null,null,null]]`, as in jq 1.7.1, where the last group was `""`.
- **jq: a directory given as an input file is a read error, as in jq, not an open error** (#6472). `jq . adir nums.json` printed `jq: error: Could not open file adir: Is a directory` and jq 1.7.1 prints `jq: error: Is a directory`; `jq -n input adir` named `<stdin>` in `jq: error (at <stdin>:0): break` where jq names `adir`; `jq -s . adir` printed the open error beside `[]` where jq prints no message. `fopen` succeeds on a directory and the first read fails, so the directory is a source with no bytes, and jq's reader says so when it moves on to the next file: once for each directory that a file follows, before that file, and not at all for the last. The exit status is 2 either way. A directory is an input file that opened, so `input_filename` names it and the run stops after the next value, as it does after a file that would not open. The `-R`, `--stream`, `-s` and chunked routes agree on 17 rows captured from jq 1.7.1; the rows where the program stops reading before it reaches the file (`jq -n 'input' nums.json adir`) still report it early, as a missing file does.
- **jq: a loop whose body has two or more ways that match nothing only where an anchor holds leaves where Oniguruma does** (#6473).
  A second exit with a consuming way after it, three or more exits, and a way that holds an anchor
  beside an item that may match nothing (`\Aa*`, `\B(\w*)`) are now written way by way, each kind of
  loop head (`\b` or `\B`, and `\A` at the first head) behind its own anchors: `"a b" |
  [match("(\\Aa*|\\B){2,}?";"g") | .string]` is `[""]`, as in jq 1.7.1, where it was `["a"]`. Over three
  draws of 1,500 anchored loops the patterns that differ from jq fall from 55 to 24, almost all of the
  rest a loop with a capture group in a pattern holding `$` or `\z`, whose groups the `fancy-regex`
  route does not copy.
- **jq: under `-n`, `input` no longer reports a file it never reaches** (#6475). `jq -n input nums.json missing` printed the first value of `nums.json`, then `jq: error: Could not open file missing: No such file or directory`, and exited 2; jq 1.7.1 prints the value and exits 0, because its reader opens a file only when it has read the one before and asks for more. Each file that will not open (or is a directory, #6472) is now said when a read of the `input` queue reaches it, or finds the stream at its end, before that read returns, and fails the run then: `jq -n '[input,input,input,input]' nums.json missing b.json` reports it on the fourth read, and `jq -n '[inputs]' nums.json missing` at the end. The queue has a read hook for it. The rows pinned in `tests/jq_cli/i6475.rs` were captured from jq 1.7.1. A file whose last value is a bare number or literal with no newline after it (`printf 1`) completes only at its end, which sends jq's reader on to the next file (past any empty ones), so a failure after it is still reported up front, as is the chunked `--stream` walk's.
- **jq: a text that ends inside a value, then a file that does not open, reports the open error first and exits 2** (#6476). `jq . t1.json missing` with `t1.json` holding `[1,` printed only `jq: parse error: Unfinished JSON term at EOF ...` and exited 5; jq 1.7.1 prints `jq: error: Could not open file missing: ...` and then the parse error, and exits 2, as it does whenever an input file failed. jq's reader moves on to the file after the last one that opened before its parser meets the end-of-text fault, so the open errors of the files past it come first; a fault in the middle of the text still stops the run before them. Under `-s` the open error was already printed but the run exited 5. Pinned over `.`, `-c`, `-s`, `--stream` and `--seq` against jq 1.7.1 in `tests/jq_cli/i6476.rs`. A directory as the last file gives the same, with #6472's message left out.
- **jq: under `-n`, a text that ends inside a value reports the files after it that did not open** (#6480). `jq -n '[inputs]|length' t1.json missing` with `t1.json` holding `[1,` printed only the parse error and exited 5, and `jq -n 'try input catch "c"' t1.json missing` printed `"c"` and exited 0: since #6475 a missing file is reported when a read reaches it, and the read of the fault at the end of the text was taken to stop in `t1.json`. jq 1.7.1 prints `jq: error: Could not open file missing: ...` before the fault and exits 2, because its parser asks the reader for more before it gives up on `[1,`, which opens the next file. The read of that fault now reports every pending failure, when the text's first fault is at its end; the reads before it do not, so `jq -n input small.json missing` over `1 5[` still prints `1` and exits 0. A directory last makes the run exit 2 the same way. The fault's `(at ...)` marker names the missing file, line 0, as jq's does. Pinned over 18 rows against jq 1.7.1 in `tests/jq_cli/i6480.rs`.
- **jq: once the input is read to its end, `input_filename`, `input_line_number` and an error's `(at ...)` name a last file that did not open** (#6480). jq's reader ends at the last file named, so after `[inputs]` over `ok.json missing`, `input_filename` is `"missing"`, `input_line_number` is 0, and `error` says `(at missing:0)`; succinctly named `ok.json` at its line count, `null` after a value that ended on its own closing byte, `<stdin>` when no file opened, and `<unknown>` after `-s`. The missing file is now a source of its own past the ones that opened, on the `-n` routes (the lazy ones that read several files, or one a chunk at a time, included), `-s`, `-sR` and `--seq`, and every read past the end stays there: `[inputs], (try input catch .), input_filename` names it, where the second read used to give `null`. Only the last name matters: an empty file or a directory after it is where the reader ends. A value whose read completes at the end of the input, a fault at the end of the text, and the `--stream` and `--stream-errors` readers still name the last file that opened. Pinned over 32 rows against jq 1.7.1 in `tests/jq_cli/i6480_end.rs`.
- **jq: a last value that completes only at the end of the input is read at a last file that did not open** (#6480). jq's parser asks for more before a bare number or literal in the last bytes is complete, which sends its reader past the last file: `jq -c '[., input_filename, input_line_number]' nonl.json missing` over `1\n2` gives `[1,"nonl.json",1]` and then `[2,"missing",0]`, and `jq -c error num.json missing` over `12` prints the open error before `jq: error (at missing:0)`. succinctly named the last file that opened, at its line count, and said the open error after the last value's error. The last value is now placed at the missing file on the main loop, the `input` queue (eager and lazy, a file scanned a chunk at a time included) and `-R`'s lines when the last has no newline; under `-n` the read of that value reports the open error, so `jq -n input nonl.json missing` reads `1` and exits 0 rather than reporting the file up front. A string or container that ends on its own closing byte, and a value before white space, keep their file. `-R` without `input`, and a main loop whose program reads `input` or `input_line_number`, still report the file before the values. Pinned over 42 rows against jq 1.7.1 in `tests/jq_cli/i6480_last_value.rs`.
- **jq: a fault at the end of the text that `input` raises is raised at a last file that did not open** (#6480). `jq -n '[inputs]|length' t1.json missing` with `t1.json` holding `[1,` said `jq: error (at t1.json:0): Unfinished JSON term at EOF at line 1, column 3`; jq 1.7.1 says `(at missing:0)`, because its parser asks the reader past the last file before it gives up. When the text's first fault is at its end, the queue now raises it at the missing file, line 0, on the eager and lazy routes (a file scanned a chunk at a time, and one deeper than the lazy route reads, included), under `-n`, `-n -s`, and for an `input` the program reads without `-n` (`jq -c '[., input]' b.json missing`). The message keeps its own line and column. A fault earlier in the text, or a missing file before the last that opened, keeps the fault's file. Pinned over 24 rows against jq 1.7.1 in `tests/jq_cli/i6480_eof_fault.rs`, and `tests/jq_cli/i6480.rs` no longer masks the marker.
- **jq: a slurped `--stream` or `--seq` input that ends in a fault prints no array when a file did not open** (#6481). `jq -c -s --stream . t1.json missing` with `t1.json` holding `[1,` printed `[[[0],1]]` and jq 1.7.1 prints nothing, with the same two stderr lines and exit 2; `-s --seq` printed `[]` (or the records it had read) and `--seq --stream -s` the events, where jq prints nothing. jq's reader moves on to the file that did not open in the call that consumes the last byte, so the fault is that call's result, and its main loop reads no further once a file has failed, so the array is never read. A clean stream, or a file that did not open ahead of a stream with no fault, still prints its array. Pinned over 21 rows against jq 1.7.1 in `tests/jq_cli/i6481.rs`.
- **jq: under `-s`, a file that does not open after a fault in the text is not reported, and the run exits 5** (#6485). `jq -c -s . bad.json missing` with `bad.json` holding `[1,}` printed `jq: error: Could not open file missing: ...` before the parse error and exited 2; jq 1.7.1 prints the parse error alone and exits 5, because its parser stops the main loop at the fault before its reader opens the next file. The same holds for `-s --stream`. jq reports a file when its reader reaches it, so a failure before the file the fault is in is still reported first, and so is one after a fault at the end of the text (#6476). The `--stream` routes that read a file a chunk at a time (without `-s`) still report every failure up front. Pinned over 22 rows against jq 1.7.1 in `tests/jq_cli/i6485.rs`.
- **jq: under `-s --stream`, a fault read after the array is not reported when a file failed to open before it** (#6485). `jq -c -s --stream . missing t1.json` with `t1.json` holding `[1,` printed `[[[0],1]]`, the open error and then `jq: parse error: Unfinished JSON term at EOF ...`; jq 1.7.1 prints the array and the open error only, because its main loop makes no further call once a file has failed, and the fault is read by a call after the array. Pinned over 8 rows against jq 1.7.1 in `tests/jq_cli/i6485_after_array.rs`. `--stream` without `-s`, which reads a file a chunk at a time, still reports every failure when the file is opened.
- **jq: `--stream` reports a file that does not open when its reader reaches it, not when the run starts** (#6485). `jq -c --stream . bad.json missing` with `bad.json` holding `[1,}` printed the open error first and exited 2; jq 1.7.1 prints the first event and the parse error and exits 5, because its reader stops at the fault and never opens the file after it. A second missing file after the value that follows the first failure (`nums.json missing mid.json missing`) is no longer reported either, as in jq, whose main loop reads no further once a file has failed. The same holds under `-n --stream` with `input`/`inputs`. A last file that did not open is a source of its own, so a number at the end of the file before it waits for the read that opens it (`-n --stream input a1 gone`), and a directory last fails the run when the reader reaches it. Pinned over 30 rows against jq 1.7.1 in `tests/jq_cli/i6485_chunked_stream.rs`. `--stream-errors` without `-n`, `-R`, `--seq` and DSV, which read every file first, still report every failure up front.
- **jq: a loop with capture groups in a pattern with `\z` or a `$` before its end answers as jq does** (#6488).
  Such a pattern runs on the `fancy-regex` route that reads `$` exactly, which only had the plain
  loop rewrite: that rewrite keeps a loop as written when it would copy a group, so
  `"ba b" | [match("(?:$\\z|\\B(\\w*)){2,}";"g") | .string]` was `["a",""]` where jq 1.7.1's is
  `["",""]`. The capture and group-copies rewrites now run there too, for a pattern nothing in which
  can match a newline (the rewrites read `$` as the end of the text) and with no group that holds
  only an anchor (#6492). A rewrite holding a shape `fancy-regex` merges wrongly keeps the pattern
  as it was, and a search whose copies exhaust the backtracking budget is answered by the pattern as
  written. `scripts/jq-regex-capture-loop-sweep.py` fixes 3 to 11 patterns in 4,000 per `--assert`
  seed and 11 to 22 per `--bounded` seed, under the `g`, `gi` and `gx` flags, and breaks none.
- **yq: an explicit indentation indicator on a block scalar header below a compact key with a property is measured from the key's mapping** (#6490). `printf -- '- k: &y\n  >2\n    t\n' | succinctly yq -o=json -I=0 .` printed `[{"k":"  t\n"}]` and yq v4.53.3 answers `[{"k":"t\n"}]`: the value side read the dash's column for `- k: &y` (its line does not end in the colon, so the key was not recognised as deferring its value), and only the first dash of `- - k:`. Over 400 documents (compact key with no property, `&y`, `!!str`, both, or a comment; five headers; four indents; the key under a mapping, behind two dashes or behind an anchored dash) every one that yq reads now gives its value here; a header at the column of a nested dash (`a:` / `  - - k:` / `    |`), which yq refuses and succinctly reads, is the one difference left (#6540).
- **jq: a capture group that holds only a zero-width anchor, after a nullable item in the same way, is set by the copy of the way that consumes text** (#6492). `"abc" | [match("(?:(a)|(\\w*)(\\z)){2,3}?";"g") | .captures | map(.string)]` gave `["a","bc",null]` for the first match and jq 1.7.1 gives `["a","bc",""]`: the group-copies rewrite wrote the consuming copy of `(\w*)(\z)` from the anchor's own text, `(\w+)\z`, which dropped the group around it. The copy is now written from the text of the item, group included. The issue called it latent, because the fancy-regex route it was found on does not run the rewrite; the plain route does. A grid of 1,890 patterns (7 nullable items, 9 anchor spellings, 3 other ways, 10 quantifiers) over 7 strings fixed 130 and changed none the other way, and the `--assert`, `--bounded`, `--ways`, `--nest`, `--fancy`, `--newlines` and `gx`/`gi` sweeps broke none.
- **yq: a mapping key that is a collection is written as the key node** (#6496). `printf -- '? - p\n: v\n' | succinctly yq .` printed `"": v` and yq v4.53.3 prints `? - p` / `: v`: the writer wrote the text of the key (empty) though the index held the node. A sequence, a block mapping and a flow collection key are written after `? ` with their lines one indent step in (`-I=4` too), the value after it on the `:` line, and an empty `[]` or `{}` key is the simple key `[]: v`. A compact collection inside such a key lost every item after the first of the one it opened (`? - - p` / `    - q` printed `? - - p`): the parser closed the key's first item behind the container its value had opened, which is now a frame of its own as an ordinary sequence item is. An anchor or tag on the key is kept (`? &a` on a line of its own before a block collection, `? &a [p, q]` before a flow one). Over 35 documents (the keys above, nested, among other entries, in a sequence, with values of every kind) at `-I=2` and `-I=4`, 70 outputs, every one is yq's. `-P`, `keys`, `to_entries`, `sort_keys`, `$x` and `[.]` still write `""` (#6547).
- **jq: a `(?m)` `^` inside a look-around or atomic group no longer holds at the end of a text after a final newline** (#6502).
  #6456 wrote each multi-line `^` as Oniguruma reads it, but only where `regex-syntax` could parse
  the pattern, which a look-around is not: `"a\n" | [match("(?m)(?<!^)";"g") | .offset]` was `[1]`
  where jq 1.7.1's is `[1,2]`. The pattern is now read through its plain copy, which holds the `^`
  at the same offset; that reading is shared with the group-copies rewrite (#6426). A differential
  of 1,500 `(?m)` look-around patterns on 8 subjects per seed, against `main`, fixes 83-94 and breaks none.

Separately, the `Unfinished JSON term at EOF` event of a text whose last file did not open is read at that file, line 0, so `input_filename` names it where it named `null`. Swept against jq 1.7.1 over 10 programs and 359 file lists of complete, half-read, empty, BOM-led and missing files, 3590 runs: 95 differ where 210 did, and none the other way; `--stream-errors -s`, `--stream` and `--seq --stream-errors` are unchanged. The `--seq` rows of the issue (items 3 and 4) are left to #6603 and #6609. A 3762-run matrix of first files cut inside every kind of token against next files that continue them agrees with `main` everywhere. Pinned over 19 rows in `tests/jq_cli/i6591.rs`.
- **jq: `--seq --stream` prints a record's parse-error warning before the open failure that follows its file, and not at all after the value that took the reader past a failure** (#6591). `jq -c --seq --stream . bad.seq missing` with `bad.seq` holding `\x1e1\n\x1e{"a\n\x1e2\n` printed `Could not open file missing` before `ignoring parse error: Truncated value at line 3, column 1`, and `jq -c --seq --stream . missing bad.seq` printed the warning although jq's main loop stops after the first event past the failure and never reads the fault. A plain run (no `-n`, no `-s`, a program that reads no `input`) now holds the failures it reports and prints each one before the first warning met in its own file or later, and drops a warning met reading any value after the one that took the reader past the first failure, as `--seq -s` did since #6603. Swept against jq 1.7.1 over 6 programs, with and without `-n`, and 819 file lists of up to three of nine `--seq` fixtures (complete, cut, faulted, missing), 9828 runs: `--seq --stream` differs in 154 where 292 did, and none the other way; `--stream`, `--stream-errors` and `--seq --stream-errors` are unchanged. What is left of that sweep is item 4: after a file whose last record is a top-level container with no newline (`\x1e[1]`), jq reads the closing event at the first missing file after it (`input_filename` names it) and stops there, so a later failure is not reported and a later file is not read; the pseudo-source that needs in the middle of a file list is the follow-up. Pinned over 15 rows in `tests/jq_cli/i6591.rs`.

The key branch's own lookahead had recorded the comment lines as pending, so the shared routine that places them counted them as lines above the dash. Across 450 shapes (a key, a nested key and a value's dash x five bodies x one or two comment lines x comment columns 0-4 x three indents) the output differs from yq in 0, where it was 240; a scalar below the comment (`? # c` / `  - x`) is unchanged.

- **jq: `--seq -s -n` beside a file that does not open places the failure where the program's `input` reaches it, and each fault in the file it was met in** (#6599). `--seq -s -n input bad.json gone.json`, with a record cut short in `bad.json`, reported `gone.json` up front, named it in the fault's location (`gone.json:3`) and exited 2; it now prints only the fault at `bad.json:3` and exits 5, as jq 1.7.1 does, since the fault stops the program before the reader gets to the missing file. All three now agree with jq at 255, 256 and 257 nested arrays. An object chain reaches jq's ceiling at about 128 deep (each key takes a second slot of its parser's stack), where it agreed already. A last value that completes only at the end of its file (`1` with no newline) reads on into the directory, so the program's next read now prints `jq: error: Is a directory` (`jq -c --stream input p.json dir`, `jq -n --stream '[inputs]' p.json dir`), and so does a read after the one that found the stream at its end. A plain `--stream .` and a `-n` program that stops before either never say it, as jq's main loop reads no more once a read has failed. Before, the chunked stream reader counted the directory (exit 2) and never printed it.

The slurp joins the documents into one array before it is indexed, so the position was gone; the files are now read again as one stream to place it, as the slurp's other parse errors already were (#5576). Only regular files are read again: a named pipe, a socket or a device gives its bytes once, and opening it again waited for a writer for good (`jq -sc length fifo` hung on any slurp fault); those keep the message without the position. Standard input cannot be read again, so a well-formed deep document read from it keeps the message without the position, which `limitations.md` now says; a deep document with a fault the splitter stops at is placed from stdin too. Pinned over 54 rows in `tests/jq_cli/i6631.rs`; the 14 tests that pinned the old refusal now pin jq's answer.

A text of 129 to 256 nested arrays was refused (`invalid JSON text passed to --argjson`), because the validator they went through stopped at 128 containers; jq's ceiling is its parser's stack of 256 entries. - **jq: `--seq --stream` and `--stream-errors` stop reporting open failures after a held-back closing event** (#6646). When the last file before a missing one ends in a container whose closer follows a scalar and has no byte after it (`\x1e[1]`, `\x1e{"a":1}`), jq's parser holds the closer's event until the next read, which is the open of the missing file, and its main loop ends there: a later missing file is not reported. succinctly reported all of them. Text where the closer follows a container, nothing, or has a byte after it, or that is not one well-formed value, keeps every failure. Where the closing event is placed (`input_filename`), and the programs that read `input` (`first(inputs)`), are not changed.

A failed file in the middle is now an empty source, as a directory was, and a directory in the middle is the read the loop stops at: it counts, and says nothing. A file between the held-back closer and the failure, even an empty one, takes that read, so `--seq --stream . arr.seq empty.json gone gone2` reports both failures again (the shape #6654 lost). Over a sweep of 22,128 file lists of up to three files and 29,520 of up to four (6 programs), 420 of 428 and 1,076 of 1,385 rows that differed from jq 1.7.1 now match, and none that matched changed; the rest report a later failure after a bare last number (#6708). `--seq --stream` and `--seq --stream-errors` over 46,800 lists each: 12 rows fixed, none regressed.

- **`succinctly jq --stream-errors` reports every directory at the end of the file list, as jq does** (#6661). A 15,840-row differential against jq 1.7.1 (fault texts behind and between files, 11 programs, `-n` and plain) left 144 rows fixed, 0 changed for the worse and none different from jq.
- **jq: `--stream` stops at the failed open that follows a held-back closing event** (#6680). When the last file before a missing file or a directory ends in a container whose closer follows a scalar and has no byte after it (`[1,2]`, `{"a":1}`), jq's parser holds the closer's event until the next read, which is the open of the failed file, and its main loop ends there: a failure after it is not reported and a file after it is not read (`jq -c -n --stream '[inputs]' arr.json missing.json dir` says nothing of `dir`; `jq -c --stream . arr.json dir other.json` never reads `other.json`). The chunked `--stream` reader, and `-n --stream-errors`, treated a failed file in the middle of the list as no read at all, put the closer in the file it came from, read on and reported the directory. A failed file in the middle is now an empty source of its own, as a directory already was, and a directory's failure is placed at its own read. Over a sweep of 22,128 file lists of up to three files and 29,520 of up to four (6 programs, with and without `-n`), the 308 and 706 rows that differed from jq 1.7.1 now match, and none that matched changed. `--stream-errors` without `-n`, which reads through the in-memory route, is not changed (#6646).
- **`succinctly jq --stream-errors` no longer reports files behind the value a halting program stops at** (#6683). With a program that does not read `input` (`jq --stream-errors halt_error a.json dir`), a directory given last was counted, and a file that would not open reported, before the first value ran, so `halt` exited 2 where jq keeps its own status (0, 5, `halt_error(3)`'s 3) and `Could not open file` printed where jq says nothing. They are now placed by the loop's reads, as `-R` and `--input-dsv` do (#6531, #6585): a first value that completes inside its file never reads past it, and one that needs the next file to end (a bare number with no newline) still reaches the failure on that read. A file with bytes behind the first failure no longer sends a halting program up front either: the loop reads one value, which is whole in its own file, and halts before it reaches anything (`jq -c --stream-errors halt_error pn.json dir p.json gone.json` prints `[[],1]` and exits 5). A program that goes on reading (`.`, `[inputs]`) reaches the rest, as before. A 35,090-row differential against jq 1.7.1 (11 flag sets, 10 programs, lists of up to four files with a directory and missing files) left 1,284 rows fixed and none changed for the worse; 180 rows are still apart (`--stream-errors` with a program that reads `input`, and `1 2` as a first file, #6732).
- **`succinctly jq` exits 2 when a halt follows a last value read on into a directory given last** (#6683). With plain JSON (`jq halt_error p.json dir`, `p.json` holding `1` with no newline) the bare number is read on into the directory, which counts the failure as it does for a missing last file, so `halt`, `halt_error` and `halt_error(3)` exit 2 as jq does, where they kept their own status (0, 5, 3).
- **`succinctly jq`'s `tz` prints Australian daylight time as `+11:00`** (#6690). `tz("AEDT")`, `tz("Australia/Sydney")` and `tz("Australia/Melbourne")` in daylight time added `13600` seconds, a typo for eleven hours, so `1700000000 | tz("Australia/Sydney")` printed `2023-11-15T02:00:00+03:46` where Sydney is `2023-11-15T09:13:20+11:00` (`succinctly yq` already printed that, from the zone database). Pinned for `AEDT`, both cities, in daylight and standard time, and the other Australian names beside them. Which days around the two transitions count as daylight time is still the approximate day-of-month rule of `is_dst_australia`, unchanged.
- **yq: a space inside a quoted dotted name (`."a b"`) is a lexer error, as in yq** (#6699).
  yq's path-element token takes the opening quote of a dotted name and stops at the first space, so `."a b"` is `."a` followed by
  text no rule takes (`lexer: invalid input text "b\""`); `succinctly yq` read it as the key `a b`, in a read, as a write target and
  under `del()`. It now refuses it wherever the step appears, and reads every other quoted name (a tab, a newline, any
  punctuation) as before. `.""` is the key of two quote characters, as in yq (`.""` reads `null` over a document whose key is `""`,
  `.x."" = 9` creates it). `.["a b"]` still reads a key with a space, and `succinctly jq` is unchanged. Checked against yq v4.53.3
  over 70 runs of 35 programs.
- **`succinctly jq -s --seq --stream` keeps the slurped array, and says no warning, when a stream ending in an unfinished term follows a file that did not open** (#6700). `jq -c -s --seq --stream . missing.json endf.seq` (`endf.seq` = `\x1e1\n\x1e[1,`) prints `\x1e[[[],1],[[0],1]]` and only `Could not open file`: jq reads the stream through to its end before the failure is met again, so the `Unfinished JSON term at EOF` warning is never said. succinctly printed that warning and lost the array. A failure after that file (#6481), no failure, and a stream ending on an RS are unchanged.
- **yq: `-o` defaults to `auto`, so a `.json` file prints JSON, as in yq** (#6703).
  yq's `--output-format` defaults to `auto` (the run's own input format, picked once from the first file's extension),
  so `yq '.b' data.json` prints JSON; `succinctly yq` defaulted to `yaml` and printed YAML, which broke a script that piped a JSON
  file through `yq` and read the result as JSON, and made `yq -i '.x = 1' data.json` rewrite the JSON file as YAML. The default is now `auto`: a `.json` file prints JSON (`-I`, `-P`, `-r`, `-N`,
  writes and several files included), and standard input, `.yaml`, `.yml`, any other name, `-n`, `-R`, `--front-matter` and an
  explicit `-p` keep YAML. An explicit `-o=yaml` still prints YAML for a JSON file. A mixed `--slurp -o=auto` over a YAML and a
  JSON file now keeps the JSON mapping's flow style as yq does (#1493's recorded gap). Checked against yq v4.53.3 over 32 runs.
- **yq: a flag after the file name is a flag, as in yq** (#6705).
  yq reads a flag wherever it appears, so `yq '.a' f.yaml -o=json`, `yq '.a = 1' f.yaml -i`, `-r`, `-I=4`, `-N`, `-e` and `-P` after the
  file all work; `succinctly yq` declared its `files` argument with `trailing_var_arg`, which made every word after the first file a file
  and failed with `failed to read file: -o=json` (`succinctly jq` had dropped it for the same reason, #3447). Checked against yq
  v4.53.3 over 37 command lines (flags before, between and after the filter and files, several files, `-o json`, `--indent 4`,
  `--output-format json`); the four that still differ do not depend on where the flag is (`-n` with a file, `-` as a filter,
  `--unwrapScalar=false`).
- **`succinctly jq` stops reporting open failures at the first one its reads reach when a program reads `input` without `-n`, and the first file ends in a bare number or literal** (#6708). `jq -c input one.json missing.json s.json missing2.json` (`one.json` = `1`, `s.json` = `"a"` and a newline) says `Could not open file missing.json` and prints `"a"`: the bare `1` is complete only once jq's reader has gone on into the next file, the main loop reads no further input after that, and `missing2.json` is never opened. succinctly said both up front. A program that reads on (`[inputs]`) still says both. A 45,612-row differential against jq 1.7.1 (flags, programs, and lists of up to five files with one or two missing) left 168 plain rows fixed and none changed for the worse; the rows still apart are the `--stream` closing-event shapes of #6646 and #6680 and a faulting first file ahead of two failures.
- **`succinctly jq` reports a file that did not open behind the last value of a text that faulted earlier, when a program reads `input` (#6712).** `jq -c input flt.json missing.json str.json missing2.json` (`flt.json` = `1 }`, `str.json` = `"a" 12`) says `Unmatched '}'`, `Could not open file missing.json` and `Could not open file missing2.json`, then prints `12`: the bare `12` completes only when jq's reader has gone on past the last file that opened, so the read of it meets `missing2.json`. succinctly placed that value at its own file when the text had a fault, and never said `missing2.json`. The same holds for `first(inputs)`, `[., input]` and `-n`. A program that does not read `input` (`.`) is unchanged, as is a fault after the last value. A 45,612-row differential against jq 1.7.1 left 4 rows fixed and none changed for the worse.
- **yq: a write over the node it reads keeps the source's alias** (#6716). `.b = [.b]` over `b: *x` printed `- 1` where yq prints `- *x`, and `.b = .b[-1]` over `b: [0, *x]` dropped the alias the same way, because the alias pass read the right side from the tree the write had already replaced. The first write of a chain now reads it from the document as it came in; later stages still read what the earlier ones wrote. A 85-row sweep against yq matched 17 more rows and regressed none.
- **yq: `path`, `key` and `parent` of a value a `<<` merge lists name its anchor's location** (#6723). With `a: &a {x: 1}` and `item: {<<: *a, k: 0}`, `.item.x | path` is `["a","x"]` in yq and was `["item","x"]` here; `[.item | .[] | path]` was `[["item","x"],["item","k"]]` where yq gives `[["a","x"],["item","k"]]`, and `key` and `parent` followed (`.item.x | parent` is the anchor's mapping). The path-context walk now starts its trail over at the member's real location, and a step taken from it carries on from there (`.item.x.p | path` is `["a","x","p"]`). A write through the same path still changes the mapping's own entry, where yq changes the shared anchor's. Measured over 256 rows (8 documents of merge shapes x 21 reads and 11 writes) against yq v4.53.3: 28 got right, 0 got worse, and every write row is unchanged.
- **`succinctly jq -s --stream` and `-s --stream-errors` name a last file that does not open, line 0, as jq does** (#6724). `jq -c -s --stream-errors '[., input_filename]' two.json missing.json` printed `"two.json"` and `jq -c -s --stream '[., input_line_number]' nors.json missing.json` printed the line of the file before the missing one; both now read the array at the failed file, as jq does (`"missing.json"`, line 0), and the same file is named in `error (at missing.json:0)`. A closing event held back at the end of the file before it, and an `input` read after the array, follow the same source (#6676 did it for `--seq`).
- **jq: `--seq --stream` and `--seq --stream-errors` reach a stream's warnings and a file's open failure as jq's main loop does** (#6725). Without `-n` and `-s`, these said every warning and every file that did not open before the program ran, so a program that halted or raised an error on an early value came after them, and exited 2 where jq 1.7.1 exits 0 or 5 because it never reaches the failure (`jq -c --seq --stream-errors halt arr missing` now exits 0 and says nothing). The stream's faults now wait for the main loop to pop them, as `--seq` already did for the record reader (#6147), and a failure is said when a read reaches the file. A file that did not open in the middle of the list is an empty read, so the closing event a file ending in `[1]` holds back is read at it (`error (at gone:0)`), and a directory whose read delivers that event fails the run with exit status 2 and no message. Over 1,260 file lists of up to three files per flag set, the 642 (`--seq --stream`) and 682 (`--seq --stream-errors`) rows of `halt`, `halt_error` and `error("x")` that differed from jq now match, as do 143 and 87 rows of the programs that read `input`, with and without `-n`; no row that matched changed.
- **jq: `@urid` follows jq 1.8.2 for a non-string, bytes that are not valid UTF-8 and its error text** (#6726).
  `succinctly jq` decoded valid input as jq 1.8.2 does and differed on the rest: a non-string raised `expected string, got number` where jq stringifies it first (`1 | @urid` is `"1"`, `["%41"] | @urid` is `"[\"A\"]"`), escapes that decode to bytes that are not valid UTF-8 (`%E4`, `%FF%FE`, `a%E4b`, an overlong form, a surrogate) printed U+FFFD where jq raises, and a malformed escape reported `invalid URL escape "%"` (yq's wording) where jq names the whole input, `string ("%") is not a valid uri encoding`, truncating a dump over 29 bytes to its first 25, `...` and the closing quote. All three now match a jq 1.8.2 binary on 172 rows (4 programs over 43 inputs) and a 1,500-input sweep that weights the inputs towards bad bytes. `succinctly yq` is unchanged (`url.QueryUnescape`: it stringifies a scalar, reads `+` as a space, raises its own `invalid URL escape`, substitutes U+FFFD), and `format("urid")` keeps jq 1.7.1's `urid is not a valid format`, the pin; the split is recorded in `docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`.
- **`succinctly jq -n -s --stream` says a file that did not open, and exits 2, when a text faults before it** (#6730, family 2). `jq -c -n -s --stream '(try input catch .),(try input catch .)' bad.json missing.json` (`bad.json` = `1 }` and `2` on lines) prints the fault, the slurped array and `Could not open file missing.json`, and exits 2: jq's slurp reads every file before it closes the array, so the program's `input` meets the fault and then the array, and the array is read past the last file that did not open. succinctly handed out the fault and the array and reached no failure: nothing said, exit 0. A failure behind a text that faults is now left to those reads, as the plain `-n -s` text's is, and the array of a stream whose last file did not open is read at that file, line 0. The array's `input_filename` and `input_line_number` follow (the missing file, line 0), as in jq. A last directory, a program that stops at the fault and the other flags keep their rows. A 13,200-row differential against jq 1.7.1 (11 flag sets, 10 programs, 15 fixtures, lists of up to three files with missing files and a directory) left 121 rows fixed and none changed for the worse. The rows still apart under `-n -s --stream` start with a file that ends in a container or a truncated one (`[1,2]`, `[1,`): the closing-event and open-token shapes of #6646 and #6730's family 1.
- **`succinctly jq -s --stream` and `-s --stream-errors` meet the fault of a token left open across files at the read jq does, when a file after it did not open** (#6730, family 1). `jq -c -s --stream . ptr pa missing` (`ptr` = `[1,`, `pa` = `[1]`, so the text `[1,[1]` ends open) printed nothing and `parse error: Unfinished JSON term`; it now prints the array `[[[0],1],[[1,0],1],[[1,0]]]` and says `Could not open file missing`, as jq does, because the read of the failed file only brings out the closing event `pa` held back and the fault waits for a read jq's main loop never makes. A directory last is the same read (`-s --stream-errors . ptr pa dir` no longer prints the fault as a second output), and with two files after it that did not open the fault is in the array under `--stream-errors` (`-s --stream-errors . ptr pa missing missing2`; `-s --stream` still says it as a parse error and prints nothing, as jq does): each failed file is now one more empty read of the stream, as it already was for `--stream-errors` without `-s` (#6646).
