Its `length` stays that literal, as jq 1.8.2's does (#7534), so `-Infinity | length > 1e1000` is `true` on every route.
- **`succinctly jq`'s `input_line_number` and `(at FILE:N)` marker count past 4,294,967,295 lines** (#7472). jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 count input lines in a `size_t`, so a value on line 4294967302 is on that line; `succinctly jq` answered `6` on the routes that read through the `input` queue (`input_line_number`, `-n 'reduce inputs ... | error(..)'`, `--seq`, `--stream`, `-R`), and a value on exactly line 4294967295 read as `<unknown>`. Lines are 64 bits now; the per-value line tables keep their 8-byte entries and add a run of high words only where a line passes 2^32, so nothing grows below that. The library's `current_input_location`, `ProducedInput` and `UNKNOWN_INPUT_LINE` carry the line as `u64`, and `seed_remaining_inputs_with_line_highs` seeds a queue from a `LineTable`.
- **`succinctly jq` runs a builtin once per value of a generator argument, as jq does** (#7474). A builtin whose argument jq binds per value (`ltrimstr`, `has`, `getpath`, `setpath`, `test`/`match`/`capture`/`scan`, `sub`/`gsub`'s regex and flags, `split`, `join`, `contains`, `indices`, `flatten`, `nth`, `bsearch`, `strftime`, `format`, `pow` and every two- and three-argument math function, 81 builtin/argument positions in all) ran that argument to the end before its first output, so `"xa" | first(ltrimstr(repeat("x")))` never answered and grew memory, and `first(ltrimstr(inputs | tostring))` read every input. The argument is now bound first, in jq's own nesting order, so `first`, `limit` and an error stop it where jq does; a call whose arguments each yield one value is unchanged.
- **jq: a program too long for the native stack is a compile error, not a crash** (#7475).
  About 48,000 chained `E as $x |` bindings, or 500,000 chained definitions, overflowed the stack and aborted the
  process (exit 134). A binding's body now checks the native-stack floor (ADR-0025), and a module-level chain of
  definitions, which the parser reads in a loop, is charged a share of the floor's room per definition for the
  walks after the parse; past either, the program is refused as jq refuses a program too long for its own parser,
  `jq: error: memory exhausted at <top-level>, line 1:` and `jq: 1 compile error`, exit 3. jq refuses far sooner
  (about 2,500 bindings, and between 5,000 and 10,000 definitions); succinctly from about 23,000 bindings and 65,000
  definitions in a release build. `succinctly yq` refuses the same chains (`Error: parse error: ... memory
  exhausted`, exit 1), where yq answers them.
- **CLI: a standard error that cannot be written no longer turns a diagnostic into a panic** (#7476).
  With standard error on `/dev/full`, a full disk or a file past `ulimit -f`, every error report of
  `succinctly jq` (a runtime error, a parse error, a missing file, a compile error) exited 101, and so did
  `json validate` and `yaml validate` on a standard error pipe with no reader. The message is now dropped,
  as jq drops its failed `fprintf(stderr, ...)`, and the run keeps the status it would have had: 5, 2 or 3
  in `succinctly jq` (as jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 do), 1 in `succinctly yq` (as yq does).
- **`succinctly jq` reads its input files with one free file descriptor, as jq does** (#7477). Under `ulimit -n 4` (descriptors 0, 1 and 2 open) every input file failed with `Could not open file a.json: Too many open files` and exit 2, where jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 print every file and exit 0. The cause was #7214's standard output, a duplicate of descriptor 1 that took the one free descriptor before the first input was opened. It now writes to descriptor 1 itself through a handle that never closes it, which still reports a descriptor that cannot be written (`jq . 1<file`, #7214). Over 15 programs (`-c .`, `-s`, `-R`, `--stream`, `--seq`, `-n '[inputs]'`, `--slurpfile`, `--rawfile`, `-f`, a missing file between two good ones) at `ulimit -n` 4, 5 and 6, stdout, stderr and exit status match jq 1.7.1 on every one of the 13 programs that failed at `ulimit -n 4` before. Pinned in `tests/jq_cli/i7477.rs`.
- **jq: an input named as a pipe (`<(cmd)`, a FIFO path, `-`, `/dev/stdin`) is read as standard input is** (#7478).
  A lone such source was read to its end before the program ran, so `-n 'first(inputs)'`, `-n input`, `halt` and `-R -n input` over a producer that never ends its stream grew until killed, where jq 1.7.1 answers at once.
  The lazy `input`/`inputs` route now starts on its front, and the plain filter and `-R` read it a window at a time, as for an unnamed pipe on standard input.
- **jq: `input`/`inputs` over several files with a document cut across a file's end reads on a window at a time** (#7480).
  The cut document (or a number or literal a file ends in) is carried onto the front of the next file and the lazy route reads on from there, where the rest of the stream was handed to the eager reader, which turned every later document into a value before the first was read: 474.1 MiB at 100 MB of NDJSON in three files on an Apple M4 Pro, now 5.3 MiB, flat from 10 MB (467.9 MiB on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, now 15.3 MiB, the benchmark driver's own size before exec); as `/dev/fd/N`, which are read whole, the text and the next file's buffer.
  Output is unchanged.
- **`succinctly jq -f` runs a shell/jq polyglot program file, as jq 1.7.1 does** (#7481). A file that opens `#!/bin/sh`, `# \`, `exec jq -n -f "$0" "$@"` and then holds the program failed with `unexpected character 'j'` at its third line; jq 1.7.1 drops those three lines (`skip_shebang` in its `src/main.c`, which applies to `-f` files only) and runs the rest, and jq 1.8.2 runs it too, through its Tcl-style comment continuation. The rule is exact and is now matched over a 2,229-file matrix (a shebang or none, a second line with 0 to 4 trailing backslashes, CRLF, the third line, what follows): stdout and exit status agree with jq 1.7.1 on every file but one, a file with a NUL byte, which follows jq 1.8.2 (#7434). A comment that ends in a backslash anywhere else still ends at its newline, as in jq 1.7.1; jq 1.8.2's continuation of every such comment is a language change and is not adopted. Pinned over 156 files in `tests/jq_cli/i7481.rs`.
- **A malformed JSON document left with containers open at end of input no longer panics** (#7482). `{"a":` and 44 `[` closed by one `}` panicked `succinctly jq .` with an index out of bounds in `BalancedParens::is_open` (exit 101) on the file and pipe routes, `-s`, `-n input`/`inputs` and `--slurpfile`; it now prints jq's `parse error: ':' not as part of an object at line 1, column 55` (exit 5), as a shallower document already did. The standard JSON index takes its parenthesis length as two bits per open and the closes such a document lacks as the zero bits after the last one written; once they crossed a word boundary the length ran past the stored words, so the index now stores them. `succinctly jq-locate` on such a document now names a path, as it already did when the missing closes fit in the index's last word, where it answered `Could not locate position`.
- **jq: `now` is a whole number of microseconds on every platform, as jq's is** (#7484). jq reads `gettimeofday` (`tv_sec + tv_usec / 1000000.0`, the same in jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2), so every reading of `[range(200)|now*1e6|.-round|fabs<0.001]|all` is true; `succinctly jq` converted the clock with `as_secs_f64`, which keeps the nanoseconds a Linux clock has, so about one reading in four was whole and the rest printed a seventh decimal (`1795225997.4185658` against jq's `1795225997.418565`). macOS clocks have microseconds, so the difference was Linux only. The nanosecond reading is cut to microseconds before it becomes a number. `succinctly yq` keeps its nanosecond timestamp text. Pinned by a unit test of the conversion and by `tests/jq_cli/i7484.rs`, which checks 300 readings.
- **jq: `TZ` is read as libc reads it** (#7486). `localtime`, `strflocaltime` and `localtime | mktime` looked `TZ` up in jiff's zone database, so `TZ=posix/Asia/Tokyo`, `TZ=right/Europe/Paris` and `TZ=Asia//Tokyo` were UTC (on macOS too for the last), `TZDIR` was not read as glibc reads it, and `TZ=asia/tokyo` loaded Tokyo on Linux. `TZ` is now a tz file under the zoneinfo directory (`$TZDIR` on Linux, `/usr/share/zoneinfo` on macOS, whose libc ignores `TZDIR`) or at a path, before it is a POSIX string, as jq 1.7.1 reads it on glibc and on macOS. Over 49 spellings of `TZ` under six `TZDIR` settings on x86_64 Linux, `localtime`, `localtime | mktime` and `strflocaltime` now give jq's local times for 271 of the 294 pairs (214 before); the rest are `right/` zones, whose offsets now load but whose leap seconds are not counted (recorded in the limitations page), and POSIX rules applied before 1967, unchanged.
- **jq: an environment entry with an empty name is listed in `$ENV` and `env`, as jq lists it** (#7487). jq splits each `environ` string at its first `=`, so the entry `=v` (made by a raw `execve`, or `Command::env("", "v")`) is `"": "v"` and `=X=1` is `"": "X=1"`; jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 agree. `succinctly jq` read the environment through `std::env::vars_os`, which skips `=v` and reads `=X=1` as `X`, so `{"":"v","Y":"1"}` printed `{"Y":"1"}`. Unix now reads the `environ` strings themselves (the read `std` makes, without its lock: a thread that calls `set_var` while another builds `$ENV` is as unsound as for C's `getenv`; the CLI sets nothing). Pinned over 5 environments and `$ENV`, `env | keys` and `env == $ENV` in `tests/jq_cli/i7487.rs`.
- **`succinctly jq` keeps reading options after a positional word that starts with `-`** (#7494). jq reads `-1`, `-.a`, `-(1)` and `-[1]` as positional words wherever they sit and goes on reading options after them, so `jq -1 -n` prints `-1` and `jq . a.json -1 -c` prints compactly. `succinctly jq` made every later word a file (`Could not open file -n`, and `--arg` and `--` read as files too). And after `--args --`, an option-shaped word is the program in jq (`jq -n --args -- -c .` is the compile error `c/0 is not defined`), where `succinctly jq` skipped it and ran `.`. Over 5,000 random orderings of options, `--args`/`--jsonargs`, `--` and positional words, the rows where `succinctly jq` differed from both jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 in stdout or exit status fell from 149 to 91, and every one left gives the malformed file `bad.json` (`{"a":1,}`) to a program that does not read its input: jq still reports the parse error and exits 5, and `succinctly jq` does not, which is input validation, not the command line.
- **jq: a fold that writes an array slot by a float-represented whole index is linear again** (#7495).
  `reduce range(1e4) as $i ([]; .[$i] = 1)`, and the same with `|=`, `+=`, `//=`, inside `foreach`, or with an
  index such as `$i * 1.0` or an element of `[range(1e4)]`, rebuilt the whole accumulator on every step, so
  the time grew with the square of the step count where `range(10000)` (an integer index) was linear.
  A whole float key now names the slot its integer spelling does and takes the same in-place write; a
  fractional, non-finite or out-of-range key keeps the evaluator's route, and the answers are unchanged.
- **jq: a number literal directly followed by `else`, `elif` or `end` is read as the number and the keyword** (#7496). `if 1 then 2else 3 end` and `if 0 then 2 else 3end` were refused as `invalid number` (exit 3); they now run as in jq (`2`), and so do `.5end`, `3.end` and `1.5else`. The lexer took an `e` after a number for a malformed exponent; as jq's, it now reads an exponent only when digits follow (`[eE][+-]?[0-9]+`) and otherwise ends the number before the `e`, so `2e`, `1e1else` and `0x10` are still syntax errors.
- **jq: a postfix after a negated number literal negates the postfixed term** (#7497). `-1[0]`, `-1.5[0]`, `-1[]?`, `-1.[]?` and `-1 [0]` were refused as `unexpected character '['` (exit 3); they now parse as jq's `-(1[0])`: `-1[0]` is a run-time `Cannot index number with number` (exit 5) and `-1[]?` prints nothing. The same holds for an object value (`{a: -1[0]?}`). The `-` is no longer folded into the literal when a `[` follows it, as it already was not for a `.`, `?`, `as` or a multiplicative operator.
- **jq: `--indent` refuses a malformed value, as jq 1.8 does** (#7501). `--indent abc`, `--indent ""`, `--indent 3x`, `--indent " 2"`, `--indent 3.0` and `--indent -c` ran, reading the value with `atoi` as jq 1.7.1 does; jq 1.8 fixed that (jqlang/jq#3195) and exits 2 with `--indent takes a number between -1 and 7`, and so does `succinctly jq` now. An optional sign and ASCII digits in -1 to 7 are still accepted (`+3`, `007`, `-1` for a tab). `--indent 0` prints newlines with no indentation, as jq 1.8 does (#7605).
- **jq: `last(f)` of an `f` that yields nothing yields nothing** (#7518). `[last(empty)]`, `[last(range(0))]` and `[[] | last(.[])]` were `[null]`, `[last(empty)] == [first(empty)]` was `false`, and `path(last(.[]))` over an empty array raised `Invalid path expression with result null`; now they are `[]`, `true` and no path, where jq 1.7.1 answered the `reduce`'s `null` seed. `succinctly jq` follows jq 1.8.2, which fixed this (jqlang/jq#3179). The difference from the pinned 1.7.1 is recorded in `docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md` and as the `syntax:man-last-empty` ledger entry.
- **jq: `foreach` with a generator INIT runs its source on the real input for every INIT output** (#7519). `[1, 2] | [foreach .[] as $x (0, 1; . + $x)]` raised `Cannot iterate over null`, as jq 1.7.1 does: its `DUPN` hands every INIT output after the first a `null` input. jq 1.8.0 fixed that as a bug (jqlang/jq#3266), and `succinctly jq` now follows jq 1.8.2 and prints `[1,3,2,4]`, in value mode, in `path()` and in assignment targets. `reduce` keeps the 1.7.1 behaviour, as jq 1.8.2 does. The difference from the pinned 1.7.1 is recorded in `docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md` and the ledger's `syntax:foreach-gen-init`.
- **jq: an optional capture group that takes no part in an empty match is unmatched** (#7520). `"a" | match("(b)?") | .captures` reported `{"offset":0,"string":"","length":0}` for the group, and `capture("(?<x>b)?")`, `scan("(b)?")` and `sub("(?<x>b)?"; "[\(.x)]")` showed `""` for it, as jq 1.7.1 does; now the group is `{"offset":-1,"string":null,"length":0}` and the others show `null`, as in jq 1.8.2 (jqlang/jq#3238), which fixed this. A group that took part in the empty match is unchanged. The difference from the pinned 1.7.1 is recorded in `docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`.
- **jq: `tonumber` refuses a string with a NUL byte in it** (#7521). `"1\u00002" | tonumber` was `1` and `"12\u0000abc" | tonumber` was `12`, because the text was cut at the NUL as in jq 1.7.1; now they raise `string ("1\u00002") cannot be parsed as a number`, and `tonumber?` is empty, as in jq 1.8.2 (jqlang/jq#3496), which upstream fixed. The difference from the pinned 1.7.1 is recorded in `docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`.
- **jq: a NaN with a payload is an invalid numeric literal, as in jq 1.8** (#7522). `NaN1`, `nan123`, `sNaN12` and `-NaN10` were read as NaN (printed `null`) from input, `--stream`, `--seq`, `fromjson`, `tonumber`, `--argjson`, `--jsonargs` and `--slurpfile`, as jq 1.7.1 reads them. jq 1.8.0 dropped them as a security fix (CVE-2024-53427): `Invalid numeric literal`, exit 5 for a document and exit 2 for a named argument. `succinctly jq` now follows jq 1.8.2 on every one of those, with its line and column. `NaN`, `nan`, `-NaN` and a zero payload (`NaN0`) are still numbers, and `succinctly yq` is unchanged. Recorded as a difference from the pinned 1.7.1 in `docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`.
- **jq: `--slurp --stream` keeps the last closing event in the array** (#7523). `printf '[1][2]' | jq -c -s --stream .` printed `[[[0],1],[[0]],[[0],2]]` and then `[[0]]` (the same for `[1,2]` and `{"a":1}` with no newline after them), as jq 1.7.1 does; now it prints one array of every event, `[[[0],1],[[0]],[[0],2],[[0]]]`, as jq 1.8.2 does (jqlang/jq#3279), which fixed this. `-n`, `input`/`inputs` and `--stream-errors -s` follow. This replaces the held-back event of #5548. The difference from the pinned 1.7.1 is recorded in `docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`.
- **jq: an error message that cuts a long value never splits a multi-byte character** (#7524). The cut now moves back to the start of the character and nothing replaces it, as in jq 1.8 (jqlang/jq#3249): `"x" * 8 + "☆" * 5 | try -. catch .` is `string ("xxxxxxxx...) cannot be negated`, where it had a U+FFFD before the `...` (#6434 matched jq 1.7.1's, which wrote one). The preview budget stays 1.7.1's 11 bytes; jq 1.8.2's wider previews (jqlang/jq#3478) are not adopted. The `succinctly yq` messages that reuse jq's wording follow.
- **jq: a bare `n` token is `Invalid numeric literal` on every route** (#7525). `printf '\036"iu"\n\036n\n' | jq --seq -c .` reported `Invalid literal`, and `printf '"iu" n' | jq --stream -c .` (also `--stream-errors`) reported `Invalid literal at EOF`, because the readers modelled jq 1.7.1's read of a stale byte from an earlier token (`check_literal` read `tokenbuf[1]` without checking the token's length); the plain, `-n` and `-s` routes already said `Invalid numeric literal`. They now follow jq 1.8.2, which fixed the uninitialised read (jqlang/jq#3324), so one set of bytes has one fault word on every route. A token that starts `nu` (`nul`) stays `Invalid literal`.
- **jq: a regex may nest groups up to 511 deep** (#7528). `"a" | test("(" * 251 + "a" + ")" * 251)` was refused with the `regex` crate's own `regex parse error ... exceed the maximum number of nested parentheses/brackets (250)`, where both jq 1.7.1 and jq 1.8.2 answer it. `succinctly jq` now answers every pattern with up to 511 nested groups (capturing, `(?:`, with a repeat or an alternation between them, under any flags) and refuses 512 or more with jq 1.8.2's `Regex failure: parse depth limit over` (jq 1.8.1's oniguruma stack-overflow fix, GHSA-f946-j5j2-4w5m; jq 1.7.1 accepted up to 2,047). Look-arounds and atomic groups nested more than 63 deep are still refused, by the second regex engine's own limit.
- **jq: `toboolean`, `trim`, `ltrim` and `rtrim` word their errors as jq 1.8.2 does** (#7529). A string `toboolean` refuses is quoted with JSON escapes (`\u0001`, `\u007f`, `\u0000`), where it showed Rust's (`\u{1}`, `\u{7f}`, `\0`), and the refusal of a non-string names the value (`null (null) cannot be parsed as a boolean`, `array ([1]) ...`), which it left out. The three trim builtins say `trim input must be a string` on a non-string, where they said `trim requires string`, `ltrim requires string` and `rtrim requires string`. These are 1.8 builtins, so 1.8.2 is the only reference.
- **jq: a circular module import is reported as `circular import of <path>`** (#7530). `import "cycle_a" as a; null` with `cycle_a.jq` and `cycle_b.jq` importing each other printed `module cycle detected: cycle_a -> cycle_b -> cycle_a`; it now prints jq 1.8.2's `jq: error: circular import of <absolute path of the re-entered module>` (CVE-2026-44777; jq 1.7.1 segfaults on these programs), also for `include`, a self-import and a cycle through three modules. The path is the resolved file, so `include "./alia"` inside `alia.jq` names `alia.jq`. The cycle now counts as an error of its own level, as in jq 1.8.2, so the walk goes on after it and a program with several cycles or other failures reports all of them with their count.
- **jq: `mktime`, `strftime`, `strflocaltime` and `todate` read a broken-down time as jq 1.8.2 does** (#7532). A NaN field was read as 0 (`[2024,0,1,0,0,nan,0,0] | mktime` was `1704067200`, `nan | todate` was `"1970-01-01T00:00:00Z"`), an array shorter than 8 was refused (`[2024,0,1] | mktime`), and a year past the C `int` range wrapped (`[-1e20,0,1,0,0,0,0,0] | strftime("%Y")` was `"2147483648"`), as in jq 1.7.1, whose `jv2tm` casts each field unchecked. `succinctly jq` now follows upstream's fixes (jqlang/jq#3070, #3162): NaN is `<name> requires parsed datetime inputs`, missing fields are 0 (`[2024,0,1] | mktime` is `1704067200`), and each field saturates to `int` after the year has had 1900 taken off (`[1e20,0,1,0,0,0,0,0] | mktime` is `67768036160140800`). The difference from the pinned 1.7.1 is recorded in `docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`.
- **jq: `strftime` and `strflocaltime` word a non-string format as jq 1.8.2 does** (#7533). `0 | strftime([])` raised `expected string, got strftime format`; it now raises `strftime/1 requires a string format` (`strflocaltime/1 requires a string format` for the local-zone one), as jq 1.8.2 does (upstream commit 1411ce6), whose fix replaced jq 1.7.1's assertion abort. The array-input case already read that way. The difference from the pinned 1.7.1, which aborts, stays recorded in `docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`.
- **jq: `length` of a number literal keeps its digits, as in jq 1.8.2** (#7534). `length` of a number took the absolute value of its double, as jq 1.7.1 does, so `-100000000000000000001 | length` was `1e+20`, `1E-400 | length` was `0` and `1.50 | length` was `1.5`. jq 1.8 fixed that (jqlang/jq#3275), and `succinctly jq` now follows it: the result is the literal's absolute value with every digit (`100000000000000000001`, `1E-400`, `1.50`), and a negative zero is `0` (`-0.0 | length` is `0.0`). It holds for input documents, `-s`, `inputs`, `--argjson`, `--slurpfile` and program literals. A computed number, NaN, the infinities and non-numbers are unchanged, and so is `succinctly yq`. The difference from the pinned 1.7.1 is recorded in `docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`.
- **jq: an index write past 2^29 elements says `Array index too large`** (#7536). `null | .[536870912] = 1`, `[] | .[1e12] = 1` and `setpath([536870912]; 1)` (also the `|=` and `+=` forms) were refused as `Cannot grow array to 536870913 elements`; `succinctly jq` now answers jq 1.8.2's sentence (CVE-2024-23337, which bounded `jv_array_set` at the same 2^29 elements; jq 1.7.1 maps gigabytes and dies on the larger indexes). The bound is unchanged. `succinctly yq` keeps its own `Cannot grow array to <n> elements`, as yq has no sentence to copy.
- **`succinctly jq` indexes a JSON document of 4 GiB or more** (#7537). Since #7425 such a document was read into a tree without an index, and a program that needed the whole-document index (`map(length) | add`, `[.[] | f]`, `first(.[])`, `sort`, `to_entries`, `del(.[0])`, `.[0] = 1`, `[paths]`), and every document that was not plain JSON (a repeated key, `nan`, nesting past 128), was refused at exit 5 where jq 1.7.1 answers. The index's 32-bit fields are counts of interest bits and parentheses, not text positions (the one position it cached, the sequential-select hint, is now 64-bit), so it now holds a text of any length with at most `u32::MAX` of each, that is at most 2,147,483,647 values (keys included): only a document past that, about two bytes a value, is still read without an index. On a 4,296,011,781-byte array of 1 MiB strings (measured once on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, not an interleaved benchmark), `map(length) | add` prints `4295999485` as jq does, in 3.8 s at 4.9 GB peak RSS, and the programs that copy the array take 11.6-14.4 s at 9.0 GB. Index size on ordinary inputs is unchanged (the hint is packed into 12 bytes, which fit where the 8-byte one did), and every document shorter than 4 GiB is still indexed in place, without the length-past-4-GiB count: instructions rise 0.01-0.16% on record-by-record NDJSON and 0.00-0.28% on single documents over 1 and 10 MB inputs (cachegrind, Ryzen 9 7950X).
- **CLI: a standard output that cannot be written no longer panics** (#7538). With standard output on `/dev/full`, a full disk or a file past `ulimit -f`, `json generate`, `dsv generate`, `yaml generate`, `jq-locate`, `yq-locate`, the `--version` and `--build-configuration` reports of `succinctly jq` and `succinctly yq`, and the `bench` tables exited 101 after a Rust panic message (`failed printing to stdout`). They now print `succinctly: error: writing output failed: <strerror>` once on standard error and exit 2, as `succinctly jq` ends a failed write to standard output (jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2: `jq: error: writing output failed: ...`, exit 2). A closed pipe (`| head`) ends them with SIGPIPE, as it ends `succinctly jq`, instead of a panic on `EPIPE`.
- **The NEON and SVE2 JSON index builders agree with the portable one when a `"` follows a bare value** (#7539). On aarch64 they took the quote in `a"` or `[1"a"]` as the start of a new string, so the semi-index of such malformed text (and every position after it) differed from the one x86_64 and the portable PFSM builder produce; the quote now ends the value and opens nothing, as the state machine says. `tests/json_builder_differential_properties.rs` checks every builder the target compiles (scalar, PFSM, dispatcher, SSE2/AVX2 or NEON/SVE2, Standard and Simple Cursor) against the portable one over every short byte combination at each chunk boundary, byte soups, and generated and mutated documents. No `jq` output difference was found before the fix.
- **jq: `strftime("")` and `strflocaltime("")` return the empty string** (#7542). They raised `strftime/1: unknown system failure` (`strflocaltime/1: ...`), as jq 1.7.1 does; now `0 | strftime("")` is `""`, and so is a format that is empty once a NUL ends it (`strftime("\u0000x")`), as in jq 1.8.2, which fixed this with its `strftime` crash fix (jqlang/jq#3271). A non-empty format whose result is empty, or one past the `strlen(fmt) + 100` byte buffer, still raises. The difference from the pinned 1.7.1 is recorded in `docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`.
- **jq: bare `first` on an array with a stray, doubled or missing `,` raises jq's parse error, as `.[0]` does** (#7554). `[,1] | first` printed `1` with exit 0, and so did `[1,]`, `[1 2]`, `[1,,2]` and `[true false]`, at the top level, nested, as an NDJSON line and after a 5 MiB line, where `.[0]`, `nth(0)` and jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 reject the document. jq defines `first` as `.[0]`, so it now makes `.[0]`'s length walk and prints jq's message with its line and column, exit 5.
- **jq: `all(f)` and `any(f)` over an array with a stray, doubled or missing `,` raise jq's parse error, as `all(.[]; f)` does** (#7555). `[1,] | all(. < 5)` answered `true` and `[1 2] | all(. == 1)` answered `false`, computed from the `2` after the missing comma, where jq (which defines `all(f)` as `all(.[]; f)`) rejects the document. The walk now checks each element's `,` as it reaches it and the gap before the `]` when it runs out, as `.[]` does, so an answer decided before the fault still stops there. Arity-0 `any`/`all` on the zero-member `{,}` raise too, as they already did on `{"a":1,}`; on an array they still answer, by design (#2692).
- **jq: a postfix after `break $label` parses** (#7557). `label $f | break $f.a`, `break $f[0]`, `break $f.[]`, `break $f[1:2]` and the rest of the postfix forms were a compile error (`unexpected character '.'`, exit 3); `break $name` is a term in jq's grammar, so they parse as in jq and the postfix never runs (`[label $f | 1, break $f.a, 2]` is `[1]`).
- **jq: a failure after a value of a `?//` bind in `in`, `halt_error`, `split`/`splits`' flags or `combinations`' count retries the bind's next alternative** (#7558). `"a" | in([[1], {"a":1}] as [$a] ?// [$b, $a] | $a)` raised `Cannot check whether array has a string key` where jq answers `true`, `split(","; ([1, "g"] as [$a] ?// [$b, $a] | $a))` raised `"g"` and `1` cannot be added where jq splits, and `combinations` reported the first alternative's `Range bounds must be numeric`. `halt_error`'s argument is now bound first, as #7474 binds the other builtins', `in(xs)` with such an argument runs as its definition (`. as $x | xs | has($x)`), and the flags and count, which jq reads inside the array it collects, are checked value by value where the failure can still retry. Arguments without a `?//` are unchanged.
- **jq: `=` through a negative index that names no element, followed by `.[]`, collects the path before refusing the write** (#7559). `.[-2][]? = 0` on `[1]` (or `null`, `[]`, `[[]]`) raised `Out of bounds negative array index` and exited 5; it is now the input unchanged, as in jq, because the `.[]` over the `null` at that index yields no path. Without the `?`, `.[-2][] = 0` now raises jq's `Cannot iterate over null (null)` instead of the bounds error. `|=`, `+=`, `//=` and `del` already agreed with jq.
- **jq: `split(re; flags)` and `splits(re; flags)` whose FLAGS argument yields nothing slice a non-string input whole, as jq 1.7.1 does** (#7560). With no FLAGS value jq's definition runs no `match`, so nothing checks the input's type and the one piece is `$s[0:($s | length)]`: `null | split("b"; empty)` is `[null]`, `[1] | [splits("b"; empty)]` is `[[1]]`, a boolean raises `boolean (true) has no length`, and a number or an object raises `Cannot index number with object` (`object`). `succinctly jq` raised `null (null) cannot be matched, as it is not a string` for all of them. A string input was already answered as 1.7.1 answers it (`["abc"]`). jq 1.8.2 yields nothing for every input here, strings included, as a side effect of a refactor of `splits` (jqlang/jq#3260) that upstream does not describe as a fix, so the pinned 1.7.1 stays the reference.
- **jq: `|= empty` over several paths queues an array-key deletion until every path is collected** (#7562). `(.[recurse]) |= empty` on `[1,[2,3],{"a":"b"}]` reported `Cannot delete array element of array` for its first path, where jq's `_modify` collects every path first and reports the later object index, `Array/string slice indices must be integers`; `(.[[1]], .a) |= empty` and `(.[[1]], .[[2]][0]) |= empty` now report jq's error too. The deletion is queued like any other and refused by the final `delpaths`.
- **`succinctly jq` finishes `map(f)` before a following `map(g)` starts** (#7565). The lazy `map` chain ran `map(f) | map(g)` element by element, so `g`'s error, `debug` line or `input` came before `f` had run on a later element: `[1,"x"] | try (map(if . == "x" then error("first") else . end) | map(error("second"))) catch .` answered `"second"` where jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 answer `"first"`. A `map(g)` now joins the chain only when `g`, or every stage already on it, can neither raise nor have an effect; otherwise the chain is drained first, its cursors kept as cursors.
- **jq: a UTF-8 byte-order mark cut across the first input files is skipped** (#7566). `EF BB` in one file and `BF [2]` in the next, or a byte of the mark in each of three files, was `Invalid numeric literal at line 1, column 4` (exit 5) under `.`, `-s`, `-n input`/`inputs`, `--stream` and `--stream-errors`, where jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 skip the mark and read `[2]`: jq reads its files as one stream and its parser matches the mark a byte at a time. A stream that ends inside a mark cut that way (`EF` then `BB BF`) is empty input, as a lone `EF` has been since #7454. The routes that read several files a window at a time leave such a list to the route that reads the files whole.
- **`-` among the input files leaves a redirected stdin where jq does after an early stop** (#7568). `jq -n input -`, `jq halt -` and `jq -n input f -` over a regular file on standard input left it at its end, where jq 1.7.1 leaves it at the end of the line that completed the last value read from it, or untouched when the run never got past the files before the `-`; the files before the first `-` are now read again and counted as jq's reader takes them (one text, a value a file leaves unfinished completed by the next), with `--stream` and `-R` too.
- **jq: `/dev/stdin` named as an input file leaves a redirected stdin where jq does, and `--stream` reads it** (#7568). On macOS, where `/dev/stdin` and `/dev/fd/0` open as descriptor 0 itself, `{ jq -n input /dev/stdin; head; } < f` and `jq halt /dev/stdin` left the file at its end, where jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 leave it at the end of the line that completed the last value; it is now put back as a `-` is. `jq --stream . /dev/stdin < f` (and `/dev/fd/7 7<f`) failed with `Invalid numeric literal at line 1, column 2`, because the probe of the file's first bytes moved the shared offset; it is moved back, and the stream reads as jq reads it. On Linux, where the path opens the file again from its start, a `-` after it (`jq -n input /dev/stdin - < f`) left the file at its end, where jq's reader never reaches the `-` and leaves it untouched; the path is now read again by its name to count what jq read of it, as a named file is.
- **jq: `input_line_number` and `(at FILE:N)` after a leading UTF-8 BOM count jq 1.7.1's reads** (#7569). jq's `fgets` reads the byte-order mark in its first 4,095-byte read though its parser skips it, so on a first line longer than 4,092 bytes the read that holds the line break starts 3 bytes earlier in the text. Every route counted from the text after the mark, so values near the end of such a line reported line 0 where jq reports 1 (`BOM` + 2,048 `1 ` values + a newline: 2,047 values on line 0 here, 2,046 in jq). Fixed on the routes that read the files whole, a window at a time and through the stream reader (`--stream`, `--stream-errors`, `-n`), on standard input, and for a mark cut across files.
- **A `--stream` run that stops on a close at a chunk's last byte leaves a redirected stdin where jq does** (#7570). When the closer right after a scalar (`[2]`, `{"a":2}`, `[[[2]]]`) was the last byte of one of jq's 4095-byte reads, a run that stopped on the close (`--stream -n 'limit(k; inputs)'`, a main-loop `halt`) left standard input at the end of that read; jq hands that event out only after reading the next chunk, and the offset is now left at the end of that one, as jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 leave it.
- **`succinctly jq` reads one input at a time under `fromstream(inputs)`, `inputs[k]` and `in(inputs)`** (#7572). Each collected every output of its generator before looking at the first, so it read the whole input first: an error on an early input named the end of the input (`printf '1\n2\n' | jq -n 'fromstream(inputs)'` said `(at <stdin>:2)` where jq 1.7.1 says `:1`; `[inputs[.]]` over `[1,2,3]` said `<unknown>` where jq says `:0`), and the inputs jq leaves unread for the main loop and for a `catch` were gone (`printf '1 2 3' | jq '[.] | in(inputs)'` exited 5 where jq exits 0). They now take one output at a time and stop at an error, as jq's `foreach`, `E | .[$k]` and `xs | has($x)` do, so a `stderr` or `debug` of a later output no longer runs either.
- **jq: a depth refusal in the first read of a long first line names line 0 over several files** (#7573). `jq -c -n '[inputs]' a.json b.json` with `a.json` a line of 300 `[` and 5,000 spaces printed `jq: error (at a.json:1): Exceeds depth limit for parsing at line 1, column 257`; jq 1.7.1 prints `(at a.json:0)`, as `succinctly jq` already did for one file: jq reads in 4,095-byte chunks and counts a line only when it reads the chunk that ends in the break, and the refusal is met in the first chunk. The route that carries an unfinished document from one file to the next counted the whole line instead; it now ends a read at 4,095 bytes from the start of the line, as the single-file route does. jq 1.8.2 has no 256-level parse depth limit, so the refusal stays 1.7.1's.
- **A run that meets a parse error leaves a redirected stdin where jq does** (#7575). A run over a regular file on standard input that stopped at a parse error (the main loop, an uncaught `input` error) left it where its own reads had taken it, often its end, where jq 1.7.1 leaves it at the end of the line (or 4095-byte read) that held the error; a run that catches the error and reads on (`try input catch ...`) now also resumes counting from the next line, as jq's reader drops the rest of the error's. A standard input that shares its open file with the output (`<> f >&0`) is no longer moved at all; `--stream` parse errors, `--seq` and `--stream-errors` are unchanged.
- **jq: an input read whole that there is no room for is jq's `cannot allocate memory`, not an empty input** (#7576). Under a `ulimit -v` smaller than the file, `-s`, `-R -s`, `--slurpfile`, `--rawfile`, `-f` and standard input read whole reported the failed allocation as a file that would not open (`jq: error: Could not open file f: out of memory`, exit 2) and ran on without it, so `-s length` printed `0` and `-c -s .` printed `[]`; on standard input the read stopped where the room ran out (`-R -s length` printed the length it got) or a later copy aborted with `memory allocation of ... failed`. Each now prints `jq: error: cannot allocate memory` and aborts (exit 134), as jq 1.7.1 does on every one of those routes (x86_64 Linux, 300 MiB NDJSON under `ulimit -v 400000`). `--seq` over a stream with no RS, which jq streams, gets the same answer and is recorded in the limitations page.
- **jq: a `?//` in a builtin's argument inside `map(f)`, `with_entries(f)` or `walk(f)` retries the next alternative, as jq does** (#7602). `["x"] | map(startswith([1,"x"] as [$a] ?// [$b,$a] | $a))` raised `startswith() requires string inputs` where jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 answer `[true]`, and `to_entries | map(has(...))`, `with_entries(...)` and `walk(...)` over such an `f` raised likewise. Such an `f` now runs under jq's own definitions of the three builtins, where the builtin's refusal of the first alternative retries the bind.
- **jq: `--stream-errors` and `--stream` over input that opens with a broken byte-order mark say `Malformed BOM`, as jq does** (#7603). `printf '\xef1\n' | jq -c --stream-errors .` printed a `["Invalid numeric literal at line 2, column 0",[]]` event and exited 0, where jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 print `jq: parse error: Malformed BOM` and exit 5: jq's parser returns that error before it scans a byte, on every read, and `--stream-errors` does not turn it into an event. Under `-n` every `input` now raises `Malformed BOM` (`[try input catch ., try input catch .]` is `["Malformed BOM","Malformed BOM"]`), and `--stream` words the fault that way too.
- **jq: a data module with a byte that is not valid UTF-8 is read with U+FFFD** (#7604). `import "d" as $d;` over a `d.json` holding such a byte was refused with `error loading data file <path>: stream did not contain valid UTF-8` (exit 3), where jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 read it: `"\xff"` imports as `["�"]`. The file's strings are decoded as the main input's and a `--slurpfile` file's are (#7436).
- **`succinctly jq --indent 0` prints newlines with no indentation, as jq 1.8 does** (#7605). jq 1.7.1 printed `--indent 0` as `-c`; jq 1.8 calls that a bug (jqlang/jq#3232) and prints one element or key per line with the space after each `:` and no indentation, for `-0`, `00` and `+0` too, and for `-c --indent 0` and `--tab --indent 0` (the last of `-c`, `--tab` and `--indent` still wins). Every print route follows it, and `-C` keeps its colours in the new layout.
- **jq: `strftime`, `strflocaltime`, `todate` and `todateiso8601` normalise a broken-down time before formatting it, as jq 1.8.2 does** (#7606). The fields were formatted as given, as in jq 1.7.1: `[2024,0,1,0,0,0,0,0] | strftime("%a")` was `"Sun"` for a Monday, `[2024,1,30,0,0,0,0,0] | todate` was `"2024-02-30T00:00:00Z"` (now `"2024-03-01T00:00:00Z"`), `[2024,13,35,25,61,61,0,0] | todate` was `"2024-14-35T25:61:61Z"`, which jq 1.7.1's own `fromdate` refuses, a short array (#7532) printed a date neither release prints (`[2024,5] | todate` was `"2024-06-00T00:00:00Z"`, now `"2024-05-31T00:00:00Z"`), and `-1.0000000000000002 | todate` was `"1969-12-31T23:59:60Z"` (now `"1970-01-01T00:00:00Z"`). `strflocaltime` reads the fields as local wall-clock time, as `mktime` does. A consistent broken-down time and every other number print as before; the difference from the pinned jq 1.7.1 is recorded in `docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`. Also: `strflocaltime("%s")` of a reading that is `-1` seconds from the epoch as UTC printed `-1` instead of that reading's instant in the local zone (`TZ=Europe/Paris`, `[1969,11,31,23,59,59,3,364] | strflocaltime("%s")` is `"-3601"` in both jq releases).
- **jq: `module not found` with `HOME` unset names the search entry jq could not expand** (#7608). jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 cannot expand `~/.jq` (or a `-L ~/x`, or a `~/` in `search` metadata) without `HOME` and append the last such error: `module not found: zz (Could not expand ~/.jq. (Could not find home directory.))`. `succinctly jq` printed the bare `module not found: zz`; it now writes jq's text for `import`, `include`, a data import and `modulemeta`.
- **jq: an undefined name inside the arguments of an undefined call no longer shifts the cited position of a later error** (#7609). `def d0: ua(ub(1));` then `ub(2)` reported `ub/1 is not defined` at the `ub(1)` of line 1 (and echoed that line), where jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 cite the `ub(2)` of line 2; the same held for a variable or a `break` inside the arguments, and for `ua(ub(1)),` then `ub(2)` in the main program. jq never compiles such arguments, so they are still not diagnosed, but their sites are now counted.
- **jq: a data import with `{raw: true}` binds the file's text** (#7645). `import "r" as $r {raw: true};` parsed `r.json` as JSON, so a file that was not JSON was `error loading data file` (exit 3) and one that was imported as `[value]`, where jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 bind its text as one string (`"abc def"`), read as `--rawfile` reads its file. Only `raw: true` itself does this, as in jq: `raw: 1`, `raw: "true"` and `raw: null` still parse the file.
- **`succinctly jq` reads a `?` or `+` after a blank, a `#` comment or a `(?#..)` comment as a new quantifier, as jq does** (#7654). Under the `x` flag `"" | [match("a{1,2} ?$"; "gx")] | length` is `1` and `"aaa" | [match("(a)? +"; "xn")] | map(.length)` is `[3]`, as in jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2, where they were `0` and `[1]`: Oniguruma ends a quantifier at the gap, so `a{1,2} ?` is `(?:a{1,2})?` and `(a)? +` is `(?:(a)?)+`, which the pattern the regex engine reads now says, where it had read the lazy `a{1,2}?` and the possessive `(a)?+`. The same holds without `x` across a `(?#..)` comment, inline `(?x)` and `(?x:...)` included; and `{,n}`, which jq reads as literal text, is no longer taken for a quantifier there (`"a{,2}}b" | test("a{,2}+b")` is `true`). Over 17,956 generated patterns 643 rows that differed from jq 1.7.1 now match it; two that matched by accident now show two older, separate faults.
- **jq: a module or data import that names a directory, or a file that will not open, reports it as jq does** (#7663). `import "d" as $d;` with a directory `d.json` said `module not found: d`, where jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 say `error loading data file <path>: Could not open <path>: It's a directory`; the same holds for `import "d" as m;` and `include "d";` (a directory `d.jq`), for the `d/jq/main.jq` and `d/d.jq` spellings, and for a directory in an earlier `-L` entry ahead of a file in a later one, which jq stops at. An unreadable file now carries jq's `Could not open <path>:` before `Permission denied`, a symlink loop moves on to the next search directory as in jq, and `modulemeta` on a module that will not read is `null` with nothing on stderr.
- **`succinctly jq` reads a lazy fixed interval `x{n}?` as exactly `n` repeats on every regex route** (#7669). `"a" | test("(?>a){2}?a")` is `false` and `"aa" | [match("(?>a){2}??") | .length]` is `[2]`, as in jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2, where they were `true` and `[0]`: on a pattern with an atomic group, a look-around, a backreference or the `l` flag, the second engine read the `?` as another quantifier, Ruby's `(?:x{n})?`, where jq's Perl_NT syntax makes it the reluctant (and so still fixed) `x{n}`. A quantifier after it now repeats `x{n}` as in jq (`x{n}?+` is `(?:x{n})+`).
- **`succinctly jq` keeps a repeated group's last, empty iteration under the `n` flag, as jq does** (#7670). `"a" | match("(a*)*"; "n") | .captures[0].offset` is `1` and `"a" | match("(?:(a?)+)?"; "n") | .captures[0].offset` is `1`, as in jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2, where both were `0`: without `n` the capture rewrite of #6069 writes Oniguruma's final empty iteration into the pattern, and under `n`, whose pattern goes to the second regex engine, it now runs there too. A pattern that engine reads with an atomic group (a possessive quantifier) and a bounded repeat (`(a??){1,3}`) keep their old answers. Over 24,956 generated patterns 181 rows that differed from jq 1.7.1 now match it, and none that matched changed.
- **jq: a first use of a prelude definition at the native-stack floor refuses instead of panicking** (#7676).
  Since #7475 the parser refuses at the native-stack floor (ADR-0025), and two parses of the crate's own text can
  happen there: the path-mode interpreter parses a prelude definition (`to_entries`, `map`, `select`, `paths`,
  `walk`, ...) on its first use, and a program's `_nwise` call parses jq's template inside the program's own parse.
  Either one, reached within a few KiB of the floor, panicked (`prelude: ParseError { message: "memory exhausted"`,
  or `jq's _nwise template parses`) where the run should have been refused. Both texts are now parsed with the
  floor lifted, and a unit test pins that each parses at the floor within a stated stack bound, so the call is
  refused as every other at the floor (`exceeded maximum recursion depth`), or the program as a binding chain too
  long for the floor (`memory exhausted`).
- **`succinctly jq` reads a quantifier that follows a quantifier as jq's Oniguruma does** (#7682). Only a `?` or `+` right after a quantifier is its lazy or possessive marker; any further quantifier is a new one on the quantified atom, which Oniguruma reduces with the one before (`a??+` is `a*?`). `"aaa" | [match("(a)??++"; "gn")] | length` is `0` and `"aaab" | test("^(?:a|aa){2}+b")` is `false`, as in jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2, where the first was refused (`possessive quantifier is not supported`) and the second `true`: such a run is now written as the tree Oniguruma builds, one quantifier per item, so a lazy quantifier followed by `+`, a quantifier after a possessive one, a possessive `{n}+` on an item that matches in several ways and a zero count over a quantified group all match as in jq. Over 37,067 generated rows the differences from jq 1.7.1 went from 2,567 to 1,401. `"aaaaaa" | [match("b|a{2,}?{2}"; "l")]` still differs, the `l` flag's documented no-op on a lazy pattern.
- **Regex shapes the quantifier fuzz left differing from jq** (#7689). Under the `n` flag an alternative that can only match empty (`(a){0}`, `[^\s\S]?`) no longer hides a later one (`"ab" | [match("(a){0}|b"; "n")]` finds `b`, as in jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2). Under `l` and `n` a repeated group whose body is a `?` repeat, and under `n` a `*` repeat, keeps jq's final empty iteration instead of a span that merges every iteration (`"aaa" | match("(a?)+"; "l").captures[0]` is at `[3,0]`, was `[0,3]`), possessive repeats included (`"ba" | match("(a?)++$"; "n")`). A `{1}` marked lazy or possessive beside another quantifier (`(a){1}?++(a)`) is read as jq reads it instead of refused, a `{1}` on a plain group of letters lets the next quantifier repeat its last character as Oniguruma's string node does (`(?:ab){1}*` matches `abbb`), and a count of zero after a gap, a `{1}` or before another count keeps its group's capture entry. Over a regenerated net of 34,308 quantifier rows, the rows differing from jq 1.7.1 went from 767 to 629.
- **`succinctly jq` reports a module that cannot be opened at every directive that reaches it** (#7709). A directory named `m.jq`, or a module file this user cannot read, reached by two `import`/`include` directives (directly, through other modules, or with other failures between) printed one `error loading data file ... Could not open ...` report and `jq: 1 compile error`; jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 never cache a file they could not open, so they report it each time and count each report (`import "dm" as a; import "dm" as b; 1` is `jq: 2 compile errors`). A 192-program matrix of {directory, mode 000, syntax error, missing} x {`import`, data `import`, `include`} x {repeated, nested, mixed} now matches jq 1.7.1 on the kind, order and count of every report, where 48 rows differed.
- **`succinctly jq` refuses an interpolated `import`/`include` path with jq's `Import path must be constant`** (#7710). `include "\(1)"; 0` said `invalid escape sequence '\('`, and `import "\("x")" as $d; 0` added a spurious `expected 'as' in import directive` and counted `2 compile errors`; the path is now read as the string it is and refused as jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 refuse it, at the start of the string, after any bad escape inside it and counted with the errors around it, in the main program, a `-f` file and a module. `succinctly dev compare jq`'s upstream-suite dimension now compares a `%%FAIL` case's error messages and their lines, not only its stdout and exit status, which is how this upstream case (`include "\(a)"; 0` in `jq.test`) had gone unnoticed; `%%FAIL IGNORE MSG` cases and bison's syntax-error wording are not compared.
- **`succinctly jq` names the line jq names for a syntax error at the end of a program** (#7711). A program, `-f` file or module ending in a newline or blank lines reported its end-of-text syntax error on the empty line after the last one (`printf '[1,\n 2,\n\n\n'` as a `-f` file: line 5 with an empty echo); jq places it at the start of its lexer's last match, the trailing whitespace run or else the last comment or token, so jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 say line 2 and echo ` 2,`. `succinctly jq` now places it the same way, with jq 1.7.1's echoed line and padding; in a 3,000-program sweep the first error's line now differs from jq 1.7.1 in 35 of 2,638 compile errors (none at the end of the text), where 800 differed.
- **`succinctly jq` reports option errors in argv order, as jq does** (#7712). jq stops at the first word of its command line it refuses, so a bad `--argjson` text, an unreadable `--slurpfile`/`--rawfile` file or a `--jsonargs` word that is not JSON before `-h`, `-V` or `--build-configuration` is an error (exit 2) where `succinctly jq` printed the help or version with exit 0, and an unknown option, a missing value or a refused `--indent` later in argv no longer pre-empts an earlier error. A missing value is now reported in jq's words (`jq: --arg takes two parameters (e.g. --arg varname value)`). Over a generated matrix of 6,845 orderings of option pairs and triples, 1,702 differed from jq 1.7.1 in the error reported or the exit status (700 of them exiting 0), and none do now; jq 1.8.2 agrees with jq 1.7.1 on all of them.
- **`succinctly jq` answers a tree recursion whose definition uses `try`, `label`, `reduce`, an object, `first`, a local def or another def** (#7713). After #7460 a call at a pipe's head or as an operand was run to its value first only when its definition's body was made of the shapes a tail loop runs ahead of its call, so `def count: if type == "array" then (.[0] | count) + (.[1] | count) else 1 end; count` over a binary tree 13 deep, and `def t($n): if $n == 0 then own else t($n - 1) + t($n - 1) end` with `own` defined as `try 1`, `label $l | 1`, `reduce ...`, `{a: 1}.a`, `first(1)`, `length` or `tostring`, were refused with `exceeded maximum recursion depth` at about 8,192 leaves where jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 answer. The question now also reads those shapes when they answer at most once, a pipe that ends in such a call, and a call with arguments to another def; an operator settles two operands that are such calls, and a tail loop's stage that calls into a module reaching a second one (its forwarding stub is a def declared in the body) runs in place again. Those programs also run faster (60-90% less time on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, 10-54% on an Apple M4 Pro, output identical); other programs move within noise, at most +1-2% for two pipe operands ending in a builtin (`(.score | tostring) + (.id | tostring)`, +0.95% instructions).
- **jq: a malformed object key is two compile errors, as in jq** (#7716). `{1+2:3}`, `{.a:1}`, `{"a"+"b":1}` and `. as {1:$a} | $a` report the syntax error and then jq's `May need parentheses around object key expression`, counted `jq: 2 compile errors`, where `succinctly jq` stopped at the first. The parse goes on past the key as jq's grammar recovers there, to the next `:`, `,` or `}`, so the errors after it are reported too (`{1:3, 2:4}` is four, `{1} | {2:3}` three), and a syntax error within three tokens of the recovery is not, as bison does (`{1:}` is one error).
- **jq: `--seq` reads a record after the last newline** (#7718). `printf '\x1e1\n\x1etrue' | jq --seq -c .` printed `1` alone and exited 0, as jq 1.7.1 does: an empty record that was the first thing jq's last read held ended the stream silently, so `\x1e"a"\n\x1e"b"` lost `"b"`, `\x1e\x1etrue` printed nothing, `[inputs]` over `\x1e[1]\n\x1e[2]` was `[[1]]`, and a last record cut short after a newline went without its warning (#2998). Now every record is read, as jq 1.8.2 does (jqlang/jq#3279), on every `--seq` route (a file, several files, standard input, a pipe or a file read in windows, and `--seq --stream`). The same upstream change makes a byte-order mark that breaks off wipe the end-of-text warning, makes `--seq -s` print that warning before the program runs, and puts every event of `--seq --stream -s` in the array; all three follow 1.8.2. Where the run stands after the last input (`<unknown>` positions) stays jq 1.7.1's (#7607). The difference from the pinned 1.7.1 is recorded in `docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`.
- **jq: a `break` caught by `try` is jq's `{"__jq":N}`, a label stops on an equal error, and a `break` stops at the label it is bound to** (#7719, #7724). `label $f | try (1, break $f) catch error` printed `1` and then failed with `(not a string): null` (exit 5); it now prints `1` and exits 0, as jq does, and `catch .`/`catch type` see `{"__jq":0}`/`"object"` instead of `null`. A hand-made `error({"__jq":0})` is the break of the first label (`[limit(3; 1, error({"__jq":0}), 2)]` is `[1]`), the number counts every label entered, including the ones jq's own `first`, `limit`, `isempty` and `|=` enter, and keeps counting across inputs; and a `break` passed through a same-named label (`def f(g): label $out | g; [label $out | f(break $out), 2]`) stops at its own label, `[]` where succinctly printed `[2]`. A program that can observe any of this runs on the path-mode interpreter; every other program keeps the shipped route unchanged. A sentinel built from data or a computed key, without `__jq` spelled in the program, is still not honoured (recorded in the jq limitations page).
- **jq: `mktime`, `fromdate` and `fromdateiso8601` raise `mktime not supported on this platform` for the instant -2 (1969-12-31T23:59:58Z), as jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 do** (#7722). jq's `f_mktime` reads a `timegm` result of `-2` as its "no `timegm`" sentinel, as it reads `-1` as `invalid gmtime representation`; `succinctly jq` copied the `-1` case only and answered `-2`. `strftime("%s")` still prints `-2`, as jq does.
- **jq: `mktime` raises `invalid gmtime representation` when the normalised year less 1900 leaves C's `int`, as jq 1.8.2 does** (#7723). `[2147485547,12,1,0,0,0,0,0] | mktime` answered `67768036191676800`; `timegm` cannot store that year back, and `strftime("%s")` of it now prints `-1`. The overflow of a minute, hour or day carry, which macOS's `timegm` also refuses, is the C library's and stays converted here; the difference is recorded in `docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md` (glibc not captured).
- **jq: negating the number 2^63 keeps a value that agrees with its own text** (#7725).
  `9223372036854775808 | -.` kept the double `-9.223372036854776e18` under the text `-9223372036854775808`, which reads back as the integer `i64::MIN`, so a debug build panicked on two internal consistency checks (`[-.] | tojson`, `scalb(nan; -.)`).
  Release builds already answered as jq 1.8.2 does and still do; a debug-versus-release sweep of 68,761 unary and 48,672 binary number cases over the `i64`, 2^53, `-0`, subnormal, overflowing and 17-plus-digit boundaries, through input, `--argjson`, `--jsonargs`, `fromjson`, `tonumber` and program literals, now finds no difference.
- **jq: `combinations` and `combinations(n)` hand each row on as it is built, as jq does** (#7726).
  Both built the whole product before the first row, so a consumer that stops early still paid for all of it: `[1,2] | first(combinations(22))` took 4.7 GB and 2 to 6 s on an Apple laptop (now 3.9 MB and under 0.01 s; laptop, indicative), and `[limit(3; combinations(1000))]` was refused with `Cannot allocate 2^1000 elements for combinations` where jq answers at once.
  `first`, `limit`, `nth`, `label`/`break`, `isempty`, `any`/`all`, `reduce` and `foreach` now read only the rows they take (`reduce` over 2^20 rows: 1.1 GB to 4 MB), on both the document and the `-n` routes; collecting the whole product (`[combinations(18)] | length`) retires the same instructions as before, within 0.1%.
  A product collected whole that cannot be held is still refused, and so is `combinations(n)` with `n` past 2^29 (`{"a":[1]} | first(combinations(4294967297))` grew to 3 GB before), which neither jq can answer.
- **`succinctly jq` and `succinctly yq` print the computed double `2^-24` as `5.960464477539063e-08`** (#7730), as jq 1.7.1, jq 1.8.2 and yq v4.53.3 do. It printed `5.960464477539062e-08`, which reads back as the next lower double (`1/16777216 | tojson | tonumber == 1/16777216` was `false`): `2^-24` is the exact midpoint of the two 16-digit candidates, and the #2542 tie correction took the even one without checking it round-trips, which it does not at a power of two, where the double below is half as far away as the one above. Of every double, only `±2^-24` was affected.
- **`succinctly jq` steps an all-integer `range` past `2^53` in doubles, as jq does** (#7731). It walked exact `i64` integers at every magnitude, so `[range(-9007199254740994; -9007199254740990)]` had four values where jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 have three (`-9007199254740994 + 1` is the double `-9007199254740992`), `[range(9223372036854775806; 9223372036854775807)]` was `[9223372036854775806]` where jq's bounds are both the double 2^63 and the range is empty, and `[limit(3; range(-9223372036854775808; 0))]` counted up where jq repeats `-9223372036854776000`. Within ±2^53, where the two walks agree value for value, the `i64` walk is unchanged; past it the first value is still `$from` itself, `range/3` between two integer literals compares them as decimals first as jq's `<` does, and a walk whose sum rounds back to itself (jq loops forever) raises `range: maximum iterations exceeded` at the existing cap. `succinctly yq --jq-extensions` keeps yq's exact `int64` walk. The divergence `docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md` recorded for #2131 and #2219 is closed.
- **jq: a run started with SIGPIPE ignored keeps it ignored, as jq does** (#7732). Under a parent that ignores SIGPIPE (a systemd unit, Python's `subprocess` with `restore_signals=False`, `trap '' PIPE`), a closed standard output killed `succinctly jq` with SIGPIPE (status 141) and a closed standard error did too, because every run set SIGPIPE to its default (#5547). The disposition the process inherited is now read before `main`, ahead of Rust's runtime, and kept: a closed standard output is `jq: error: writing output failed: Broken pipe`, exit 2, on every output route (plain, `-r`, `-j`, `--stream`, `--seq`, `halt_error`, `debug`, `stderr`, the `jq` and `sjq` aliases), and a closed standard error is ignored, as in jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 on Linux and macOS (36 of 96 matrix rows differed, none now). With SIGPIPE inherited at its default nothing changes. `succinctly yq` still dies of SIGPIPE whatever it inherited, as yq does; the other subcommands report the closed pipe as `succinctly: error: writing output failed: Broken pipe`, exit 2, when started with SIGPIPE ignored. The route that writes a whole-file result straight from the document's index (`jq . file`) dropped the write's own error and printed `Error: write error`, exit 1, for a closed pipe and for a full disk alike; it now reports both as jq does (`writing output failed: <strerror>`, exit 2).
- **jq: a run at the user's process or thread limit answers instead of failing to start** (#7733). Under `ulimit -u`, `prlimit --nproc` or a container's pids limit, `main` could not create the evaluation thread it runs on at any stack size (`EAGAIN`), and every run, even `jq -n 1`, ended with `failed to spawn the evaluation thread ... (os error 11)`, exit 1, where jq 1.7.1, which is single-threaded, runs. The run now goes on the main thread, with ADR-0025's native-stack floor registered at that thread's real stack (on Linux the soft `RLIMIT_STACK` is first raised to 64 MiB when it is lower and the hard limit allows), so deep recursion is still refused with jq's depth error instead of overflowing, at a shallower depth than on the evaluation thread. `succinctly yq` and the other subcommands take the same route.
- **jq: an environment entry with no `=` is read as jq reads it, in `env` and in `$ENV`** (#7734). Such an entry (only a raw `execve` makes one) was skipped in both, where jq's `env` lists it as `"NAME": null`, setting it in place in `environ` order, and jq's `$ENV` deletes the name, so under `A=1`, `B=2`, `A`, `C` jq prints `{"A":null,"B":"2","C":null}` for `env` and `{"B":"2"}` for `$ENV` and `succinctly jq` printed `{"A":"1","B":"2"}` for both. 38 of 133 rows of a 19-environment matrix differed (several bare entries, bare after and before an assignment, an empty entry, a bare non-UTF-8 name); none does now, against jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 on macOS and jq 1.7.1 on Linux. #7487's note that such entries are skipped by both was wrong.
- **jq: a `?//` destructuring alternation in the loop of a `while` or `repeat` under `limit`, `first`, `isempty`, `any`/`all` or `nth` retries its next alternative when their `break` is raised after it, as jq does** (#7736). `[1] | [limit(3; while(. as [$x] ?// $x | $x; .))]` is six `[1]`s, as in jq, where succinctly gave three. A `?//` in the update of `|=` stays on the shipped route, whose remaining difference (`.[] |= select((. as [$x] ?// $x | $x) != null)`) is recorded in the jq limitations page.
- **jq: a character device as the lone input (`/dev/urandom`, a terminal that streams lines), named or on standard input, is read as a pipe is** (#7737).
  It was read to its end before the program ran, so `-R -n 'input|length' /dev/urandom`, `-c . < /dev/urandom` and `-c halt /dev/pts/N` over a terminal that kept streaming grew until killed, where jq 1.7.1 answers at once.
  Every route #7478 opened to pipes now takes any source that is not a regular file or a directory: the plain filter and `-R` read it a window at a time, and the lazy `input`/`inputs` start on its front; a terminal typed into still ends at its `^D` and is read whole as before.
- **jq: `-n input`, `first(inputs)` and `limit` over a stream that is not UTF-8, or holds a parse fault, answer at once** (#7738).
  The lazy route handed such a stream (a pipe, a FIFO, a device, a terminal) to the route that reads it whole, which never ends on a stream that does not (`cat /dev/urandom | jq -n input`), where jq 1.7.1 reports the parse error, or replaces the byte in a string with U+FFFD, as its reader gets there.
  A stream is now substituted a window at a time and a fault reported from what has been read; a regular file keeps the read whole its length bounds.
- **jq: a `def` named like an operator jq compiles into a call replaces the operator, as in jq** (#7739). jq's parser turns `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%` and the comparisons into calls to `_plus` ... `_greatereq` (unless both operands are constants), unary minus into `_negate`, `@name` and string interpolation into `format`, `..` into `recurse`, `|=` and the update-assignments into `_modify` and `=` into `_assign`, so a definition of that name and arity in scope takes the operator's place: `def _plus(a;b): "P"; 1 | . + 2` is `"P"`, `def format(f): "<" + f + ">"; "id=\(1)"` is `"id=<text>"` and `def recurse: "R"; [..]` is `["R"]`, where succinctly ran the operator. Only a program that defines one of these names parses differently; `label`'s comparison through `_equal` is recorded rather than followed.
- **jq: `--stream` and `--stream-errors` over a terminal named by its path (`/dev/pts/N`, `/dev/ttysNNN`, `/dev/stdin` on a terminal) keep its first bytes** (#7740).
  The 3-byte probe's handle was kept only for a FIFO or socket, and a terminal reopened and seeked back went on after the probed bytes, so `{"a":1}` and `[2]` on two lines gave `jq: parse error: Unfinished string at EOF at line 3, column 0`, where jq 1.7.1 prints the four events.
- **jq: `--stream` and `--stream-errors` with a terminal on standard input end at jq's `^D`** (#7741).
  The reader read standard input again after a read that had returned end of file, and a terminal returns end of file once per `^D`, so an empty input, a blank line or `1` and Enter needed a second `^D` and `1` with no newline a third, where jq 1.7.1 needs one and two.
  Standard input's end of file is now sticky for the run, as jq's stdio makes it.
- **jq: `-n` with no input files reads a terminal on standard input when `input`/`inputs` asks** (#7742).
  The read was left out on purpose (#723), so `input` raised `break` and `[inputs]` printed `[]` before anything was typed, where jq 1.7.1 reads the terminal.
  A terminal is now read by the lazy route a line at a time and only once the program asks for its first input, so `-n input` answers the first line as it is typed (named as `-` or by its path too), and a program that never gets to `input` never waits for it.
- **`succinctly jq -n 'inputs'` over standard input longer than 256 KiB reads a NUL glued to a number in the first 256 KiB as jq does** (#7748). `[12`, a NUL, `x,34]` and a newline past the first 4 KiB of such a stream was refused with `Invalid JSON text: expected ',' or ']', found '\0'` (exit 5) by `-n '[inputs]|length'`, `first(inputs|...)`, `reduce inputs` and main-loop programs that read `input_line_number`, where jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 read `[12,34]`, as `succinctly jq` already did for the same bytes in a file of any size and on standard input past that front; a file's first 16 KiB had the same gap. The lazy route now rewrites the front it starts on as it rewrites each window read after it, taking the NUL check from the UTF-8 validation of the front it already made.
- **A NUL glued to a number before a closer is reported at jq's column, and a top-level number it ends is not printed before jq's error** (#7749). jq ends the token at the next structural byte, not at the NUL, so `[[1]1`, a NUL, `]` is `Expected separator between values at line 1, column 7` and `1`, a NUL, `}` is `Unmatched '}' at line 1, column 3` with nothing printed, in jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2, where `succinctly jq` reported column 6 and printed `1` first, on every route. The rewrite #7437 makes of such a token now puts the number at the token's end, with the spaces before it, also when the token starts in an earlier file.
- **A fault followed by a stray quote on its line no longer carries the rest of a file onto the next one** (#7750, #7751, #7753). The stitch that joins a token a file ends inside to the next file judged an open container or string by its brackets and quotes alone, so `0 [x"]` then `1\n2\n` looked like a string the next file goes on with; jq's parser stops at the fault and parses on from the next line of the same file. A program reading past the fault with `try input` lost every value after a file that did not open later in the list (`"E" 2` where jq prints `"E" 2 4 101`), `input_filename` named the next file for the values after the fault, and a fault in a document still open at the end of its file was reported after a later file that did not open, with exit 2 where jq exits 5. A tail is now carried only when jq's parser meets no fault reading it. Over 54,216 lists of split files with a missing file, a directory or a mode-000 file among them (`scripts/jq-filelist-differential.py`), the differences from jq 1.7.1 went from 1,259 to 0 with the companion fixes for #7752 and #7754.
- **A number or literal the fault completes, read past a file that did not open, reports the parse error** (#7752). `jq . missing.json n.json` over `1}` printed `1` and lost `Unmatched '}'`; jq's main loop stops once it is past a failure, after the one value it fetches, and that fetch returns the fault, because the byte that would complete the `1` is the faulty `}`. The cut to one value past the failure now comes after the check that drops such a token, as it already did without a failure (#4311).
- **`-s` with a file that did not open reports a fault the program does not read, as jq does** (#7754, #7755). `jq -s length c.json missing.json one.json` over `[1,x]` printed `2` and exited 0 with nothing on stderr: the failure after the fault was rightly left unreported (jq's slurp stops at the fault, #6485), but the lazy slurp never raised the fault either. jq's slurp ends at the first fault before the end of the text, which its main loop reports as a parse error after the failures before it, and the program does not run. The scan that places the failures has found that fault, so it is now reported that way; a directory in the list no longer makes the slurp word a later fault, or the first in the evaluator's words. With every file open nothing is scanned and `-s length` over `[1,x]` still prints `2`, as recorded.
- **`-e` changes the exit status and nothing else** (#7757). A fault the program reached did not end the document under `-e`: `printf '[2,]\n' | succinctly jq -c -e '.,1'` printed jq's parse error and then `1`, and `.,.` reported the fault twice, where jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 print the error alone, as `succinctly jq` without `-e` did. `-e` materialized every output to learn whether it was truthy, and on a fault reported it and went on with the document; it now records the truthiness of each output once it is written, on every route, so it no longer raises on a string the run without it forwards (#5308) either. Over a matrix of 7 faults, 5 contexts, 15 programs and 11 routes, 381 of 5,775 runs printed something different with `-e` than without it (jq: none); none do now.
- **`input` and `inputs` refuse an escape jq refuses with jq's catchable parse error** (#7758). A high surrogate escape with no low one after it (`"\ud83d"`, `"\ud83dx"`, `"\udc00\ud83d"`) made `input` raise `invalid unicode escape sequence`, which `try` and `?` could not catch (`[inputs?]` exited 5), and in an object key it, or an invalid `\x` or short `\u` escape, went through as the key's source text. jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 raise `Invalid \uXXXX\uXXXX surrogate pair escape at line 1, column 8` (or `Invalid escape ...`), catchable, and read on with the next document; so does `succinctly jq` now, and `--slurpfile` words the same faults as jq does. The main loop's forwarding of such a string is unchanged (#5308). Of 1,512 runs over 28 escape shapes, 404 on the `input`/`inputs` (windowed and `-n -s` included) and `--slurpfile` routes answered differently from jq; none do now.
- **jq: `--slurpfile` and a data import word a file that is not JSON as jq does** (#7769). The detail after `Bad JSON in --slurpfile NAME FILE: ` (exit 2) and `error loading data file PATH: ` (exit 3) is jq's parser's message and position (`Unfinished JSON term at EOF at line 2, column 0`, `Expected separator between values at line 1, column 7`), where it was `serde_json`'s (`Invalid JSON in stream: EOF while parsing a value at line 1 column 3`), for every fault kind: a truncated value, a stray closer, a bad literal, a missing separator, a trailing comma, a NUL, bytes that are not UTF-8 (one column each, as jq counts them), and a fault in a later document. A number with a NUL glued to it ends at the NUL, as in jq (`1.5e3`, a NUL, is `[1.5E+3]`), where such a file was refused.
- **jq: a POSIX `TZ` takes any number of digits in its offsets and rule times, as macOS libc and glibc read it** (#7783). `TZ=XYZ5:30:5`, `XYZ1:5`, `XYZ005`, `XYZ+005:00`, `EST5EDT4:5,M3.2.0,M11.1.0` and `EST5EDT,M3.2.0/2:3,M11.1.0` were read as UTC by `localtime`, `strflocaltime` and `strptime`'s `%Z`, because the zone parser took exactly two digits for minutes and seconds and at most two for an offset's hours; jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 apply them on both platforms. The forms the two C libraries read differently (a name shorter than three characters, a minute of 60, a trailing `:`) keep their reading, recorded in `docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`.
- **jq: `strptime` reads `%+`, and on macOS `%+` is the locale's own layout, as jq prints and reads it there** (#7784). `strptime("%+")` never matched (`0 | strftime("%+") | strptime("%+") | mktime` raised `does not match format "%+"`; jq answers `0`), and `%+` was printed in the C layout under every locale, where macOS's libc expands it to the locale's `date_fmt` both ways (`LC_ALL=de_DE.UTF-8`: `"Di. 14 Nov. 2023 23:13:20 CET"`). `%v` takes the locale's month abbreviation on macOS too (`de_DE`: `" 1-Jan.-1970"`, was `" 1-Jan-1970"`). A `+` before the end of the format, a `%` or white space is the conversion, as Apple's `strptime` reads it, and a `+` before a specifier is still a flag (`%+Y`). glibc has neither (a glibc jq prints them as written); off macOS the C layout is printed and read, as recorded in `docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`.
- **jq: a chain of defs that each call the one below twice no longer takes exponential time before it runs** (#7786).
  `def g0: 1; def g1: g0 + g0; ...; def g60: g59 + g59; reduce empty as $i (0; g60)` and the same chain under `map`,
  `sort_by`, `any`, `.[] |= f`, `with_entries`, `empty as $x | f`, a Fibonacci-shaped chain and a layered module DAG
  (each module's def calling the three modules below) answered only after a walk exponential in the chain's length,
  where jq answers at once: the analyses run before a fold, a `map`, an update or an `as` body walked a called def's
  body again at every call that reached it. `walk::search_subexpr` now walks each shared def body and argument once
  per walk, and the two walks that count occurrences count a shared subtree once and add it at each call, so the
  time is linear in the program's size where it was exponential; output is unchanged.
- **`succinctly jq` answers a tree recursion over many more leaf and combination shapes, and retries a `?//` inside `first` again** (#7787). The test that decides whether a call is run to its value before its consumer (#7460, #7713) was a list of shapes; a recursion over any other one, such as `def t($n): if $n <= 0 then [1] | first else t($n-1) + t($n-1) end; 0 | t(13)`, a leaf written with `limit(1; ...)`, `foreach`, `until`, `env`, `input_line_number` or a local def with parameters, or a combination through `first`, `//`, `label`, an object, `getpath`, `and`, `or`, a string interpolation or an `if` condition, was refused with `exceeded maximum recursion depth` at about 8,192 leaves where jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 answer. The test now reads every form of the language by what it yields (at most one output, and nothing observable left to run after it), for an expression that holds a call to a def that may recurse; an operator settles such an operand when the other one answers once (`and`/`or` when both hold such a call). Which expressions hold one is a shape test plus a flag remembered on each definition, so an operator, object or interpolation over plain paths asks nothing more. #7713's list had also admitted `first(...)` without looking inside, so `def f: first([1] as [$a] ?// $a | $a); f | if . == 1 then error("e") else . end` raised `e` where jq retries the `?//` and answers `[1]`; a `?//` anywhere in the expression now keeps it streaming. A filtered generator as a leaf (`(1, 2) | select(. == 1)`) and a `?//` leaf are still refused at the same depth: limitations.md says why.
- **jq: `strftime("%OB")` is the locale's alternative month name on macOS, as jq prints it** (#7790). Under `cs_CZ`, `pl_PL`, `ru_RU`, `uk_UA`, `el_GR`, `lt_LT`, `be_BY`, `kk_KZ` and `mn_MN`, macOS's libc gives `%OB` the nominative name a month standing alone takes, where `%B` is the genitive of a date (`0 | strftime("%OB")` is `"leden"` and `strftime("%B")` is `"ledna"` under `cs_CZ`); `succinctly jq` printed `%B` for both. `strflocaltime` follows, and `strptime("%OB")` reads those names (`leden`, not `ledna`). Every other `%E`/`%O` form was already the plain one, as in macOS's libc under every installed locale.
- **`succinctly jq` retries a `?//` inside `first(...)` in a def again** (#7795). Since #7744 a call whose definition's body is `first(f)` was run to its value before its consumer without looking inside `f`, so `def f: first([1] as [$a] ?// $a | $a); f | if . == 1 then error("e") else . end` raised `e` where jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2 retry the bind with its next pattern and answer `[1]`. A `first(f)` whose `f` holds a `?//` keeps the streaming route; nothing else changes.
- **A `#` or a Unicode blank inside a class under the regex `x` flag keeps jq's empty matches on multibyte text** (#7804). Oniguruma reads a `#` in a class as the character and keeps every blank there, where the `regex` crate reads the `#` as a comment and drops U+3000, U+00A0 and the other Unicode blanks; such a class did not parse, and the pattern went to the second engine, which left out the extra empty match jq makes one byte after an empty match (#6326). `"é" | [match("[#]?"; "gx") | .offset]` is `[0,1,1]` as in jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2, where it was `[0,1]`, and the same holds for `[#a]*`, `(?x)[#]{0,1}`, `[　]?` and the rest. Over a 14,976-row matrix of class forms, quantifiers, texts and the flags `g`, `gx`, `gxn` and `gxl`, the rows differing from jq went from 4,272 to 314 (all of them are the `l` flag on a lazy quantifier, a recorded limit).
- **A regex group name is accepted or refused as jq does** (#7805). The first character of a `(?<name>…)` or `(?'name'…)` must be a word character other than an ASCII digit, as Oniguruma's `fetch_name` reads it: `(?<(>x)` and `(?<€>x)` are `invalid char in group name <…>` and `(?<-a>x)` and `(?<+a>x)` `invalid group name <…>` (exit 5), where they were accepted, while `(?<²a>x)` and `(?<‿a>x)` are still accepted. Every later character up to the closing delimiter belongs to the name and is no pattern text, so `"a" | test("(?<a[>a)")` is `true` instead of `premature end of char-class`, and `(?<a$>x)` and `(?<a{>x)` report the groups `a$` and `a{`. A `)` or the end of the pattern before the delimiter is `invalid group name` with Oniguruma's cut of the name (`(?<ßx` is `<ß>`), and `(?<` alone is `end pattern with unmatched parenthesis`, all as in jq 1.7.1 and 1.8.2.
- **jq: `-s` prints no array before a fault at the end of the text** (#7807). Over a text whose last byte completes a value while the parser still holds an unfinished one, `-s` printed the array and then the error, as jq 1.7.1 does: `printf '2[' | jq -c -s .` printed `[2]`, `--stream -s` printed `[[[],2]]` for `2"` and `[[[0],1]]` for `[1,`, and a file that did not open before the text hid the error altogether. Now the error is printed alone, as jq 1.8.2 does (jqlang/jq#3279, the change #7523 adopted for `--stream -s`), on every route that slurps: plain `-s`, which had answered `2"` that way already and `2[` the old way, `--stream -s`, `--stream-errors -s` (the fault event is the array's last) and `-n -s` (the first `input` raises the fault, the second returns the array). Positions stay jq 1.7.1's (#7607). The difference from the pinned 1.7.1 is recorded in `docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`.
